kinds.label: Religious institutions
kinds.def: Sexual abuse of children by clergy, religious, lay leaders or members of a church, order, mosque, madrasa, temple, synagogue or other faith body, and the body's handling of it (transfers, secrecy, failure to report).

kinds.label: Cults, sects and closed communities
kinds.def: Abuse inside high-control groups or separated communities (sects, communes, polygamous groups, closed colonies) where leaders control contact with outsiders, schooling and marriage, so abuse is hidden or authorised from within.
kinds.src: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (Australia), Final Report, 15 Dec 2017, Volume 16 'Religious institutions' (closed faith communities); Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (child protection in religious organisations and settings)

kinds.label: Children's homes, orphanages and residential care

kinds.label: Scouting, youth, arts and hobby groups
kinds.def: Abuse in scouting and guiding, church youth societies, holiday camps, choirs and other recreation, arts and hobby groups run for children.
kinds.src: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (Australia), Final Report, 15 Dec 2017, Volume 14 'Sport, recreation, arts, culture, community and hobby groups'

kinds.label: Hospitals, psychiatric care and medical professionals
kinds.def: Abuse of child patients by doctors, surgeons, psychiatric staff or people given access to hospitals, and the health bodies' handling of it.
kinds.src: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (Australia), Final Report, 15 Dec 2017 (health and allied institutions examined, e.g. Tasmania; and Volume 6 'Making institutions child safe'); Lampard investigation of the NHS (2015) on Savile

kinds.label: Youth detention and custody
kinds.def: Abuse of children held in juvenile halls, youth detention centres, training schools and secure units, by staff or with staff knowledge.
kinds.src: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (Australia), Final Report, 15 Dec 2017, Volume 15 'Contemporary detention environments'; Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (children in custodial institutions, incl. Medomsley)

kinds.label: Immigration detention and migrant children in state custody
kinds.def: Sexual abuse or exploitation of children held in immigration detention, offshore processing or state-run shelters for unaccompanied migrant children, and children who go missing from reception into trafficking.
kinds.src: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (Australia), Final Report, 15 Dec 2017, Volume 15 'Contemporary detention environments' (includes immigration detention)

kinds.label: Armed forces, military training and cadets
kinds.def: Abuse of child recruits, apprentices and cadets inside military training establishments and cadet forces, and abuse of local children by service personnel stationed at bases, outside combat.
kinds.src: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (Australia), Final Report, 15 Dec 2017, Report of Case Study 40 (Australian Defence Force) and Volume 15

kinds.label: Child migration programmes
kinds.def: Children sent overseas by governments and charities under child migration schemes (e.g. UK to Australia, Canada, Rhodesia) who were sexually abused in the receiving institutions.
kinds.src: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (child migration programmes, report 2018)

kinds.label: Entertainment, broadcasting and media
kinds.def: Abuse by broadcasters, performers, talent agents, writers or modelling figures, using fame and access, and the employers' or industry's failure to act.
kinds.src: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (and Dame Janet Smith Review for the BBC, 2016)

kinds.label: Politicians and public officials
kinds.def: Abuse or exploitation by politicians, diplomats or officials, or their protection of offenders and obstruction of cases; includes allegations of elite rings that inquiries tested and found unsupported.
kinds.src: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (allegations of child sexual abuse linked to Westminster; Cambridge House/Knowl View; Lord Janner)

kinds.label: Group-based grooming and exploitation networks
kinds.def: Several offenders acting together who groom, pass around and sexually exploit children in a town or region, often targeting children in care; includes 'loverboy' recruitment.
kinds.src: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (child sexual exploitation by organised networks); Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section H 'Solicitation of children for sexual purposes' (grooming)

kinds.label: Prostitution, brothels and paid sexual exploitation
kinds.def: Children exploited for money or goods in brothels, bars, karaoke venues, mining camps, online sex advertising or 'compensated dating', by pimps, families or criminal groups.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section E 'Exploitation of children in/for prostitution' and D.4.i 'Commercial sexual exploitation of children'

kinds.label: Travelling offenders and sexual exploitation in travel and tourism
kinds.def: Offenders who travel or move abroad (as tourists, expatriates, volunteers or workers) to abuse children, and the tourism venues and states' responses (passport bans, notifications, deportations).
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section I 'Sexual exploitation of children in the context of travel and tourism'; Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (children outside the United Kingdom)

kinds.label: Online abuse-material sites, forums and sharing networks
kinds.def: Websites, darknet forums, messaging groups and peer-to-peer networks whose members share child sexual abuse material, and the platforms' and police responses.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section F 'Child pornography / child sexual abuse material' and G.4.ii 'Child sexual exploitation online'; Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (England and Wales), investigation strands announced 2015-16 (internet-facilitated abuse)

kinds.label: Commercial production and sale of abuse material
kinds.def: Studios, producers and paid websites that make or sell abuse material for money, including 'model' studios and pay-per-view operations.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section E.4.vii 'Use of children for pornographic performances' and section F

kinds.label: AI-generated and digitally altered abuse material
kinds.def: Abuse material made or altered with software or AI, including 'nudified' or deepfake images of real children and training data containing abuse material.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section F.4.ii 'Digitally generated child sexual abuse material'

kinds.label: Live-streamed abuse to order
kinds.def: Abuse performed live on webcam for paying remote viewers, often arranged by adults close to the child, with payments through money-transfer services.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), sections G.4.iii 'Live online child sexual abuse', G.4.iv 'Live streaming', G.4.v 'Child sexual abuse to order' and G.4.vi 'Webcam child sex tourism'

kinds.label: Sextortion and online coercion networks
kinds.def: Offenders or groups who obtain sexual images from children and then blackmail them for more images, money or self-harm, including organised groups such as 764 and the 'Com'.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section H.4.iii 'Sexual extortion of children (sextortion)'

kinds.label: Grooming through games, chat and social platforms
kinds.def: Adults contacting and grooming children through games, chat sites and social media, and the legal and regulatory action against the platforms.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section H.4.i 'Grooming of children for sexual purposes' (online solicitation)

kinds.label: Cross-border trafficking for sexual exploitation
kinds.def: Children recruited in one country and moved to another to be sexually exploited, by criminal groups, family networks or 'loverboys'.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section K 'Trafficking of children'; UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation ('trafficking for sexual exploitation')

kinds.label: Trafficking for sexual exploitation within a country
kinds.def: Children recruited and moved within their own country (from rural areas to cities, mining or tourist zones, or across state lines) to be sexually exploited.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section K 'Trafficking of children' (no border crossing required); UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation (domestic trafficking flows)

kinds.label: Child and forced marriage used for sexual exploitation
kinds.def: Girls married off, sold as 'brides', given in 'contract' or temporary marriages, or forced into 'marriage' by leaders or armed groups, where the marriage is the means of sexual exploitation.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section L 'Child/early marriage'; UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation ('trafficking for forced marriages'); UNODC GLOTIP 2018 Booklet 2 (forced marriage by armed groups)

kinds.label: Illegal and fraudulent intercountry adoption
kinds.def: Children sent abroad for adoption with falsified papers, without real parental consent or for payment, through agencies, notaries, orphanages or officials.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section J 'Sale of children' (improperly inducing consent for adoption); UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation ('illegal adoption', 0.3% of detected victims in GLOTIP 2022)

kinds.label: Sale of babies, stolen newborns and 'baby factories'
kinds.def: Newborns bought, stolen from maternity wards or bred in 'baby factories' and surrogacy operations, and sold to buyers at home or abroad.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section J 'Sale of children'; UNODC GLOTIP 2020 (baby selling listed among forms detected)

kinds.label: Children taken by regimes and given false identities
kinds.def: Children of detained, disappeared or 'undesirable' parents taken by a state or regime and placed with other families under falsified identities.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), section J 'Sale of children' (transfer of a child for consideration or any other advantage); UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation ('illegal adoption')

kinds.label: Abduction, recruitment and sexual slavery by armed forces and groups
kinds.def: Children abducted or recruited by armed forces, militias, armed groups or gangs and used as fighters, 'wives' or sex slaves, or raped in conflict.
kinds.src: UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons 2018, Booklet 2 'Trafficking in persons in the context of armed conflict' (recruitment of children; sexual slavery; forced marriage)

kinds.label: Peacekeepers and aid workers
kinds.def: Sexual exploitation and abuse of children by UN and regional peacekeepers, international police and contractors, and humanitarian workers, often in exchange for food, money or aid.
kinds.src: UN Secretary-General's Bulletin 'Special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and sexual abuse' (ST/SGB/2003/13): sexual activity with anyone under 18 is prohibited

kinds.label: Customary and ritual servitude with sexual exploitation
kinds.def: Children given to shrines, temples, households or powerful men under custom (trokosi, devadasi, bacha bazi, restavek, criadazgo, ngozi, ritual oaths), where sexual exploitation is part of the practice.
kinds.src: Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (Luxembourg Guidelines; 1st ed. adopted Luxembourg 28 Jan 2016; 2nd ed. ECPAT/Interagency Working Group, March 2025), sections E and J (exploitation and transfer of children under any arrangement); UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation ('other forms' of exploitation)

kinds.label: Orphanage trafficking and voluntourism
kinds.def: Children recruited from families into orphanages (often 'paper orphans') to attract donations and foreign volunteers, where they are exposed to exploitation and sale.
kinds.src: Parliament of Australia, Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade, 'Hidden in Plain Sight' (6 Dec 2017), Part 8: orphanage trafficking as modern slavery

kinds.label: Forced begging and forced criminality run by trafficking networks
kinds.def: Children controlled by trafficking networks or exploitative schools and forced to beg, steal or commit crimes, often also exposed to sexual abuse.
kinds.src: UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (2022 and 2024 editions), forms of exploitation ('trafficking for begging'; 'trafficking for forced criminality')

C.n: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
C.place: Buenos Aires (ESMA naval school and other clandestine detention centres)
C.who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
C.cover: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.
C.d: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.
C.cite: Tribunal Oral Federal No. 6, Buenos Aires, case 1351 (Plan Sistemático), verdict 5 July 2012, as summarised by the International Crimes Database and MercoPress (6 July 2012)

C.n: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
C.vn: about 500 children estimated kidnapped or born in detention centres; 140 identified by 7 July 2025; around 300 still unfound per Buenos Aires Times
C.who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
C.cover: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.
C.d: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.
C.cite: Buenos Aires Times, 7 July 2025; AP, 28 July 2023 (133rd); Wikipedia 'Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo'

C.n: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
C.vn: violations confirmed in at least 56 of 367 petitions; more than 140,000 (TRC) to about 200,000 (AP) Korean children sent abroad since the 1950s
C.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
C.cover: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.
C.d: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
C.cite: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Korea, findings announced 26 March 2025 (Reuters via The Star); Wikipedia 'International adoption of South Korean children'

C.n: Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished
C.who: Gynaecologist Eduardo Vela
C.d: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987. It was the first trial in Spain over the 'stolen babies' of the Franco era and after. A judge had recorded about 30,000 cases of Spanish children taken, according to the report.
C.cite: RTÉ News, 8 October 2018 (Madrid Provincial Court verdict)

C.n: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
C.vn: up to 20,000 estimated by investigators; the 2018 criminal probe covers about 8,000 overseas adoptions 1970–1999
C.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
C.d: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.
C.cite: Al Jazeera, 'How Chile's stolen children are finding their way home', 20 September 2023

C.n: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
C.place: 18 institutions incl. Tuam (Co. Galway), Bessborough (Cork), Sean Ross Abbey (Roscrea)
C.vn: about 56,000 women and 57,000 children passed through the investigated homes; about 9,000 children died
C.who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
C.cover: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).
C.d: The Commission of Investigation's final report (published 12 January 2021) covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 9,000 children died in them between 1922 and 1998, about one in seven births and about twice the general infant mortality rate. Several homes had been linked to illegal domestic and foreign adoptions, many to the United States. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for a 'profound generational wrong'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
C.cite: Mother and Baby Homes Commission of Investigation, Final Report, 12 January 2021, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
C.place: Occupied Poland (Łódź region, Zamość and others)
C.vn: Polish official estimate about 200,000; other estimates 20,000–200,000; only 10–20% returned
C.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
C.d: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.
C.cite: US Holocaust Memorial Museum, 'Subsequent Nuremberg Proceedings, Case #8: The RuSHA Case'; DW, 30 December 2017

C.n: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
C.vn: more than 11,000 babies adopted to Western countries in the 1980s (Zembla); about 4,000 to the Netherlands
C.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
C.cover: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.
C.d: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
C.cite: The Guardian, 20 September 2017 (Karen McVeigh); BBC News, 14 March 2021

C.n: Vietnam — Nam Dinh ring: 266 babies sold for foreign adoption
C.who: Heads of two provincial social welfare centres; doctors and nurses at village clinics
C.d: In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, for 'abuse of power and authority'. They allegedly solicited infants from poor families and falsified documents saying the babies were abandoned; 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi had reported desertion numbers rising 17-fold or more at orphanages in 7 provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired in September 2008.
C.cite: The Independent, 23 September 2009; Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Vietnam' adoption timeline

C.n: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
C.place: Hengyang, Hunan (six orphanages); babies brought from Guangdong
C.vn: nearly 1,000 children bought by six orphanages in three years (court documents reviewed by ABC News)
C.who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
C.d: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.
C.cite: Schuster Institute for Investigative Journalism (Brandeis), 'China' adoption page, citing Xinhua and ABC News

C.n: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
C.vn: about 800 adoptions facilitated 1997–2001; guilty plea covered 17 cases
C.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
C.d: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.
C.cite: ABC News 20/20, 24 March 2005; Schuster Institute (Brandeis) Cambodia page

C.n: Samoa — Focus on Children (Utah) adoption fraud
C.vn: 80 adoptions 2002–2005; 37 questioned in the indictment
C.who: Focus on Children, Utah agency run by Scott and Karen Banks
C.d: Samoan parents were told their children would go to the US temporarily for schooling, but the children were adopted permanently. A federal indictment on 28 February 2007 charged Scott and Karen Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. All pleaded guilty on 6 January 2009 to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of an alien, and the agency to a felony conspiracy; in February 2009 Judge David Sam sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Samoa' adoption page, citing ICE press release 1 March 2007

C.n: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen 'baby mill' adoption scheme
C.vn: Utah investigators believed more than 40 pregnant women were brought through Utah
C.who: Paul Petersen, Maricopa County (Arizona) Assessor and adoption lawyer
C.d: Petersen, an elected Arizona official, paid recruiters to bring pregnant Marshallese women to the US, paying them about $10,000 to give up their babies and charging adoptive couples about $35,000, although the Compact of Free Association bars Marshallese travel to the US for adoption. Charged in October 2019 in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas, he pleaded guilty in all three courts in June 2020 (human smuggling, fraud, communication fraud) and was sentenced in December 2020 in federal court in Arkansas to more than six years in prison. He also fraudulently obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds for the women.
C.cite: Utah Attorney General press release, 19 June 2020; USA Today, 1 December 2020 (via Wikipedia 'Paul Petersen (criminal)')

C.n: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
C.vn: more than 30 Ugandan children
C.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
C.cover: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.
C.d: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
C.cite: US Department of Justice press release, 17 August 2020; The Guardian, 18 August 2020

C.n: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
C.vn: 5,577 adopted abroad in 2007 alone, 4,728 to the US; up to 500 kidnapping cases believed linked to children adopted overseas; a 2003 government commission documented 1,084 missing children incl. 500 under one presumed abducted for adoption
C.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
C.d: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.
C.cite: CICIG, Report on Players Involved in the Illegal Adoption Process in Guatemala, 2010 (via Wikipedia); Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Guatemala'

C.n: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
C.who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
C.d: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.
C.cite: The Guardian (staff and agencies), 13 August 2007

C.n: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
C.who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
C.d: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'India', citing Frontline (28 April 2001, 2005) and The Hindu (26 Dec 2002, 31 Aug 2005)

C.n: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
C.vn: police suspected more than 350 children; files for 120 sent overseas, at least 13 to Australia
C.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
C.d: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'India', citing Boloji (12 June 2005) and TIME (21 August 2008)

C.n: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
C.vn: agency placed 518 children 2004–2006, most internationally
C.who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
C.d: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'India'

C.n: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
C.vn: 394 intercountry adoptions in 2006, up from 8 in 2000
C.who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
C.d: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Nepal'; Wikipedia 'International adoption'

C.n: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions
C.vn: about 5,000 children estimated stolen; 3,000 placed in New York and California alone 1940–1950
C.who: Tennessee Children's Home Society (Shelby County branch) under Georgia Tann
C.d: From 1924 to 1950 Georgia Tann used the Memphis branch of the Tennessee Children's Home Society to take children from poor families and sell them, charging up to $5,000 for out-of-state adoptions when Tennessee adoptions cost about $7. A state investigation into adoption fraud led to the home's closure in 1950; Tann died before its findings were published.
C.cite: Tennessee State Library and Archives, Georgia Tann/Tennessee Children's Home Society Investigation Scrapbooks, 1950 (via Wikipedia 'Georgia Tann')

C.n: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
C.vn: at least 31 children improperly sent overseas (TRC, Feb 2025); AP found evidence of 19 adoptions 1979–1986
C.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
C.d: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.
C.cite: AP, 9 November 2019; Korea Times, 22 February 2025 (TRC finding)

C.n: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
C.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
C.cover: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).
C.d: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
C.cite: Commissie Onderzoek Interlandelijke Adoptie (Joustra), report 8 February 2021, as reported by BBC News, 14 March 2021; Dutch Wikipedia 'Interlandelijke adoptie'

C.n: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
C.vn: DCI listed over 4,000 children to 22 countries Aug 1990–Feb 1991; figures as high as 10,000 for March 1990–June 1991 (Selman 2002)
C.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
C.d: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.
C.cite: Deutsche Welle, 22 June 2004; Selman, Population Research and Policy Review 21 (2002); Romania annual statistics to HCCH

C.n: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
C.vn: more than 15,000 Ethiopian children adopted in the US since 1999 (BBC)
C.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
C.d: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.
C.cite: BBC News, 10 January 2018; Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Ethiopia'

C.n: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
C.place: Calebasse and Le Citron, near Port-au-Prince → Dominican border
C.who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
C.d: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained trying to take 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic without proper documentation; their interpreters said group members had spoken with the children's parents. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association. In February a judge released eight, concluding they had not knowingly committed a crime, and later a ninth; the kidnapping and criminal association charges were dropped. On 17 May 2010 the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel under a 1980 law restricting movement out of Haiti and sentenced to the 3 months and 8 days she had already served.
C.cite: CNN, 4 February 2010; NBC News/AP, 17 May 2010

C.n: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
C.vn: close to 1,000 documented cases of disappeared children
C.who: Salvadoran armed forces
C.cover: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.
C.d: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
C.cite: Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Serrano-Cruz Sisters v. El Salvador, 1 March 2005; Wikipedia 'Pro-Búsqueda'

C.n: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
C.vn: about 160,000 children sent abroad since 1992, more than half to the US (New Yorker)
C.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
C.d: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.
C.cite: The New Yorker (Barbara Demick), 19 September 2024; FOX 6, 5 September 2024

C.n: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
C.place: Women's prisons and Auxilio Social homes across Spain
C.vn: 30,960 children removed from Republican mothers 1944–1954; Garzón: more than 30,000 under state 'tutelage'
C.who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
C.cover: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.
C.d: A 1940 law allowed imprisoned mothers to keep children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 Republican children were in state custody in 1943. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón characterised the removals as crimes against humanity and said the Falange was involved in kidnapping or forcibly repatriating children and changing their names. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from hospitals over about fifty years took their cases to the attorney general; lawyers' estimates of up to 300,000 were rejected by a 2026 forensic study, which did not dispute about 30,000 children placed in state care.
C.cite: Audiencia Nacional, Garzón ruling (El País, 2008); Wikipedia 'Lost children of Francoism'

C.n: Kenya — babies stolen and sold in Nairobi, incl. from a government hospital (BBC Africa Eye)
C.place: Nairobi (Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital; Kayole street clinics)
C.vn: Missing Child Kenya worked on about 600 missing-child cases in four years; no official statistics exist
C.who: Street child-snatchers working for a buyer; illegal street clinics; a clinical social worker at a government hospital
C.d: A year-long BBC Africa Eye investigation (November 2020) found children snatched from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350–550, illegal street clinics selling newborns (one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70), and a clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000) using legitimate transfer paperwork. The reporters delivered all the children to a children's home. The BBC said the official appeared to keep his job and the clinic appeared to still operate.
C.cite: BBC Africa Eye, 'The baby stealers', 15 November 2020

C.n: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
C.who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
C.d: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).
C.cite: The Guardian, 2 June 2011; Makinde et al., Trauma, Violence & Abuse (2015)

C.n: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
C.d: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.
C.cite: BBC News (AFP), 26 April 2018

C.n: Indonesia — baby trafficking syndicate selling infants to Singapore
C.place: Pontianak (West Kalimantan) and Tangerang; babies from West Java
C.vn: at least 25 babies sold since 2023; six rescued
C.who: Syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers
C.d: In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some 'reserved while still in the womb', for 11–16 million rupiah each, after preparing fraudulent family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested and six babies about to be trafficked were rescued; police sought Interpol help to trace the adopters.
C.cite: BBC News, 17 July 2025

C.n: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
C.who: Baby 101 company
C.d: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.
C.cite: HuffPost (AFP), 24 February 2011

C.n: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
C.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
C.d: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.
C.cite: CNN, 26 December 2007; BBC News, 29 October 2007; The Guardian, 1 April 2008

C.n: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
C.vn: 800–1,500 babies born there 1928–1946
C.who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
C.d: The Ideal Maternity Home in Nova Scotia, run by William and Lila Young from the late 1920s until 1947, promised discreet birthing and adoption for unmarried mothers. According to author Bette Cahill, people paid up to $10,000, usually disguised as a donation, to adopt babies from the home, while babies considered 'unmarketable' were fed only molasses and water; many died and were buried in butter boxes. Wikipedia, citing Cahill, adds that mothers were charged $500, that the provincial Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934, and that the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act; a 1946 Montreal Standard article described their 'baby farm rackets'.
C.cite: CBC News, November 2016 (citing Bette Cahill, Butterbox Babies, 1992)

C.n: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
C.who: French government and adoption associations
C.cover: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.
C.d: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.
C.cite: French inter-ministerial inspection report on illicit practices in intercountry adoption, March 2024, as quoted by AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024

C.n: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
C.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
C.d: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).
C.cite: AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024; The Oslo Desk, 23 September 2025

C.n: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
C.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
C.d: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.
C.cite: Van Steen, History & Policy (2025), on the Swedish report of 2 June 2025; AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024

C.n: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
C.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
C.d: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.
C.cite: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland (HLS/DHS), 'Adoption', version of 1 December 2025

C.n: Sierra Leone — 29 Makeni children sent to US adopters without parents' consent (HANCI)
C.who: Help A Needy Child International (HANCI)
C.d: In 1998 about 29 children at HANCI's centre in Makeni were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded the biological families 'cannot be said to have genuinely consented'.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Sierra Leone', citing AP (3 June 2010) and Slate (E.J. Graff, 11 May 2012)

C.n: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
C.vn: Hannah B. Williams Orphanage: 89 of 102 'orphans' returned to families in 2005; US orphan visas rose from 183 (2005) to 353 (2006)
C.who: Private orphanages and adoption facilitators
C.d: After the civil war ended in 2003 the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 'orphans' returned to their families. A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.
C.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Liberia', citing BBC (13 Nov 2008), UNICEF/Holt (2007), UNMIL (2007)

C.n: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
C.who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
C.cover: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.
C.d: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.
C.cite: Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Gelman v. Uruguay, judgment 24 February 2011 (Series C No. 221)

C.n: Colombia — 1981 ring selling Andean children abroad with forged papers
C.vn: 'hundreds of poor Andean children'
C.who: Adoption trafficking ring
C.d: In 1981 the New York Times (Warren Hoge) reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. In 2003 Interpol issued a detention order for the manager of an uncertified Costa Rica-based adoption agency suspected of trafficking babies from Colombia in 2000–2002 (suspect, not convicted).
C.cite: New York Times, 1981, via Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Colombia'

C.n: Haiti — 2007: children trafficked for international adoption returned to parents
C.vn: 47 children returned (IOM); a later report cited 50 returned and 100 awaiting rescue
C.who: A Haitian centre holding children awaiting international adoption
C.d: In 2007 a Haitian centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting international adoption to their families, after misleading parents with payments and holding the children in 'inhumane conditions' for months or years, according to the International Organization for Migration. An October 2007 report said officials had returned 50 trafficked children with 100 more awaiting rescue.
C.cite: IOM press briefing notes, 'Trafficked Children Returned Home', 2007; Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Haiti'

C.n: Malaysia — online baby-selling trade (Al Jazeera 101 East)
C.who: Online brokers; baby sellers
C.d: An undercover Al Jazeera 101 East investigation (24 November 2016) documented an online trade in which babies were advertised with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. Some babies went to couples wanting a child; others, it reported, were sold to traffickers. Immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia were among those giving up babies.
C.cite: Al Jazeera 101 East, 'Malaysia: Babies for Sale', 24 November 2016

C.n: United States / UK — 'internet twins' sold twice through an online adoption broker
C.place: St Louis, Missouri; broker in El Cajon, California; twins taken to Wales
C.who: Internet agency A Caring Heart (broker in California)
C.d: In 2000–01 a California-based internet adoption broker placed six-month-old twin girls first with a Californian couple, who paid about £4,000 and were then persuaded to return them to the birth mother, and then with a couple from north Wales who paid about £8,200 and adopted them in Arkansas. After the Welsh couple publicised the purchase in January 2001, Prime Minister Tony Blair promised action against trading children for adoption, Flintshire council took the twins into care under an emergency protection order, and on 9 April 2001 the High Court ruled they should be returned to the US. The FBI searched the broker's home near San Diego on 14 March 2001. The case led to UK adoption reform, including penalties for bringing children into the UK for adoption without approval.
C.cite: The Guardian, 'The internet twins: timeline', 9 April 2001; CBS News/AP, 14 March 2001

C.n: North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'
C.place: Clwyd and Gwynedd, North Wales (Bryn Estyn, Wrexham, among others)
C.who: Clwyd and Gwynedd county councils' children's homes, incl. Bryn Estyn; North Wales Police criticised
C.cover: The earlier Jillings report (commissioned 1994, completed 1996) was shelved and only released in redacted form in 2012 after a BBC Freedom of Information request. North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers rather than having them independently investigated.
C.d: Sir Ronald Waterhouse's tribunal took evidence from about 650 people who had been in care and published 'Lost in Care' in February 2000, finding widespread abuse over about 20 years in children's homes in North Wales. Allegations were reported across almost 40 homes, with the report concentrating on seven. Seven former care workers were convicted after a 1991 police inquiry, five of them from Bryn Estyn. The report found responses were 'too little and too late' and that children's interests were sacrificed to protect professional positions; officers of North Wales Police were among those accused.
C.cite: Waterhouse Tribunal, 'Lost in Care', February 2000, as summarised by CRIN

C.n: Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings
C.place: Kincora Boys' Home, east Belfast, Northern Ireland
C.who: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast Welfare Authority / Eastern Health and Social Services Board); RUC investigations; MI5
C.cover: Hart found MI5 'consistently obstructed a proper line of inquiry' during the 1980s RUC Caskey Phase Three investigation, and found numerous missed opportunities to detect and stop the abuse.
C.d: The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart reported on 20 January 2017. It confirmed that 38 boys at Kincora were sexually abused; three staff members, Joseph Mains, Raymond Semple and William McGrath, were convicted. Hart found that Kincora was not a homosexual brothel, that no security agency used it to entrap or blackmail men, and that there was 'no credible evidence' that prominent people such as civil servants, businessmen or Sir Maurice Oldfield were involved; he called the honey-trap claims 'unfounded myths'. He did criticise MI5 for obstructing the 1980s police investigation. Some former residents rejected the conclusions.
C.cite: Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (Hart Report), 20 January 2017, as reported by The Irish Times

C.n: Northern Ireland Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (22 institutions, 1922–1995)
C.who: 22 children's homes and institutions run by the state, voluntary bodies and religious orders in Northern Ireland
C.d: The Hart Inquiry's 10-volume, roughly 2,300-page report, published 20 January 2017, examined abuse in 22 residential institutions in Northern Ireland between 1922 and 1995, reviewing hundreds of government and intelligence files. It found systemic failings and abuse including sexual abuse across state, voluntary and church-run homes and recommended redress and a public apology.
C.cite: Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry report, 20 January 2017, as reported by The Irish Times

C.n: Jersey care system and Haut de la Garenne — Independent Jersey Care Inquiry
C.place: Haut de la Garenne, St Martin, Jersey
C.who: States of Jersey children's services; Haut de la Garenne children's home
C.cover: The inquiry found the authorities failed to build a culture of transparency, feeding perceptions of collusion and cover-up, and a 'small island culture' that was not countered.
C.d: The Independent Jersey Care Inquiry reported in July 2017 after hearing from about 450 people connected with Jersey's care system since 1945. It found the States of Jersey had been 'an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent', that its child-welfare law was decades behind, and that some children in care might still be at risk. Haut de la Garenne, centre of the 2007–2010 police investigation Operation Rectangle, was described as a symbol of the turmoil and the inquiry recommended its buildings be demolished. Chief Minister Ian Gorst apologised: 'We failed children who needed our care.'
C.cite: Independent Jersey Care Inquiry report, July 2017, as reported by LocalGov

C.n: Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA
C.place: Lambeth, London (Shirley Oaks home located near Croydon)
C.vn: 705 former residents had made sexual abuse complaints to the council by June 2020; the inquiry said the true scale is likely much higher. At Shirley Oaks alone, allegations against 177 staff or associated people involving at least 529 former residents.
C.who: London Borough of Lambeth; Shirley Oaks, South Vale and Angell Road children's homes
C.cover: Over 40 years only one senior employee was disciplined. The council did not tell a coroner that a boy found dead at Shirley Oaks in 1977 had alleged sexual abuse by his 'house father' Donald Hosegood; the inquiry asked the Metropolitan Police to consider a criminal investigation into this.
C.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 27 July 2021 that children in Lambeth's care were subjected to decades of cruelty and sexual abuse from the 1960s. By June 2020 the council had complaints from 705 former residents; at Shirley Oaks, allegations were made against 177 staff or associated people involving at least 529 former residents. At Angell Road, children including some under five were systematically exposed to sexual abuse. The inquiry found racism, nepotism, corruption and mismanagement in the council, and that most children at Shirley Oaks (1980) and South Vale (1990–91) were Black.
C.cite: IICSA, Children in the care of Lambeth Council investigation report, 27 July 2021

C.n: Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA
C.place: Nottingham and Nottinghamshire (Beechwood Children's Home, Mapperley)
C.vn: About 350 people reported sexual abuse in the councils' care; the inquiry said the true number is likely much higher.
C.who: Nottinghamshire County Council and Nottingham City Council residential and foster care; Beechwood Children's Home
C.cover: Only two disciplinary actions, both inadequate, followed the many allegations at Beechwood; known perpetrators were allowed to continue fostering and abused again.
C.d: IICSA reported on 31 July 2019 that sexual abuse was widespread in the two councils' residential and foster care in the 1970s–1990s. About 350 people reported abuse. From the late 1970s to 2019, 16 residential staff and 10 foster carers were convicted of sexually abusing children in their care, plus 12 convictions for harmful sexual behaviour by children against other children. The inquiry concluded that 'neither of the Councils learned from their mistakes'.
C.cite: IICSA, Children in the care of the Nottinghamshire Councils investigation report, 31 July 2019

C.n: Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff
C.vn: Durham Constabulary's Operation Seabrook recorded 1,848 men reporting physical or sexual abuse; later reports say over 2,000 came forward.
C.who: Medomsley Detention Centre for young offenders (Home Office Prison Service)
C.cover: The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman (November 2025) found that knowledge of the abuse held by the Prison Service, police and Home Office was 'ignored and dismissed', families' complaints led to no action, and successive wardens were 'either complicit or incompetent'.
C.d: Medomsley held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, an officer who ran the kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and again in 2005 and died in 2010; the Ombudsman called him 'possibly the most prolific sex offender in British history'. Operation Seabrook (from 2013) identified 32 living suspects; five former officers were convicted in 2019 and another in 2023, eight former staff jailed in total. The Ombudsman's report of 12 November 2025, based on 8,000 documents and 74 witnesses, found the authorities failed in their duty to keep detainees safe.
C.cite: Prisons and Probation Ombudsman, Operation Deerness report on Medomsley, 12 November 2025; ITV News, 28 Feb 2024; LBC

C.n: Islington Council children's homes, London
C.who: London Borough of Islington children's homes and foster placements (42 homes)
C.cover: A 2018 report by Sarah Morgan QC found that councillor Sandy Marks knew of abuse allegations before the Evening Standard published them in 1992; the council leadership publicly denied the newspaper's reports at the time.
C.d: Survivors say children in Islington's 42 children's homes and in foster care were abused between the 1960s and 1990s; the Evening Standard exposed abuse in the homes in 1992. A 2018 independent report by Sarah Morgan QC into former councillor Sandy Marks found evidence linking her to the 'Fallen Angels' group (which she denies) but no evidence it affected her council duties or that she learned of organised abuse. Islington later set up a support payment scheme for survivors.
C.cite: Leigh Day on Sarah Morgan QC report for Islington Council, 7 November 2018

C.n: Kendall House girls' home, Gravesend — Proctor review
C.who: Kendall House, a Church of England children's home taking girls placed by social services
C.d: An independent review chaired by Dr Sue Proctor, commissioned by the Bishop of Rochester and published in July 2016, found that from 1967 girls as young as 11 were routinely given antidepressants, sedatives and antipsychotics, sometimes without medical assessment. Former residents were physically, emotionally and sometimes sexually abused, including two rapes while girls were held in isolation. The review heard from 20 former residents and examined records of 44. A 1980 television programme had already exposed the home.
C.cite: Kendall House Review (Proctor), July 2016, as reported by Church Times and the National Secular Society

C.n: Quarriers, Aberlour and Barnardo's homes — Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry
C.place: Scotland (Quarriers Village, Bridge of Weir, and other homes)
C.who: Quarriers, Aberlour Child Care Trust and Barnardo's residential homes in Scotland
C.d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's third case study findings, published 7 January 2020, concluded that children in residential care run by Quarriers, Aberlour and Barnardo's between 1921 and 1991 suffered physical, emotional and sexual abuse. These voluntary providers cared for children placed by local authorities across Scotland.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 3 findings (Quarriers, Aberlour, Barnardo's), 7 January 2020

C.n: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales)
C.place: England and Wales (inquiry based in London)
C.vn: More than 6,200 victims and survivors shared accounts with the Truth Project; this is not a total of victims.
C.who: Institutions across England and Wales: local authority care, churches, schools, custodial institutions, political parties, police
C.d: IICSA published its final report in October 2022 after 19 investigation reports, 325 days of public hearings, more than 700 live witnesses and almost 1,000 written statements, and over 200,000 documents. More than 6,200 victims and survivors took part in its Truth Project. It made 107 recommendations, including mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse. Its investigations found institutional failures by councils, police, churches and government departments.
C.cite: IICSA Final Report, October 2022, Part A.2 'The Inquiry's activities'

C.n: British child migration programmes — IICSA
C.place: Sent from the UK to Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia
C.vn: About 4,000 children migrated after the Second World War, mostly to Australia; earlier migration (from the 19th century) was much larger.
C.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
C.cover: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.
C.d: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
C.cite: IICSA, Child Migration Programmes Investigation Report, 1 March 2018

C.n: 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers
C.place: West Berlin (network nodes also in Göttingen, Hannover, Lüneburg, Tübingen, Heppenheim)
C.who: Berlin Senate youth administration and state youth office (Landesjugendamt); sexologist Helmut Kentler (Pädagogisches Zentrum Berlin, later TU Hannover); network incl. Gerold Becker of the Odenwaldschule
C.cover: University of Hildesheim researchers found the abuse was carried out and institutionalised under the responsibility of the Landesjugendamt and the Berlin Senate administration; Kentler died in 2008 without prosecution.
C.d: From the late 1960s (Kentler held a post at the Senate's Pädagogisches Zentrum from 1967 to 1976) West Berlin youth authorities, on the advice of Helmut Kentler, placed homeless boys and other children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, as a form of 'resocialisation'. University of Hildesheim reports (2020 and final report 22 February 2024) reconstructed a nationwide network in science, youth welfare and administration that supported, legitimised or tolerated paedophile positions and sexual violence, continuing beyond 2000. Some children were about five years old when placed. Berlin says known victims have received compensation.
C.cite: University of Hildesheim final report on the Kentler network, presented by Berlin Senator Katharina Günther-Wünsch, 22 February 2024 (epd/evangelisch.de; News4teachers)

C.n: Odenwaldschule, Heppenheim — abuse by headmaster Gerold Becker and teachers
C.vn: At least 132 pupils according to the 2010 lawyers' report, which said documentation was incomplete.
C.who: Odenwaldschule (private, state-recognised progressive boarding school); headmaster Gerold Becker, music teacher Wolfgang Held
C.cover: After victims came forward in 1998 and the Frankfurter Rundschau reported it in November 1999, a promised review did not take place; prosecutors in Darmstadt dropped the case under the statute of limitations. Becker died in 2010 without facing legal consequences.
C.d: Lawyers Claudia Burgsmüller and Brigitte Tilmann, a former judge, were called in by the school to investigate; their 2010 report identified more than a dozen perpetrators, with former headmaster Gerold Becker and a music teacher named as the main abusers from the late 1960s, and 17 witnesses testifying against Becker. Later counts put the victims at at least 132 pupils abused by teachers between the 1960s and 1990s; the victims' association says at least 20 teachers were responsible. The abuse, long covered up, became widely public in 2010; pupil numbers and funding fell and in April 2015 the school's sponsoring association announced its closure. Becker also appears in the Hildesheim research as a figure in the Kentler network.
C.cite: Der Spiegel International, 'The Roots of Abuse: Decades of Molestation Haunt Odenwaldschule', 2010; News4teachers/dpa, 3 Oct 2014; Abendzeitung München/dpa, 27 Apr 2015

C.n: Lügde campsite abuse — youth office placed foster child with offender
C.who: Two men at a permanent campsite; youth welfare offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont; Lippe police
C.cover: Welfare authorities placed a foster girl with the main offender despite allegations about him. Police failed to act on repeated complaints, evidence disappeared from police archives, and a case worker manipulated and deleted files. The NRW parliamentary inquiry found 'authority failure' and said the men could have been stopped two years earlier.
C.d: On 5 September 2019 the Detmold regional court sentenced Andreas V. to 13 years and Mario S. to 12 years, both followed by preventive detention, for abusing 32 children at a campsite in Lügde from 1998 to 2018; police found 32,000 files of abuse material. Youth welfare authorities had placed a foster daughter with Andreas V. The North Rhine-Westphalia Landtag inquiry (interim report 24 March 2022) found failures by police and the youth offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont.
C.cite: Irish Times, 5 Sep 2019; NRW Landtag Untersuchungsausschuss interim report, 24 March 2022 (epd)

C.n: Round Table on Residential Care (Runder Tisch Heimerziehung) — West German children's homes 1950s–70s
C.vn: About 800,000 children grew up in church and state homes; this is the number in care, not the number abused. About one in three people contacting the Round Table's contact point reported sexual abuse.
C.who: State and church-run children's homes in West Germany
C.d: The Bundestag-appointed Round Table on residential care in the 1950s and 1960s presented its final report in December 2010. It found brutal discipline, humiliation, beatings and forced labour were common, and about one in three of those who contacted it reported sexual abuse. It recommended a fund of at least €120 million to be paid in equal thirds by the federal government, the states and the churches.
C.cite: Runder Tisch Heimerziehung, final report, December 2010 (epd/evangelisch.de, 10 Dec 2010)

C.n: De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945
C.who: Dutch residential youth care, foster care, juvenile justice institutions, closed youth care, shelters for unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors, institutions for disabled children
C.d: The commission led by Professor Micha de Winter published 'Onvoldoende beschermd' on 14 June 2019 after interviewing about 1,000 people who had lived in foster families or youth institutions. It found that a considerable share of children in Dutch youth care since 1945 were not adequately protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, that supervisors did not intervene enough, and that the government did too little to prevent it. The cabinet said the violence 'should never have happened' and set up a payment scheme for victims.
C.cite: Commissie Onderzoek naar geweld in de jeugdzorg (De Winter), final report, 14 June 2019 (Leiden University)

C.n: Samson Commission — sexual abuse of children in Dutch state care
C.vn: 800 claims received (65% care homes, 30% foster families); not a total.
C.who: Dutch children's homes and foster care (Jeugdzorg)
C.d: The commission chaired by former procurator-general Rieke Samson reported in October 2012 on sexual abuse of children in state-arranged care since 1945. It received 800 claims, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. It found the government, care homes and foster care services did not do enough to protect children and, once aware, lacked professionalism and courage to act.
C.cite: Samson Commission final report, October 2012 (DutchNews, 8 Oct 2012)

C.n: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
C.kind: sexual abuse + forced labour + child removal
C.vn: More than 60,000 people interned without judicial order in the 20th century; not all were children and not all suffered sexual abuse.
C.who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
C.d: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).
C.cite: Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention (UEK), final report, 2 September 2019 (JusticeInfo.net)

C.n: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report
C.who: City of Vienna children's home at Wilhelminenberg
C.cover: Municipal staff in the overseeing department knew of widespread abuse and did not act; city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it.
C.d: A commission set up by the City of Vienna presented a 344-page report on 12 June 2013, based on 217 interviews including 140 former residents. It found children at the city-run home (1948–1977, girls only from 1962) were rampantly abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and outside men, with girls as young as about six. Findings were sent to prosecutors. Some former residents received payments of up to €35,000.
C.cite: Wilhelminenberg Commission report, 12 June 2013 (AP via CBS News)

C.n: Godhavn Report — Danish state children's homes 1945–1976
C.place: Godhavn boys' home, Tisvilde, North Zealand (and 18 other state homes)
C.who: Danish state-run children's homes incl. Godhavn boys' home
C.d: The Godhavn Report, published 9 May 2011, examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other state homes from 1945 to 1976, finding neglect, physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22% of Godhavn residents had been given psychiatric drugs by psychiatrist Ib Ostenfeld. No prosecutions followed. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised to hundreds of victims in 2019.
C.cite: Godhavn Report, 9 May 2011; SBS News on PM apology, August 2019
