C.n: Swedish inquiry into abuse in children's homes and foster care (Vanvårdsutredningen)
C.who: Swedish municipal children's homes and foster care
C.d: The government inquiry into abuse and neglect in Swedish children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980 reported in February 2011, recommending a public apology and SEK 250,000 for each person who suffered serious abuse; the apology ceremony was held at Stockholm City Hall in 2011. A compensation board set up on 1 January 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015 and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.
C.cite: Vanvårdsutredningen, February 2011 (The Local, 10 Feb 2011); SVT Nyheter, 4 July 2015

C.n: Norwegian children's homes and special schools 1945–1980 (NOU 2004:23)
C.who: Norwegian municipal children's homes and state special schools
C.d: The official report NOU 2004:23 'Barnehjem og spesialskoler under lupen' found neglect and abuse, in part of a serious nature and including sexual abuse, in children's homes and special schools between 1945 and 1980. Bergen and other municipalities ran their own investigations and compensation schemes; in 2005 the Storting committee recommended adapting the state 'rettferdsvederlag' scheme with payments up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof.
C.cite: Stortinget, Innst. S. nr. 217 (2004–2005), on NOU 2004:23

C.n: Finland — maltreatment in child welfare substitute care 1937–1983
C.who: Finnish child welfare institutions and foster care
C.d: A Ministry of Social Affairs and Health study interviewed about 300 people who had been in child welfare substitute care between 1937 and 1983 and found maltreatment and violence in all forms of care. The Finnish government made an official apology on 20 November 2016, Universal Children's Day.
C.cite: Finnish Ministry of Social Affairs and Health, official apology, 20 November 2016

C.n: France — children in state child welfare (ASE) exploited in prostitution
C.place: France (cases raised in Bouches-du-Rhône and Essonne)
C.vn: Parliamentary commission estimate of children in ASE care who are victims of prostitution (as reported by RFI/AFP).
C.who: Aide sociale à l'enfance (departmental child welfare services)
C.d: A French parliamentary commission of inquiry report published in April 2025 estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services (ASE), which hold about 396,900 minors, are victims of prostitution. Lawyers asked the Bouches-du-Rhône and Essonne departments for administrative reviews over children in care who were prostituted; teenagers are often housed in hotels with little supervision. A complaint was filed with the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.
C.cite: RFI/AFP report on French child welfare and prostitution, 2025, citing National Assembly commission of inquiry

C.n: Notre-Dame de Bétharram school — National Assembly commission of inquiry
C.vn: About 200 complaints filed since early 2025.
C.who: Notre-Dame de Bétharram, a Catholic private school under contract with the state; Ministry of Education inspection
C.cover: The commission wrote that 'in the absence of action from a minister who was informed and in a position to intervene', abuse continued for years; it found state inspection of private schools under contract was weak and sanctioned teachers could move between schools undetected.
C.d: Priests, teachers and staff are accused of sexual and physical abuse of pupils from 1957 to 2004, with about 200 complaints filed in 2025. The National Assembly commission of inquiry (rapporteurs Violette Spillebout and Paul Vannier) published its report on 2 July 2025 with 50 recommendations, including rebuilding state inspections. It did not directly implicate François Bayrou, who said he had not grasped the seriousness of information he received; Vannier separately accused him of misleading parliament.
C.cite: Assemblée nationale commission of inquiry report, 2 July 2025 (AP via BishopAccountability; Le Club des Juristes)

C.n: Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims
C.place: Canada (schools in every province and territory except NB, PEI and NL)
C.vn: 37,951 claims for injuries from physical and sexual abuse were made by end-2014 (TRC figure); the Independent Assessment Process ultimately received 38,276 claims. About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended.
C.who: Government of Canada; schools operated by the Catholic, Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
C.cover: Under the settlement, claimants' IAP records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep or share them.
C.d: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher. By the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been made for injuries from physical and sexual abuse and 30,939 resolved. The Independent Assessment Process received 38,276 claims in total; adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants and the government compensated 4,415 more directly.
C.cite: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, Final Report, December 2015 (CBC 'By the numbers'); Globe and Mail on IAP totals

C.n: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission
C.place: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's, Newfoundland
C.who: Mount Cashel Orphanage run by the Irish Christian Brothers, with privileged foster-home status from Newfoundland Social Services; Royal Newfoundland Constabulary; provincial Department of Justice
C.cover: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.
C.d: Complaints of abuse at Mount Cashel surfaced in 1974 and 1975 but neither led to charges. Police reopened the case in February 1989; nine Christian Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission (156 hearing days, over 200 witnesses, report 31 May 1991) found neither the police nor the Justice Department handled the 1975–76 files normally, and that child welfare director Frank Simms insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.
C.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Response of the Newfoundland Criminal Justice System to Complaints (Hughes), 31 May 1991, as summarised by Heritage Newfoundland and Labrador

C.n: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children — Restorative Inquiry
C.who: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children (provincially funded orphanage for Black children)
C.d: Former residents of the home, which operated from 1921, described neglect and emotional, physical and sexual abuse. A class action was settled and the provincial government apologised in 2014 to former residents and the African Nova Scotian community for harm caused by systemic racism. The Restorative Inquiry delivered its final report on 28 November 2019 in Halifax.
C.cite: Government of Nova Scotia news release on Restorative Inquiry final report, 28 November 2019

C.n: Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse
C.who: Cornwall Community Police Service, Ontario Provincial Police (Project Truth), local probation office, Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria-Cornwall
C.cover: Commissioner Glaude found the Diocese's $32,000 settlement with complainant David Silmser contained an illegal clause, and called Cornwall police's investigation of his complaint 'deeply flawed', though he found no conspiracy between police and diocese.
C.d: The Cornwall Public Inquiry under Commissioner G. Normand Glaude reported in December 2009 at a cost of over $50 million. It found systemic failures by police, probation and the Catholic diocese in responding to historical sexual abuse allegations against adults in positions of trust in Cornwall. On the long-rumoured paedophile 'clan', Glaude made no finding, saying no investigation had provided conclusive evidence.
C.cite: Report of the Cornwall Inquiry (Glaude), December 2009, as reported by the Standard-Freeholder via BishopAccountability

C.n: Grandview Training School for Girls, Galt, Ontario
C.vn: The survivors' group grew to over 300 women.
C.who: Ontario provincial training school for girls (juvenile reformatory)
C.cover: Complaints of serious sexual abuse made by girls while at the school were reportedly ignored and never investigated.
C.d: Hundreds of women reported physical and sexual abuse while held as girls at the Grandview Training School, a government-run school for 'troubled' girls in Galt (now Cambridge), Ontario, which closed in 1976. Eight former staff members were charged and two were convicted. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite an investigation by Ontario Provincial Police and Waterloo Regional Police after the abuse became public in 1991, a survivors' group of more than 300 women seeking compensation, and a 1999 apology by MPP Jim Flaherty in the Ontario legislature on the province's behalf (these three points not re-confirmed in this pass).
C.cite: CBC News, 'Grandview school to be demolished'

C.n: Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation
C.place: United States (417 schools in 37 states or territories)
C.vn: At least 973 children's deaths confirmed — an undercount; not a count of abuse victims.
C.who: US Department of the Interior / federal government; many schools run by churches with federal funding
C.d: The Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative's Volume I (May 2022) and Volume II (July 2024) identified 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or then-territories between 1819 and 1969, at least 973 children's deaths, and at least 74 marked and unmarked burial sites at 65 schools. The report states that many Indian children suffered 'physical, sexual, and emotional abuse' at the schools and recommended a formal US apology.
C.cite: US Department of the Interior, Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report Vol. II, July 2024 (Equal Justice Initiative summary)

C.n: Boy Scouts of America — 82,000+ abuse claims and bankruptcy settlement
C.vn: More than 82,000 claims filed in the bankruptcy by the November 2020 deadline.
C.who: Boy Scouts of America (now Scouting America) and local councils
C.cover: BSA kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers; 1,247 files from 1965–1985 were ordered released by the Oregon Supreme Court in June 2012 after a 2010 civil jury award of nearly $20 million.
C.d: BSA filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2020. By the November 2020 claims deadline more than 82,000 people had filed sexual abuse claims, which lawyers said was larger than all Catholic Church cases combined. A $2.46 billion settlement trust pays survivors between $3,500 and $2.7 million; the US Supreme Court declined to review the plan in January 2026. BSA's internal 'ineligible volunteer' files, which the Oregon Supreme Court ordered largely released in 2012, recorded suspected abusers over decades.
C.cite: JURIST, Nov 2020; KSL/AP on settlement; ABA Journal on Oregon Supreme Court ruling, 14 June 2012

C.n: Los Angeles County juvenile halls and MacLaren Children's Center — $4bn settlement
C.place: Los Angeles County, California (MacLaren Children's Center, El Monte, and juvenile halls)
C.vn: More than 6,800 claims.
C.who: Los Angeles County Probation Department juvenile facilities; MacLaren Children's Center (closed 2003); county foster care
C.d: On 29 April 2025 the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a $4 billion settlement of more than 6,800 claims of sexual abuse, mostly in Probation Department juvenile facilities and at the MacLaren Children's Center in El Monte, plus foster care, dating back to the 1980s. It was the costliest such payout in county history.
C.cite: ABC7 Los Angeles, 29 April 2025

C.n: New Hampshire Youth Development Center, Manchester
C.vn: More than 1,100 former residents had filed lawsuits by May 2024.
C.who: State of New Hampshire Youth Development Center (juvenile detention)
C.d: More than 1,100 former residents of New Hampshire's state youth detention centre have sued over physical, sexual and emotional abuse spanning six decades, and 11 former state workers have been arrested. In the first trial, on 3 May 2024, a jury found the state negligent and awarded David Meehan, who went to police in 2017, $38 million. The state argued it was not liable for 'rogue' employees. A state settlement fund had paid $102 million on 206 claims by October 2024, with 448 more pending.
C.cite: Concord Monitor/AP, 3 May 2024

C.n: US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018
C.who: State and locally run juvenile detention and correctional facilities
C.d: The Bureau of Justice Statistics surveyed 6,049 youth in 327 juvenile facilities between March and December 2018. 7.1% reported sexual victimisation in the previous 12 months, and 5.8% reported sexual misconduct by staff (down from 7.7% in 2012). Youth-on-youth forced or coerced victimisation was reported by 1.9%.
C.cite: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Sexual Victimization Reported by Youth in Juvenile Facilities, 2018 (released 11 Dec 2019)

C.n: Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'
C.place: Texas (case heard in Corpus Christi federal court)
C.who: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services; Health and Human Services Commission
C.cover: Judge Jack held Texas in contempt three times (2019, 2020, April 2024) for failing to investigate abuse complaints and protect children; in 2019 she said she could no longer find the department credible.
C.d: In a class action filed in 2011 on behalf of children in long-term state care, US District Judge Janis Graham Jack ruled in December 2015 that Texas violated foster children's constitutional rights by placing them in a system where 'rape and over-medication were the norm'. She later ordered 24-hour awake supervision and flagging of children who were victims or perpetrators of sexual violence. In April 2024 she found the state in contempt for a third time and fined it $100,000 a day over failures to investigate abuse reports.
C.cite: KUT, 5 Nov 2019; AP via KTVZ, 16 Apr 2024

C.n: 'Troubled teen' residential programmes — GAO 2007 investigation
C.who: Private residential treatment programmes, boot camps and wilderness programmes for youth
C.d: In testimony to Congress on 10 October 2007 (GAO-08-146T), the Government Accountability Office reported it had found thousands of allegations of abuse, some involving death, at residential treatment programmes for troubled youth, reviewing closed cases back to 1990. GAO did not verify each allegation.
C.cite: GAO-08-146T, Residential Treatment Programs: Concerns Regarding Abuse and Death in Certain Programs for Troubled Youth, 10 Oct 2007

C.n: Youth residential treatment facilities — US Senate Finance Committee 2024
C.who: Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health, Vivant Behavioral Healthcare (incl. former Sequel facilities); funded by Medicaid and child welfare agencies
C.d: A two-year Senate Finance Committee investigation released on 12 June 2024 found that 'horrific instances of sexual abuse persist unremediated' inside residential treatment facilities for children run by four large companies, along with physical abuse, overuse of restraints and overmedication. Facilities often receive more than $1,200 per child per day from Medicaid; states including Oregon sent foster children to out-of-state facilities.
C.cite: US Senate Finance Committee (Chairman Wyden), 'Warehouses of Neglect', 12 June 2024

C.n: Illinois state youth detention centres and Cook County JTDC — mass abuse lawsuits
C.place: Illinois (incl. Illinois Youth Center St. Charles and Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center, Chicago)
C.vn: 667 people had sued over abuse at state and county youth facilities between May and September 2024 (allegations by plaintiffs).
C.who: Illinois Department of Juvenile Justice (nine state youth detention centres, five since closed); Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center
C.d: Between May and September 2024, 667 former detainees sued alleging sexual abuse by staff at Illinois state youth detention centres and the Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center; three suits filed on 23 September 2024 alone covered 272 plaintiffs and abuse from 1996 to 2021. The lawsuits name repeat alleged abusers, including a chaplain at St. Charles, and say at least one accused employee still worked for the state. These are allegations not yet tested in court.
C.cite: AP via BishopAccountability, 24 September 2024

C.n: Ontario training schools class action (Brown v. Ontario)
C.place: Ontario (13 training schools incl. Pine Ridge, Bowmanville; Hillcrest, Guelph; Brookside, Cobourg; Cecil Facer, Sudbury)
C.who: Government of Ontario provincial training schools (juvenile reformatories)
C.d: In the class action Brown v. Ontario, the province agreed to a settlement of up to CAD 60 million, signed 21 January 2026 and approved by the Ontario Superior Court on 21 May 2026, for former residents of 13 provincial training schools between 1953 and 1984. It covers physical and sexual assault and solitary confinement. Ontario denies liability and the court did not decide the merits.
C.cite: Brown v. Ontario settlement notice (Open Class Actions), 2026

C.n: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report
C.vn: 8,013 private sessions held May 2013–November 2017; more than 16,000 people contacted the Commission. Not a count of all victims.
C.who: Religious, government and other institutions; evidence related to 3,489 institutions
C.cover: Case studies documented destroyed or unkept records and the protection of institutional reputation over children, e.g. the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat ('records were deliberately not made or kept or were destroyed').
C.d: The Royal Commission, announced in November 2012, delivered its final report on 15 December 2017 with a total of 409 recommendations across its reports. It held 8,013 private sessions, received 1,344 written accounts and heard evidence relating to 3,489 institutions. 58.1% of survivors in private sessions reported abuse in a religious institution, 32.5% in a government-run institution and 10.5% in other non-government institutions. The average age at first abuse was 10.4 years. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began on 1 July 2018.
C.cite: Royal Commission final report, 15 December 2017, as summarised by knowmore legal service and by The Guardian (republished by BishopAccountability)

C.n: Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7
C.place: Parramatta, New South Wales (and Hay, NSW)
C.vn: Sixteen women gave statements to the 2014 public hearing; the home held thousands of girls between 1887 and 1974.
C.who: NSW state child-welfare department; Parramatta Girls Home (Parramatta Training School for Girls), Hay Institution for Girls
C.cover: Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated; some resigned or were dismissed after inquiries; no criminal charges were laid.
C.d: Parramatta Girls Home was a NSW state-run institution for girls from 1887 to 1974, many of them Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations. The Royal Commission's February 2014 hearing (Case Study 7, report October 2014) heard evidence about 11 men, most of them superintendents or deputies, accused of physical and sexual abuse. Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated and no criminal charges were laid. A 2004 Senate inquiry had earlier taken statements from 20 former residents.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 7, October 2014 (via Wikipedia)

C.n: Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry
C.vn: 535 Aboriginal people gave testimony; more than 600 further submissions. The report said that in certain regions and periods the share of Indigenous children forcibly removed was 'undoubtedly much greater than one in ten'.
C.who: Commonwealth, state and territory governments; church and state institutions, foster and adoptive families
C.cover: The report documented officials misrepresenting capable parents as unfit and telling some parents their children had died when they had not.
C.d: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 'Bringing Them Home' report on the forced removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children was released on 26 May 1997 with 54 recommendations. Survivors described abuse, including sexual abuse, in institutions and foster care. Recommendation five, a national apology, was refused by the Howard government and delivered by Prime Minister Kevin Rudd in 2008; the recommended national compensation scheme was refused by successive governments. The report recorded rates of sexual assault among its witnesses (record cites 17% of women and 7.7% of men among 502 witnesses; not re-checked from the report itself).
C.cite: The Guardian, 'Australia's stolen generations: a legacy of intergenerational pain and broken bonds', 25 May 2017 (20th anniversary of the Bringing Them Home report)

C.n: Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions
C.who: 159 government and non-government orphanages, reformatories and detention centres in Queensland
C.d: The Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions, chaired by former governor Leneen Forde, was set up on 13 August 1998 and reported in May 1999. It examined 159 institutions from 1911 to 1999, found that abuse had occurred and made 42 recommendations. Some findings were sealed because matters were still before the courts. It led to state apologies, the Queensland Government Redress Scheme and the Forde Foundation.
C.cite: Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions (Forde Inquiry), May 1999 (via Wikipedia and Qld Government)

C.n: Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia
C.who: South Australian state guardianship system (Families SA and predecessors)
C.d: Commissioner Ted Mullighan's inquiry began in November 2004 and was widened in 2007 to children on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands. Its March 2008 report found 'that in the past 65 years the State has failed to protect some of the children in its care from sexual abuse' and that record-keeping on 924 children who died in state care was manifestly inadequate. It made 54 recommendations, and 400 suspected abusers were reported to South Australia Police.
C.cite: Children in State Care Commission of Inquiry (Mullighan Report), March 2008 (via Wikipedia)

C.n: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale)
C.place: Don Dale Youth Detention Centre, Berrimah, Darwin, NT
C.who: Northern Territory Government youth detention and child protection systems
C.cover: A 2014 media release falsely said six boys had escaped when CCTV showed one; two earlier reports (January 2015 review and the August 2015 Children's Commissioner report) were not acted on.
C.d: The Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory was set up in July 2016 after ABC Four Corners broadcast footage of boys at Don Dale being tear-gassed, hooded with spit hoods and shackled. Its final report, released on 17 November 2017 by commissioners Margaret White and Mick Gooda, found children had been subjected to 'regular, repeated and distressing mistreatment in detention' and that the law was often not followed, and recommended closing Don Dale, raising the age of criminal responsibility to 12 and not detaining children under 14.
C.cite: SBS NITV, 'Close Don Dale: NT juvenile justice inquiry final report delivered', 17 Nov 2017

C.n: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
C.place: Ireland (Larch Hill, Co. Dublin national office)
C.vn: 275 known or suspected perpetrators across the two predecessor associations; by November 2018 108 alleged victims had been identified and records review was ongoing.
C.who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
C.cover: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.
C.d: Child-protection consultant Ian Elliott's 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published by Scouting Ireland on 14 May 2020, found a cover-up and failure to report abuse in the former Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and Scout Association of Ireland. It described 'a culture driven by self-interest', said 'cronyism thrived', and found that people suspected or known to be sex offenders gained positions of power and became 'largely impregnable'; records had been lost or destroyed, so the full extent could not be determined. An earlier audit reported to the Oireachtas in November 2018 had found evidence of 108 alleged victims and 71 alleged abusers, with numbers expected to rise considerably.
C.cite: RTÉ News, 'Report finds failure to report Scouting Ireland abuse', 14 May 2020; The Irish Times, 21 Nov 2018

C.n: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
C.vn: NZ$10.7 million paid to 183 former patients after a 2001 apology; police interviewed 63 former patients.
C.who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
C.cover: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.
C.d: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.
C.cite: RNZ, 'Lake Alice survivors to get $150,000 each in redress', 18 Dec 2024; The Guardian, 'Victims allegedly tortured by New Zealand psychiatrist fear time is running out for justice', 7 Jul 2021

C.n: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
C.vn: Medical tests confirmed sexual abuse of 34 of 42 girls aged 7–17.
C.who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
C.cover: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.
C.d: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Brajesh Thakur's NGO; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The Supreme Court took up the case and, at the CBI's request, transferred the trial to a POCSO court at Saket, Delhi, because the accused were influential in Bihar. On 20 January 2020 that court convicted Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment and has appealed.
C.cite: The Hindu, 'Muzaffarpur shelter home case: Brajesh Thakur challenges verdict', 2020; The Hindu, 'Supreme Court transfers Muzaffarpur shelter home sexual assault case from Bihar to Delhi'; Indian Express, 5 Aug 2018

C.n: Lumos — 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights'
C.vn: About 30,000 children in about 750 orphanages; the Government of Haiti estimates 80% have at least one living parent.
C.who: Mostly privately run, foreign-funded orphanages in Haiti; donors 92% from the US and 90% faith-based
C.d: Lumos researched Haiti's orphanages from October 2016 to February 2017, including a 2016 evaluation of 140 children in four orphanages with the government agency IBESR, and published its report in June 2017. It found at least US$70 million a year going to about a third of orphanages, with total funding estimated above $100 million a year; only 15% of orphanages were registered and at least 140 had conditions putting children at severe risk. It documented violence and severe neglect and, in a few cases, sexual abuse, trafficking and avoidable deaths, and evidence of orphanages recruiting children away from families — an 'orphanage business' it describes as increasingly recognised as trafficking.
C.cite: Lumos, 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights', executive summary, June 2017

C.n: TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes
C.place: Bihar (38 districts; incl. Muzaffarpur, Motihari, Bhagalpur, Munger)
C.who: Children's and girls' homes funded by the Bihar Social Welfare Department, many NGO-run
C.cover: In the audited Bhagalpur home staff refused to give the audit team the key to the complaint box, saying it was lost; the department's director evaded questions about action on the other 14 homes.
C.d: At the Bihar government's request, the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences visited 110 children's homes in 38 districts and submitted its audit to the Social Welfare Department on 27 April 2018, grading homes as better, administrative negligence or criminal negligence. The Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti was graded criminal negligence, and the report raised harassment or abuse at 14 other homes, including a girls' home with complaints of severe sexual harassment and violence and homes where children were routinely beaten. The audit triggered the Muzaffarpur FIR of 31 May 2018 and later CBI cases against other Bihar shelter homes.
C.cite: Tata Institute of Social Sciences (Koshish), social audit report to Bihar Social Welfare Department, 27 April 2018, as reported by Newslaundry, 29 July 2018

C.n: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
C.vn: Estimate: of about 655,000 children, young people and adults in state and faith-based care 1950–2019, about 200,000 were abused and more were neglected.
C.who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
C.cover: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.
C.d: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.
C.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, 'Whanaketia', final report, 24 July 2024; RNZ, 24 July 2024

C.n: Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care
C.place: Tasmania (Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Deloraine; Launceston General Hospital)
C.who: Tasmanian Government: Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital paediatric ward, public schools, Child Safety Services, Tasmania Police
C.cover: Launceston General Hospital failed to act on a 2011 or 2012 disclosure about nurse James Griffin, leaving children at risk for eight years; Tasmania Police failed to act on 'highly probative' evidence from the Australian Federal Police in 2015; the government had been on notice about unlawful isolation at Ashley since at least 2013.
C.d: The commission, called in 2020 after a podcast aired allegations against Launceston General Hospital paediatric nurse James Griffin (who died in 2019 after being charged with child sexual offences), released a 3,500-page final report in 2023 with 75 findings and 191 recommendations. It found the state's response to child sexual abuse since 2000 had too often been inadequate, sometimes to protect reputations. Children at Ashley Youth Detention Centre had experienced systematic harm and abuse for decades and sexual abuse remained a 'live and current' risk; the commission repeated its call for Ashley to close. Premier Jeremy Rockliff apologised in parliament.
C.cite: Commission of Inquiry into the Tasmanian Government's Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in Institutional Settings, final report, 2023; AAP

C.n: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
C.vn: 41 girls aged 14–17 died in the 8 March 2017 fire (the count is of fire deaths, not of abuse victims); the Human Rights Ombudsman had received 45 abuse reports 2012–2016.
C.who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
C.cover: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.
C.d: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.
C.cite: Associated Press, '6 ex-officials in Guatemala convicted in deaths of 41 girls in 2017 fire at state facility', 12 Aug 2025; BBC News, June 2017

C.n: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
C.place: Mexico City (also CAIFAC, Monterrey; 'La Casita', Cancún)
C.vn: 126 children removed from the shelter in January 2009; as of March 2012, 14 children remained missing.
C.who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
C.cover: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.
C.d: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter, run by a church group, went missing. In October 2010 Mexico's federal Attorney General offered rewards for information on 14 children who disappeared in February 2009 from the Casitas del Sur shelter in Mexico City and from related homes in Nuevo Laredo and Quintana Roo, and about 5 million pesos for three people sought in the case, saying the children may have been taken by child traffickers. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite the removal of 126 children by police and human rights staff on 29 January 2009 and obstruction charges against seven staff (not re-checked for this map).
C.cite: CNN, 'Mexico offers reward in missing children case', 9 Oct 2010

C.n: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
C.vn: 432 children (174 girls, 278 boys) and 138 adults freed on 15 July 2014.
C.who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
C.cover: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.
C.d: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.
C.cite: Justice in Mexico (University of San Diego), 27 July 2014; Expansión, 3 June 2018

C.n: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
C.place: Chile (incl. Centro Galvarino, Estación Central, Santiago)
C.vn: SENAME reported 1,313 children, adolescents and adults died 2005–mid-2016 across its protection and juvenile justice programmes; the UN Committee counted 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016 and found 6.8% of children in centres had been sexually abused in the past year.
C.who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
C.d: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.
C.cite: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, inquiry under the Optional Protocol (report released 30 July 2018), via BioBioChile; SENAME figures October 2016 (via Spanish Wikipedia)

C.n: Élan School, Poland, Maine — troubled-teen programme
C.who: Élan School (private behaviour-modification boarding school; NATSAP member)
C.cover: In the late 1970s staff refused a sheriff's lieutenant entry past the lobby after rumours of abuse.
C.d: Élan operated from 1970 until 1 April 2011, when it closed after decades of abuse reports from former students. Illinois officials removed eleven children in 1975 alleging mistreatment, and in 2007 New York education officials, who paid tuition for special-education students, alleged students were made to restrain peers and were sleep-deprived. The New Yorker (2000) and Time (2011) described 'the ring', in which students were made to fight one another. Maine State Police reopened the 1982 death of a 15-year-old student in 2016 but filed no charges. The record of sexual abuse rests on former students' accounts; no official sexual-abuse finding was located.
C.cite: New Yorker (2000); Time (2011); Lewiston Sun Journal; Maine State Police 2016 (via Wikipedia)

C.n: Provo Canyon School, Utah — licences revoked 2026
C.who: Provo Canyon School, owned by Universal Health Services (2000–2026)
C.d: Provo Canyon School opened in 1971 and has faced abuse allegations for more than 50 years; former students including Paris Hilton (who attended in the 1990s under different ownership) have publicly described abuse. In 2026, after a 13-year-old boy was seriously injured in a fight and staff did not call 911 or seek immediate care, Utah's Department of Health and Human Services revoked the licence of the school's Springville campus and, on 17 July 2026, of its original Provo campus, citing failure to protect children from harm and abuse, 'cruel and unnecessary' pain-compliance techniques, prolonged restraints and humiliating discipline. Owner Universal Health Services (since 2000) said it disagreed and was reviewing appeal options. No official sexual-abuse finding was located; the licence revocations concerned abuse, mistreatment and safety.
C.cite: The Salt Lake Tribune, 'Utah revokes license for Provo Canyon School's original campus, ending notorious teen program', 17 Jul 2026

C.n: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
C.place: Romania (incl. Siret children's psychiatric hospital; Sighetu Marmației institution)
C.vn: About 100,000–170,000 children were in orphanages in 1989; an estimated 500,000 were raised in them overall.
C.who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
C.d: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.
C.cite: Wikipedia 'Romanian orphans' (citing BBC 2009 and academic sources)

C.n: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
C.place: Kathmandu Valley (Bagmati Province); children from Karnali and other rural districts
C.vn: 10,905 children were in 417 registered child care homes in 2021/22 (National Child Rights Council); UNICEF says about 85% have at least one living parent or guardian.
C.who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
C.d: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).
C.cite: National Child Rights Council (NCRC) report 2021/22 and UNICEF, via The Annapurna Express

C.n: Scouts Canada — KPMG review of unreported abuse
C.vn: KPMG reviewed 468 files of suspected sexual misconduct over 64 years and found at least 65 incidents not reported to authorities.
C.who: Scouts Canada
C.cover: A 2011 CBC investigation found Scouts Canada had signed confidentiality agreements with more than a dozen abuse victims; KPMG found abusers had in some cases been 'removed discreetly' and records were inconsistent and poorly kept.
C.d: After a CBC investigation in autumn 2011 found confidentiality agreements that kept victims from speaking, Scouts Canada apologised and asked KPMG to audit 64 years of records. The review, released in 2012, examined 468 files and found the organisation failed at least 65 times to report sexual misconduct allegations to authorities, 13 of them after 1992 when reporting became mandatory. Scouts Canada then gave police all records it could find. In 1979 the Boy Scouts of America had sent a known abuser back to Canada without warning Scouts Canada; he was convicted in Victoria, BC in 1996 of assaulting four boys.
C.cite: KPMG review of Scouts Canada records, 2012, via Global News; CBC 2011 (via Wikipedia 'Scouting sex abuse cases')

C.n: The Scout Association (UK) — abuse claims and payouts
C.vn: At least 260 claims taken on by eight law firms in a decade; more than £6m paid across 166 settled cases (BBC File on 4, 2023).
C.who: The Scout Association (UK)
C.d: A BBC File on 4 investigation in June 2023 found, from data from eight specialist law firms, that at least 260 child sexual abuse claims had been taken on against the Scouts in the previous decade and more than £6m paid out across 166 settled cases. The Scouts said 96% of claims highlighted by a survivors' campaign related to offences before 2013 and that the payouts broadly matched what it knew. In 2014 the BBC had reported more than 50 historical claims and £897,000 in damages; an MP called for an inquiry into failures to pass abuse records to police.
C.cite: BBC File on 4, June 2023, via Civil Society; BBC 2014 (via Wikipedia)

C.n: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinder (VCP) — independent study of sexualised violence
C.vn: At least 344 victims since 1973; at least 161 people committed or were accused of sexualised violence.
C.who: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (VCP), Protestant scouting federation
C.cover: The study found 'old cases' from the 1980s and 1990s were long ignored for lack of any idea of reappraisal (Aufarbeitung).
C.d: A study by the Munich Institut für Praxisforschung und Projektberatung (IPP) and the Dissens Institute, presented in Kassel on 27 January 2026, found at least 344 people had suffered sexualised violence within the VCP since 1973. It drew on 79 interviews and about 1,300 pages of files on 100 cases. About 60% of victims were girls, two-thirds were aged 13–17 when it began, nearly half the acts occurred after 2000, and more than half on camps or trips. Perpetrators came mostly from within the organisation, often adult group leaders.
C.cite: IPP München and Dissens-Institut, VCP Aufarbeitungsstudie, 27 January 2026, via evangelisch.de

C.n: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
C.who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
C.d: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.
C.cite: VRT NWS, 23 April 2014; Belga News Agency, 23 February 2025

C.n: Moldova — children leaving residential institutions targeted by traffickers
C.vn: More than 14,000 children lived in residential care, over 70% of them 'social orphans' with living parents (UNICEF 2006). UNICEF said children in institutions were 'several times' (elsewhere '10 times') more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.
C.who: Moldovan state residential institutions and boarding schools (Ministry of Education, Health, Labour)
C.d: Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children in the mid-2000s; children left them at 15–16 with no support beyond about US$70 and no follow-up. UNICEF reported that research showed institutionalised children were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children and that 'they often become easy prey for traffickers'. The US State Department's March 2007 human rights report said women and children were trafficked for sexual exploitation to Russia, Turkey, Israel, the UAE and other countries, and that 12% of trafficking victims assisted by IOM were minors.
C.cite: UNICEF (2005, 2006) and US State Department Country Report on Human Rights Practices 2006 (March 2007), compiled by ACCORD (Austrian Centre for Country of Origin and Asylum Research), query a-5839

C.n: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
C.place: Ukraine (33 institutions visited, incl. Vinnytsia oblast)
C.vn: UNICEF estimated at least 82,000 children in Ukraine's residential institutions; DRI put the number near 100,000.
C.who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
C.d: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.
C.cite: Disability Rights International, 'No Way Home: The Exploitation and Abuse of Children in Ukraine's Orphanages', 2015 (citing La Strada Ukraine, IOM Ukraine, UNICEF, US State Department TIP 2014)

C.n: Haiti — orphanage assessment identifies 3,019 potential trafficking victims
C.vn: Potential trafficking victims identified in institutions by Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR.
C.who: Private orphanages in Haiti; Institut du Bien-Être Social et de Recherches (IBESR)
C.d: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states that Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR, 'after completing an assessment of more than 750 orphanages with another government and international NGOs, identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in those institutions'. IBESR closed eight non-compliant orphanages in the reporting period and expanded foster care to 121 accredited families to reduce children's vulnerability to trafficking.
C.cite: US Department of State, Trafficking in Persons Report 2019 (Haiti), as quoted by Better Care Network

C.n: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
C.place: Cambodia (incl. Siem Reap and Phnom Penh)
C.who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
C.cover: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.
C.d: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.
C.cite: US Department of State, Trafficking in Persons Report 2019 (Cambodia), as quoted by Better Care Network

C.n: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
C.place: Canberra (Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade)
C.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
C.d: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.
C.cite: Parliament of Australia, Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade, 'Hidden in Plain Sight', December 2017 (via Better Care Network)

C.n: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
C.vn: 24 girls rescued on 5 August 2018 from a home registering 42 inmates; 18 were missing.
C.who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
C.cover: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.
C.d: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.
C.cite: PTI, 6 August 2018 (via Morung Express); PTI/CBI, 2019 (via ACT database)

C.n: Nyumbani Children's Home, Nairobi — USAID found abuse claims credible
C.vn: Six former residents told the Washington Post they were sexually abused 2002–2018; a USAID investigation identified other cases.
C.who: Nyumbani Children's Home for HIV-positive children, run by Children Of God Relief Institute (COGRI), a Catholic charity
C.cover: A USAID memo (21 July 2022) said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006, 'neglected to document violence against children', permitted victim-blaming and 'systematically failed to respond to widespread sexual misconduct'; some survivors were made to write letters of apology.
C.d: Nyumbani, opened in 1992, was among Africa's first homes for HIV-positive children and attracted large US donations. After a whistleblower complaint, a 2021 USAID investigation found abuse claims 'credible', including rape of children by volunteers, caregivers and other children. The Washington Post reported the findings on 27 November 2023 from court documents filed by the orphanage's Kenyan board. The co-founder stepped down after the Post's questions.
C.cite: USAID investigation (2021) and memo of 21 July 2022, filed in Kenyan court, as reported by The Washington Post, 27 November 2023 (republished by BishopAccountability)

C.n: Serbia — 'Torment not Treatment' investigation of institutions for children and adults with disabilities
C.place: Serbia (Kulina, Stamnica, Vršac and other institutions)
C.who: Serbian state institutions for people with mental disabilities
C.cover: In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave; Serbian officials called the allegations 'dark propaganda'.
C.d: Mental Disability Rights International's four-year investigation, released on 14 November 2007, covered conditions affecting more than 17,000 people with disabilities in Serbian institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy conditions, contagious disease and no oversight, treatment it said was 'tantamount to torture'. It warned of a danger of sexual exploitation: at Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards and staff said they made no effort to determine whether sex was consensual.
C.cite: Mental Disability Rights International, 'Torment not Treatment: Serbia's Segregation and Abuse of Children and Adults with Disabilities', November 2007

C.n: Colombia — ICBF investigation of 21 substitute (foster) homes
C.place: Colombia (Soacha, Antioquia, Bogotá, Meta and other departments)
C.vn: 44 children and 14 adolescents relocated from 21 foster homes under investigation.
C.who: Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar (ICBF) substitute-home (hogar sustituto) programme
C.d: In March 2018 the ICBF opened 21 investigations into foster homes nationwide for alleged verbal abuse, poor food and neglect and relocated 44 children and 14 adolescents, with about 3,100 homes still to review. The review followed a case in Soacha in which a man was jailed on charges of sexually abusing two girls aged 7 and 8 who were in ICBF custody in a foster home; he did not accept the charges.
C.cite: Blu Radio, 21 March 2018 (ICBF director Karen Abudinen)

C.n: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
C.vn: Medical evidence confirmed sexual abuse of a 9-year-old; 22 other children were taken into NCPA custody.
C.who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
C.cover: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.
C.d: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.
C.cite: Groundviews, 2 January 2014

C.n: Panama — legislative subcommission and prosecutors on abuse in state-supervised shelters
C.vn: At least 20 children identified as victims of sexual, physical and psychological abuse among about 280 interviewed in 57 shelters.
C.who: Private and NGO shelters (albergues) under the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf)
C.cover: The Ombudsman found 70% of 44 shelters inspected lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.
C.d: A National Assembly subcommission report in early February 2021 found cases of abuse in shelters for children at social risk. By March 2021 the Public Ministry had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected.
C.cite: La Prensa (Panama), 10 March 2021; Panamá América, 10 December 2021

C.n: Japan — Yomiuri survey of sexual misconduct by staff in children's homes
C.vn: At least 47 staff confirmed to have committed indecent acts and 69 children victimised in the five years to fiscal 2020 (Yomiuri survey).
C.who: Children's homes (児童養護施設) in Japan
C.d: A Yomiuri Shimbun survey published in December 2021 found that in the five years to fiscal 2020 at least 47 staff at children's homes across Japan were confirmed to have committed indecent acts against children in their care, and that 69 children were victims. Only a summary of the survey was accessible; the full article was withdrawn by the provider.
C.cite: Yomiuri Shimbun survey, 26 December 2021 (summary via Livedoor News)

C.n: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
C.vn: At least nine deaf students came forward; more were believed to have stayed silent.
C.who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
C.cover: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.
C.d: A 2005 investigation found that six people at the school, including the headmaster, had sexually harassed or raped at least nine deaf students from 2000 onward. Four received prison terms, two of which were later suspended; two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations had expired. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police opened a new investigation, the city moved to close the school in November 2011, and on 28 Oct 2011 the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for sexually assaulting an 18-year-old student in April 2005.
C.cite: The Korea Times, 'Film ignites call for probe into assaults', Sept 2011; 'Dogani school to be shut down', Oct 2011; 'National Assembly passes Dogani Law', 28 Oct 2011; 'Gwangju school sex offender gets 12 years in prison', 5 Jul 2012

C.n: Uganda — over 500 unlicensed children's homes outside state oversight
C.place: Uganda (Kampala, Wakiso, Mukono, Jinja and other districts)
C.vn: 185 licensed homes hold 9,486 children; more than 500 unlicensed homes are estimated to operate.
C.who: Uganda Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development; unlicensed children's homes, many foreign-funded
C.d: Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development says only 185 children's homes are fully licensed (holding 9,486 children) and that more than 500 unlicensed institutions operate without oversight, exposing children to neglect, exploitation and abuse. The ministry's principal probation officer said many children in homes are not orphans, and that some are survivors of trafficking or sexual abuse. The government has closed unregistered homes, including Hope Center Uganda (American board) after a raid that found children in poor conditions.
C.cite: Daily Monitor (Uganda), 2025, quoting the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development; Global Press Journal

C.n: Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes)
C.place: Chile (incl. a home in Arica; Punta Arenas)
C.who: SENAME-accredited residential care homes (hogares), run by private organisations under state supervision
C.cover: The report was delivered to the Judiciary in March 2013 but held back over methodological criticism until CIPER published it in July 2013; legislators said the Justice Minister had known since March.
C.d: Family-court judges led by Judge Mónica Jeldres, with UNICEF, interviewed children in residential homes between July and November 2012. The report found sexual abuse was a constant in the homes and that 10% of children in state protection had been involved in some form of sexual abuse as victim or perpetrator. In one Arica home it found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers: 24 girls left the home and returned drugged at dawn. After publication the government ordered 34 homes intervened, SENAME closed four residences, the prosecutor's office opened investigations and deputies announced a congressional investigating commission.
C.cite: Poder Judicial / UNICEF 'Informe Jeldres' (2013), revealed by CIPER; El Dínamo, 11 July 2013

C.n: Apna Ghar shelter, Rohtak — CBI court convictions
C.vn: More than 100 residents, including children and minor girls, rescued in May 2012 (Onmanorama); Scroll reports about 20 rescued by the NCPCR.
C.who: Apna Ghar, a government-funded shelter run by Jaswanti Devi and relatives
C.d: The case began in 2012 when three girls escaped from the government-funded Apna Ghar shelter and told police residents were physically and sexually abused and used as bonded labour. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights raided it in May 2012; Haryana sealed it in June 2012 and the CBI charge-sheeted ten people in August 2012. On 18 April 2018 a special CBI court in Panchkula convicted nine, including of rape, abortion without consent, bonded labour and offences under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act and Juvenile Justice Act; on 27 April 2018 Jaswanti Devi, her son-in-law and a driver were sentenced to life. A former child development project officer who oversaw the shelter was acquitted.
C.cite: Special CBI Court, Panchkula, verdict 18 April and sentence 27 April 2018 (PTI via Scroll; Onmanorama)

C.n: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
C.place: Refugee camps, Guéckédou area (Guinea), Liberia and Sierra Leone
C.vn: UNHCR/Save the Children UK field mission interviewed about 1,500 people; OIOS fully investigated 43 cases
C.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
C.d: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.
C.cite: OIOS, Investigation into sexual exploitation of refugees by aid workers in West Africa, UN doc A/57/465, 11 October 2002; Wikipedia 'Sexual exploitation and abuse in humanitarian response' (summarising UNHCR/SCF-UK report, Feb 2002)

C.n: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
C.who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
C.d: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.
C.cite: Report of the Secretary-General on the activities of OIOS: investigation into SEA in MONUC, UN doc A/59/661, 5 January 2005; A/59/710 (Zeid report), 24 March 2005

C.n: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
C.place: Martissant and other contingent locations, Port-au-Prince
C.vn: AP (2017) counted at least 9 children in UN files; OIOS said acts against children were 'frequent'
C.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
C.cover: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.
C.d: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
C.cite: Wikipedia 'MINUSTAH' and 'Sexual abuse scandal in Haiti' (citing OIOS findings and AP, 12 April 2017)

C.n: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
C.vn: UN-commissioned confidential report (leaked April 2015) cited at least about ten children; boys aged 9–13 among them
C.who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
C.cover: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.
C.d: An internal UN document revealed by The Guardian in April 2015 recorded interviews with six boys aged 9 to 13 who said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport, in exchange for food rations. The Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014; the investigation eventually covered accusations by fifteen children, most interviewed in Bangui in 2015 and 2016. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case (non-lieu) for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony; the prosecutor said 'it cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged.
C.cite: Le Figaro / AFP, 15 January 2018

C.n: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
C.vn: 136 alleged victims initially identified in two allegations; the 2016 UN data tables list 46 child victims for Burundi and 43 for Gabon contingent allegations
C.who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
C.d: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.
C.cite: Report of the Secretary-General, Special measures for protection from SEA, UN doc A/71/818, 28 Feb 2017 (annex tables); Wikipedia 'Sexual abuse by UN peacekeepers'

C.n: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
C.vn: 8 cases documented by HRW, including a 14-year-old girl
C.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
C.d: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.
C.cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Central African Republic: Rape by Peacekeepers', 4 February 2016

C.n: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
C.place: Central African Republic (deployment areas incl. Ouaka)
C.vn: 807 = size of the battalion, not number of accused
C.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
C.d: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.
C.cite: Reuters via The Peninsula (Qatar), 10 January 2016; UN Secretary-General report A/71/818, annex tables (allegations reported in 2016)

C.n: MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021)
C.vn: UN did not give ages in the announcement; the SG's 2022 report says most multi-victim 2021 MINUSCA allegations involved one TCC whose troops were repatriated in September 2021, and that 25 allegations in 2021 (all missions) involved 51 children
C.who: Gabonese military contingent, MINUSCA
C.d: On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA (about 450 personnel) would be repatriated after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse; Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most multiple-victim MINUSCA allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.
C.cite: UN News, 15 Sept 2021; Report of the Secretary-General A/76/702 (2022)

C.n: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
C.place: Prijedor, Bijeljina, Tuzla, Arizona Market (Brčko) and other towns
C.vn: HRW cites a programme total of 601 women and girls of whom 498 were repatriated; girls under 18 among them (e.g. a 17-year-old Romanian in Prijedor)
C.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
C.cover: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.
C.d: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
C.cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Hopes Betrayed: Trafficking of Women and Girls to Post-Conflict Bosnia and Herzegovina for Forced Prostitution', Vol. 14 No. 9(D), November 2002; Bolkovac v DynCorp Aerospace Operations (UK) Ltd, Employment Tribunal, 2 Aug 2002

C.n: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
C.vn: A Kosovo victim-support group reported that of locally trafficked girls a third were under 14 and 80% under 18
C.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
C.cover: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.
C.d: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
C.cite: Amnesty International, 'So does it mean that we have the rights?' (Kosovo), May 2004, as reported by The Guardian, 7 May 2004

C.n: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
C.who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
C.d: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.
C.cite: Wikipedia 'United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia' and 'Sexual abuse by UN peacekeepers'; Machel, Impact of Armed Conflict on Children, A/51/306 (1996)

C.n: ONUMOZ Mozambique — soldiers recruited girls aged 12–18 into prostitution (Machel study)
C.who: UN Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ) soldiers
C.d: The UN study 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children' led by Graça Machel (August 1996) found that after the 1992 peace treaty, ONUMOZ soldiers recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. It also found that in 6 of 12 country studies on sexual exploitation of children in armed conflict, the arrival of peacekeeping troops was associated with a rapid rise in child prostitution.
C.cite: Report of the expert of the Secretary-General, Graça Machel, 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children', UN doc A/51/306, 26 August 1996

C.n: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued
C.who: Oxfam GB staff in the 2010 earthquake response, including the country director
C.cover: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.
C.d: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. The Charity Commission's June 2019 inquiry found that not all lines of enquiry about minors were pursued and that Oxfam did not adequately investigate allegations in an email of 18 July 2011 that minors were being sexually abused by Oxfam employees, nor report them to the Commission or law enforcement. The Commission said it was no longer possible to conclude with certainty whether minors were involved or at risk.
C.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, Inquiry Report: Oxfam GB — summary findings and conclusions, 11 June 2019

C.n: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
C.place: Beni, Butembo, Mangina (North Kivu) and Ituri
C.vn: testimony from 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; nine rape allegations; 29 pregnancies
C.who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
C.d: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.
C.cite: Final Report of the Independent Commission on the review of sexual abuse and exploitation during the response to the 10th Ebola virus disease epidemic in North Kivu and Ituri, DRC, 28 September 2021

C.n: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
C.place: AMISOM base camp and Burundian contingent base, Mogadishu
C.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
