C.cover: Complaints reached House staff and leaders around 2000–2005. The House Ethics Committee (Dec 2006) found Speaker Hastert and other leaders 'negligent' but recommended no sanctions. Florida's FDLE closed its probe in 2008 citing insufficient evidence and said Congress and Foley denied it access to data.
C.d: In late September 2006 sexually suggestive emails and instant messages from Rep. Mark Foley to teenage boys who had served as House pages became public; he resigned on 29 Sept 2006. On 8 Dec 2006 the House Ethics Committee found Republican members and staff had been negligent in handling earlier warnings about his conduct but that no House rules were broken, and recommended no punishment. No criminal charges were brought; Florida's state investigation was closed in September 2008 citing insufficient evidence.
C.cite: NPR, 'House Leadership Chided for Foley Scandal', 8 Dec 2006

C.n: Joel Greenberg conviction and House Ethics findings on Matt Gaetz
C.who: Joel Greenberg (Seminole County tax collector); Rep. Matt Gaetz (not charged)
C.d: Greenberg pleaded guilty in May 2021 to six federal crimes, including sex trafficking of a minor (a 17-year-old girl in 2017), identity theft, stalking, wire fraud and conspiracy to bribe a public official, and was sentenced to 11 years on 1 Dec 2022. DOJ investigated Rep. Gaetz over whether he paid the same 17-year-old for sex but did not charge him. The House Ethics Committee report (23 Dec 2024) said it received testimony that Gaetz twice had sex with the 17-year-old at a 2017 party and paid her, and found that this violated Florida law, but found insufficient evidence that he violated the federal sex-trafficking statute. Gaetz denies having sex with a minor and has not been charged.
C.cite: CBS News/AP, 'Joel Greenberg ... sentenced to 11 years for sex trafficking of a minor', 1 Dec 2022; CBS News, 'Matt Gaetz ethics report says his drug use and sex with a minor violated state laws', 23 Dec 2024; House Ethics Committee report, Dec 2024

C.n: R. Kelly — racketeering and child sexual abuse material convictions
C.who: Robert Kelly (singer) and his entourage (racketeering enterprise)
C.cover: He was acquitted in 2008 of child pornography charges brought in 2002, despite Chicago Sun-Times reporting from 2000.
C.d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Kelly on 27 Sept 2021 of racketeering, including acts of bribery and sexual exploitation of a child, and of Mann Act sex-trafficking offences; he was sentenced to 30 years. In September 2022 a Chicago federal jury convicted him of three counts of producing child sexual abuse material and three of enticing a minor; in February 2023 he was sentenced to 20 years, 19 of them to run concurrently with the New York term. The 2019 documentary 'Surviving R. Kelly' led to the new prosecutions.
C.cite: CNN, 'R. Kelly convicted of racketeering and sex trafficking by a federal jury in New York', 27 Sep 2021; CNN, 'R. Kelly ... sentenced to 20 years in federal child porn case', 23 Feb 2023

C.n: Jared Fogle (Subway spokesman) — child abuse material and paid sex with minors
C.who: Jared Fogle; Russell Taylor (co-conspirator); Subway
C.cover: Allegations surfaced in 2007 but the FBI acted only in 2015. A franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 about Fogle's messages seeking sex with a minor; Subway says it has no record.
C.d: After his Indianapolis home was raided in July 2015 in a child abuse material investigation, Fogle pleaded guilty to receiving child abuse material and travelling to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor, and on 19 Nov 2015 was sentenced to 188 months (15 years 8 months). He had already paid $100,000 restitution to each of 14 victims ($1.4m); two were 16 and 17 when he travelled to have sex with them.
C.cite: NBC News, 'Jared Fogle, ex-Subway pitchman, gets 15 years in prison for child porn charges', 19 Nov 2015

C.n: USA Swimming — coaches banned for abuse; claims mishandled
C.vn: 'hundreds' of swimmers' claims allegedly mishandled (Orange County Register, 2018)
C.who: USA Swimming
C.d: USA Swimming banned prominent coach Rick Curl for life in September 2012; a former swimmer said he had abused her from age 12 in 1983–1986. A February 2018 Orange County Register investigation reported that hundreds of swimmers were sexually abused over decades and that people in charge knew and ignored it, and that USA Swimming had banned 138 coaches and officials for life for sexual abuse and misconduct. Former coach Andy King, reported to Pacific Swimming officials in 2003, was arrested in 2009 and sentenced to 40 years after pleading no contest to 20 counts of felony child molestation, some victims as young as 10.
C.cite: Orange County Register, '100s of USA swimmers were sexually abused for decades and the people in charge knew and ignored it, investigation finds', 16 Feb 2018; ESPN/AP, 'USA Swimming bans Rick Curl for life', 19 Sep 2012

C.n: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska
C.who: Claims against Lawrence E. King Jr. (Franklin Community Federal Credit Union) and prominent Nebraskans
C.d: After the Franklin Community Federal Credit Union in Omaha failed in late 1988 and its manager Lawrence King was accused of embezzling millions, rumours spread that its money had paid for the sexual abuse of minors by prominent Nebraskans. In July 1990 a Douglas County grand jury called the claims a 'carefully crafted hoax' and indicted two people for perjury; a federal grand jury in September 1990 also found the allegations unfounded. King called the sexual allegations 'garbage'. A later civil default judgment against King, who did not respond, is not a finding of fact.
C.cite: PolitiFact, 'Grand juries determined alleged sex trafficking Franklin scandal in Omaha was a hoax', 29 Apr 2022, citing New York Times 29 Jul and 27 Sep 1990 and AP 26 Sep 1990

C.n: 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria
C.who: Online conspiracy theory targeting Democratic politicians
C.d: In Oct–Nov 2016 online posts, citing leaked Podesta emails, falsely claimed that the Comet Ping Pong pizzeria in Washington was home to a child sex-abuse ring involving top Democrats. No victims or evidence emerged. On 4 Dec 2016 Edgar Maddison Welch fired an AR-15 rifle inside to 'investigate'; he pleaded guilty in March 2017 to federal assault with a dangerous weapon and transporting a firearm across state lines, and was sentenced to four years in June 2017.
C.cite: NPR, 'Pizzagate gunman sentenced to 4 years in prison', 22 Jun 2017

C.n: McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals
C.who: McMartin Preschool (accused: Ray Buckey, Peggy McMartin Buckey)
C.d: Claims of abuse at the McMartin Pre-School in Manhattan Beach, California, began in autumn 1983 with one small boy's report and grew to include allegations of 'satanic-like ritual'; interview techniques were later widely criticised. In January 1990, after nearly three years of trial, Peggy McMartin Buckey was acquitted of all 12 counts and Ray Buckey of 40 counts, with the jury deadlocked on 13; a retrial of Ray Buckey on eight counts ended in a deadlocked jury in July 1990, and the prosecution was dropped. None of the seven people charged was convicted of anything. The case cost taxpayers about $14m. Included as the template for 'ritual abuse' claims.
C.cite: Los Angeles Times, 'A Mistrial for Buckey: Jury Hopelessly Deadlocked in McMartin Case', 27 Jul 1990; Los Angeles Times, 19 Jan 1990

C.n: Johnny Kitagawa — Johnny & Associates talent agency
C.vn: Smile-Up (successor company) had received 1,044 claims by 14 Aug 2026 and decided to compensate 585
C.who: Johnny Kitagawa (founder, Johnny & Associates; now Smile-Up)
C.cover: Media silence: Shukan Bunshun's 2001 reports were upheld on the sexual allegations by the courts (damages reduced 2003; Supreme Court rejected appeal 2004), yet Japanese media barely covered them; journalists attributed this to the agency's power over talent bookings. Earliest cited report: Weekly Sankei, 1965.
C.d: An external investigation set up by Johnny & Associates concluded on 29 Aug 2023 that founder Johnny Kitagawa had sexually abused minors aspiring to be pop singers for decades; the BBC summarises the finding as abuse of hundreds of boys and young men over a six-decade career. The company admitted the abuse in September 2023, split into a new talent agency (Starto Entertainment) and Smile-Up, which handles compensation through a relief committee of three former judges. The BBC documentary 'Predator' (March 2023) and a former trainee's public allegations in April 2023 triggered the reckoning. In March 2024 Smile-Up's CEO told the BBC he believed two more perpetrators had worked at the agency. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Two more abusers at J-pop predator's company', 27 Mar 2024; Kyodo News, 'Probe finds Johnny's talent agency founder abused minors for decades', 29 Aug 2023; The Guardian, review of BBC 'Predator', 7 Mar 2023

C.n: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
C.who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
C.cover: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.
C.d: Sengar, then a BJP MLA in Uttar Pradesh, was convicted in December 2019 by a special CBI court in Delhi of raping a minor girl in Unnao district in 2017, and sentenced to life imprisonment; the BJP had expelled him. In December 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; on 29 Dec 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order on the CBI's appeal, and in May 2026 it set the suspension aside, directing the High Court to decide his appeal against conviction within three months or pass a fresh order.
C.cite: LiveLaw, 'Supreme Court stays Delhi HC order granting bail to Kuldeep Sengar in Unnao rape case', 29 Dec 2025; The Wire, 'SC sets aside Delhi HC order suspending Kuldeep Sengar's sentence', 15 May 2026

C.n: Kasur child abuse video scandal (Hussain Khanwala)
C.vn: Media estimate 280–300 children; the Punjab joint investigation team confirmed 19 genuine complaints
C.who: Local gang filming abuse of children; Punjab police; local MPA (alleged)
C.cover: Punjab police and the local PML-N provincial assembly member Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan were alleged to have tried to cover it up; the Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. Police clashed with protesting villagers on 8 Aug 2015.
C.d: In August 2015 it emerged that in Hussain Khanwala village, Kasur district, a gang had filmed the sexual abuse of children and blackmailed their parents by threatening to leak the videos. Pakistani media put the number of children at 280 to 300; the joint investigation team set up by the Punjab government confirmed 19 genuine complaints, examined 47 video clips and charged 17 people (Express Tribune, 14 November 2015). Police, who had failed to act despite pleas from parents, made arrests only after clashes between relatives and authorities drew media attention. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court in Lahore sentenced two men to life imprisonment; Arab News reported in February 2018 that 12 other accused men were acquitted.
C.cite: Wikipedia 'Kasur child sexual abuse scandal' (citing The Nation, Aug 2015)

C.n: Knox Grammar School — headmaster failed to report teachers' abuse
C.who: Knox Grammar School; Uniting Church
C.cover: The Royal Commission (Sept 2016) found headmaster Ian Paterson never reported a student's abuse allegation to police in about 30 years, despite a duty from 1988; he let accused teachers resign and gave some positive references, and withheld information from a police officer.
C.d: After abuse was reported to police in 2009, five former Knox Grammar teachers were convicted of child sexual offences against students. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse held Case Study 23 on the school in February–March 2015, examining its handling of concerns about teachers between 1970 and 2009, and heard from 12 former students. Its September 2016 report found that former headmaster Ian Paterson (1969–1998) deliberately covered up allegations, placing the school's reputation ahead of student welfare; he had told the commission he did not tell police what he knew about teachers who were later convicted.
C.cite: Sydney Morning Herald, 'Former Knox Grammar headmaster Ian Paterson covered up abuse, Royal Commission finds', 13 Sep 2016; ABC News, 6 Mar 2015

C.n: Geelong Grammar School — Royal Commission case study 32
C.who: Geelong Grammar School (Anglican)
C.cover: The Royal Commission found the school repeatedly failed to investigate or report credible allegations, particularly under principal John Lewis (1980–94), and 'placed its own interests ahead of those of victims'. A 2007 settlement with victims of a boarding-house assistant was minuted as 'a very satisfactory financial outcome for the school'.
C.d: The Royal Commission's Case Study 32 heard from 13 former students who said they were abused by staff between 1956 and 1989. Five staff members were convicted of child sex offences against Geelong Grammar students, including a live-in boarding-house assistant who pleaded guilty in April 2005 to 41 counts of gross indecency and indecent acts and was convicted of offences against 40 students between 1985 and 1995 (six and a half years' jail), and a teacher convicted in 2008 over a 2007 offence. The report was published in December 2016.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, 'Report of Case Study No. 32: Geelong Grammar School', December 2016 (copy hosted by ICMEC; official site childabuseroyalcommission.gov.au unreachable)

C.n: Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling
C.vn: about 70 former Brisbane Grammar students sued over counsellor Kevin Lynch
C.who: Brisbane Grammar School; St Paul's School; Anglican Diocese of Brisbane (Archbishop Peter Hollingworth)
C.cover: Brisbane Grammar quietly investigated complaints about counsellor Kevin Lynch in the early 1980s; he moved to St Paul's. A 2003 diocesan inquiry found Archbishop Hollingworth in 1993 allowed a known abuser to keep working as a priest.
C.d: School counsellor Kevin John Lynch, who worked at Brisbane Grammar and then at the Anglican St Paul's School in the 1980s and 1990s, abused students; music teacher Gregory Knight at St Paul's was a convicted paedophile. Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001. An Anglican church inquiry report, tabled in the Queensland parliament on 1 May 2003, found he had acted unfairly in some cases, notably in allowing a known paedophile to continue as a priest; he resigned as Governor-General on 25 May 2003. In November 2015 the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse examined the two schools' handling of the abuse, and Hollingworth apologised to victims.
C.cite: ABC News, 'Child abuse royal commission: Peter Hollingworth ... apologises to victims of paedophile teachers', 14 Nov 2015; ABC News, 'Timeline: Peter Hollingworth's career', 26 May 2003

C.n: T.B. Joshua (SCOAN) — BBC investigation into abuse of disciples
C.who: T.B. Joshua; Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN)
C.d: A BBC Africa Eye investigation published on 8 January 2024 reported corroborating testimony from more than 25 former disciples from seven countries that TB Joshua, founder of the Synagogue Church of All Nations in Lagos, had sexually assaulted and raped followers and subjected them to abuse including solitary confinement, with the most recent experiences in 2019. One woman said he first raped her when she was 17 and that she was made to have forced abortions. Joshua died in June 2021. The church did not respond to the BBC's allegations but has called previous claims unsubstantiated. No official finding. Religious figure placed here for celebrity and political influence.
C.cite: BBC News Africa Eye, 'TB Joshua: Megachurch leader raped and tortured worshippers, BBC finds', 8 Jan 2024

C.n: Haitian Football Federation — Yves Jean-Bart banned by FIFA
C.who: Yves Jean-Bart (FHF president since 2000)
C.d: On 30 April 2020 The Guardian reported accusations that Jean-Bart, president of the Haitian Football Federation since 2000, coerced young female players at the national training centre in Croix-des-Bouquets into sex; he denies the allegations. On 18 Nov 2020 FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him from football for life. On 14 Feb 2023 the Court of Arbitration for Sport annulled the ban; FIFA appealed to the Swiss Federal Tribunal in March 2023 (outcome not checked). Human Rights Watch said witnesses and survivors had faced threats and intimidation. He has not been convicted by any court.
C.cite: FIFA media release, 'FIFA files appeal to Swiss Federal Tribunal against CAS award in proceedings involving Yves Jean-Bart', 20 Mar 2023; The Guardian, 30 Apr 2020 and 20 Nov 2020; Human Rights Watch, 22 Feb 2023

C.n: Whyte Review — British Gymnastics
C.who: British Gymnastics
C.d: Anne Whyte QC's independent review of British Gymnastics, published in June 2022 and covering August 2008 to August 2020, received more than 400 submissions (133 from current and former gymnasts) and conducted 190 interviews. More than 40% of submissions described physical abuse by coaches and more than 50% emotional abuse; more than 25% referred to excessive weight management; some 30 submissions included allegations of sexual abuse, such as sexual assault, inappropriate touching and kissing as a punishment.
C.cite: BBC Sport, Whyte Review published, 16 Jun 2022

C.n: Westchester County grand jury — Archdiocese of New York (2002)
C.place: White Plains, Westchester County, New York
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of New York
C.cover: Grand jury called the church's handling of complaints 'an orchestrated effort to protect abusing clergy members from investigation, arrest and prosecution'
C.d: A Westchester County grand jury issued a 13-page report in June 2002 after a two-month inquiry that reviewed tens of thousands of pages of archdiocesan documents and heard from eight alleged victims. It found the church's handling of abuse claims was an orchestrated effort to shield abusing clergy from investigation and prosecution. It recommended making it a felony for church officials not to report allegations and ending the statute of limitations for crimes against minors. The archdiocese called the report unfair.
C.cite: Westchester County Grand Jury report, June 2002, as reported by CBS News / AP, 20 June 2002

C.n: Suffolk County grand jury — Diocese of Rockville Centre (2003)
C.place: Rockville Centre, Long Island, New York
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Rockville Centre
C.cover: Accused priests moved from parish to parish; a diocesan 'intervention team' and legal-affairs team used to silence victims and suppress claims; secret archives on 43 priests
C.d: A Suffolk County grand jury report of about 180 pages, presented by District Attorney Thomas Spota in February 2003 after a nine-month investigation, found that at least 58 abusive priests had been protected by the Diocese of Rockville Centre. Officials used sham policies, a bogus 'intervention team' that silenced victims and a 'legal affairs' team that worked to block claims, moved abusers between parishes where they often had access to children, and disregarded advice to give them psychiatric care. The grand jury said the failures could not be attributed to incompetence.
C.cite: Suffolk County Supplementary Grand Jury report, February 2003, as reported by The Irish Times, 13 February 2003

C.n: New Hampshire Attorney General — Diocese of Manchester (2003)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Manchester
C.cover: The Attorney General cited 'flagrant indifference' to the danger posed by abusive priests and found church officials made false statements while testifying in civil suits; a December 2002 agreement let the diocese avoid criminal indictment after the AG said it had evidence likely to sustain a conviction
C.d: On 3 March 2003 the New Hampshire Attorney General released a 154-page report, with about 9,000 pages of supporting documents, after a 10-month investigation. It found 50 priests credibly accused of abusing minors over 60 years and cited the diocese's 'flagrant indifference' to the danger to children. Under a December 2002 agreement the diocese avoided criminal indictment, after the Attorney General said it had evidence likely to sustain a conviction against the diocese, and accepted annual monitoring by the Attorney General for at least five years.
C.cite: New Hampshire Attorney General, Report on the Investigation of the Diocese of Manchester, 3 March 2003, as reported by The Boston Globe, 4 March 2003

C.n: Maine Attorney General — Diocese of Portland (2004)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Portland (Maine)
C.cover: Church officials kept abuse complaints secret and reassigned at least seven accused priests to parishes; one was later accused of abusing at least 10 girls
C.d: In February 2004 the Maine Attorney General reported on allegations reaching back 75 years against 63 men: diocesan priests, members of religious orders and church or school employees. The report found that church officials kept abuse charges secret and reassigned some accused priests, placing children at risk. No accusations of abuse after 1996 were found, and no one could be charged because of the statute of limitations.
C.cite: Maine Attorney General report on the Diocese of Portland, February 2004, as reported by the Portland Press Herald, 25 February 2004

C.n: Philadelphia grand jury — Archdiocese of Philadelphia (2005)
C.vn: 'Hundreds' of minors, per the grand jury
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia
C.cover: Grand jury found Cardinals John Krol and Anthony Bevilacqua knew of the abuse and covered it up; the archdiocese disputes this
C.d: A Philadelphia grand jury released a 418-page report in September 2005 finding that at least 63 priests of the archdiocese had abused hundreds of minors over several decades. It found that Cardinals John Krol and Anthony Bevilacqua knew of the abuse and concealed it. No charges were brought because most cases fell outside the time limit for prosecution.
C.cite: Report of the County Investigating Grand Jury, Philadelphia, 21 September 2005, as reported by JURIST

C.n: Second Philadelphia grand jury — priests still in ministry (2011)
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia
C.cover: A senior archdiocesan official was charged with moving priests with abuse complaints to new parishes without warning; up to 37 priests with credible allegations remained in ministry
C.d: A second Philadelphia grand jury reported in February 2011 that as many as 37 priests remained in active ministry despite credible allegations of sexual abuse. Two priests, a former priest and a Catholic school teacher were charged with raping boys, and Monsignor William Lynn, a former senior archdiocesan official, was charged and accused of transferring problem priests to new parishes without warning anyone of earlier complaints. On 8 March 2011 the archdiocese suspended 21 priests while their cases were reviewed.
C.cite: Report of the Grand Jury, Philadelphia, released February 2011, as reported by CBS News, March 2011

C.n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown (2016)
C.vn: 'Hundreds of children' over about 40 years
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown
C.cover: Two bishops concealed the abuse; the grand jury said the church had such sway over law enforcement that it helped select a police chief
C.d: A statewide investigating grand jury, in a report released by the Pennsylvania Attorney General on 1 March 2016, found that more than 50 priests and religious leaders abused hundreds of children in the Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown over about 40 years. Two bishops, including Bishop Joseph Adamec, concealed the abuse. The report said the diocese had enough influence over local law enforcement to help choose a police chief.
C.cite: Pennsylvania 37th Statewide Investigating Grand Jury, Report I, 1 March 2016, as reported by AP / The Columbian

C.n: Colorado Attorney General special master — three Catholic dioceses (2019)
C.who: Archdiocese of Denver; Dioceses of Colorado Springs and Pueblo
C.cover: On average 19.5 years passed between a credible allegation and restricting the priest; more than half of victims were abused after the diocese already knew the priest was an abuser; euphemisms used in records
C.d: A report by special master Bob Troyer, a former US Attorney appointed by Attorney General Phil Weiser, was released on 23 October 2019. It found that 43 priests sexually abused at least 166 children in Colorado's three Catholic dioceses over about 70 years, the most recent reported case in 1998. On average it took 19.5 years from a credible allegation to a restriction on the priest, and more than half the victims were abused after the church already knew of the priest. A supplemental report followed on 1 December 2020.
C.cite: Special Master's Report on Colorado's Roman Catholic Dioceses, 22 October 2019, as reported by Colorado Public Radio, 23 October 2019

C.n: Florida Office of Statewide Prosecution — Catholic clergy abuse (2020)
C.who: Catholic dioceses of Florida
C.cover: Florida was a state where accused priests were 'routinely relocated'; the report found acts by the church that enabled sexual abuse of minors
C.d: Florida's Office of Statewide Prosecution closed a two-year investigation, opened after the 2018 Pennsylvania grand jury report, with a report released on 6 November 2020. It found historical sexual abuse allegations against 97 priests in Florida, none of whom could be prosecuted because of the statute of limitations, earlier prosecution or death. It found that accused priests had been routinely relocated and that church acts had enabled abuse of minors, but found no evidence of ongoing unreported abuse. More than 260 tips were received.
C.cite: Office of Statewide Prosecution, Report on Sexual Abuse in the Catholic Church in Florida, 6 November 2020, as reported by ABC Action News / Tampa Bay 28

C.n: St. Joseph's Orphanage, Burlington — Vermont task force (2020)
C.who: St. Joseph's Orphanage, run with roles for the Catholic Diocese of Burlington, the Sisters of Providence and Vermont Catholic Charities
C.cover: The Attorney General blamed police and prosecutors for not investigating allegations when they were first made; the Sisters of Providence had not produced documents the task force requested by the time the report was finished
C.d: A task force of the Vermont Attorney General, Burlington's mayor, the Chittenden County State's Attorney, the Vermont State Police and Burlington police investigated former residents' allegations for two years after a 2018 BuzzFeed News report. Its report of about 300 pages, released on 14 December 2020, said 'it is clear abuse happened and children suffered', including physical and sexual abuse, but found too little evidence to prove alleged murders. Attorney General T.J. Donovan said police and prosecutors had failed to investigate complaints when first made; no charges were possible because of time limits.
C.cite: St. Joseph's Orphanage Task Force report, 14 December 2020; Vermont Attorney General press release; WCAX, 14 December 2020

C.n: Iowa Attorney General — clergy abuse review (2021)
C.who: Archdiocese of Dubuque; Dioceses of Des Moines, Davenport and Sioux City; other faith leaders
C.cover: Survivors told the Attorney General their allegations had been ignored or covered up by the church
C.d: Iowa Attorney General Tom Miller's office released its review on 23 June 2021 after an inquiry begun in late 2018. It examined 50 complaints, 45 involving the Catholic Church, with records involving 70 priests and alleged abuse from the 1930s to 1997. It described a painful history of abuse and extensive cover-ups in Iowa's Catholic dioceses but found the four dioceses had made reforms in good faith over the past two decades. None of the complaints against Catholic clergy could be prosecuted because of the statute of limitations.
C.cite: Iowa Attorney General, Clergy Abuse Report, 23 June 2021, as reported by Iowa Public Radio

C.n: Nebraska Attorney General — three Catholic dioceses (2021)
C.vn: 258 victims of sexual abuse; about 60% were minors at the time; the office said the count is incomplete
C.who: Archdiocese of Omaha; Dioceses of Lincoln and Grand Island
C.cover: The church knew of the assaults and did not properly report them to law enforcement
C.d: The Nebraska Attorney General's Office released a report on 4 November 2021 after a three-year investigation of the state's three Catholic dioceses. It identified 258 victims, nearly 60% of them minors at the time, and 57 abusers, with abuse dating back to the 1930s. It found that the church knew of assaults and failed to report them properly to law enforcement. No charges were possible because the statute of limitations had expired.
C.cite: Nebraska Attorney General, Report on Catholic Church Sexual Abuse, 4 November 2021, as reported by Nebraska Public Media

C.n: Kansas Bureau of Investigation — Catholic clergy abuse (2023)
C.vn: Investigators spoke with nearly 140 victims, witnesses and suspects in 15 states
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Kansas City in Kansas and other Kansas dioceses
C.cover: The KBI found the church protected suspected clergy for decades, often by transferring priests to other churches; some victims were bound by non-disclosure agreements
C.d: A four-year Kansas Bureau of Investigation inquiry, requested by Archbishop Joseph Naumann and reported in January 2023, reviewed five decades of church records and identified 188 clergy suspected of crimes such as rape and sexual misconduct with children. Investigators spoke with nearly 140 victims, witnesses and suspects in 15 states and referred 30 cases to prosecutors, all of which were too old to charge. The KBI found the church had protected these men for decades, often by moving them to other parishes.
C.cite: Kansas Bureau of Investigation summary report, January 2023, as reported by Kansas News Service / NPR (WFAE), 15 January 2023

C.n: New York Attorney General v. Diocese of Buffalo (2020–2022)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Buffalo; retired Bishop Richard Malone and Auxiliary Bishop Edward Grosz
C.cover: The Attorney General alleged diocesan leaders protected more than two dozen accused priests by not sending their cases to the Vatican
C.d: In November 2020 the New York Attorney General sued the Diocese of Buffalo and its retired bishops, alleging that they protected more than two dozen priests accused of child sexual abuse. In a settlement filed on 25 October 2022 the diocese accepted enhanced child-protection measures and an independent compliance auditor, and the two bishops were barred from fiduciary roles in New York charities.
C.cite: People of the State of New York v. Diocese of Buffalo, complaint 23 November 2020; stipulation of settlement 25 October 2022, as reported by America magazine

C.n: New York Attorney General — Diocese of Brooklyn agreement (2024)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn
C.cover: The diocese did not consistently follow its own procedures, sometimes did not disclose credible allegations and did not adequately monitor accused clergy; a priest who admitted abusing minors was defrocked in 2007 on condition of confidentiality and this was kept secret until 2017; another priest was moved between parishes after complaints
C.d: On 16 April 2024 the New York Attorney General announced an agreement after finding that the Diocese of Brooklyn had not consistently followed its own procedures for abuse complaints, applied inconsistent standards of proof and did not adequately monitor credibly accused clergy. In one case a priest who admitted repeatedly abusing minors was removed from duties without parishioners being told, and his 2007 defrocking was kept confidential until 2017; in another a priest was transferred between parishes after earlier concerns and went largely unmonitored despite a 2006 complaint. The diocese accepted new procedures, referral of all complaints to law enforcement and an independent secular monitor for at least three years.
C.cite: New York Attorney General, press release on agreement with the Diocese of Brooklyn, 16 April 2024; Insurance Journal / AP

C.n: Michigan Attorney General — diocese-by-diocese reports (2022–2026)
C.who: Catholic Dioceses of Marquette, Gaylord, Kalamazoo, Lansing, Grand Rapids and Saginaw (Archdiocese of Detroit pending)
C.d: After search warrants were executed at all seven Michigan dioceses in October 2018, the Attorney General's office published one report per diocese: Marquette (27 October 2022), Gaylord (8 January 2024), Kalamazoo (22 May 2024), Lansing (16 December 2024, 56 people accused, 48 of them priests), Grand Rapids (15 December 2025, 51 priests) and Saginaw (25 June 2026, 37 priests and one deacon). By June 2026 the investigation had received 1,276 tips, brought 11 criminal cases and obtained 9 convictions covering 38 survivors. The office states that inclusion in a report does not mean an allegation was substantiated.
C.cite: Michigan Department of Attorney General press releases on the Dioceses of Grand Rapids (15 December 2025) and Saginaw (25 June 2026); CBS Detroit on Lansing (16 December 2024)

C.n: Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia — Atlanta and Savannah (2023)
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Atlanta; Diocese of Savannah
C.cover: Some accused priests were reassigned without notice to officials at their new posts; historical church policies 'enabled sexual abuse of minors'
C.d: A review by the Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia, dated 20 March 2023 and covering both dioceses that together span the whole state, found credible allegations of child sexual abuse against 28 priests while serving in Georgia, dating back to the 1940s. It found that some accused priests were reassigned without notice and that historical policies enabled abuse; Savannah began taking allegations seriously in the late 1980s and Atlanta in the 1990s. No case could be prosecuted.
C.cite: Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia report, 20 March 2023, as reported by Catholic News Agency / EWTN News, 29 March 2023

C.n: Rhode Island Attorney General — Diocese of Providence (2026)
C.vn: 'Over 300' victims abused between 1950 and 2011
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Providence
C.cover: The diocese kept abuse secret and failed to report it to civil authorities; under Bishops McVinney and Gelineau accused priests were moved or sent to 'treatment' and returned to ministry, where some abused again; the diocese refused in-person interviews
C.d: Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha published a report on 4 March 2026 after an investigation begun in 2019. It identified 75 credibly accused clergy and more than 300 victims abused between 1950 and 2011. It found the diocese kept abuse secret, did not report it to civil authorities, and under Bishops Russell McVinney and Louis Gelineau moved accused priests or returned them to ministry after 'treatment'. Four current or former priests were charged during the investigation.
C.cite: Rhode Island Attorney General, report on child sexual abuse in the Diocese of Providence, 4 March 2026 (press release)

C.n: Massachusetts Attorney General — Worcester, Fall River and Springfield dioceses (2026)
C.place: Boston, Massachusetts (Attorney General); dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield
C.vn: Nearly 1,000 children
C.who: Catholic Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield
C.d: On 30 September 2026 Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell released a report finding that more than 270 Catholic clergy abused nearly 1,000 children in the Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield, with abuse dating back to the 1950s. She called it the first full public accounting of the abuse, misconduct and institutional failures in those dioceses. The report recommended proper investigation of allegations and transparent, accurate records, and Campbell called on Worcester, the only one of the three without a public list of credibly accused priests, to publish one.
C.cite: Massachusetts Attorney General report on the Fall River, Springfield and Worcester dioceses, 30 September 2026, as reported by WBUR

C.n: Ramsey County v. Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis (2015–2016)
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis
C.cover: The archdiocese admitted it 'failed to adequately respond and prevent the sexual abuse' of three boys by a priest
C.d: In June 2015 the Ramsey County Attorney filed six gross misdemeanor child endangerment charges against the archdiocese itself over its handling of priest Curtis Wehmeyer, later imprisoned for abusing three brothers. The charges were dropped on 20 July 2016 after the archdiocese admitted in court papers that it had failed to adequately respond to and prevent the abuse. A December 2015 civil settlement placed the archdiocese under court oversight until February 2020.
C.cite: Ramsey County Attorney criminal complaint and civil petition, 5 June 2015; settlement and admission, 20 July 2016, as reported by MPR News

C.n: US Senate inquiry — Olympic movement and the FBI failed to protect athletes (2019)
C.vn: 260 women and girls said Larry Nassar assaulted them
C.who: US Olympic Committee; USA Gymnastics; FBI; Michigan State University
C.cover: The report found the USOC, USA Gymnastics and other governing bodies took actions to conceal their negligence, and that the USOC and the FBI 'fundamentally failed' to protect gymnasts
C.d: An 18-month investigation by the Senate Commerce subcommittee led by Senators Jerry Moran and Richard Blumenthal reported on 30 July 2019. It found that the US Olympic Committee and the FBI 'fundamentally failed' to protect gymnasts from Larry Nassar, and that the USOC, USA Gymnastics and other governing bodies took actions to conceal their negligence. It found institutions repeatedly failed to report wrongdoing to law enforcement. The senators proposed the Empowering Olympic and Amateur Athletes Act to reform oversight of Olympic sport.
C.cite: US Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Manufacturing, Trade and Consumer Protection, Olympic abuse investigation report, 30 July 2019, as reported by UPI

C.n: Ropes & Gray report for the US Olympic Committee — Nassar (2018)
C.who: US Olympic Committee; USA Gymnastics
C.cover: USA Gymnastics' CEO told the USOC's CEO and chief of sport performance of allegations against Nassar in 2015; neither shared it and the USOC took no action until press reports in September 2016
C.d: A 233-page report by the law firm Ropes & Gray, commissioned by the US Olympic Committee and released on 10 December 2018, was based on more than 100 interviews over 10 months. It found that in 2015 USA Gymnastics' chief executive told the USOC's chief executive and its chief of sport performance that national team members had alleged abuse by Larry Nassar, and that the USOC took no action from July 2015 until the Indianapolis Star published in September 2016. The USOC fired its chief of sport performance the day the report was released.
C.cite: Ropes & Gray, Report of the Independent Investigation: The Constellation of Factors Underlying Larry Nassar's Abuse of Athletes, 10 December 2018, as reported by CNN via WTVR

C.n: Daniels review of USA Gymnastics (2017)
C.who: USA Gymnastics
C.cover: Reporting rules were so unclear and poorly enforced that the reviewer described the result as 'inadvertent suppression'
C.d: Former federal prosecutor Deborah Daniels, commissioned by USA Gymnastics in late 2016 after lawsuits over abuse by coaches and team doctor Larry Nassar, released her review on 27 June 2017. She found reporting protocols unclear and poorly enforced, a culture that put performance ahead of protection, and an opaque process for investigating claims. She made 70 recommendations, which the board adopted unanimously.
C.cite: Deborah J. Daniels, review for USA Gymnastics, June 2017, as reported by AP / Sports Illustrated, 27 June 2017

C.n: Justice Department inspector general — FBI mishandling of Nassar allegations (2021)
C.vn: At least 40 girls and women said they were abused over a 14-month period while the FBI knew of allegations
C.who: FBI Indianapolis field office; USA Gymnastics
C.cover: FBI Indianapolis officials took months to open a formal investigation, interviewed only one of three athletes (by phone), and later gave incomplete and inaccurate information to internal FBI inquiries
C.d: The Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General reported on 14 July 2021 that the FBI made 'numerous and fundamental errors' after USA Gymnastics reported allegations against Larry Nassar to its Indianapolis office in 2015. Months passed before a formal investigation was opened; agents interviewed only one of three athletes, by phone. Officials later gave incomplete and inaccurate information when their handling was questioned. At least 40 girls and women reported being abused during the 14 months the FBI knew of the allegations.
C.cite: US Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General, Investigation and Review of the FBI's Handling of Allegations of Sexual Abuse by Former USA Gymnastics Physician Lawrence Gerard Nassar, 14 July 2021, as reported by AP / OPB

C.n: GAO-11-200 — US schools hired or kept staff with histories of sexual misconduct (2010)
C.who: Public and private K-12 schools in 11 US states
C.cover: School officials let teachers resign rather than face discipline and in some cases gave positive references that helped them get jobs at other schools; some schools did no criminal history check
C.d: The US Government Accountability Office released GAO-11-200 on 16 December 2010 after examining 15 cases in 11 states where schools hired or retained people with histories of sexual misconduct. In at least 11 cases the offenders had previously targeted children and in at least 6 they abused more children after being hired. Officials sometimes allowed resignations instead of discipline and wrote positive references; some schools did no fingerprint-based checks. GAO found no federal law governing the employment of sex offenders in schools.
C.cite: US Government Accountability Office, GAO-11-200, K-12 Education: Selected Cases of Public and Private Schools That Hired or Retained Individuals with Histories of Sexual Misconduct, December 2010; House Education and Labor Committee release

C.n: Indian Health Service — Presidential Task Force after pediatrician Stanley Patrick Weber (2020)
C.place: Pine Ridge, South Dakota (IHS hospital); also Browning, Montana
C.who: US Indian Health Service (IHS)
C.cover: After complaints the IHS transferred Weber to another IHS hospital, where he practised for another 21 years; staff did not know their reporting obligations
C.d: Stanley Patrick Weber, an Indian Health Service pediatrician, was convicted of sexually abusing young boys at IHS hospitals in Montana and South Dakota. A White House task force chaired by US Attorney Trent Shores released a report on 23 July 2020 finding that officials across the agency did not understand their legal duties to report suspected abuse, that the agency sometimes overlooked doctors' troubled work histories to fill posts, and that parts of its child-protection policy conflicted with federal law. After complaints, the agency had moved Weber to another IHS hospital, where he practised for another 21 years.
C.cite: Presidential Task Force on Protecting Native American Children in the Indian Health Service System, report, April 2020 (released 23 July 2020), as reported by PBS Frontline

C.n: Justice Department finds sexual abuse in five Texas juvenile facilities (2024)
C.place: Gainesville State School and four other TJJD facilities, Texas
C.who: Texas Juvenile Justice Department (TJJD)
C.cover: The US Attorney said Texas state agencies and the Texas Rangers had substantiated sexual abuse allegations at these facilities as early as the 2000s and that the problem persisted
C.d: On 1 August 2024 the US Justice Department announced findings that the Texas Juvenile Justice Department fails to protect children from sexual abuse by staff and other children at all five of its secure facilities (Evins, Gainesville, Giddings, McLennan County and Ron Jackson), in violation of the Constitution. It also found excessive force, prolonged isolation and inadequate mental-health care. The department noted that state investigations had substantiated sexual abuse at these facilities since the early 2000s.
C.cite: US Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division findings report on the Texas Juvenile Justice Department, 1 August 2024 (press release)

C.n: Texas Youth Commission sexual abuse scandal — Rangers report and legislative takeover (2007)
C.place: West Texas State School, Pyote, Texas
C.who: Texas Youth Commission (state juvenile corrections)
C.cover: Complaints at the West Texas State School from 2001 to 2005 were largely ignored; a TYC headquarters inquiry found no abuse; the local district attorney never took the Texas Rangers' case to a grand jury
C.d: A Texas Ranger's 229-page report documented sexual abuse of boys by two senior administrators at the West Texas State School in Pyote, where complaints from 2001 to 2005 had been largely ignored and the local prosecutor did not take the case to a grand jury; the two were indicted in April 2007. When this became public in February 2007, investigators counted more than 750 sexual abuse complaints across all 13 Texas Youth Commission facilities from January 2000 to February 2007. The TYC board resigned on 16 March 2007, the legislature approved a conservator for the agency, and by May 2007, 93 employees had been suspended, fired or forced to retire.
C.cite: Texas Rangers investigative report on the West Texas State School; Texas Senate Criminal Justice Committee actions, 2007, as reported by Prison Legal News, 15 February 2008

C.n: Law Commission of Canada — 'Restoring Dignity': child abuse in Canadian institutions (2000)
C.who: Government-run and government-funded institutions for children, including Indian residential schools
C.d: In November 1997 the federal Minister of Justice asked the Law Commission of Canada to report on processes for dealing with physical and sexual abuse of children in government-run, government-funded and government-sponsored institutions. Its report, Restoring Dignity: Responding to Child Abuse in Canadian Institutions, was presented in March 2000. It reviewed the history of residential schools and other institutions and assessed redress options, recommending programmes negotiated with survivors that avoid causing further harm, together with public education and prevention measures.
C.cite: Law Commission of Canada, Restoring Dignity: Responding to Child Abuse in Canadian Institutions, March 2000 (Department of Justice Canada archive)

C.n: Jericho Hill School for the Deaf, Vancouver — Berger special counsel and BC Ombudsman (1992–1993)
C.vn: More than 300 former students applied and received payments under the 1992 compensation plan
C.who: Jericho Hill Provincial School for the Deaf (BC Ministry of Education)
C.cover: A boy's 1982 disclosure to a school psychologist was passed to a government social worker, but school authorities stopped the planned investigation; in 1987 police could not gather enough evidence for charges; the province fought a class action through the courts before settling in 2004
C.d: In 1982 a teenage boy told a psychologist working for the provincial school for deaf children that a counsellor had sexually abused him, but school authorities stopped the planned investigation. More students disclosed abuse in 1987; police could not gather enough evidence for charges, and more than 20 students were found to have abused other students. Former judge Thomas Berger, appointed special counsel in 1992, concluded that the abuse had occurred, and the BC Ombudsman issued Public Report No. 32 on the abuse of deaf students on 8 November 1993. More than 300 former students received payments under a 1992 compensation plan, and in 2004 the province committed $15.6 million to settle a class action.
C.cite: BC Ombudsman, Public Report No. 32: Abuse of Deaf Students at Jericho Hill School, 8 November 1993; The Tyee, 13 April 2004

C.n: Nova Scotia — Kaufman review of the response to institutional abuse (2002)
C.vn: The compensation programme received 1,264 claims; Kaufman found both that abuse occurred and that there were false and exaggerated claims
C.who: Nova Scotia provincial youth institutions and the province's compensation programme
C.d: Retired judge Fred Kaufman, asked by Nova Scotia's government in November 1999 to review its response, delivered 'Searching for Justice: An Independent Review of Nova Scotia's Response to Reports of Institutional Abuse' to Justice Minister Michael Baker on 31 January 2002. The province's compensation programme for people abused in provincial youth institutions, expected to draw about 300 claims, had received 1,264 by the time it closed in 2000 and paid about $39 million in compensation and counselling. Kaufman stated that sexual and physical abuse did occur, but found the programme 'seriously flawed', found significant evidence of false and exaggerated claims, and found that employees were branded as abusers without recourse. He made 105 recommendations.
C.cite: Fred Kaufman, Searching for Justice, 31 January 2002; Nova Scotia government news release; The Irish Times, 9 February 2002

C.n: Quebec National Assembly special commission on the sexual exploitation of minors (2020)
C.who: Pimping networks and sex-trade establishments exploiting minors in Quebec
C.d: A cross-party special commission of Quebec's National Assembly studied the sexual exploitation of minors for 18 months, with hearings in Quebec City, Montreal and Val-d'Or, and tabled its final report on 3 December 2020. It estimated about 600 establishments in Quebec, such as strip clubs, massage parlours and escort agencies, where a man could find a teenager for sex, described Montreal as a national hub, and said pimps could earn up to $300,000 a year. It made 58 recommendations, the first being to make the fight against sexual exploitation of minors a national priority.
C.cite: Commission spéciale sur l'exploitation sexuelle des mineurs, final report, December 2020, as reported by Global News, 3 December 2020

C.n: Victoria — 'Betrayal of Trust' parliamentary inquiry into religious and other organisations (2013)
C.who: Catholic Church and other religious and non-government organisations in Victoria
C.cover: The inquiry found the Catholic Church's early-1990s response continued to conceal abuse; senior church representatives conceded steps intended to conceal wrongdoing
C.d: The Family and Community Development Committee of the Parliament of Victoria tabled 'Betrayal of Trust', its report of the Inquiry into the Handling of Child Abuse by Religious and Other Non-Government Organisations, in November 2013. It found 'substantial criminal child abuse' over a long period by priests and members of religious orders in Victoria, and a culture in religious organisations that allowed systemic criminal abuse. Its recommendations would compel religious leaders to report child abuse to police and strip the Catholic Church of its virtual immunity from being sued.
C.cite: Parliament of Victoria Family and Community Development Committee, Betrayal of Trust, 13 November 2013, as reported by The Tablet and The Guardian

C.n: Wood Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service — paedophile inquiry (1997)
C.who: A Sydney paedophile network linked to convicted sex offender Colin Fisk; a group of NSW police detectives
C.cover: The network bribed a group of detectives for advance warning of police scrutiny; the Commission was highly critical of how police, prosecutors and public servants handled child sex-offence cases
C.d: The Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service under Justice James Wood (1994–1997) had its terms widened in 1995 to cover paedophile networks, the care of at-risk minors and police guidelines for investigating sex offences against minors; Volume IV of its final report is the paedophile inquiry. It found a network involving convicted offender Colin Fisk that shared child abuse material, procured under-age sexual partners and invested in an under-age male brothel in Surry Hills, and that it had a corrupt relationship with a group of detectives who sold it advance warning of police scrutiny. The Commission found no compelling evidence for claims of a large ring of prominent professionals protected by senior police.
C.cite: Royal Commission into the New South Wales Police Service, Final Report, Volume IV: The Paedophile Inquiry, 1997, as summarised by Wikipedia (citing the report)

C.n: Senate 'Lost Innocents' — child migrants abused in Australian institutions (2001)
C.place: Bindoon, Western Australia (Christian Brothers' Boys Town)
C.who: Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia (Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf, Tardun) and other receiving institutions for British and Maltese child migrants
C.d: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Lost Innocents: Righting the Record — Report on child migration' in August 2001. Of 207 former child migrants who made submissions, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.
C.cite: Senate Community Affairs References Committee, Lost Innocents: Righting the Record, 30 August 2001; summarised in IICSA, Child Migration Programmes investigation report, Part B

C.n: Senate 'Forgotten Australians' — children in institutional care (2004)
C.vn: About 500,000 people were placed in institutional or foster care (Senate estimate); the inquiry received 614 submissions
C.who: Australian orphanages, children's homes, foster care and other out-of-home care run by states, churches and charities
C.d: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Forgotten Australians: A report on Australians who experienced institutional or out-of-home care as children' on 30 August 2004. It received 614 submissions and estimated that about 500,000 people had been placed in institutions or foster care, and heard accounts of neglect, beatings, psychological cruelty, forced labour and sexual assault and rape by carers, other children, visitors and foster families. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised in Parliament to Forgotten Australians and former child migrants on 16 November 2009.
C.cite: Senate Community Affairs References Committee, Forgotten Australians, tabled 30 August 2004 (tabling speeches); 2009 apology as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: South Australia — Child Protection Systems Royal Commission, 'The Life They Deserve' (2016)
C.who: Families SA (state child protection agency); carer Shannon McCoole
C.cover: The inquiry examined how Families SA failed to prevent abuse by a carer it employed
C.d: Former Supreme Court Justice Margaret Nyland led a two-year royal commission into South Australia's child protection system, set up in 2014 after Families SA carer Shannon McCoole was charged with sexual offences against children in his care; McCoole was later jailed for 35 years. Her report, 'The Life They Deserve', was delivered to the Governor on 5 August 2016 with 260 recommendations. It found that many children in state care had been abused and neglected not only by their families but also let down by the system meant to protect them.
C.cite: Child Protection Systems Royal Commission, The Life They Deserve, 5 August 2016; SBS News

C.n: Australian Human Rights Commission — 'Change the Routine', gymnastics review (2021)
C.who: Gymnastics Australia and the sport of gymnastics in Australia
C.cover: Complaints of abuse and harm were not adequately addressed and athletes' voices were silenced
C.d: Gymnastics Australia engaged the Australian Human Rights Commission in August 2020 after repeated abuse claims; the Commission's report 'Change the Routine' was released on 3 May 2021. Drawing on 57 interviews and 138 submissions, it heard of emotional, physical and sexual abuse in a sport whose participants are predominantly young girls, found that complaints were not adequately addressed and that children were not effectively safeguarded, and described a 'win-at-all-costs' culture. It made 12 recommendations, including an apology, which Gymnastics Australia accepted.
C.cite: Australian Human Rights Commission, Change the Routine: Report on the Independent Review into Gymnastics in Australia, May 2021; SBS News, 3 May 2021

C.n: Western Australia — St Andrew's Hostel Katanning special inquiry (Blaxell, 2012)
C.who: St Andrew's Hostel, Katanning (state country high school hostel); warden Dennis McKenna
C.cover: Most officials who received allegations took no action; the inquiry made adverse findings against a police officer and a local councillor
C.d: Former judge Peter Blaxell was appointed special inquirer on 22 November 2011 to examine how government agencies and officials responded to allegations of sexual abuse at St Andrew's Hostel, a state-run hostel for rural high-school students. Its warden from 1976 to 1990, Dennis McKenna, was convicted in 1991 of 19 offences against five boys and pleaded guilty in 2011 to 10 more, a total of 29 offences against 11 boys aged 14 to 16. The report, 'How the system and society failed our children', found that most officials took no action on allegations and made adverse findings against one police officer and one local councillor.
C.cite: Special Inquiry into St Andrew's Hostel, Katanning, report 'St Andrew's Hostel Katanning: How the system and society failed our children', 2012 (Government of Western Australia)

C.n: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015)
C.who: Australian-funded Regional Processing Centre on Nauru; contracted guards and staff
C.cover: Staff wrote in an open letter in April 2015 that the Australian government had known of alleged abuses against women and children for more than 18 months
C.d: The Moss Review, commissioned by the Australian government and published in March 2015, was aware of three rape allegations at the Australian-run Regional Processing Centre on Nauru, one involving a minor, confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child, and concluded that guards trading marijuana with detainees for sexual favours was possibly occurring. In April 2015 staff alleged multiple instances of sexual abuse of women and children in an open letter. A Senate select committee reported on 31 August 2015 in 'Taking responsibility: conditions and circumstances at Australia's Regional Processing Centre in Nauru'.
C.cite: Philip Moss, Review into recent allegations relating to conditions and circumstances at the Regional Processing Centre in Nauru, published March 2015 (Al Jazeera, 21 March 2015); staff open letter, 7 April 2015, and Senate Select Committee report 'Taking responsibility', 31 August 2015 (as cited by Wikipedia)

C.n: Poland — State Commission on Paedophilia, first and second reports (2021–2022)
C.vn: 188 girls and 173 boys in 345 cases and 245 court proceedings analysed
C.who: Polish justice system; Catholic clergy (almost 30% of perpetrators in the cases studied)
C.d: Poland's State Commission on Paedophilia, set up by the government after a 2020 documentary on abuse and alleged cover-ups in the Catholic Church, published its first report on 29 July 2021. It analysed 345 cases and 245 court proceedings involving 188 girls and 173 boys, most aged 11 to 15. Almost 30% of perpetrators were clergy and 35% were relatives. In half the cases no one had noticed signs of abuse. The commission sent 137 notifications to prosecutors and made 22 recommendations, including ending the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse. Its second report, published on 2 August 2022, covered 513 cases; among abusers who were not relatives, clergy were the largest professional group (57 cases, about 47%).
C.cite: Państwowa Komisja do spraw przeciwdziałania wykorzystaniu seksualnemu małoletnich poniżej lat 15, first report, July 2021 (Notes from Poland, 29 July 2021); second report, 2 August 2022 (Prawo.pl)

C.n: Poland — Diocese of Sosnowiec independent commission (2026)
C.vn: at least 50 children; 96% under 15
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Sosnowiec
C.cover: Bishops were repeatedly alerted, including by reliable sources, but often took no action; where they acted, they usually moved the priest to another parish.
C.d: The independent commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', set up in October 2024 and chaired by journalist Tomasz Krzyżak, presented its findings on 12 February 2026 after reviewing diocesan files from 1992 to January 2025. It found at least 50 children harmed, 96% of them under 15, and 29 people accused, 23 of them diocesan clergy; 19 of the 23 priests were confirmed offenders in church or state proceedings. Bishops were repeatedly alerted but in some cases took no action, and accused priests were often transferred rather than punished. The commission reported eight people to prosecutors.
C.cite: Commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', report on the Diocese of Sosnowiec, 12 February 2026 (Notes from Poland, 13 February 2026)

C.n: Spain — Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo audit for the Episcopal Conference (2023)
C.vn: at least 2,056 minors, counted from complaints and lawsuits; the Episcopal Conference said the real number is higher
C.who: Spanish Episcopal Conference; Catholic clergy, religious and lay church staff
C.d: The Spanish Episcopal Conference hired the law firm Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo in February 2022 to audit sexual abuse in the Church. The church announced its findings on 21 December 2023: at least 2,056 minor victims and 1,383 complaints, without saying how many clergy were accused. The figure is far below the estimate of more than 200,000 victims since 1940 published in October 2023 by an independent commission appointed by parliament, and the bishops said it was 'obvious that the number is higher'.
C.cite: Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo audit for the Conferencia Episcopal Española, December 2023 (The Local Spain / AFP, 21 December 2023)

C.n: Belgium — Chamber special committee on sexual abuse in the Church (Lalieux, 2011)
C.who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
C.d: After the June 2010 police raids that ended the Adriaenssens commission, the Belgian Chamber set up a special committee on the handling of sexual abuse in relationships of authority, especially within the Church, chaired by Karine Lalieux. Its report, approved unanimously on 30 March 2011, found abuse in every sector of the church and across the country, especially in Catholic boarding schools, with families reporting at least 13 suicides. It recommended an independent arbitration body for compensation and extending the limitation period from 10 to 15 years after a victim turns 18. The arbitration centre and its compensation scheme followed in 2012.
C.cite: Chambre des représentants, Commission spéciale relative au traitement d'abus sexuels et de faits de pédophilie dans une relation d'autorité, report adopted 30 March 2011 (AP via Deseret News, 30 March 2011)

C.n: France — CIIVISE final report on sexual violence against children (2023)
C.vn: estimate of children who are victims of sexual violence each year in France
C.who: French justice, health and child-protection systems; families and institutions
C.d: The Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence against Children (CIIVISE), created by the government on 11 March 2021 and chaired by juvenile judge Édouard Durand, delivered its final report on 20 November 2023 with 82 recommendations. It estimated that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence each year in France. It found that victims wait 10 to 13 years on average for specialised care and that only 5% of reports come from doctors. The commission's work covers abuse in families and in institutions, and the failures of courts, police and health services to act.
C.cite: CIIVISE, 'Violences sexuelles faites aux enfants : on vous croit', 20 November 2023 (Fondation Raja summary, 8 December 2023)

C.n: France — National Assembly inquiry into failings of sports federations (2024)
C.vn: Signal-sports cell: 1,800+ reports concerning 1,200+ people by Nov 2023; 8 in 10 victims were minors
C.who: French sports federations (incl. judo, ice sports, football), sports ministry
C.cover: The commission described a culture of silence 'at every level', reaching the highest level of the state; the ministry did not give the rapporteur its Signal-sports tracking table, and the data it did provide were 'very incomplete'.
C.d: A National Assembly commission of inquiry chaired by Béatrice Bellamy, with Sabrina Sebaihi as rapporteur, worked from July 2023 and presented its report in January 2024 after 92 hearings. It found that by November 2023 the ministry's Signal-sports cell had handled over 1,800 reports involving more than 1,200 people, with eight in ten victims minors at the time. Background checks on volunteers, required since 2006, only began working in 2021, and 42 federations were behind. The report described a culture of silence and concealment in federations and in the state.
C.cite: Assemblée nationale, Commission d'enquête relative à l'identification des défaillances de fonctionnement au sein des fédérations françaises de sport, report no. 2012, press kit 23 January 2024

C.n: France — Senate mission on sexual offences against minors by people working with children (2019)
C.who: Catholic Church in France, sports federations, schools, holiday camps, centres for disabled children
C.d: A French Senate joint information mission chaired by Catherine Deroche, with Marie Mercier and Michelle Meunier as rapporteurs, presented its conclusions on 29 May 2019 after hearing more than 60 people. Meunier described a 'systemic problem' in the Catholic Church, which the report put down to the sacred status of priests, the lack of checks on power, fear of scandal and a strong culture of secrecy; it flagged centres for disabled minors and sports federations as high-risk. It made 38 recommendations, including checking the sex-offender register (FIJAISV) before every hire to work with minors. A request by Socialist senators for a full commission of inquiry into the Church was refused by the law committee.
C.cite: Sénat, mission commune d'information sur la répression des infractions sexuelles sur mineurs, report no. 529, 28 May 2019 (Public Sénat, 29 May 2019)

C.n: Netherlands — De Vries Commission on sexual abuse in organised sport (2017)
C.vn: 686 cases reported to the sport confidential line 2001–2017, 60% under 16; survey: about 12% of athletes had such experiences as children
C.who: Dutch sports clubs and federations; NOC*NSF
C.d: The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF set up a commission led by former minister Klaas de Vries in May 2017; it reported on 12 December 2017. A survey found about 12% of athletes had experienced sexually transgressive behaviour as children and about 4% sexual assault or rape. The commission analysed 686 cases reported between 2001 and 2017, in which 60% of victims were under 16 and 70% of perpetrators were coaches or supervisors, and received 103 new reports. It recommended a reporting duty for sports boards.
C.cite: Commissie De Vries, 'Onderzoek naar seksuele intimidatie en misbruik in de sport', December 2017 (NOS, 12 December 2017)

C.n: Germany — Conference of Religious Superiors (DOK) survey of abuse in Catholic orders (2020)
C.vn: at least 1,412 children, adolescents or wards (80% male); DOK says unreported cases cannot be counted
C.who: Catholic religious orders in Germany (100 of 291 responding orders)
C.d: The German Conference of Catholic Religious Superiors (DOK) surveyed 392 orders and published the results on 26 August 2020. The 291 orders that answered, covering 88% of members, recorded accusations against at least 654 members and 58 other staff, from at least 1,412 children, adolescents or wards, about 80% of them male. Accusations were recorded in 53 of 77 male orders and 47 of 214 female orders. About 80% of the accused had died. The DOK said there were further unreported cases and that its survey was not a scientific study comparable to the bishops' 2018 study.
C.cite: Deutsche Ordensobernkonferenz, survey results, 26 August 2020 (America magazine / CNS, 26 August 2020)

C.n: Germany — Independent Commission case study on abuse in sport (2022)
C.who: German sports clubs and federations (West and East Germany)
C.d: Germany's federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a case study on sport on 27 September 2022, based on 72 reports from victims and witnesses and three personal accounts. Most abuse happened in organised club sport, especially competitive sport, by mostly male coaches, trainers or teachers in positions of power, and two-thirds of victims were abused repeatedly. Nearly a fifth of reports concerned sport in the GDR. Few cases had been uncovered or dealt with; victims often found their accounts denied, played down or covered up.
C.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, 'Sexualisierte Gewalt und sexueller Kindesmissbrauch im Kontext des Sports', 27 September 2022 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Germany — Independent Commission case study on child sexual abuse in the GDR (2019)
C.vn: based on accounts of about 100 people abused as children in the GDR
C.who: GDR children's homes and Jugendwerkhöfe (youth work homes); families
C.d: The federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse presented a case study on the GDR on 6 March 2019, based on the recollections of about 100 men and women abused as children. Girls were more often abused in their own families and boys more often in homes such as the Jugendwerkhöfe (youth work homes). Cases were also documented in which children were organised and sold for sexual services. The study, which is not representative, found that child sexual abuse remained taboo in the GDR considerably longer than in West Germany.
C.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, Fallstudie DDR, 6 March 2019 (Deutsches Ärzteblatt, 6 March 2019)

C.n: Germany — Federal Independent Commissioner (Bergmann) final report (2011)
C.vn: about 13,000 letters and 2,000 calls from victims and relatives
C.who: Churches, schools, sports clubs, homes and families in Germany
C.d: After the 2010 revelations at Canisius-Kolleg and other schools, the federal government appointed former minister Christine Bergmann as Independent Commissioner. Her final report, presented on 24 May 2011 to the Round Table on Child Sexual Abuse, drew on about 13,000 letters and 2,000 phone calls from victims and relatives about abuse in churches, schools, sports clubs and families. It recommended that institutions where abuse occurred make one-time payments based on what courts would award, that therapy costs be covered, and that an independent body oversee implementation. A permanent federal commissioner's office followed, and in 2016 an Independent Commission for the investigation of child sexual abuse began work.
C.cite: Abschlussbericht der Unabhängigen Beauftragten zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, 24 May 2011 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Germany — SOS-Kinderdorf independent commission report (2024)
C.vn: 226 known cases of boundary violations (physical, psychological and sexual), incl. rapes in individual cases
C.who: SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. (Germany) — children's villages and group homes
C.d: An independent commission appointed by SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. investigated from 2021 and presented its report in Munich on 2 October 2024. It recorded 226 known cases of boundary violations since the organisation's founding in 1955, 189 from its internal reporting office and 37 from a 2023 newspaper appeal, including sexual assaults and in some cases rape. About half were committed by staff such as house parents and about 20% by other young people in care. The commission said the closed nature of SOS family units was a risk and that more cases are likely unrecorded.
C.cite: Unabhängige Kommission SOS-Kinderdorf, Abschlussbericht, 2 October 2024 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Germany — Nordelbian Lutheran Church expert commission (Ahrensburg, 2014)
C.who: Former Nordelbian Evangelical Lutheran Church (now Nordkirche)
C.cover: The Ahrensburg pastor went unpunished because the offences were time-barred, as were many others; Hamburg bishop Maria Jepsen resigned over the scandal.
C.d: An independent commission published its final report in October 2014 on sexual abuse in the former Nordelbian Lutheran Church. It examined 14 pastors against whom the church opened 16 disciplinary proceedings between 1993 and 2012, for acts from 1973 to 2011 against children, adolescents and adults. The case that started it was a pastor in Ahrensburg who abused at least a dozen boys and girls over more than 20 years and went unpunished because the acts were time-barred. Hamburg bishop Maria Jepsen resigned over the scandal, and Bishop Kirsten Fehrs called the report shameful and shocking.
C.cite: Unabhängige Expertenkommission, report on sexual abuse in the Nordelbian Church, October 2014 (epd via evangelisch.de, 15 October 2014)

C.n: Germany — Ettal Benedictine abbey boarding school, IPP study (2013)
C.who: Benedictine Abbey of Ettal and its boarding school
C.d: After abuse at the Ettal abbey school became public in 2010, the abbey commissioned the Munich Institute for Practice Research and Project Consulting (IPP; Heiner Keupp, Florian Straus). Its roughly 160-page study, presented on 7 March 2013 and based on 41 interviews with former pupils, relatives and priests and on abbey records, found physical, psychological and sexualised violence over at least three decades, mostly from the 1960s to the 1980s. Keupp described a 'culture of enabling' and said there was no strategic plan or 'System Ettal'.
C.cite: IPP München (Keupp, Straus et al.), study on violence at Ettal boarding school, 7 March 2013 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Germany — Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (BdP) study (2024)
C.vn: 103 identified, 123 incl. cases that could not be dated or assigned
C.who: Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (non-denominational scout association)
C.d: The BdP commissioned IPP Munich, working with the Dissens institute, to study sexualised violence in the association from its founding in 1976 to 2006. Presented on 29 February 2024, the study identified 103 victims (123 including cases that could not be dated or assigned) and 36 accused (50 with the same additions), almost all male; most incidents were in the 1980s and 1990s. It found two main perpetrator types, older adult leaders and adolescents or young adults who used leadership roles, and named weak oversight of young leaders, informal power imbalances, strong group loyalty and silence about sexuality as risk factors.
C.cite: IPP München / Dissens, study for the Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder, 29 February 2024 (IPP press release)

C.n: Germany — Catholic scouts (DPSG) study on sexualised and spiritual violence (2026)
C.vn: no count given; study not representative; victims mainly girls and young women
C.who: Deutsche Pfadfinder*innenschaft Sankt Georg (DPSG), Catholic scout association
C.d: Researchers from the universities of Marburg and Gießen, led by Sabine Maschke and Ludwig Stecher, studied sexualised and spiritual violence in the Catholic scout association DPSG from 1929 to 2022 and presented the results in Cologne on 5 February 2026. They found sexualised violence was a widespread structural problem, especially on camps and trips, mostly by male leaders against underage girls, and that the association had looked away and played incidents down. Over 90% of the accused were male. The DPSG accepted institutional responsibility.
C.cite: Universities of Marburg and Gießen, study for the DPSG, 5 February 2026 (JLU Gießen press release; epd)

C.n: Germany — Archdiocese of Cologne, Gercke report (2021)
C.vn: more than half under 14
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Cologne
C.cover: The report counted 75 breaches of duty by eight senior archdiocesan officials; an earlier report by Westpfahl Spilker Wastl was withheld by the archdiocese.
C.d: Criminal lawyer Björn Gercke, mandated by the archdiocese, presented an 800-page report on 18 March 2021 covering 1975 to 2018. It found 314 victims, more than half under 14, and 202 accused clergy and lay staff. It counted 75 breaches of duty by eight senior officials, among them the later Archbishop of Hamburg Stefan Heße, while clearing Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki of breach of duty. Woelki had withheld an earlier report by another law firm, which caused a long crisis in the archdiocese.
C.cite: Gercke Wollschläger, 'Pflichtverletzungen von Diözesanverantwortlichen im Erzbistum Köln …', 18 March 2021 (The Local / AFP; KNA via Vatican News)

C.n: Germany — Diocese of Münster, University of Münster study (2022)
C.vn: at least 610 minors; authors estimate the real number 8 to 10 times higher
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Münster
C.cover: The study found a 'massive leadership failure' under the bishops from 1947 to 2008; most accused priests were transferred rather than restricted.
C.d: Historians at the University of Münster, including Thomas Großbölting, published a study of the diocese on 13 June 2022 after about two and a half years of research. It found at least 610 minors abused by 196 clerics between 1945 and 2020, about 4% of the diocese's priests in that period, and estimated the real number of victims at 8 to 10 times higher. Bishops and diocesan leaders were often fully informed, covered up cases or intervened only superficially, and usually transferred accused priests.
C.cite: University of Münster, study on sexual abuse of minors by clergy in the Diocese of Münster 1945–2020, 13 June 2022 (AP via Religion News Service)

C.n: Germany — Archdiocese of Freiburg commission report (2023)
C.vn: more than 540 people assumed affected; earlier count at least 442
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Freiburg
C.cover: The report found that Archbishop Robert Zollitsch (from 2003) ignored canon law, did not report abuse suspicions to the Vatican although required from 2002, and that files were manipulated; Archbishop Oskar Saier (1978–2002) transferred offenders without informing parishes.
C.d: The archdiocese's independent reappraisal commission presented a roughly 600-page report on 18 April 2023, examining 24 cases in depth from 1945 onward. The commission chair, Magnus Striet, said more than 540 people were assumed to have been victims of more than 250 clerics; an earlier count had found at least 442 victims. It found that former archbishop Robert Zollitsch, who also chaired the German Bishops' Conference from 2008 to 2014, failed up to the point of deliberate concealment and ignored canon law, and that his predecessor Oskar Saier transferred offenders without informing parishes.
