C.cite: Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission / AG Aktenanalyse, Erzdiözese Freiburg, report of 18 April 2023 (Vatican News; KNA/Pillar via BishopAccountability)

C.n: Germany — Diocese of Mainz, EVV study (2023)
C.vn: 657 possible victims identified, 401 after review
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Mainz
C.cover: The study faulted Cardinal Karl Lehmann's early years (1983–2001) as 'deflecting and dissembling' and also criticised Bishop Albert Stohr and Cardinal Hermann Volk; Bishop Peter Kohlgraf said that for his predecessors protecting perpetrators and the Church mattered more than those affected.
C.d: The study 'Erfahren. Verstehen. Vorsorgen.' by lawyer Ulrich Weber, commissioned by the diocese, was released on 3 March 2023. It identified 657 possible victims and 392 suspects for 1945 to 2019, of whom 401 victims and 181 accused remained after review. Weber said Cardinal Karl Lehmann, bishop from 1983 to 2016, never met his own public standard for handling abuse. Bishop Peter Kohlgraf acknowledged major misconduct and omissions under Lehmann, Cardinal Hermann Volk and earlier leaders.
C.cite: Ulrich Weber, 'Erfahren. Verstehen. Vorsorgen.' (EVV), Diocese of Mainz, 3 March 2023 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability, 4 March 2023)

C.n: Germany — Diocese of Aachen, Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2020)
C.vn: at least 175 cases with indications of abuse of children and adolescents, most aged 8 to 14
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Aachen
C.cover: The report assigned personal responsibility to former Bishop Heinrich Mussinghoff and his vicar general Manfred von Holtum.
C.d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the diocese, presented its report on 12 November 2020 after reviewing files from 1965 to 2019. It found indications of at least 175 cases of sexual abuse of children and adolescents by 81 clerics (79 priests and two deacons), most victims aged 8 to 14. It assigned personal responsibility to, among others, former bishop Heinrich Mussinghoff and his former vicar general Manfred von Holtum.
C.cite: Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, Gutachten for the Diocese of Aachen, 12 November 2020 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Germany — Diocese of Essen, IPP study (2023)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Essen
C.cover: Accused priests were often moved to other posts, sometimes in other dioceses; parishes were not informed, and until 2010 the diocese made no effort to support victims.
C.d: The Munich IPP institute, with the Berlin institute Dissens, published its study of the diocese's 65 years on 14 February 2023. It found 226 people who reported abuse and 190 accused clergy in the records, with most offences in the 1950s to 1970s. Accused priests were often reassigned, sometimes to other dioceses, without parishes being told, and until 2010 the diocese did nothing to support victims. Bishop Franz-Josef Overbeck acknowledged the failures; about 1.9 million euros had been paid to victims.
C.cite: IPP München / Dissens (Helga Dill et al.), study of sexualised violence in the Diocese of Essen, 14 February 2023 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Germany — Archdiocese of Berlin, Redeker Sellner Dahs report (2021)
C.vn: at least 121 known victims
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Berlin
C.d: The law firm Redeker Sellner Dahs, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Berlin, presented its report in part on 29 January 2021, covering the period from 1946. It identified 61 accused clergy and at least 121 known victims. A part on the responsibility of named officials was kept back for data-protection reasons, reviewed by another firm and presented at the end of June 2021.
C.cite: Redeker Sellner Dahs, Gutachten for the Archdiocese of Berlin, 29 January 2021 (KNA via Vatican News; German Bishops' Conference overview, 13 December 2022)

C.n: Germany — Diocese of Trier independent commission (2022 onward)
C.vn: identified so far in the August 2022 interim report
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Trier
C.cover: Bishop Bernhard Stein (1967–1980) is accused of covering up cases; the commission said it would also examine the terms of Reinhard Marx (bishop 2002–2008) and Georg Bätzing (vicar general 2012–2016).
C.d: The diocese's independent commission, launched in June 2021 with Gerhard Robbers as spokesman, released its interim report in August 2022 covering 1946 to 2021. It had identified 513 victims and 195 perpetrators so far. University of Trier historians working for the inquiry later published interim reports on abuse during the terms of bishops Bernhard Stein (2022) and Hermann Josef Spital (2024).
C.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Missbrauchs im Bistum Trier, interim report, August 2022 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability, 13 October 2022)

C.n: Germany — Diocese of Osnabrück, University of Osnabrück study (interim report 2022, final report 2024)
C.vn: 349 identifiable victims and firm indications of at least 60 more (more than 400) from 1945 to 2024; the study says the hidden number may be up to ten times higher
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Osnabrück
C.cover: The interim report found Bishop Franz-Josef Bode repeatedly left accused priests in office and gave some roles, including youth ministry, that enabled further offences; Bode resigned in March 2023.
C.d: Historians and lawyers at the University of Osnabrück led by Hans Schulte-Nölke and Siegrid Westphal, commissioned by the diocese, presented a roughly 600-page interim report on 20 September 2022 on sexual violence by clergy since 1945; it criticised the handling of allegations under Bishop Franz-Josef Bode (from 1995) and his predecessors, finding he repeatedly left accused priests in office and assigned some to posts that enabled further abuse. Bode accepted responsibility and resigned in 2023. The final report, presented on 2 October 2024, named 122 accused clerics, about 4% of priests who served in the diocese since 1945 (an area that until 1995 included today's Archdiocese of Hamburg), and 349 identifiable victims with firm indications of at least 60 more; the study says the hidden number may be up to ten times higher.
C.cite: University of Osnabrück (Schulte-Nölke, Westphal et al.), interim report, 20 September 2022 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability) and final report, 2 October 2024 (statement of Vicar General Ulrich Beckwermert, 9 October 2024; Vatican News, 9 October 2024)

C.n: Austria — Kremsmünster Abbey school abuse, diocesan commission and IPP study
C.vn: 24 boys abused by the convicted former boarding-school director; the 2015 IPP study counted 350 cases of sexual, physical or psychological violence (1945-2000) and 24 accused people
C.who: Benedictine Abbey of Kremsmünster and its Stiftsgymnasium
C.d: Abuse at the boarding school of the Benedictine abbey of Kremsmünster in Upper Austria became public in 2010. In July 2013 an Austrian court sentenced a former priest who had been the boarding-school director to 12 years in prison for abusing 24 boys in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s. A study by the Munich Institute for Practice Research (IPP), commissioned by the abbey and published in March 2015, drew on interviews covering 1945 to 2000 and identified 350 cases of sexual, physical or psychological violence and 24 accused people.
C.cite: Court report on conviction of former Kremsmünster boarding-school director, July 2013 (news report reprinted by BishopAccountability.org); APA via Vienna.at, 'Studie zum Missbrauch im Stift Kremsmünster', 27 March 2015

C.n: Italy — Il Forteto community, Tuscany: abuse of children placed by courts
C.who: Il Forteto agricultural cooperative and community; Tuscany Region, juvenile court and local authorities that placed and accredited it
C.cover: The founder already had a final conviction in 1985, yet courts and social services kept placing children there; parliament's 2024 commission is to establish why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on sexual abuse and mistreatment.
C.d: Il Forteto, a cooperative and community at Vicchio in the Mugello near Florence, received children placed by juvenile courts and social services for decades. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, was definitively sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse, although a conviction had already become final in 1985 and placements continued. Two Tuscan regional council inquiry commissions examined the case; a parliamentary inquiry in the previous legislature did not finish with a final report, and a new bicameral commission of inquiry was created by Law 47 of 25 March 2024 and installed on 1 August 2024. Its task is to establish institutional responsibilities and why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on abuse and mistreatment.
C.cite: Camera dei deputati, Law 47/2024 on the parliamentary commission of inquiry on Il Forteto (temi.camera.it); La Nazione, 1 August 2024

C.n: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
C.vn: 936 children adopted from Ethiopia to Flanders 1996–2017; investigations opened for 12 families
C.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
C.d: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.
C.cite: Flemish expert panel on intercountry adoption (findings 2021, final report dated 15 February 2023); Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie, Ethiopia investigation (Brussels Times, 23 November 2023); Belga News Agency

C.n: Archdiocese of Paderborn — University of Paderborn study (2026)
C.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Paderborn; archbishops Lorenz Jaeger and Johannes Joachim Degenhardt
C.cover: The study found sexual violence against children was concealed over decades; the tenures of Cardinals Jaeger and Degenhardt were assessed critically.
C.d: Historians at the University of Paderborn, commissioned by the archdiocese, published their study on 12 March 2026. It identified 210 accused people and 489 victims and found that sexual violence against children was concealed for decades under Archbishops Lorenz Jaeger and Johannes Joachim Degenhardt. Paderborn city council then voted to rename streets named after both cardinals and to remove them from its honorary citizens. In September 2026 the archdiocese's independent review commission reported 262 accused clergy and church employees known by the end of June 2026.
C.cite: Universität Paderborn, historical study of sexual abuse in the Archdiocese of Paderborn 1941–2002, 12 March 2026 (epd via evangelisch.de, 26 March 2026); Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission Paderborn, fourth annual report (epd, 4 September 2026)

C.n: Diocese of Passau — University of Passau study (2025)
C.vn: at least 672 minors sexually abused or physically mistreated by clergy; authors think the real number may be double
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Passau — priests, deacons and religious brothers
C.cover: Bishops and vicars general often put protecting the institution and the priesthood above victims; judges, prosecutors, medical experts and school and youth authorities are named as bystanders.
C.d: A University of Passau team led by historian Marc von Knorring, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission, published its study online on 8 December 2025 covering 1945 to 2022. It found at least 672 minors, mostly boys, who were sexually abused or physically mistreated (or both) by 154 clergy, about 6.4% of some 2,400 priests, deacons and religious clergy in the period; 128 of them sexually abused minors, and about 86% were likely repeat offenders. Abuse took place in boarding schools and homes, religious lessons and altar-server duties. The study found bishops and vicars general often protected the institution and the priesthood rather than victims.
C.cite: Marc von Knorring and team, Universität Passau, study for the Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission of the Diocese of Passau, December 2025 (ZDFheute)

C.n: Diocese of Würzburg — Schneider report for the review commission (2025)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Würzburg (43 of 51 accused were clergy)
C.cover: Until the early 2000s some accused clergy received 'systematic protection'.
C.d: Lawyer Hendrik Schneider, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission (UKAM), presented his report on 8 April 2025 covering 1949 to 2019. It counted 51 accused, 43 of them clergy, and 226 victims subject to 449 documented acts, which the report extrapolated to about 3,053 acts. The average age of victims at the first act was 9.8 years. It found systematic protection of some accused clergy until the early 2000s. Earlier, in 2019, lawyer Hans-Jochen Schrepfer reviewed nearly 3,000 personnel files, and the Würzburg law firm Cornea Franz reviewed the records of the diocese's three Kilianeen boys' boarding schools.
C.cite: Hendrik Schneider, report for the Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung des sexuellen Missbrauchs im Bistum Würzburg, 8 April 2025 (epd via evangelisch.de); epd, 19 November 2019, on the Schrepfer personnel-file review and the Kilianeen review

C.n: Diocese of Hildesheim — Niewisch-Lennartz expert group on the Janssen era (2021)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Hildesheim under Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen
C.cover: Priests accused of abusing children were generally only moved to another parish; perpetrators got support and protection while victims got no help.
C.d: An external expert group led by former Lower Saxony justice minister Antje Niewisch-Lennartz, with former senior prosecutor Kurt Schrimm and the IPP institute, presented its report on 14 September 2021 on the tenure of Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen (1957–1982). Its interviews identified 71 suspects, 45 of them clergy, the others lay staff, members of religious orders and youths in children's homes; 51 were active during Janssen's tenure. Accused priests were generally only transferred, in one case to South America, and children were left unprotected in tent camps, priests' homes and church children's homes. The group found no further evidence against Janssen himself but did not refute the two allegations made against him in 2015 and 2018. An earlier IPP study for the diocese appeared in 2017.
C.cite: Bistum Hildesheim, press kit for the presentation of the Niewisch-Lennartz/Schrimm/IPP report, 14 September 2021; epd via evangelisch.de, 14 September 2021

C.n: Diocese of Augsburg — independent review commission study (2025)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Augsburg; bishops and vicars general 1949–2019
C.cover: Diocesan leaders did not respond appropriately to allegations for decades: share of inappropriate handling 54.5% under Freundorfer, 63.6% under Stimpfle, 68.8% under Dammertz, 33.3% under Mixa, 5.9% under Zdarsa.
C.d: The diocese's independent review commission (UAKA) presented a 206-page study on 30 October 2025, built on the diocese's MHG-study data covering 1,507 personnel files of diocesan clergy. It found 77 accused linked to 193 offences against 156 victims, about two-thirds male and 42.5% under 14, with offences back to 1948. Diocesan leaders handled allegations inappropriately for decades, in up to 68.8% of cases under one bishop; handling improved after the 2002 guidelines. Bishop Bertram Meier said the diocese bore grave guilt.
C.cite: Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission des Bistums Augsburg (UAKA), study presented 30 October 2025 (epd via Sonntagsblatt)

C.n: Diocese of Fulda — independent review commission final report (2025)
C.vn: 120 identified; the commission says the true total is several times higher
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Fulda; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp (personnel chief 1977–2003)
C.cover: Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently to protect the church's reputation and transferred without stated reasons; victims were ignored until 2010.
C.d: The independent commission for the Diocese of Fulda, chaired by former Fulda mayor Gerhard Möller, presented its final report on 17 June 2025 after reviewing 2,124 files covering about 80 years. It identified 120 victims and 37 accused priests and chaplains, with 239 provable sexual offences, and said the true number is several times higher. Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently and moved without explanation, and victims were ignored until 2010; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp, in charge of personnel from 1977 to 2003, was named as mainly responsible. Bishop Michael Gerber said the diocese had incurred guilt and church structures had failed.
C.cite: Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexualisierter Gewalt im Bistum Fulda, final report, June 2025 (epd via evangelisch.de, 17 June 2025)

C.n: Diocese of Speyer — University of Mannheim study, part 1 (2025)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Speyer; religious orders working in it
C.cover: Accused priests were either punished individually or protected; structural problems, including weak oversight of religious orders, were ignored.
C.d: Historian Sylvia Schraut of the University of Mannheim, in a study begun in April 2023 at the initiative of the diocese's independent review commission, presented part 1 on 8 May 2025. It identified 109 accused clergy since 1946, two-thirds born before 1920; half the offences took place in the 1950s and 1960s, in church homes, lessons, confession and parish work. The church either punished accused priests individually or shielded them, and oversight of religious orders was weak. Part 2, with case analyses, is due in 2027. Separately, in 2020 the Darmstadt social court granted victim compensation to a man abused in the former Niederbronn Sisters' children's home in Speyer; he said the nuns brought children to abusers, and he and two other men independently said a former vicar general abused them there between 1963 and 1975.
C.cite: Sylvia Schraut, 'Sexueller Missbrauch im Bistum Speyer seit 1946 – Teilstudie 1', Universität Mannheim, press release 8 May 2025; epd report on the Engelsgasse children's home, 11 December 2020

C.n: Diocese of Limburg — 'Betroffene hören – Missbrauch verhindern' project (2020)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Limburg; bishops, vicars general and personnel directors
C.cover: The file review named diocesan leaders responsible for 'cover-up and silence' and found that protecting the institution guided decisions.
C.d: The Diocese of Limburg ran a project with about 70 mostly external experts from September 2019 to June 2020 as its response to the 2018 MHG study; the 415-page final report was presented on 13 June 2020 in Frankfurt's Paulskirche. Its file review covered 46 cases and found that diocesan leaders had played down the crimes and treated the accused as a threat to the clerical system rather than a danger to children. It named the leaders responsible for cover-up and silence and produced 61 measures against abuse. Survivors who took part criticised how little affected people were involved.
C.cite: Bistum Limburg, 'Betroffene hören – Missbrauch verhindern. Konsequenzen aus der MHG-Studie', final report, 13 June 2020

C.n: Archdiocese of Hamburg — University of Ulm study of abuse in Mecklenburg 1946–1989 (2023)
C.who: Catholic Church in Mecklenburg (Archdiocese of Hamburg); East German Ministry for State Security (Stasi)
C.cover: The Stasi recruited suspects as informers, so no prosecutions followed; church leaders knew, and church–state arrangements such as moving suspects to West Germany kept cases quiet.
C.d: Forensic psychiatrists at the University of Ulm led by Manuela Dudeck, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Hamburg, presented their study in Schwerin on 24 February 2023. Reviewing 1,503 church and Stasi files, they identified 19 suspects and 40 victims; the 13 victims interviewed had been about 10 years old on average when the abuse began. Parishes and church leaders knew of abuse, and the study found a culture of silence and partly active cover-up. The Stasi recruited suspects as informers and used them, so prosecutions did not follow, and church–state arrangements such as moves to West Germany kept cases quiet.
C.cite: Manuela Dudeck and Laura Rinser, Universität Ulm, study for the Archdiocese of Hamburg, 24 February 2023 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Salesians of Don Bosco, German Province — working group report (2011)
C.vn: 120 complaints; about half concern sexual abuse, half physical violence
C.who: Salesians of Don Bosco, German Province — homes and schools
C.d: A working group with internal and external members set up by the German Province of the Salesians of Don Bosco reported on 23 February 2011. It had received 120 complaints concerning Salesian facilities from 1950 into the 1980s, about half about sexual abuse and half about physical violence, against members of the order and employees. About two-thirds of the cases had been clarified, and cases were referred to prosecutors.
C.cite: Salesianer Don Boscos, Deutsche Provinz, Arbeitsgruppe zur Aufklärung von Misshandlungs- und Missbrauchsfällen, report of 23 February 2011

C.n: German Capuchin Province — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2011)
C.vn: at least 11 of the accused friars are believed to have abused minors; no total victim count
C.who: Capuchin Order, German Province (former Bavarian and Rhine-Westphalian provinces); Burghausen seminary
C.cover: Files of deceased friars appear to have been purged; before 2009 no sanctions against suspects were found; no church-law preliminary investigation was opened in any case, and the reviewers found no evidence that the province passed reports to prosecutors.
C.d: Lawyer Martin Pusch of Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the German Capuchin Province, reported on 30 November 2011. He found 32 accused friars, 19 of them accused of sexual abuse and at least 11 believed to have abused minors, mostly in schools and training institutions including the Burghausen seminary; no criminal or church-court conviction was found in any case. Files of deceased friars appeared to have been purged, and no sanctions were found before 2009, when three suspects were suspended and one elderly friar transferred. No church-law investigation was opened in any case, and before 2010 victims received no response or support.
C.cite: Martin Pusch (Westpfahl Spilker Wastl), report for the Provincial of the German Capuchin Province, 30 November 2011

C.n: Redemptorists in Germany — interim reports (2010–2024) and IPP study (2026)
C.vn: at least 90, mostly pupils
C.who: Redemptorist order in Germany — schools including the Collegium Josephinum, Bonn
C.d: Between 2010 and 2024 the Redemptorist order in Germany commissioned six interim reports on sexual violence, mainly at its schools. They documented at least 90 victims, mostly pupils, and at least 29 perpetrators from 1950 to 2011, including at the order's Collegium Josephinum grammar school in Bonn. In September 2026 the order presented a 276-page study by the Munich IPP institute (Heiner Keupp), commissioned jointly with survivors, on how it handled the cases from 2010.
C.cite: Redemptorist order, interim reports 2010–2024; IPP München (Heiner Keupp), study presented in Bonn, September 2026 (epd via evangelisch.de, 25 September 2026)

C.n: Franciscan Minorites (German province) — independent study (2024)
C.vn: one friar alone abused 20 people; many victims were children in the order's boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg
C.who: Order of Friars Minor Conventual (Minorites), German province
C.cover: Some accused abused for almost 30 years before sanctions took hold; threatened consequences were not enforced across changes of superiors.
C.d: Lawyers Petra Ladenburger and Martina Lörsch presented a 152-page study on 10 June 2024, the first independent, externally overseen study of a Catholic order in Germany under the 2021 agreement between the orders' conference (DOK) and the federal abuse commissioner. It assessed allegations against nine friars since the 1960s; one friar was accused of abusing 20 people, and many victims were children in the order's boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg. The committee overseeing the study said some accused abused for nearly 30 years before effective sanctions, because successive superiors did not enforce threatened consequences.
C.cite: Petra Ladenburger and Martina Lörsch, study for the German Province of the Franciscan Minorites, 10 June 2024 (Vatican News)

C.n: German Franciscan Province — IPP study (2026)
C.vn: more than 100, mostly minors; about 75% male; 'tip of the iceberg'
C.who: German Franciscan Province (OFM) — educational institutions incl. Vossenack school and boarding school
C.d: The Munich IPP institute, led by Peter Caspari, presented its study for the German Franciscan Province on 25 February 2026, covering the period since 1945. It identified more than 100 victims, mostly minors aged 10 to 15 when the abuse began and about three-quarters male, and 98 suspected perpetrators; most abuse took place in educational institutions. The provincial minister acknowledged structural problems and the order's guilt. A survivor from the Vossenack school accused the leadership of years of cover-up.
C.cite: IPP München (Peter Caspari), study for the Deutsche Franziskanerprovinz, 25 February 2026 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Aloisiuskolleg Bonn (Jesuit school) — Zinsmeister report (2011)
C.vn: 58 reports of abuse and other violations; authors said far from complete
C.who: Society of Jesus — Aloisiuskolleg boarding school, Bonn
C.cover: A priest responsible for more than half the reports, later rector, was never stopped.
C.d: An independent team led by Cologne law professor Julia Zinsmeister presented its report on the Jesuit Aloisiuskolleg on 15 February 2011, covering about 60 years. It received 58 reports of abuse and other violations against 23 staff, 18 Jesuit priests and 5 lay employees, most active in the 1950s and 1960s. Ten cases concerned the former headmaster, who led and lived at the school from 1968 to 2008, and would count as sexual abuse under strict criminal-law standards. The authors blamed the order's closed organisational culture.
C.cite: Julia Zinsmeister et al., final report on the Aloisiuskolleg, 15 February 2011 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Collegium Josephinum, Bad Münstereifel — Archdiocese of Cologne project report (2017)
C.vn: about 100 former pupils gave accounts; no total victim count
C.who: Archdiocese of Cologne — Collegium Josephinum boarding school (closed 1997)
C.cover: The archdiocese, as operator, set no rules for educational methods and did not monitor practice.
C.d: A project led by educational scientist Claudia Bundschuh, with Bettina Janssen as operational lead and commissioned by the Archdiocese of Cologne, published its final report on 13 September 2017. About 100 former pupils described violence at the boarding school from at least the 1950s; the report found a 'system of abuse of power' up to at least the 1970s. Seven staff, all but one priests, were accused of sexual violence and twelve of physical violence. The archdiocese set no rules and did not supervise the school.
C.cite: Claudia Bundschuh, Bettina Janssen and Arnfried Bintig, final report on the Collegium Josephinum Bad Münstereifel, 13 September 2017 (Archdiocese of Cologne press release via domradio.de)

C.n: Albertinum Gerolstein — Diocese of Trier boarding school report (2022)
C.vn: 54 former pupils came forward
C.who: Diocese of Trier — Bischöfliches Internat Albertinum, Gerolstein; its three priest-directors
C.cover: The diocese lacked effective oversight; pupils who reported beatings were not believed and survivors received no help.
C.d: Bettina Janssen and Claudia Bundschuh presented their final report of about 140 pages on the diocesan boarding school Albertinum in Gerolstein on 11 February 2022, covering 1946 until it closed in 1983. Fifty-four former pupils came forward. Violence, mostly physical but including sexualised violence, was part of daily life; all three directors, who were priests, and one lay employee committed sexualised violence. Bishop Stephan Ackermann apologised and admitted the diocese had lacked effective oversight; by February 2023 the diocese had paid more than 650,000 euros to former pupils.
C.cite: Bettina Janssen and Claudia Bundschuh, 'Gewalt am Bischöflichen Internat Albertinum Gerolstein', final report, February 2022 (epd via evangelisch.de, 12 February 2022)

C.n: Korntal Brüdergemeinde children's homes — final report (2018)
C.vn: 56 of 105 interviewees reported sexualised violence; 93 reported physical violence
C.who: Evangelische Brüdergemeinde Korntal — three children's homes in Korntal and Wilhelmsdorf
C.d: Retired judge Brigitte Baums-Stammberger and educational scientist Benno Hafeneger presented their 400-page report 'Uns wurde die Würde genommen' in Stuttgart on 7 June 2018, after 115 interviews with former residents. Of the 105 accounts used, 56 reported sexualised violence and 93 physical violence in three homes of the Protestant Brüdergemeinde in Korntal and Wilhelmsdorf from 1949 to the 1980s. A caretaker forced at least 30 children into sexual acts; a stable worker, a baker and a children's doctor were also named as serious offenders. The Brüdergemeinde apologised and paid recognition payments, usually 5,000 euros.
C.cite: Brigitte Baums-Stammberger and Benno Hafeneger, final report on the Korntal children's homes, 7 June 2018 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: West German children's cure homes ('Verschickungskinder') — Humboldt University report (2025)
C.vn: an estimated 11.4 million children (range 9.8–13.2 million) stayed in cure and recreation homes 1951–1990; the study says no count of mistreated children is possible
C.who: Children's cure homes run by welfare organisations, municipalities and private operators, financed by health and pension insurers; Deutsche Rentenversicherung, Caritas, Diakonie and German Red Cross
C.d: A Humboldt University team led by historian Alexander Nützenadel published the first nationwide report on West German children's cure homes on 15 May 2025, jointly with the German pension insurance (DRV), Caritas, Diakonie and the German Red Cross. It estimates that 11.4 million children stayed in such homes between 1951 and 1990 and describes humiliation, intimidation and violence as structural, caused by underfunding, staff shortages and inadequate supervision; many children faced physical, psychological and sexualised violence, though the study says no count is possible. No home was closed because of complaints. The four organisations expressed regret and accepted responsibility.
C.cite: Alexander Nützenadel et al., Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, research report on children's cure homes 1945–1989, 15 May 2025 (Deutsche Rentenversicherung press release; epd, 19 May 2025)

C.n: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen — review of paedophile advocacy in the party (2014–2016)
C.vn: 12 victims of child sexual abuse contacted the party's working group; 3 received payments for abuse in the Emmaus community at Dachsberg, Kamp-Lintfort, in the early 1980s
C.who: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen (federal party and Berlin branch); paedophile activist groups of the 1970s–80s
C.d: The Göttingen Institute for Democracy Research led by Franz Walter, commissioned by the Greens, presented its report in November 2014: paedophile activists got demands to legalise sex between adults and children into several Green resolutions in the 1980s, until a clear break at federal level in 1989, while in the Berlin branch the debate continued into the mid-1990s. A Berlin state-party commission reported in May 2015. The party's working group was contacted by 12 victims of child sexual abuse; three received payments for long-term abuse in the early 1980s in the Christian Emmaus community at Dachsberg in Kamp-Lintfort, where the party's institutional co-responsibility could not be ruled out. The party apologised in November 2014.
C.cite: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen, 'Aufarbeitung und Verantwortung' (2016), summarising Franz Walter et al., Göttinger Institut für Demokratieforschung (2014) and the Berlin commission report (May 2015)

C.n: Independent Commission (UKASK) study of paedosexual networks in Berlin (2021)
C.who: Paedosexual networks in Berlin; supporters among scientists, the Greens, child-rights groups and parts of the left-liberal and autonomist scene; Berlin authorities
C.cover: Authorities looked away for a long time and held victims partly responsible; in the 1960s–70s foster children were placed with paedosexual men, partly on the advice of educators.
C.d: The federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a preliminary study by Iris Hax and Sven Reiß on 24 February 2021 on paedosexual networks in Berlin from the 1970s to the 2000s. It found that groups of men who sexually exploited boys used social movements and had support from scientists, for a time from the Greens, and from child-rights groups and parts of the left-liberal and autonomist scene, while the women's movement opposed them. Authorities looked away and partly blamed victims; boys were also commercially exploited around Bahnhof Zoo. The commission called for a nationwide investigation of such networks.
C.cite: Iris Hax and Sven Reiß, preliminary study on paedosexual networks in Berlin, Unabhängige Kommission zur Aufarbeitung sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs, 24 February 2021 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Saarland University Hospital (UKS) — independent review commission (2023)
C.vn: 52 confirmed of more than 80 suspected cases
C.who: Universitätsklinikum des Saarlandes, Homburg — an assistant physician (died 2016) and hospital leadership
C.cover: The hospital and prosecutors decided not to inform potentially affected families; relatives and the public learned of the suspicions only in 2019.
C.d: An independent commission chaired by former BKA president Jörg Ziercke presented its final report on 24 May 2023 on suspected abuse at Saarland University Hospital. An assistant physician carried out medically unnecessary intimate examinations of children between 2010 and 2014; the hospital reported him at the end of 2014 and dismissed him, and the investigation ended when he died in 2016. The commission confirmed 52 of more than 80 suspected cases and found a lack of consistent leadership; the decision by the hospital and prosecutors not to inform families until 2019 was the main cause of lost trust. It recommended compensation of 5,000 to 50,000 euros per case.
C.cite: Unabhängige Aufarbeitungskommission am Universitätsklinikum des Saarlandes, final report, 24 May 2023 (epd via evangelisch.de)

C.n: Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart — diocesan abuse figures (2023)
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart — clergy, religious sisters and lay staff
C.d: The Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart's third report on investigation and recognition, with figures as of 1 September 2023 and published in October 2023, counted 207 accused (114 priests, deacons and male religious with a diocesan contract, 17 other religious priests, 54 lay people and 21 religious sisters) and 421 known victims for 1946 to 2023. Cases are handled by the diocese's abuse commission (KsM), set up in 2002. The diocese's independent review commission, formed in December 2021, published its first report in February 2023.
C.cite: Diözese Rottenburg-Stuttgart, 'Aufklärung, Aufarbeitung, Anerkennung des Leides, Prävention', 3rd edition, figures as of 1 September 2023 (press release 10 October 2023)

C.n: Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015)
C.vn: by July 2015, 362 people in Tyrol had received compensation and 159 people in Vorarlberg had received financial support since 2010
C.who: State welfare system and residential homes of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, incl. Jagdberg (Schlins), St. Martin (Schwaz), Mariatal (Kramsach), Kleinvolderberg
C.cover: The study found the institutional system produced, tolerated and failed to prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence.
C.d: A University of Innsbruck team led by Michaela Ralser, commissioned by the state governments of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, presented its overall study of welfare and residential care on 6 July 2015. It examined four state institutions in detail (Jagdberg, St. Martin, Mariatal and Kleinvolderberg) and found a total institution of isolation and dependence that produced, tolerated and did not prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence until the 1980s. By then 362 people in Tyrol and 159 in Vorarlberg had received compensation from the states since 2010.
C.cite: Michaela Ralser et al., 'Gesamtstudie zur Geschichte der Fürsorge- und Heimerziehung in Tirol und Vorarlberg', presented 6 July 2015 (Universität Innsbruck iPoint)

C.n: Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022)
C.who: Seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol (Martinsbühel, Scharnitz, Josefinum/Volders, Bubenburg/Fügen, St. Josef/Mils, Thurnfeld/Hall, Elisabethinum/Axams); Diocese of Innsbruck; Tyrolean youth welfare
C.cover: Survivors said the state youth welfare office and school authorities looked too little; church and state officials acknowledged institutional responsibility.
C.d: A commission set up in 2019 by the State of Tyrol, the Diocese of Innsbruck and religious orders, chaired by Margret Aull, presented its final report 'Demut lernen' on 7 December 2022, written by historians Ina Friedmann and Friedrich Stepanek. Based on 75 interviews, it covered seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol after 1945, where former residents described structural, physical, psychological and sexualised violence; at Martinsbühel in the 1970s one sister looked after up to 50 girls. Survivors said state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely enough. Bishop Hermann Glettler called the findings 'total pedagogical failure' in church and state institutions, and the state social affairs councillor apologised.
C.cite: Dreierkommission Martinsbühel, final report 'Demut lernen. Kindheit in konfessionellen Kinderheimen in Tirol nach 1945', 7 December 2022 (Amt der Tiroler Landesregierung press release)

C.n: Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019)
C.vn: 3,139 reports handled; 2,384 people received financial aid; sexual-abuse share not stated
C.who: City of Vienna youth welfare — municipal, church and private children's homes and foster care, incl. the Kinderübernahmestelle (KÜST)
C.d: A historians' commission led by Reinhard Sieder reported in May 2012 on Vienna's municipal, church and private children's homes after 1945, through which roughly 100,000 children passed; it described sadistic sexual abuse by some staff alongside widespread violence. The City of Vienna commissioned the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring in 2010 to handle claims of people harmed in Vienna youth welfare institutions between 1945 and 1999. Its final report (2019) records 3,139 reports and financial aid to 2,384 people, with 42.13 million euros paid directly to victims. The separate Wilhelminenberg commission is already on the map.
C.cite: Reinhard Sieder et al., historians' commission on Vienna children's homes, May 2012 (profil, 21 May 2012); Weisser Ring, Abschlussbericht 'Hilfe für Opfer von Gewalt in Einrichtungen der Wiener Jugendwohlfahrt', 2019

C.n: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
C.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
C.cover: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.
C.d: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
C.cite: Independent Special Commission, Final Report Part One (Summary Report), SOS Children's Villages, 6 June 2023; Vorarlberg Online, 12 November 2025

C.n: SOS-Kinderdorf Austria — abuse at Imst and Moosburg, founder Hermann Gmeiner, and the Griss reform commission (2025–2026)
C.vn: 8 men abused as boys by founder Hermann Gmeiner at four villages (per SOS Austria, Oct 2025); an investigation report later listed 16 suspected cases against him
C.who: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich — children's villages incl. Imst (Tyrol) and Moosburg (Carinthia); founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986)
C.cover: The allegations against Gmeiner were known internally for years (victims came forward 2013–2023) but were made public only in 2025.
C.d: After a Falter report in September 2025 on abuse by staff at Austrian SOS children's villages, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich said on 23 October 2025 that there were credible allegations that its founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986) sexually and physically abused eight boys at four villages between the 1950s and 1980s; victims had come forward from 2013 and received compensation and therapy, but the organisation had not made this public. A later investigation report listed 16 suspected cases of sexualised violence by Gmeiner. An external reform commission chaired by former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss presented its results on 25 June 2026, focusing on abuse at Moosburg and Imst, handling of earlier studies and possible cover-ups, and the lack of external oversight. Prosecutors in Klagenfurt, Innsbruck and Salzburg opened investigations.
C.cite: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich statement (dpa via Blue News, 23 October 2025); Reformkommission (Irmgard Griss), results presented 25 June 2026 (ORF); investigation report on Gmeiner (stol.it, 26 June 2026)

C.n: Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2025)
C.vn: 59 victims in proven or probable cases, 16 more unclear; 51% female
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone (South Tyrol)
C.cover: Handling of abuse cases until 2010 was a systemic failure; one priest was removed only in 2010 despite allegations from the 1960s.
C.d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, published its 631-page report on 20 January 2025, described as the first fully independent study of its kind in Italy, covering 1964 to 2023. It found 29 clerics against whom allegations were proven or highly probable, in 67 cases of sexual assault with 59 victims, plus 16 unclear cases; one priest abused girls as young as seven and was removed only in 2010. It described the handling of cases until 2010 as a general and highly systemic failure. Bishop Ivo Muser said 'every case is one too many' and that victims' suffering should fill the church with shame.
C.cite: Westpfahl Spilker Wastl (Wastl, Pusch, Gladstein, Schenke), report for the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, January 2025 (Politiko via BishopAccountability.org, 21 January 2025)

C.n: Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI) — national safeguarding reports (2022–2025)
C.vn: 89 people in 2020–21 reports; 115 alleged victims in 2023–24; 613 clergy files sent to the Vatican 2000–2022
C.who: Conferenza Episcopale Italiana — diocesan listening centres and the national child-protection service
C.cover: Critics, including Rete l'Abuso, said the reports cover only recent diocesan-desk data and omit court and Vatican cases; the first report mentions no reports to civil authorities.
C.d: The Italian Bishops' Conference published its first national report in November 2022, prepared with experts of the Università Cattolica: 80 diocesan listening centres had received 86 contacts in 2020–2021 concerning 89 people, against 68 alleged abusers, 44% of them clerics. CEI also said dioceses had sent 613 files on clerics to the Vatican's doctrine office since 2000. Its third survey, presented in May 2025, counted 115 alleged victims (64 boys, 51 girls) and 67 alleged perpetrators, 44 of them clergy, in 2023–2024. Critics said the reports are too narrow and Italy has no independent national inquiry.
C.cite: CEI, 'Proteggere, prevenire, formare' first report, 17 November 2022 (Il Post); CEI Servizio Nazionale per la tutela dei minori, third territorial survey, 28 May 2025 (Sky TG24)

C.n: Society of Jesus in Spain — report on abuse since 1927 (2021)
C.vn: 81 minors and 37 adults (118 cases)
C.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Spain — 65 of the 96 accused abused children
C.d: In January 2021 the Jesuits in Spain published a report admitting 118 cases of sexual abuse since 1927, 81 of them against children and 37 against adults. It named 96 accused Jesuits, about 1.08% of members since 1927; of the 65 who abused children, 48 had died and 17 were alive. AP described it as the first comprehensive internal inquiry into abuse by a religious order in Spain. Victims' groups criticised it for not naming perpetrators or those who covered up abuse.
C.cite: Compañía de Jesús en España, report on abuse cases since 1927, January 2021 (JURIST, January 2021; AP, Aritz Parra and Nicole Winfield, 22 January 2021)

C.n: Marist Brothers in Spain — independent commission recognises 25 victims (2020)
C.who: Marist Brothers (Hermanos Maristas) schools in Spain, incl. Barcelona
C.d: On 3 December 2020 the Marist congregation in Spain announced that an independent commission it had set up to review all cases had recognised 25 victims of sexual abuse by former teachers in its schools, with compensation reported at about 400,000 euros in total, including for time-barred cases. The Barcelona cases, from 1970 to 2010, were exposed by local press in 2016. Only one teacher, lay PE teacher Joaquín Benítez, was tried; in 2019 he was sentenced to 21 years and nine months for abusing four pupils, other complaints being time-barred.
C.cite: Hermanos Maristas, announcement of 3 December 2020 (AFP via Semanario Universidad)

C.n: Catalonia — Síndic de Greuges (ombudsman) report on child sexual abuse in the Catholic Church (2020)
C.who: Catholic religious congregations and dioceses in Catalonia
C.cover: Congregations generally did not seek out other cases or offer reparation.
C.d: A commission within the Catalan ombudsman's office (Síndic de Greuges), under Rafael Ribó, published its report on 2 October 2020. Most cases it heard concerned boys aged 5 to 17, abused repeatedly in the 1960s and 1970s on camps and excursions, on church premises and in abusers' flats, with three cases from the 1990s; documents pointed to many more victims than came forward. Religious congregations generally had not looked for other cases or offered reparation. Among seven recommendations, it asked the Catalan Parliament to create an inquiry commission, which the Parliament approved on 27 April 2022.
C.cite: Síndic de Greuges de Catalunya, report on sexual abuse of children in the Catholic Church, 2 October 2020 (betevé)

C.n: Mallorca — Consell de Mallorca commission on sexual exploitation of children in IMAS care (2021)
C.vn: about 16 cases known in January 2020
C.who: Institut Mallorquí d'Afers Socials (IMAS), the island's child-protection agency
C.d: A commission of the Consell de Mallorca, chaired by vice-president Jaume Tortella, reported on 23 April 2021 on the sexual exploitation of minors in the care of the island's child-protection agency IMAS; about 16 cases were known in January 2020, 13 of them from 2017 to early 2019. With the PP and Vox refusing to take part, it found no political, technical or criminal responsibility and no network linking the cases, matching the prosecutors' investigation. Reporting had changed in February 2020 so that suspicions go to the national police, and five cases not previously reported were sent to prosecutors. In late 2020 two men were convicted of corrupting girls in care, and in April 2022 a European Parliament Petitions Committee delegation visited Palma to examine the cases.
C.cite: Consell de Mallorca commission on minors in care, report presented 23 April 2021 (Ultima Hora)

C.n: Belgian Chamber commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church after 'Godvergeten' (2024)
C.who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
C.cover: The commission noted 58% of cases are dismissed by prosecutors and called for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' raids after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions.
C.d: The federal Chamber set up a parliamentary commission of inquiry into sexual abuse in the Church and elsewhere, chaired by Sophie De Wit (N-VA), after the 2023 VRT series 'Godvergeten'. Its final report of 2 May 2024 made 137 recommendations, including that the Church proactively trace perpetrators through its archives and give police and courts access to relevant church files, and a legal study on retroactively ending the limitation period for child sexual abuse. It called for reducing the 58% of sexual-violence cases dismissed by prosecutors, and for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' investigation after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions. It proposed an abuse commissioner, a centre of expertise and an arbitration body for time-barred cases.
C.cite: Chamber of Representatives, special commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church and elsewhere, report of 2 May 2024 (VRT NWS)

C.n: Deetman Commission — supplementary inquiry into abuse of and violence against girls in the Catholic Church (2013)
C.vn: 79 new reports, 37 of them without sexual abuse; 26 earlier reports from women reconsidered
C.who: Roman Catholic Church in the Netherlands — dioceses and religious orders
C.d: The Deetman Commission presented a supplementary inquiry on 11 March 2013 into sexual abuse of and violence against girls and young women who were minors in the Dutch Catholic Church from 1945 to 2012, after its 2011 report had found over 77% of identified victims were male. It received 79 new reports, of which 37 concerned only physical or psychological violence, and reconsidered 71 earlier reports of violence, 26 from women. It called on bishops and religious superiors to reach out to these victims; reports involving sexual abuse go to the Church's reporting point and compensation committees.
C.cite: Commissie-Deetman, aanvullend onderzoek 'Seksueel misbruik van en geweld tegen meisjes in de Rooms-Katholieke Kerk', 11 March 2013 (rkkerk.nl)

C.n: Territorial Abbey of Saint-Maurice — independent working group report (2025)
C.who: Abbey of Saint-Maurice (canons regular) and its boarding school, Valais
C.d: An independent working group formed at the request of the abbey, then under a Vatican-appointed apostolic administrator, by Neuchâtel attorney general Pierre Aubert presented its findings on 20 June 2025. Historians of the University of Fribourg (Anne-Françoise Praz, Stéphanie Roulin and others) and retired judge Claire-Lise Mayor Aubert heard about 50 witnesses and 24 clergy and examined sexual violence at the abbey and its boarding school from 1960 to 2024. They found sexualised touching by canons, ambiguous photo sessions, exhibitionism and use of child abuse material; since 1970 five criminal penalty orders had been issued against three canons and a novice, and members with ambiguous or unlawful conduct were left in office without precautions. The mandate did not cover the abbey's collège.
C.cite: Groupe de travail indépendant (Université de Fribourg), 'Violences sexuelles à l'Abbaye de Saint-Maurice 1960–2024', 20 June 2025

C.n: Malta — Church Response Team figures on clergy abuse 1991–2010
C.vn: 45 cases of abuse involving minors (not a victim count)
C.who: Catholic Church in Malta — Response Team set up by the Maltese bishops (chair Judge Victor Caruana Colombo)
C.d: In April 2010 the Maltese Curia said the Church's Response Team, set up by the bishops in 1991 and chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 remained open, four priests were found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. The convictions over St Joseph Home are already on the map.
C.cite: Archdiocese of Malta, statement on the Response Team, 13 April 2010 (Blitz Quotidiano)

C.n: Slovakia — bishops' commission evaluation report on abuse 2018–2023 (2024)
C.vn: more than 44 victims in 39 confirmed cases; likely higher
C.who: Catholic Church in Slovakia — Latin dioceses, Greek Catholic eparchies and religious orders
C.d: The Slovak bishops' commission for the protection of minors published its 'Evaluation Report 2018–2023' in March 2024, the first such report in Slovakia, counting complaints from 1990 onward. Of 68 complaints, 39 were confirmed and closed, 17 remained open, 7 could not be resolved and 5 were not confirmed; the confirmed cases involved more than 44 victims. Fifty complaints concerned Latin-rite dioceses, three Greek Catholic eparchies and 15 religious orders.
C.cite: Slovak Bishops' Conference, commission for the protection of minors, 'Evaluation Report 2018–2023', March 2024 (The Pillar via BishopAccountability.org, 6 March 2024)

C.n: Latvia — Logos Centrs child exploitation network, Riga (1999–2002 convictions)
C.vn: 67 people sexually exploited, 61 of them minors; the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors (figures from Wikipedia citing Latvijas Vēstnesis, not independently confirmed)
C.who: Logos Centrs video and model agency, Riga (director Jurijs Jurjevs)
C.d: After a September 1999 Latvian TV report, prosecutors investigated the Riga agency Logos Centrs, headed by Jurijs Jurjevs, which The Baltic Times described as a bogus modelling agency running a child pornography and prostitution ring; seven people were charged. Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors as a customer and sentenced to ten years, the maximum; pageant agency manager Ainārs Eisaks received 2.5 years; Ingus Tūns' case was tried separately. According to Wikipedia, citing Latvijas Vēstnesis and Delfi, 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited, the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors, Jurjevs received more than four years and Tūns five. Claims that senior politicians were clients were investigated and found false (see the Saeima commission record).
C.cite: The Baltic Times, 'Two child abusers get sentences, others line up', 19 October 2000; Wikipedia, 'Logos Centrs pedophilia case', citing Latvijas Vēstnesis (2000) and Delfi

C.n: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false
C.who: Saeima investigation commission chaired by MP Jānis Ādamsons; former PM Andris Šķēle, ex-justice minister Valdis Birkavs, State Revenue Service head Andrejs Sončiks (accused, cleared)
C.d: After a September 1999 TV report on the Logos Centrs case, the Saeima set up an investigation commission chaired by opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons, who on 17 February 2000 publicly linked former prime minister Andris Šķēle, former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and revenue service head Andrejs Sončiks to the paedophilia case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them, stating it was 'fully proved' that the information given to the commission about them was false. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander; in February 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats. None of the officials was charged.
C.cite: Prosecutor General's Office of Latvia, decision of 1 August 2000 (The Baltic Times, 3 August 2000); The Baltic Times, 'Court upholds verdict against Adamsons', 21 February 2007

C.n: Australian Defence Force — HMAS Leeuwin, Balcombe and ADF Cadets (Royal Commission Case Study 40)
C.vn: Defence Abuse Response Taskforce: allegations from more than 200 junior recruits aged 15-17 at HMAS Leeuwin alone
C.who: Royal Australian Navy (HMAS Leeuwin), Army Apprentice School Balcombe, Australian Air Force Cadets
C.cover: Senior staff at HMAS Leeuwin knew of the abuse and tolerated it; in 2000 a 15-year-old Air Force cadet faced disciplinary proceedings and discharge after an adult instructor's inappropriate relationship with her, which the commission said should never have happened.
C.d: The Royal Commission's Case Study 40 report (23 August 2017) found that physical and sexual abuse of child recruits was widespread at the navy base HMAS Leeuwin from the 1960s to 1972, that senior staff knew and tolerated it, and that the navy failed in its duty of care. At the Army Apprentice School, Balcombe, in the 1970s and 1980s an unofficial rank hierarchy let senior apprentices sexually and physically abuse junior ones. In the Air Force Cadets, policies from at least 2000 gave the age of consent as 14, which the commission said increased the risk of abuse. In June 2014 the Defence Abuse Response Taskforce had reported allegations from more than 200 junior recruits aged 15 to 17 at HMAS Leeuwin.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 40 (Australian Defence Force), 23 Aug 2017; Minister for Defence statement on the DART report on HMAS Leeuwin, 18 June 2014

C.n: UK cadet forces — 363 sexual abuse allegations in five years (BBC Panorama, MoD figures)
C.who: Army Cadet Force, Air Training Corps and Sea Cadets (sponsored by the Ministry of Defence)
C.cover: Former cadets and families told the BBC that officials discouraged them from going to the police.
C.d: A BBC Panorama investigation in July 2017, using Freedom of Information figures from the Ministry of Defence, found 363 allegations of sexual abuse across the army, air and sea cadet forces between 2012 and 2017, both current and historical. Of these, 282 were referred to police and 99 adult instructors were dismissed. The programme reported that the MoD had paid more than £2 million to victims and that some victims and families had been urged not to tell police. The MoD said it had robust procedures and encouraged victims to report to police.
C.cite: BBC Panorama (July 2017), reported by Forces News, 4 July 2017, citing MoD Freedom of Information figures

C.n: YMCA NSW — Royal Commission Case Study 2 (Caringbah childcare worker Jonathan Lord)
C.vn: 12 boys aged 6-11 (convicted on 29 charges, per The Leader and SBS); Australasian Leisure Management reported 13 children aged 6-11
C.who: YMCA NSW (Caringbah out-of-school-hours care and holiday programmes)
C.d: The Royal Commission's first hearing (October 2013) examined how YMCA NSW and police responded to 2011 allegations that childcare worker Jonathan Lord sexually abused children in its care at Caringbah; Lord was convicted and jailed with a minimum term of six years. The commission heard he was hired after improper reference checks and that staff did not pass concerns to senior management. Its 165-page report, published 2 July 2014, found staff training insufficient and YMCA NSW's policies deficient, and said the case 'calls into question the child safety practices of YMCA NSW'.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 2 (YMCA NSW), 2 July 2014

C.n: Amsterdam daycare abuse case (Het Hofnarretje) and the Gunning commission
C.vn: charged with abusing 67 children; admitted abusing 87 (later reports say confessed to 83)
C.who: Robert Mikelsons (childcare worker at Het Hofnarretje and Jenno's Knuffelparadijs) and his partner Richard van O.
C.cover: An anonymous tip to Meld Misdaad Anoniem in 2008 was not acted on; the Gunning commission called it a missed opportunity.
C.d: Childcare worker Robert Mikelsons abused babies and toddlers at two Amsterdam daycare centres and as a babysitter between February 2007 and January 2010. On 21 May 2012 the Amsterdam district court sentenced him to 18 years plus compulsory psychiatric detention (TBS); he was charged over 67 children and admitted abusing 87, and the appeal court raised the sentence to 19 years on 26 April 2013. His partner Richard van O. was sentenced to six years as an accessory. On 15 April 2011 a commission chaired by Louise Gunning-Schepers found that daycare centres, government bodies and others had failed, that risk signals were missed, and that a 2008 anonymous report had not been acted on.
C.cite: Amsterdam District Court verdict, 21 May 2012 (DutchNews); Commissie-Gunning report, 15 April 2011 (AT5)

C.n: Australia — 'The Forgotten Children': national inquiry into children in immigration detention
C.place: Sydney (seat of the Australian Human Rights Commission)
C.who: Australian Government immigration detention (onshore centres and Nauru regional processing centre)
C.d: The Australian Human Rights Commission's national inquiry, 'The Forgotten Children', was tabled in Federal Parliament on 11 February 2015. It reported 33 incidents of reported sexual assault in immigration detention between January 2013 and March 2014, 'the vast majority involving children'. A separate government-commissioned review by Philip Moss (March 2015) on the Nauru centre was aware of three rape allegations, one involving a minor, and confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child.
C.cite: Australian Human Rights Commission, The Forgotten Children: National Inquiry into Children in Immigration Detention 2014, tabled 11 Feb 2015 (summarised in Medical Journal of Australia); Moss Review, March 2015 (Al Jazeera)

C.n: United States — 4,556 sexual abuse complaints from unaccompanied migrant children in ORR shelters (2014-2018)
C.place: Washington, D.C. (Office of Refugee Resettlement, HHS)
C.who: Office of Refugee Resettlement (HHS) and contracted shelters for unaccompanied migrant children
C.d: HHS records released in February 2019 by Rep. Ted Deutch showed 4,556 complaints of sexual abuse reported to the Office of Refugee Resettlement by unaccompanied migrant children in its care between October 2014 and July 2018. The Justice Department received 1,303 such complaints in fiscal years 2015-2018, of which 178 involved adult staff at the facilities. HHS said the figures were mischaracterised and that none of the allegations involved federal ORR staff.
C.cite: HHS/ORR documents on sexual assaults FY2015-18, released by Rep. Ted Deutch, 26 Feb 2019 (CBS News)

C.n: Victoria — Board of Inquiry into historical child sexual abuse at Beaumaris Primary School and other government schools (2024)
C.vn: the board said the four teachers it focused on are believed to have abused more than 100 students; more than 120 victim-survivors, secondary victims and others came forward
C.who: Victorian Department of Education; Beaumaris Primary School and 23 other government schools
C.cover: Board found a culture of covering up child sexual abuse in the Department of Education to protect the system's reputation; a teacher convicted and found guilty of misconduct in the 1980s was moved into administration and banned from teaching for only three years
C.d: A Victorian Government Board of Inquiry, set up after reports of abuse at Beaumaris Primary School, tabled its final report in Parliament on 6 March 2024. It examined the school from 1960 to 1994 (abuse there was concentrated in 1971–72) and was widened to 23 other government schools. It focused on four teachers, out of six relevant staff, who are believed to have abused more than 100 students, mostly boys aged 9 to 12. The board found the department 'woefully failed to protect children', had no policies for handling allegations or convictions, and covered up abuse. It made nine recommendations, including a parliamentary apology and accountability processes for historical abuse in all state schools.
C.cite: Board of Inquiry into Historical Child Sexual Abuse in Beaumaris Primary School and Certain Other Government Schools, final report tabled 6 March 2024, as reported by AAP and EducationHQ

C.n: Queensland — Crime and Misconduct Commission inquiry into abuse of children in foster care, 'Protecting children' (2004)
C.who: Queensland Department of Families; foster care and child protection system
C.d: In late May 2003 a woman told a Department of Families office that she had been sexually abused for 13 years in foster care by a family member who was an approved foster carer and by visitors to the household, and that other children placed with the family were also abused. In July 2003 the Premier referred concerns about the foster care system to the Crime and Misconduct Commission, which audited abuse notifications against current carers and held public hearings from 13 October 2003. Its report, released in January 2004, found the department's response 'completely inadequate' at most of nine points where children could have been protected, and concluded that the child protection system had failed Queensland children. It made 110 recommendations, including creating a separate Department of Child Safety and a Child Guardian.
C.cite: Crime and Misconduct Commission (Queensland), 'Protecting children: an inquiry into abuse of children in foster care', January 2004 (report summary)

C.n: Tasmania — Ombudsman's review of claims of abuse in state care, 'Listen to the Children' (2004)
C.vn: 1,848 eligible claimants were accepted by the Abuse in State Care program (2003–2013) that followed the review; this counts all forms of abuse, not only sexual abuse
C.who: Tasmanian state care: state, church and charitable homes (including Ashley, Rochebank, Clarendon, Kennerley, Glenara and Mt St Canice) and foster care
C.d: After a former state ward spoke publicly in July 2003 about abuse in state care, the Tasmanian Ombudsman reviewed claims from adults who had been abused as children in state care, publishing 'Listen to the Children' in November 2004 and a Phase 2 final report in June 2006. The review covered state, church and charitable homes and foster care, where sexual abuse from the 1950s to the 1970s had been described. It led to the state's Abuse in State Care program (2003–2013), which accepted 1,848 claimants and paid between $35,000 and $60,000 each. Claimants who accepted a payment had to waive future legal action against the government. Tasmania's 2023 Commission of Inquiry later found that allegations against staff and carers revealed through the program had not been acted on.
C.cite: Ombudsman Tasmania, 'Listen to the Children: Review of Claims of Abuse from Adults in State Care as Children', November 2004 (CLAN library catalogue); Victorian Government redress research summary (2022); Tasmanian Times; Canberra Times on the 2023 Commission of Inquiry

C.n: Anglican Church of Australia — Parkinson study of reported child sexual abuse, 17 dioceses (2009)
C.vn: 180 complainants in 191 reported cases, 1990–2008; the report describes them as reports, not confirmed incidents
C.who: Anglican Church of Australia (17 of 23 dioceses)
C.d: The Anglican Church of Australia's Professional Standards Commission asked for this study after the 2004 General Synod; University of Sydney researchers Patrick Parkinson, Kim Oates and Amanda Jayakody published it in May 2009. It counted 191 cases of alleged child sexual abuse reported to 17 of the 23 dioceses between 1990 and 2008, made by 180 complainants against 135 people. Nearly two-thirds of the accused were clergy or candidates for ordination, about three-quarters of complainants were male, and on average 23 years passed between the abuse and the complaint. Eight percent of cases were never investigated; of 44 cases known to have gone to court, 53% ended in conviction.
C.cite: P. Parkinson, K. Oates, A. Jayakody, 'Study of Reported Child Sexual Abuse in the Anglican Church', commissioned by the Professional Standards Commission of the General Synod of the Anglican Church of Australia, May 2009 (full report, BishopAccountability.org copy); APO summary

C.n: New Zealand — Confidential Listening and Assistance Service final report, 'Some memories never fade' (2015)
C.vn: 1,103 participants who were in state care before 1992; abuse heard included physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse and neglect
C.who: New Zealand state care: residential special education, health and welfare institutions
C.d: The New Zealand Government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, chaired by Judge Carolyn Henwood, in 2008 to hear people who had been abused or neglected in state care before 1992. It heard 1,103 participants and finished in June 2015; its final report, 'Some memories never fade', was released under the Official Information Act in August 2015. The panel described 'an alarming amount of abuse and neglect, with extreme levels of violence', including physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse, across the 50 years before 1992, and said much of it was preventable with better oversight.
C.cite: Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, 'Some memories never fade: Final Report', 2015 (Department of Internal Affairs); NZ Family Violence Clearinghouse, 27 August 2015

C.n: Charity Commission statutory inquiry — Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain (Jehovah's Witnesses), 2014–2023
C.place: Mill Hill, London (Watch Tower Britain headquarters during the inquiry)
C.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain; Jehovah's Witness congregations in Britain (now under the Kingdom Hall Trust)
C.cover: Commission found trustees were not as straightforward or transparent as they should have been about who held safeguarding responsibility; repeated legal challenges 'substantially constrained' the inquiry (insufficient evidence of deliberate obstruction)
C.d: The Charity Commission for England and Wales opened a statutory inquiry into the national Jehovah's Witness charity in May 2014 over its safeguarding policy, after a 2007 inquiry into a London congregation found it had no child protection policy and the NSPCC found in 2013 that the national policy conflicted with UK law and guidance. Watch Tower challenged the inquiry in the courts; the Supreme Court refused it permission to appeal in December 2016, and a tribunal judge said its delays created 'ongoing risks' to children. The Commission's report of 4 August 2023 closed the inquiry because responsibility for safeguarding in more than 1,000 congregations had passed to the Kingdom Hall Trust, which it placed under a compliance case. Jehovah's Witness organisations had reported 67 allegations of child sexual abuse against 67 people for 2009–2019 to IICSA.
C.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, 'Charity inquiry: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain', 4 August 2023; Civil Society News, 4 August 2023

C.n: Rotherham — IOPC Operation Linden report on South Yorkshire Police (2022)
C.who: South Yorkshire Police
C.cover: IOPC found significant failures by South Yorkshire Police to protect children from organised grooming; 8 officers had a case to answer for misconduct and 6 for gross misconduct; 43 of 164 complaint allegations were upheld
C.d: The Independent Office for Police Conduct published its Operation Linden report on 22 June 2022, after 91 investigations (begun 2014–2018) into South Yorkshire Police's response to child sexual exploitation in Rotherham from 1997 to 2013. The investigations covered 265 allegations from 51 complainants, 44 of them survivors, and the conduct of 47 officers. Eight officers had a case to answer for misconduct and six for gross misconduct; many had retired, five officers received sanctions from management action to a final written warning, and a sixth officer's misconduct case was found not proven at a 2022 hearing. The IOPC found the force was not equipped to deal with organised grooming at the scale it met in Rotherham and failed to protect vulnerable children.
C.cite: Independent Office for Police Conduct, 'The Operation Linden Report', 22 June 2022

C.n: South Yorkshire — Drew review of South Yorkshire Police's handling of child sexual exploitation (2016)
C.who: South Yorkshire Police
C.d: South Yorkshire's Police and Crime Commissioner, Alan Billings, commissioned Professor John Drew to review the force's handling of child sexual exploitation after concerns that Sheffield had seen failings similar to Rotherham's. The review, published on 23 March 2016, found the force had confronted 'a raft of weaknesses' in its earlier approach and had made strong progress over the previous three years. Drew said his picture was incomplete because he could not examine about 200 IPCC complaints about officers linked to Rotherham or speak to witnesses in ongoing criminal cases. The outgoing chief constable said the force had charged 124 people with child sexual exploitation offences since the 2014 Jay report.
C.cite: Independent review of South Yorkshire Police's handling of child sexual exploitation (Drew Review), commissioned by the South Yorkshire Police and Crime Commissioner, 23 March 2016, as reported by the Sheffield Telegraph

C.n: IICSA — sexual abuse of children in custodial institutions, 2009–2017
C.vn: More than 1,000 incidents of alleged sexual abuse in custody were reported between 2009 and 2017; this is a count of incidents, not of children.
C.who: Young offender institutions and secure training centres in England and Wales (incl. Medway and Rainsbrook STCs)
C.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its report on children in custodial institutions on 28 February 2019, after public hearings on 9–20 July 2018. It found that more than 1,000 incidents of alleged sexual abuse were reported in custody from 2009 to 2017, far more than official figures showed, and that children in young offender institutions and secure training centres remained at risk. Recent cases included staff touching detainees during searches and restraint; adult survivors also described abuse in custody decades earlier.
C.cite: IICSA, Sexual Abuse of Children in Custodial Institutions: 2009–2017, Investigation Report, 28 February 2019

C.n: IICSA — the internet and child sexual abuse (2020)
C.who: Online platforms and services (Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat named); UK government and law enforcement
C.d: IICSA's report on the internet, published 12 March 2020, found that millions of indecent images of children are in circulation and that most are on mainstream platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat, not only the dark web. It cited BT data of more than 30,000 attempts every 24 hours to view abuse material, and an NSPCC estimate that about 500,000 men in the UK had viewed such images. It recommended pre-screening of uploads, stricter age verification and international action to remove images hosted abroad.
C.cite: IICSA, The Internet, Investigation Report, 12 March 2020 (figures as summarised by Switalskis solicitors)

C.n: IICSA — sexual abuse in residential, boarding, music and special schools (2022)
C.who: Boarding schools, residential special schools and specialist music schools in England and Wales; school inspectorates and the Teaching Regulation Agency
C.d: IICSA's residential schools report (March 2022, over 220 pages) covered music and residential special schools in phase 1 and day and boarding schools in phase 2. It found that boarding pupils, children with special needs and pupils in one-to-one music teaching were especially exposed to abuse by adults and peers, and that school reputations were sometimes put before victims. It found weaknesses in inspection, teacher regulation and DBS checks and made recommendations in seven areas.
C.cite: IICSA, Sexual abuse and exploitation of children in residential schools, Investigation Report, March 2022 (summary by Farrer & Co)

C.n: IICSA — child sexual exploitation by organised networks (six areas, 2022)
C.place: England and Wales (St Helens, Tower Hamlets, Swansea, Durham, Bristol, Warwickshire)
C.who: Organised networks exploiting children; local authorities and police forces in six case-study areas
C.cover: Victims were sometimes treated as offenders while perpetrators were often not investigated or prosecuted.
C.d: IICSA's report of 1 February 2022 examined St Helens, Tower Hamlets, Swansea, Durham, Bristol and Warwickshire and found that network exploitation occurs in all parts of England and Wales and that councils and police showed extensive failures. Officials had wrongly assumed exploitation was declining; it had become more hidden, including through phones, apps and live-streaming for payment. None of the six areas recorded the ethnicity of victims or alleged perpetrators. It made six recommendations, including mandatory data collection.
C.cite: IICSA, Child sexual exploitation by organised networks, Investigation Report, 1 February 2022 (HC 1059)

C.n: IICSA — Ealing Abbey and St Benedict's School (Benedictine)
C.vn: Since 2003 four staff connected to St Benedict's were convicted of offences involving more than 20 children; at least 18 further allegations were received.
C.who: Ealing Abbey (English Benedictine Congregation) and St Benedict's School
C.cover: IICSA found a culture of cover-up and denial; very senior figures at the school or abbey were perpetrators and staff were warned to say nothing; Abbot Martin Shipperlee's handling of allegations showed serious shortcomings.
C.d: IICSA's report of 24 October 2019 found abuse at St Benedict's School over more than 30 years, in a 'sadistic and predatory' atmosphere where harsh physical punishment often led to sexual abuse. Since 2003 four staff connected to the school had been convicted of offences against more than 20 children, and the inquiry received at least 18 further allegations against them and eight other monks and teachers. It found serious shortcomings in Abbot Martin Shipperlee's handling of allegations; he resigned during the investigation, saying some of the failings were his.
C.cite: IICSA, Roman Catholic Church: English Benedictine Congregation case study — Ealing Abbey and St Benedict's School, 24 October 2019

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — child migrants sent from Scotland (Case Study 8)
C.who: Charities, religious orders and governments that ran child migration schemes from Scotland to Canada and Australia
C.d: Lady Smith published the first volume of findings on child migration on 21 March 2023 and a second volume in September 2023. She found that many thousands of children were sent from Scotland, mainly to Canada and later Australia, and that some were sexually abused at their destinations, including by men in holy orders and by members of a paedophile ring. About 80,000 children were sent from the UK to Canada by 1920 and about 7,000 to Australia between 1912 and 1970; 45 people gave evidence.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 8, Volume 1 (21 March 2023) and Volume 2 (28 September 2023)
