C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Morrison's Academy, Crieff
C.who: Morrison's Academy boarding houses
C.d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's eleventh set of findings, published on 5 March 2024, covered boarding at Morrison's Academy from 1945 to 2007, when it stopped taking boarders. Lady Smith found children were abused, mainly physically and emotionally, with some sexual abuse, including by a few older pupils. Boarding houses could operate as separate 'fiefdoms' without adequate oversight by school management until the 1990s, and a strong culture of not reporting discouraged children from speaking up.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 9 findings: Morrison's Academy, March 2024

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Queen Victoria School, Dunblane (military boarding school)
C.who: Queen Victoria School (Ministry of Defence boarding school for children of service personnel)
C.d: The inquiry's thirteenth volume of findings, published 22 October 2024, found 'dreadful abuse' at Queen Victoria School, especially from the late 1950s to the early 1990s, with weak oversight and a military culture of silence. A teacher employed 1973–1993 groomed and sexually abused several primary-age boys and the school did not act on his well-known behaviour. A drumming instructor sexually abused seven female pupils between 2011 and 2019, after child protection systems were in place.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 9 findings: Queen Victoria School, 22 October 2024

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Keil School, Dumbarton
C.who: Keil School (closed 2000); Mackinnon-Macneill Trust
C.cover: After a parent complained early on about the physics teacher's behaviour, the problem was covered up by headmaster Christopher Tongue and other senior staff.
C.d: The fifteenth volume of findings, published 20 August 2025, found abusive practices normalised at Keil School from the late 1950s to the 1980s. Physics teacher William Bain (at Keil 1987–2000) sexually abused many children, some almost daily, after a parent's early complaint was covered up by the headmaster and senior staff; Bain was convicted in 2016 and again on 30 June 2025. An English teacher, David Gutteridge, was convicted in 2024 of abusing a pupil. Publication was delayed at the Crown's request until Bain's trial ended.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 9 findings: Keil School, 20 August 2025

C.n: Scotland — Shaw historical abuse systemic review (residential care 1950–1995)
C.who: Residential schools and children's homes in Scotland (e.g. Nazareth House Kilmarnock, Quarriers Village); successive governments and local authorities
C.d: Tom Shaw, former chief inspector of education in Northern Ireland, reviewed for the Scottish Executive the laws, rules and records governing residential schools and children's homes from 1950 to 1995; his report was published in November 2007. He found the regulations were 'extensive and in many respects impressive' but that successive governments and authorities failed to make sure they were followed, and that abuse would likely have been less common had they been honoured. About 35 former residents were interviewed and about 80 other people gave evidence. He recommended a national task group, a centre for former residents and new law on children's home records.
C.cite: Historical Abuse Systemic Review (Tom Shaw) for the Scottish Executive, November 2007; The Scotsman; Community Care

C.n: Kerelaw residential school and secure unit, Stevenston — Frizzell inquiry
C.vn: Glasgow City Council reported 350–400 allegations from 159 people.
C.who: Kerelaw residential school and secure unit, run by Glasgow City Council from 1996
C.d: The Scottish Government commissioned Eddie Frizzell to inquire into Kerelaw in November 2007; his report was published in May 2009. It found abuse did take place, physical abuse was prevalent, complaints were not consistently followed up, and there were significant failures of management and leadership linked to Glasgow City Council's neglect of the school. Two staff were convicted in 2006, one receiving 10 years for 18 offences, and 14 staff were dismissed. The council had reported 350–400 allegations from 159 people.
C.cite: Independent Inquiry into Abuse at Kerelaw Residential School and Secure Unit (Frizzell), May 2009, via Scottish Law blog 12 May 2009

C.n: Catholic Church in Scotland — McLellan Commission (2015)
C.who: Catholic Church in Scotland (Bishops' Conference of Scotland)
C.cover: The report condemned a 'culture of secrecy and cover-up' that let abuse stay hidden.
C.d: At the invitation of the Bishops' Conference of Scotland, former Church of Scotland Moderator Andrew McLellan chaired a commission reviewing the Catholic Church's safeguarding policy and practice; its 99-page report was published on 18 August 2015. It called abuse 'the greatest challenge facing the whole Catholic Church in Scotland', condemned a 'culture of secrecy and cover-up', said the Church had not made significant structural changes, and made eight key recommendations. Archbishop Philip Tartaglia offered a 'profound apology' to victims.
C.cite: A Review of the Current Safeguarding Policies, Procedures and Practice within the Catholic Church in Scotland (McLellan Report), 18 August 2015; The Tablet, 18 August 2015; CathNews NZ, 21 August 2015

C.n: Scottish FA — Independent Review of Sexual Abuse in Scottish Football (2021)
C.who: Scottish football: Scottish FA and clubs including Celtic, Rangers and Hibernian (named among clubs asked to apologise)
C.d: The independent review chaired by Martin Henry, commissioned by the Scottish FA, published its final report on 11 February 2021, having been held back from 2018 until related criminal proceedings ended. It examined non-recent abuse mainly from the 1970s to the early 1990s and found that adults with a sexual interest in children moved easily through Scottish football and kept their activities hidden, with flawed decisions that sometimes meant little or no action. 33 people gave personal accounts; the review urged clubs including Celtic, Rangers and Hibernian to apologise publicly, and the Scottish FA apologised.
C.cite: Independent Review of Sexual Abuse in Scottish Football, final report, 11 February 2021

C.n: Northern Ireland — Marshall independent inquiry into child sexual exploitation (2014)
C.vn: 100–145 children identified at significant risk; the report said the real number was likely 'significantly higher'.
C.who: Individuals and groups exploiting children in Northern Ireland, some using purported paramilitary links; children in residential care
C.d: Health minister Edwin Poots commissioned Professor Kathleen Marshall after the PSNI said in September 2013 it was investigating the suspected exploitation of 22 young people. Her report, published 18 November 2014, identified 100 to 145 children at significant risk of sexual exploitation and said the real number was likely much higher. It found individuals with purported paramilitary links used fear to exploit young people, but no targeting by paramilitary groups as such, and no evidence of cover-up. It made 17 key recommendations.
C.cite: Child Sexual Exploitation in Northern Ireland: Report of the Independent Inquiry (Marshall), 18 November 2014; Irish Times

C.n: Clwyd children's homes — Jillings report (1996, published 2013)
C.vn: At least 24 victims identified; 3,755 witness statements were taken by North Wales Police.
C.who: Clwyd County Council children's homes; North Wales Police
C.cover: Compiled in 1996 but withheld for 17 years; the panel said agencies gave limited information and sometimes refused to meet it; North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers.
C.d: John Jillings led an investigation into abuse in Clwyd County Council's children's homes; the report was finished in 1996, withheld because the council's insurers feared compensation claims, and published in redacted form in July 2013. It found abuse in Clwyd homes was 'extensive and has taken place over a substantial number of years' and that responses were 'too little and too late'. It criticised North Wales Police for investigating allegations against its own officers and said the council and other agencies gave limited information, some refusing to meet the panel. It called for a judicial inquiry; the Waterhouse tribunal later examined the wider abuse.
C.cite: Jillings report on Clwyd children's homes (1996), published by the six North Wales councils, July 2013; The Scotsman

C.n: Macur Review of the Waterhouse Inquiry (North Wales, 2016)
C.who: Waterhouse Inquiry (Lost in Care); North Wales children's homes
C.d: The UK government set up the Macur Review in 2012 to check whether the Waterhouse Inquiry into abuse in North Wales children's homes had been given all relevant material and had investigated within its terms. Lady Justice Macur reported in March 2016 and found no evidence of significant failings that would undermine Waterhouse's findings. She made six recommendations, the last advising caution about re-opening past inquiries.
C.cite: The Report of the Macur Review, 17 March 2016 (UK Government); ITV News, 17 March 2016; recommendations count via Wikipedia

C.n: Clywch inquiry — Children's Commissioner for Wales on Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen
C.who: Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen (secondary school); Mid Glamorgan County Council education department
C.cover: In 1991 an education officer failed to make a child protection referral despite pupils' statements; the director of education obstructed a proper investigation, issued a misleading statement and let the teacher resign without action.
C.d: The first inquiry by the Children's Commissioner for Wales, Peter Clarke, published in 2004, concluded that drama teacher John Owen committed serious acts of sexual impropriety against pupils at Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen. Owen was charged in September 2001 after four former pupils went to police and was found dead in October 2001, before trial. The commissioner found that when sixth-formers complained in 1991 the Mid Glamorgan education officer made no child protection referral, and that the county's director of education obstructed a proper investigation and issued a misleading statement; Owen was allowed to resign without disciplinary action. It recommended independent school disciplinary tribunals for Wales and an independent children's counselling service.
C.cite: Children's Commissioner for Wales, Clywch: Report of the examination of the Children's Commissioner for Wales into allegations of child sexual abuse in a school setting, 2004; Community Care

C.n: Leicestershire children's homes — Frank Beck and the Kirkwood Inquiry
C.place: Leicestershire (The Poplars, Ratcliffe Road, The Beeches)
C.vn: Beck's 1991 sentencing covered assaults on more than 100 children; police took statements from nearly 400.
C.who: Leicestershire County Council Social Services; officer-in-charge Frank Beck
C.d: Frank Beck ran three Leicestershire council children's homes, The Poplars, Ratcliffe Road and The Beeches, between 1973 and 1986, and resigned in March 1986 after two male residential social workers complained of sexual advances. On 29 November 1991 he received five life sentences for assaults on more than 100 children; police took statements from nearly 400 children. The Leicestershire inquiry chaired by Andrew Kirkwood QC, reported in 1993, was strongly critical of the management of the county's social services, finding that early warnings were ignored, supervision was absent and complaints were poorly investigated. Its hearings were held in private.
C.cite: The Leicestershire Inquiry 1992 (Andrew Kirkwood QC), published 1993; Leicester Crown Court verdict 29 Nov 1991 (via Wikipedia 'Frank Beck')

C.n: Utting review 'People Like Us' — safeguards for children living away from home (1997)
C.place: England and Wales (Department of Health, London)
C.who: Children's homes, foster care, boarding and special schools, penal institutions in England and Wales
C.d: After allegations of widespread ill-treatment in children's homes dating back to the 1970s, the government asked Sir William Utting, former chief inspector of social services, to review safeguards for all children living away from home. His 1997 report found safeguards stronger than a decade earlier but said children in prison and in private foster care were not properly protected and that abuse of disabled children was overlooked; it called persistent sexual abusers 'a scourge of childhood'. It made 159 recommendations, leading to the Quality Protects programme.
C.cite: People Like Us: The Report of the Review of the Safeguards for Children Living Away from Home (Utting), 1997; Community Care

C.n: UK government study of 'satanic ritual abuse' claims — La Fontaine report (1994)
C.who: Claims of organised satanic/ritual abuse made in 84 cases, including those that led to removals of children in Rochdale and Orkney
C.d: Health Secretary Virginia Bottomley commissioned anthropologist Jean La Fontaine in 1991 after children were removed from homes in Rochdale and Orkney on claims of ritual abuse. Her report, made public on 3 June 1994, examined 84 cases and found no evidence supporting any allegation of satanic abuse. Only three claims of 'ritual' abuse were substantiated, and she said even those did not merit that description.
C.cite: J. S. La Fontaine, The Extent and Nature of Organised and Ritual Abuse, Department of Health, 1994; Cult Education Institute archive of 3 June 1994 report

C.n: Wanless–Whittam review — Home Office files on organised abuse claims (2014)
C.who: Home Office; Geoffrey Dickens MP's 1980s dossier; Paedophile Information Exchange funding claims
C.cover: 114 relevant Home Office files were missing, lost or destroyed; the review could not rule out that some were removed to hide abuse.
C.d: Peter Wanless and Richard Whittam QC reviewed, for the Home Secretary, how the Home Office handled information about organised child abuse in the 1980s, including Geoffrey Dickens MP's dossier. Their report, submitted 15 October 2014 and published 11 November 2014, found no evidence of an organised Home Office effort to hide child abuse, but said 114 files were missing, lost or destroyed and the imperfect records meant removal to hide abuse could not be ruled out. It found nothing to support claims that the Home Office funded the Paedophile Information Exchange.
C.cite: An Independent Review of Two Home Office Commissioned Independent Reviews Looking at Information Held in Connection with Child Abuse from 1979–1999 (Wanless and Whittam), November 2014; The Scotsman

C.n: Savile in schools and children's homes — 14 investigations with independent oversight (2015)
C.who: 14 councils, charities and schools (incl. Barnardo's, Action for Children, Henshaws Society for Blind People, Sevenoaks School) named in information about Jimmy Savile
C.d: After Michael Gove's statement of 27 March 2014, 14 investigations were carried out by councils, institutions and successor organisations into information linking Jimmy Savile to their children's homes and schools in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s. The Department for Education statement of 26 February 2015 reported that none reached firm conclusions: many informants were judged credible, but there was not enough corroborating evidence for definite findings. Lucy Scott-Moncrieff's independent oversight found the investigations had been conducted in an appropriate and robust fashion.
C.cite: Independent oversight of investigations into matters relating to Jimmy Savile at schools and children's homes (Scott-Moncrieff), DfE written statement, 26 February 2015

C.n: Children's Commissioner for England — inquiry into sexual exploitation in gangs and groups (2012–13)
C.place: England (Office of the Children's Commissioner, London)
C.vn: 2,409 children confirmed as victims in the 14 months August 2010 – October 2011; a further 16,500 judged at high risk.
C.who: Gangs and groups sexually exploiting children across England
C.d: The Office of the Children's Commissioner's inquiry, supported by the University of Bedfordshire, published interim findings on 21 November 2012. It identified 2,409 children confirmed as victims of sexual exploitation by gangs and groups in the 14 months from August 2010 to October 2011, and a further 16,500 at risk. It recorded 1,514 perpetrators of varied ethnicity (545 white, 415 Asian, 244 black, the rest not recorded) and listed warning signs professionals should act on, such as running away, self-harm and repeated sexually transmitted infections. The final report followed in 2013.
C.cite: Office of the Children's Commissioner, 'I thought I was the only one': Inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation in Gangs and Groups, interim report, 21 November 2012; Children & Young People Now

C.n: CEOP thematic assessment 'Out of mind, out of sight' — localised grooming (2011)
C.who: Groups grooming children in person ('localised grooming'); Local Safeguarding Children Boards
C.d: The Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre announced in January 2011 a thematic assessment of 'localised grooming' and published 'Out of mind, out of sight' later that year. It recorded 2,379 offenders since the start of 2008, mostly men aged 18 to 24 (38% white, 26% Asian, 3% black, ethnicity unknown in 32%), with about 90% of victims white. It found about two-thirds of Local Safeguarding Children Boards were not meeting national guidance and that victims did not expect to be believed. CEOP warned the data were not comprehensive enough to draw firm conclusions.
C.cite: CEOP, Out of Mind, Out of Sight: Breaking down the barriers to understanding child sexual exploitation, 2011; Yorkshire Post

C.n: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee — child sexual exploitation and localised grooming (2013)
C.who: Police, social services and the Crown Prosecution Service; Rochdale and Rotherham councils
C.d: The Home Affairs Committee's report of 10 June 2013 (HC 68-I) found that police, social services and the Crown Prosecution Service had failed vulnerable children in some areas and that this was still happening across the country. It found Rochdale and Rotherham councils slow to recognise organised abuse of children, many in council care, and blamed a lack of professional curiosity. It described a model of localised grooming involving mainly Pakistani-heritage men targeting young white girls but warned against focusing on that model alone, and recommended court reforms.
C.cite: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Child sexual exploitation and the response to localised grooming, Second Report of Session 2013–14, HC 68-I, 10 June 2013

C.n: Rotherham — Casey inspection of the council (2015)
C.who: Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council
C.cover: Inspectors found the council went to 'some lengths' to cover up information and silence whistleblowers, and used severance payments and compromise agreements instead of holding staff to account.
C.d: Louise Casey's government-ordered inspection, published 4 February 2015, judged Rotherham council 'not fit for purpose' and in denial about continuing failures after the Jay report. It found the council still treated child sexual exploitation as a social care issue, could not assure the public that taxi licence holders were fit and proper (86% of audited complaint investigations were inadequate), and had covered up information and silenced whistleblowers. The council leader and cabinet resigned and the government sent in commissioners.
C.cite: Report of Inspection of Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council (Louise Casey), 4 February 2015; Children & Young People Now

C.n: Manchester — Operation Augusta assurance review (2020)
C.vn: At least 57 victims and 97 potential suspects identified by Operation Augusta; the later Operation Green Jacket identified 53 potential victims, 48 of them in council care.
C.who: Greater Manchester Police; Manchester City Council children's homes; groups of men exploiting girls in care
C.cover: Senior officers closed the investigation in July 2005; minutes of the meetings on its closure disappeared and several officials declined to cooperate with the review.
C.d: An assurance review commissioned by Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, published 14 January 2020, found that Operation Augusta, set up in 2004 after the death of a 15-year-old girl in council care, had identified at least 57 victims and 97 potential suspects before senior officers closed it in July 2005. Allegations of rape and abuse were not followed up and very few perpetrators were brought to justice; some suspects visited council children's homes apparently with staff knowledge. Minutes of the closure meetings were missing.
C.cite: Greater Manchester Combined Authority, An Assurance Review of Operation Augusta (Newsam and Ridgway), January 2020; ITV News, 14 January 2020

C.n: Ofsted review of sexual abuse in schools and colleges (2021)
C.who: Schools and colleges in England (state and private)
C.d: After thousands of anonymous accounts were posted to the Everyone's Invited website, the government asked Ofsted to review sexual abuse in schools and colleges. Its report of 10 June 2021, based on visits to 32 state and private schools and colleges and talks with more than 900 young people, found sexual harassment had become normalised: 79% of girls said sexual assault of any kind happens 'a lot' or 'sometimes' between peers and 64% said so of unwanted touching. Many teachers underestimated the problem and pupils saw no point in reporting.
C.cite: Ofsted, Review of sexual abuse in schools and colleges, 10 June 2021; ITV News

C.n: Church of England — second Past Cases Review (PCR2, 2022)
C.vn: 383 new cases; 168 involved children, 149 vulnerable adults, 27 both, 39 unrecorded.
C.who: Church of England dioceses, cathedrals and national institutions
C.cover: Allegations were often handled informally, without investigation, records or referral to safeguarding professionals.
C.d: The Church of England's second Past Cases Review, reported nationally on 5 October 2022, examined more than 75,000 files, some from the 1940s, and identified 383 new cases: 168 involved children, 149 vulnerable adults and 27 both. 242 cases involved clergy, 53 other church officers and 41 volunteers working with children. It found allegations had often been handled informally without proper investigation or referral, and made 26 national recommendations. The archbishops apologised.
C.cite: Church of England, Past Cases Review 2: national report, 5 October 2022

C.n: Isle of Man — Knottfield children's home (Tynwald committee report)
C.who: Knottfield children's home (Isle of Man Government); house parent Joseph Marshall
C.d: A Tynwald scrutiny committee (Social Affairs Policy Review Committee) chaired by David Cretney reported on 6 October 2018 on the 'horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse' by Joseph Marshall while he ran Knottfield children's home with his wife between 1973 and 1983, and made 11 recommendations. Marshall had been convicted of 13 offences relating to Knottfield in 1992 and was jailed for six years in April 2022 for sexually abusing two boys there. The report was withdrawn during the criminal case; the Isle of Man Government apologised on 16 January 2023 for mistakes that contributed to the abuse and supported all 11 recommendations.
C.cite: Tynwald Social Affairs Policy Review Committee report on Knottfield, October 2018; Isle of Man Government statement, 16 January 2023; Manx Radio

C.n: Ireland — National Board's safeguarding reviews of every Catholic diocese and order (2011–2017), incl. Raphoe
C.place: All dioceses on the island of Ireland (National Board, Maynooth); Raphoe review covers Co. Donegal
C.vn: Raphoe: 52 allegations against 14 priests since 1975; four priests convicted. Other dioceses reported separately (e.g. Kerry 67 allegations, Down and Connor 59).
C.who: Catholic dioceses and religious congregations in Ireland and Northern Ireland; National Board for Safeguarding Children in the Catholic Church
C.cover: Raphoe: the review found 'significant' errors by bishops, with frequent delays in reporting allegations or none at all, and victims' needs ignored to protect the Church's reputation (Bishop Boyce's statement).
C.d: The Catholic Church's National Board for Safeguarding Children reviewed every diocese on the island of Ireland and the religious orders that ran schools and institutions, publishing in tranches from 30 November 2011 to 2017. The first tranche included Raphoe, where 52 allegations had been made against 14 priests since 1975 and four had been convicted; Bishop Philip Boyce accepted 'very poor judgements and mistakes'. A December 2013 tranche reported, for example, 67 allegations against 21 priests in Kerry and 59 against 42 in Down and Connor.
C.cite: NBSCCCI Review of Safeguarding Practice in the Diocese of Raphoe, 30 November 2011; NBSCCCI reviews of six dioceses, December 2013 (Irish Times)

C.n: Ireland — Murphy inquiry into child sexual abuse in swimming (1998)
C.vn: Coach Derry O'Rourke pleaded guilty to 29 specimen charges involving 11 girls; gardaí said up to 30 children may have been abused.
C.who: Irish Amateur Swimming Association (IASA); national coaches including Derry O'Rourke and George Gibney (Gibney never tried)
C.cover: The report found 'total systems failure' in the IASA; charges against another coach were dropped after a 1994 judicial review because of delay.
C.d: The Irish government asked senior counsel Roderick Murphy to inquire after former Olympic coach Derry O'Rourke was jailed for 12 years for abusing 11 girl swimmers. His 165-page report (1998) found that children had come to believe abuse was a normal part of their training, and a 'total systems failure' in the Irish Amateur Swimming Association. It noted Garda investigations into two other coaches and made more than 100 recommendations; the minister cut the association's funding.
C.cite: Report of the Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse in Swimming (Murphy), 1998; Irish Echo; Irish Times

C.n: Madonna House residential centre, Dublin — Department of Health inquiry (1996)
C.who: Madonna House children's residential centre, run by the Sisters of Charity
C.cover: Management failed to act on staff concerns and children's complaints; one staff member regarded as having an inappropriate relationship with a girl was paid to live elsewhere but kept his job; the sections describing abuse were removed from the published 1996 report and only revealed in 1999.
C.d: The report of the inquiry into Madonna House, a Sisters of Charity residential centre for children in Dublin, was published in 1996 with its most damaging sections removed on legal advice. The withheld sections, revealed in May 1999 after RTÉ's States of Fear team obtained them, described beatings, humiliation and sexual assaults on children by a small number of staff, and management that failed to take effective action on staff concerns and children's complaints.
C.cite: Report on the Inquiry into the Operation of Madonna House (1996); Irish Times, 13 May 1999

C.n: Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review
C.place: Dublin (St Patrick's Guild; Tusla; Adoption Authority of Ireland)
C.vn: 126 illegal birth registrations confirmed at St Patrick's Guild (2018); the review estimated 5,540–19,980 adoption files may carry similar markers.
C.who: St Patrick's Guild adoption society; Tusla and the Adoption Authority of Ireland (record holders); the Irish state
C.d: In May 2018 the Irish government announced that 126 people placed through the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had been illegally registered as the birth children of their adoptive parents. An independent review then sampled 1,496 of about 150,000 adoption records; its report, published in March 2021, found about 265 files with suspicious markers and estimated 5,540 to 19,980 files might show similar signs. Tusla reported evidence of coerced consent, children placed abroad with little documentation and altered names and birth dates; the report did not recommend a full file review.
C.cite: Independent review of incorrect birth registrations (Reynolds review), published March 2021; Irish Times Q&A, 10 March 2021

C.n: Denmark — Appeals Board finds 'systematic illegal behaviour' in Korean adoptions 1970–1989
C.vn: 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark from South Korea in 1970–1989; the report did not count affected cases.
C.who: Danish adoption agencies DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp (and Terre des Hommes); South Korean agencies
C.cover: Two Danish agencies knew that children's information was being changed.
C.d: A report released in January 2024 by Denmark's Appeals Board (Ankestyrelsen), which supervises intercountry adoption, examined adoptions from South Korea between 1970 and 1989, when 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark. It found 'systematic illegal behaviour' on the Korean side: weak regulation let organisations alter adoptees' identities and backgrounds in official documents, and large sums of money passed between organisations in the two countries. It found that DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp knew about the changing of children's information. Adoptee groups said it did not examine the Danish state's role.
C.cite: Ankestyrelsen report on adoptions from South Korea 1970–1989, January 2024; JURIST

C.n: Denmark — state investigation of abuse in special-care institutions 1933–1980 (særforsorgen)
C.place: Denmark (Ministry of Social Affairs; apology given at Horsens)
C.vn: About 15,000 children and adults with disabilities were committed to the institutions; the sources do not give a count of children sexually abused.
C.who: Danish state special-care institutions (særforsorgen) for children and adults with intellectual and physical disabilities
C.d: An investigation ordered by the Danish government in 2020, financed by the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Elderly and carried out by Danmarks Forsorgsmuseum (Svendborg Museum), was published in March 2022. It documented widespread abuse and neglect, including sexual assault, of children, young people and adults placed in state special-care institutions between 1933 and 1980, and found the state did not carry out systematic oversight. About 15,000 people with disabilities were committed. Social affairs minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil gave an official apology on behalf of the state at Horsens on 11 September 2023.
C.cite: Historisk udredning vedrørende børn, unge og voksne anbragt i særforsorgens institutioner 1933–1980, 2022; The Local Denmark, 12 September 2023

C.n: Iceland — Catholic Church investigative commission on Landakotsskóli (2012)
C.vn: Of 30 former pupils and camp attendees questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse.
C.who: Catholic Church in Iceland; Landakotsskóli school and church summer camps
C.cover: The commission reported that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest had abused him.
C.d: An investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir, reported in early November 2012. It confirmed that Rev. Ágúst Georg, principal of the church's Landakotsskóli school, and teacher Margrét Müller abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse. It found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter reporting abuse by the priest. In December 2015 the Althing passed Act No. 117/2015, extending the state compensation scheme for abuse in institutions to Landakotsskóli.
C.cite: Report of the investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, November 2012 (Iceland Review via BishopAccountability)

C.n: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
C.vn: More than 20,000 children adopted to Norway since the 1950s; the committee examined the system and selected cases, not every adoption.
C.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
C.cover: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.
C.d: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
C.cite: NOU 2026:7 Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit (Granskingsutvalget for utenlandsadopsjoner), presented 22 June 2026; Statsforvalteren i Innlandet, 3 July 2026; summary for children published by the committee

C.n: Finland — Conservative Laestadian movement (SRK) admits 70–100 child abuse cases mishandled
C.vn: 70–100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s, most within member families.
C.who: Central Committee of Conservative Laestadian Congregations (SRK), Finland's largest revivalist movement within the Lutheran church
C.cover: SRK admitted officials 'mishandled' cases, did not use expert help and did not communicate, which could look like downplaying or covering up.
C.d: In April 2011 the SRK, which has about 35,000 members, announced that an internal report had found 70 to 100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s. Most involved abuse within member families rather than by church officials, but the SRK admitted its officials had mishandled the cases and lacked the knowledge to respond. A study by Johanna Hurtig (University of Tampere) on abuse in the movement was published the same year.
C.cite: SRK statement on internal report, April 2011 (AFP via TimesLive); Yle, 31 January 2022

C.n: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
C.place: Guatemala City (Secretaría de la Paz; Hogar Elisa Martínez)
C.vn: 333 adoption files reviewed, a sample of 670 adoptions recorded for 1977–1989; UPI/CNN reported the commission found at least 333 children taken and sold; the national search commission estimates about 5,000 children disappeared
C.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
C.cover: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received
C.d: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
C.cite: Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, Secretaría de la Paz, 'Las adopciones y los derechos humanos de la niñez guatemalteca, 1977-1989', September 2009; UPI, 12 Sept 2009

C.n: Bolivia — two former Jesuit provincials convicted for not reporting Fr Alfonso Pedrajas (2025)
C.vn: 'at least 85 minors' per Pedrajas's own diary (1972–2000), many of them Indigenous scholarship students at a boarding school; 18 victims' complaints were presented at trial
C.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Bolivian province
C.cover: The court found the provincials knew of allegations against Pedrajas and did not report them to police; prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba in May 2023
C.d: On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, Jesuit provincials of Bolivia in 1993–1999 and 1999–2007, to one year in prison each, plus costs, compensation to victims and psychological treatment, for knowing of allegations against Fr Alfonso Pedrajas and not reporting them. Pedrajas, who died in 2009, wrote in a diary published by El País in 2023 that he abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000. Prosecutors presented 18 victims' complaints and 34 witnesses and said they would pursue other priests named at trial. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia.
C.cite: Bolivian court judgment, 2 Sept 2025, as reported by Reuters (via BishopAccountability.org)

C.n: Paraguay — Truth and Justice Commission: sexual slavery of girls by senior officers of the Stroessner regime
C.who: Senior military and police officers of the Stroessner regime; procurers who took girls from their families
C.d: Paraguay's Comisión de Verdad y Justicia, created by law in October 2003, presented its final report on 28 August 2008 after collecting more than 2,000 testimonies on the 1954–1989 dictatorship. Its conclusions state that sexual violence against women and girls was fostered by the repressive apparatus and reached its extreme in 'sexual slavery of girls practised by senior officers of the regime', and that young children were exploited economically and sexually in military posts at the service of officers. It recorded that 10.8% of victims were minors at the time and noted large under-reporting of sexual violence. Amnesty International reported that girls as young as seven were believed to have been taken from their homes for senior military officers.
C.cite: Comisión de Verdad y Justicia del Paraguay, Informe Final, Conclusiones y Recomendaciones, Asunción, 28 Aug 2008; Amnesty International, 13 Aug 2008

C.n: Yemen — UN Group of Eminent Experts: rape of boys and girls by armed forces; sexual violence against recruited girls
C.place: Aden (Security Belt Forces facilities); also Ta'izz, Sana'a, Ibb
C.who: Security Belt Forces; Yemeni 35th Armoured Brigade; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa; Houthi de facto authorities
C.d: The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 (A/HRC/42/17) that Security Belt Forces raped 18 women, four boys and a girl in 2016–2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden; members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy; and Houthi detention sites saw sexual violence against a 17-year-old boy. Its September 2020 report found credible accounts that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13–17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.
C.cite: Report of the Group of Eminent International and Regional Experts on Yemen, A/HRC/42/17 (Aug 2019) and A/HRC/45/6 (Sept 2020); Al Jazeera, 9 Sept 2020

C.n: Nepal — National Human Rights Commission national reports on trafficking: an estimated 5,000 children trafficked in a year
C.vn: NHRC estimate of children among about 35,000 Nepalis trafficked in 2018 (all forms, including labour); 374 trafficked children rescued inside Nepal
C.who: Trafficking networks moving women and girls across the open border to India and on to third countries
C.d: Nepal's National Human Rights Commission, through its Office of the Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons, has published national reports on trafficking since 2005. Its report released in August 2019 estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and that nearly 1.5 million were at risk. It said nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year and that poor screening at the open border makes cross-border trafficking hard to control. Its 2018 report said girls and women are trafficked to India for prostitution, orchestra dancing, circus work and marriage, and some are moved on to third countries.
C.cite: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, national report on trafficking in persons (2019); The Kathmandu Post, 6 Aug 2019

C.n: Nepal — Hague Conference mission finds regular falsification of papers to make children 'adoptable' (2010)
C.who: Child-care homes and intermediaries in Nepal's intercountry adoption system; foreign adoption agencies
C.d: At the request of Nepal's Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare, the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law sent a technical assistance mission to Nepal on 23–27 November 2009; its report is dated 4 February 2010. It cited evidence that documents were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin, age and status, and that this continued under the 2008 rules. It said the USD 5,000 per-child payment and USD 10,000 annual agency fee created strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care, and that Nepal had no data on adoptable children.
C.cite: Hague Conference on Private International Law, Permanent Bureau, 'Report of Technical Assistance Mission to Nepal, 23-27 November 2009', 4 Feb 2010

C.n: Turkey — parliamentary research commission on child abuse after the Ensar Foundation dormitory case (2016)
C.place: Ankara (Grand National Assembly); triggered by Karaman
C.vn: a teacher in Karaman was arrested for abusing 10 children (Diken)
C.who: Student houses in Karaman linked to the Ensar Foundation; student dormitories nationally
C.d: On 24 March 2016 the Turkish Grand National Assembly unanimously set up a research commission on child abuse after a teacher in Karaman was arrested for abusing 10 children in student houses, two of them owned by the Ensar Foundation. It began work on 28 April; by July its only field visit had been to Karaman, where the provincial family directorate gave members a report that blamed the victims' families. Its draft report in October 2016 recommended that the Education Ministry license and inspect student dormitories, a permanent children's rights committee in parliament, a child-protection coordination centre, background checks for people working with children and a wider penal definition of sexual abuse. Opposition (CHP) members said the report was general and theoretical and that the commission had not visited state nurseries, prisons or Syrian camps.
C.cite: TBMM Çocuk İstismarını Önleme Araştırma Komisyonu draft report (2016); Diken, 24 March and 8 July 2016; BirGün, 15 June and 13 Oct 2016; bianet, 2 Nov 2016

C.n: Zimbabwe — Gender Commission inquiry into sexual exploitation of girls and child marriage in apostolic sects (2021–2023)
C.place: Harare (Zimbabwe Gender Commission); sect sites in Marange and Marondera
C.vn: over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation received and investigated by the Commission in 2022 (all settings, not only sects)
C.who: Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect and other apostolic church branches
C.d: After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect shrine in August 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened a public investigation on 24 September 2021 into sexual exploitation and abuse of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects. It identified compulsory virginity testing, wife pledging, betrothal and forced marriage in the Marange sect, and an earlier 2020 probe of branches around Marondera found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as 'wives-in-waiting' and married at puberty. Its report for 2022 said it had received and investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation and called for legislation regulating faith-based organisations.
C.cite: Zimbabwe Gender Commission investigation into apostolic sects (call for submissions 24 September 2021), as reported by The Herald (Zimbabwe), 2021; ZGC 2022 report as reported by CITE, 15 June 2023

C.n: Brazil — Joint Congressional Inquiry (CPMI) into networks sexually exploiting children (2004)
C.who: Networks including politicians, businessmen and clergy named by the commission
C.d: A joint commission of 11 senators and 11 deputies, created in 2003 to investigate violence and networks of sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, had by May 2004 received more than 800 complaints, heard more than 300 people and visited 14 states. Its final report, approved on 13 July 2004, put more than 250 people on notice, among them 20 serving politicians (including one federal deputy, two state deputies and three mayors), about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed the cases to federal and state prosecutors. The commission's bill rewriting the Penal Code chapter on 'crimes against public morals' (PLS 253/2004) became Law 12.015 of 2009.
C.cite: Relatório final da Comissão Parlamentar Mista de Inquérito da exploração sexual de crianças e adolescentes (Senator Patrícia Saboya, president; Deputy Maria do Rosário, rapporteur), 2004; Senate speech of Sen. Patrícia Saboya, 12 May 2004; Al Jazeera, 17 July 2004

C.n: Brazil — Senate 'CPI da Pedofilia' on online abuse material and child abuse (2008–2010)
C.who: Users of the Orkut social network and offenders across Brazil; the CPI's hearings were credited with the fall of a Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, convicted at first instance in 2010
C.d: The Federal Senate's parliamentary inquiry into paedophilia, chaired by Senator Magno Malta, worked for almost three years, the longest CPI to date, and its rapporteur Demóstenes Torres handed a final report of nearly 1,700 pages to police and prosecutors in December 2010. It signed a conduct agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to lift secrecy on Orkut pages linked to child sexual abuse. Rádio Senado reported that hundreds of people were arrested or indicted after its work, and Malta credited the CPI's hearings with the fall of Belém state deputy Luiz Afonso Sefer; Sefer was convicted in 2010 of raping a child, but the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal and, as of February 2026, his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. Laws passed during its work criminalised possession of child abuse material and ordered the closure of businesses where children were exploited.
C.cite: Federal Senate, CPI da Pedofilia final report (December 2010), as reported by Rádio Senado, 13 and 16 December 2010

C.n: Brazil — Chamber of Deputies inquiry asks indictment of 37, including a mayor and state deputies (2014)
C.who: Local politicians and others in Amazonas, Minas Gerais and other states
C.d: A parliamentary inquiry of the Chamber of Deputies, installed in 2012 with Deputy Liliam Sá as rapporteur, approved its final report on 4 June 2014. It asked for the indictment of 37 people for sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, among them the mayor of Coari (Amazonas), Adail Pinheiro, a serving Amazonas state deputy, a former state deputy and a former president of the Três Corações city council.
C.cite: Câmara dos Deputados, CPI Exploração Sexual de Crianças e Adolescentes, final report approved 4 June 2014, as reported by Congresso em Foco

C.n: Argentina — CONADEP 'Nunca Más': children of the disappeared taken and given to military families (1984)
C.vn: report: no fewer than 200 children under 15 kidnapped (figure via Wikipedia, citing the report); 8,960 disappearances recorded in all (Wikipedia gives 8,961)
C.who: Argentine armed and security forces (1976–83)
C.cover: Identities of children changed; records of births in detention not kept
C.d: The National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created by President Raúl Alfonsín on 15 December 1983 and chaired by Ernesto Sábato, delivered its report Nunca Más on 20 September 1984. It recorded 8,960 forced disappearances between 1976 and 1983 and stated that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped; babies were taken with their parents or born to pregnant prisoners in detention camps and given to military families. The report was key evidence in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas.
C.cite: Comisión Nacional sobre la Desaparición de Personas, Nunca Más, 20 September 1984 (Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture; US Institute of Peace truth commission digest; Wikipedia for the child figure)

C.n: Chile — National Prosecutor's Office: 166 investigations of clergy and church workers, 248 victims (2019)
C.vn: 131 of the 248 were children or adolescents when abused; 35 adults; no information for 82
C.who: Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers; 152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders among those investigated
C.d: Chile's National Prosecutor's Office reviewed sexual abuse by members of the Catholic Church nationally. Its balance of 30 April 2019 counted 166 investigations and 221 people investigated (152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders), and 248 victims, of whom 131 were children or adolescents, 35 adults and 82 not recorded. In July 2018 the office had already reported five cases of alleged cover-up or obstruction aimed at bishops or superiors of congregations.
C.cite: Fiscalía Nacional de Chile, balance of investigations into members of the Catholic Church, 30 April 2019, as reported by El Dínamo

C.n: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
C.who: Hospital medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff, private intermediary organisations
C.cover: Some hospitals did not register or destroyed birth records from 1970 onward (e.g. Carlos Van Buren hospital, Valparaíso); the commission also found gaps in birth and departure records
C.d: A special investigating commission of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Deputy Boris Barrera, worked from January to 22 July 2019 on children taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, some of whom were made to believe their babies had died, and given for adoption, many abroad, before, during and after the 1973–1990 dictatorship. It found complicity by medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff and organisations operating outside hospitals, and noted that private intermediaries were paid for their role. It recommended an international DNA bank, a national truth commission on irregular adoptions and excluding private bodies from adoption; the Chamber approved the report on 4 October 2019 by 88 votes with 13 abstentions.
C.cite: Cámara de Diputados de Chile, Comisión Especial Investigadora sobre adopciones irregulares, report of July 2019 (approved October 2019), as reported by El Desconcierto

C.n: Ecuador — National Assembly 'AAMPETRA' commission on sexual violence in schools (2018)
C.vn: named after the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari in Quito, where 41 children were abused; government data later showed 4,221 pupils suffered sexual violence in schools 2014–May 2020 (HRW analysis)
C.who: Teachers and staff of public and private schools; Ministry of Education
C.cover: Commission found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities
C.d: Ecuador's National Assembly set up a multiparty occasional commission in 2017 after families of pupils abused at the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari (AAMPETRA) in Quito, where 41 children were abused, mobilised. It reviewed cases from 2013 to 2017 and, in a report approved unanimously on 16 February 2018, found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities and concluded that former ministers had not acted. Human Rights Watch's later analysis of government data counted 4,221 pupils who suffered sexual violence in schools between 2014 and May 2020.
C.cite: Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador, Comisión Especializada Ocasional AAMPETRA, report approved 16 February 2018; Human Rights Watch, 9 December 2020

C.n: Jamaica — Keating Report on children in state care finds sexual abuse by caregivers (2003)
C.who: Jamaican children's homes and places of safety; Child Services Division
C.cover: Nine of 15 homes visited could not recall an official inspection in the previous three years
C.d: The Government of Jamaica appointed a four-member review panel chaired by Sadie Keating in December 2002, after a public campaign about abuse in children's homes. Its report, reported by the Jamaica Observer on 15 July 2003, found that children in homes and places of safety had been sexually abused, including by care-giving staff, and that nine of the 15 homes visited could not recall a Child Services Division inspection in the past three years.
C.cite: Report on the Situation of Children in the Care of the Jamaican State (Keating Report), 2003, as reported by the Jamaica Observer, 15 July 2003

C.n: Trinidad and Tobago — Sabga task force on children's homes, kept secret for 25 years
C.vn: 30 to 40 children abused by one employee at St Dominic's Children's Home
C.who: Children's homes incl. St Dominic's Children's Home and St Jude's School for Girls
C.cover: Abuser at St Dominic's was asked to resign and allegedly helped into hospital work; report never published by government
C.d: A task force appointed by the Cabinet in 1997 and chaired by Robert Sabga visited nine children's homes. It found that a male employee at St Dominic's Children's Home had repeatedly sexually abused some 30 to 40 children and, when discovered, was asked to resign and allegedly helped to find work at a hospital; it also recorded beatings at St Jude's School for Girls. The report was never published; the Trinidad Express published its findings in May 2022.
C.cite: Report of the Cabinet-appointed Task Force on children's homes (Robert Sabga, chair), 1997, as published by the Trinidad Express, May 2022

C.n: Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022)
C.vn: 16,238 documented recruited children 1990–2017; estimated 27,101–40,828 with under-reporting; recruitment figure, not a count of sexual-violence victims
C.who: FARC-EP, ELN and other guerrillas, paramilitary groups, and state security forces (recruitment and use of minors)
C.d: Colombia's Commission for the Clarification of Truth published its volume on children and adolescents, 'No es un mal menor', in July 2022. It documented 16,238 children recruited by armed groups between 1990 and 2017 and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828, and described recruitment as intentional and systematic, including use of minors by the state security forces. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception at an early age, forced to have abortions, and subjected to harassment, rape and sexual torture.
C.cite: Comisión para el Esclarecimiento de la Verdad, Informe Final, 'No es un mal menor: Niñas, niños y adolescentes en el conflicto armado', July 2022

C.n: Sierra Leone — Truth and Reconciliation Commission: RUF and AFRC systematically abducted and raped girls aged 10 to 14 (2004)
C.vn: 2,058 abductions of women and girls reported to the TRC; 189 allegations of sexual slavery (72.5% attributed to the RUF, 11.6% to the AFRC)
C.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF), Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Civil Defence Forces (CDF), Sierra Leone Army, West Side Boys
C.d: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone released its final report in October 2004. It found that the RUF and the AFRC 'deliberately embarked on systematic strategies to abduct and rape women and girls between the ages of ten and 14 years', using them as sexual and domestic slaves and 'wives'; in a few cases the children were below ten. It also found that the CDF carried out a deliberate strategy of rape, sexual slavery and other sexual violations against girls, and that girls as young as 12 were forced to pay for aid with sex. Of 189 allegations of sexual slavery of women and girls reported to it, 72.5% were attributed to the RUF and 11.6% to the AFRC.
C.cite: Witness to Truth: Report of the Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2004), chapter 'Women and the Armed Conflict' (excerpts compiled by McMaster University Truth Commissions Digital Collection); TRC overview, October 2004 (ReliefWeb)

C.n: Special Court for Sierra Leone — RUF leaders convicted of sexual slavery, forced marriage and use of child soldiers (2009)
C.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF): Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon, Augustine Gbao
C.d: On 25 February 2009 the Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted RUF leaders Issa Sesay and Morris Kallon on 16 of 18 counts and Augustine Gbao on 14. All three were convicted of sexual slavery and of forced marriage as a crime against humanity, the first forced-marriage convictions by an international criminal tribunal; Sesay and Kallon were also convicted of using child soldiers, while Gbao was acquitted of that charge. They were sentenced to 52, 40 and 25 years, and on 26 October 2009 the Appeals Chamber upheld the convictions and sentences, overturning only Gbao's conviction for collective punishments.
C.cite: Special Court for Sierra Leone, Prosecutor v. Sesay, Kallon and Gbao (RUF case), Trial Judgment 25 February 2009; Appeal Judgment 26 October 2009 (Residual Special Court for Sierra Leone case page; UN News)

C.n: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
C.place: Freetown (Special Court; trial held in The Hague)
C.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
C.d: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.
C.cite: Special Court for Sierra Leone, Prosecutor v. Charles Ghankay Taylor, trial judgment 26 April 2012 (JusticeInfo/Hirondelle; UN News; UN Office of the SRSG for Children and Armed Conflict)

C.n: South Africa — Human Rights Commission finds sexual abuse in schools systemic (2026)
C.place: Johannesburg (SAHRC); complaint from St John's College, Mthatha
C.vn: SACE recorded 826 sexual misconduct complaints against educators 2021–2025; 9,857 child sexual abuse cases recorded nationally in 2024/25 (all settings)
C.who: Educators and other adults in South African schools; South African Council for Educators; education departments
C.cover: Professional deregistration of educators does not automatically lead to listing on the safeguarding register; a documented shortfall of 10,748 convicted offenders not yet entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders
C.d: After a complaint about alleged sexual violence by an educator at St John's College in Mthatha, Eastern Cape, the South African Human Rights Commission convened a stakeholder roundtable and on 29 June 2026 released a report describing sexual violence in schools as systemic and entrenched. It recorded 826 sexual misconduct complaints to the South African Council for Educators between 2021 and 2025 and found that professional deregistration does not automatically lead to inclusion on the safeguarding register, and that 10,748 convicted offenders had not yet been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.
C.cite: South African Human Rights Commission, report on sexual violence at schools ('a crisis of fragmentation, delayed integration and uneven enforcement'), media statement 29 June 2026

C.n: DR Congo — UN Mapping Report: rape of girls and of child soldiers in military camps by all forces (1993–2003)
C.who: All parties: FAC (later FARDC), RCD-G, MLC, RCD-K/ML, RCD-N, UPC and PUSIC, FNI and FRPI, FAPC, Mayi-Mayi, ex-FAR/Interahamwe and others
C.d: The UN human rights office's Mapping Exercise report, published on 1 October 2010, covered the most serious violations in DR Congo between 1993 and 2003. It described 'the apparent systematic use of rape and sexual assault allegedly by all combatant forces' against women and girls, including Hutu refugee children in 1996–97, and the widespread use of child soldiers by all parties, who suffered murder, rape and torture in military camps. It listed 12 parties named by the Secretary-General for recruiting children, among them the national army.
C.cite: OHCHR, Report of the Mapping Exercise documenting the most serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law committed within the territory of the DRC between March 1993 and June 2003, August 2010 (published 1 October 2010)

C.n: Central African Republic — Deschamps panel finds 'gross institutional failure' by the UN over child abuse by foreign troops (2015)
C.vn: six boys aged about 8 to 13 interviewed in May–June 2014; further children interviewed in July 2014 (nine) and May 2015 (twelve)
C.who: French Sangaris forces; Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA soldiers; UN officials who handled the allegations
C.cover: Report passed 'from inbox to inbox'; panel found abuse of authority by the head of MINUSCA's Human Rights and Justice Section, the SRSG for MINUSCA and the head of OIOS, and that staff became more concerned with whether the allegations had been improperly leaked to French authorities than with acting on them
C.d: The External Independent Review Panel appointed by the Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported on 17 December 2015. It examined accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui that soldiers, largely from the French Sangaris force, and also Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA troops, had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. It called the UN's handling a 'gross institutional failure' and found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.
C.cite: Taking Action on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse by Peacekeepers: Report of an Independent Review on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse by International Peacekeeping Forces in the Central African Republic, 17 December 2015; NPR, 18 December 2015

C.n: South Sudan — UN Commission finds rape, abduction and sexual slavery of women and girls by armed forces and groups (2022)
C.who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces, opposition forces and armed groups; intercommunal militias
C.cover: Commission described impunity for armed forces in Western Equatoria; court-ordered compensation to victims in Yei unpaid
C.d: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan presented a report on conflict-related sexual violence to the Human Rights Council on 18 March 2022. It found that parties to the conflict used rape of women and girls as a weapon of terror and political repression, and that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. It noted that a military court in Yei had convicted SSPDF soldiers of rape in late 2020 but victims had not been paid court-ordered compensation.
C.cite: UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, conference room paper on conflict-related sexual violence, presented to the Human Rights Council, 18 March 2022, as reported by AllAfrica (UN News)

C.n: Syria — UN Commission of Inquiry: rape of detained women, girls and boys; forced marriage of girls by ISIS (2018)
C.who: Syrian government forces and affiliated militias (worst offenders); Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham; Islamic State
C.d: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic released 'I lost my dignity' on 15 March 2018, based on 454 interviews covering March 2011 to December 2017. It found sexual and gender-based violence pervasive and committed by most parties: women and girls were raped in detention, at checkpoints and in house raids, and male detainees including boys were subjected to sexual torture, with government forces and allied militias named as the worst offenders. It found that Islamic State forced girls and women into marriages with its fighters, and that these acts amount to war crimes.
C.cite: Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic, 'I lost my dignity': Sexual and gender-based violence in the Syrian Arab Republic, A/HRC/37/CRP.3, 15 March 2018 (as reported by VOA)

C.n: Afghanistan — Human Rights Commission national inquiry into bacha bazi (2014)
C.who: Powerful men who keep boys for dancing and sexual abuse
C.cover: The Commission's chair said the law did not properly prevent the practice and called for an end to the 'culture of impunity'
C.d: The Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission concluded a national inquiry into the causes and consequences of bacha bazi, the sexual abuse of boys kept by powerful men to dance, in August 2014. It held 71 focus groups and 17 public hearings in 17 provinces, attended by almost 2,200 people, and two-thirds of victims said they received money from the perpetrators. Its chair, Sima Samar, said the practice was a crime that the law did not properly prevent and called on the government to fight the culture of impunity.
C.cite: Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission, Causes and Consequences of Bacha Bazi in Afghanistan (National Inquiry Report), 2014, as reported by the Asia Pacific Forum (21 August 2014) and Anadolu Agency

C.n: Malaysia — government task force confirms rape of Penan schoolgirls by timber workers in Sarawak (2009)
C.who: Workers of Malaysian logging companies in Sarawak (no company named)
C.cover: Sarawak police said three complaints the year before had been probed and none taken to court
C.d: A team from Malaysia's Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development investigated in Sarawak in November 2008, and its report, made public in September 2009 after the Associated Press obtained it, found that timber workers had raped or tried to sexually abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10, including girls given lifts to school in logging trucks. The team interviewed four women with direct experience and many others who said abuse was common; it named no company. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the previous year without enough evidence to prosecute.
C.cite: Report of the National Task Force on the sexual abuse of Penan women and girls (Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development), released September 2009, as reported by the Associated Press (via CRIN)

C.n: Timor-Leste — Truth commission finds over 4,000 children taken to Indonesia, renamed and converted (2005)
C.vn: at least 4,000 (CAVR)
C.who: Indonesian military; Islamic and other organisations and individuals that took children
C.d: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, in 2005, covering 1974 to 1999. It found that at least 4,000 children were forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the occupation, by military units, some of which used them as child soldiers or servants, and by Islamic organisations that converted them; children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. It called separating a child from their true identity, culture, religion or language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. CAVR and the joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, which was never created.
C.cite: Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation in Timor-Leste (CAVR), Chega!, 2005, as reported by JusticeInfo.net

C.n: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
C.place: Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUC) and other missions; report issued at UN Headquarters, New York
C.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
C.d: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.
C.cite: A comprehensive strategy to eliminate future sexual exploitation and abuse in United Nations peacekeeping operations, UN doc A/59/710, 24 March 2005

C.n: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
C.place: DR Congo (MONUSCO, 44 allegations) and other UN missions; report issued at UN Headquarters, New York
C.vn: 2024 only: 125 victims in peacekeeping and political missions, 98 adults and 27 children
C.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
C.cover: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action
C.d: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
C.cite: Report of the Secretary-General, Special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (A/79/789, 2025), as reported by AP via NPR/WHQR, 19 March 2025

C.n: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
C.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
C.cover: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.
C.d: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
C.cite: US Department of Justice press release, 16 October 2019; BBC News, 16 October 2019 and 6 July 2020

C.n: Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days
C.place: North Carolina (sentencing court); operator from Florida
C.who: Playpen (Tor site; administrator Steven W. Chase, convicted)
C.cover: After seizing the server the FBI kept Playpen running from 19 February to 4 March 2015 under a court warrant and used malware (a 'Network Investigative Technique') to unmask users; the EFF criticised the operation as continued distribution, and the 11th Circuit (2019) held the warrant invalid but did not exclude the evidence (good-faith exception). In 2017 the FBI dropped charges against one defendant rather than disclose the NIT.
C.d: Playpen operated on Tor from August 2014 to March 2015 and had over 215,000 users (Europol: more than 150,000) at shutdown. The FBI arrested the administrator and ran the site itself for about two weeks, unmasking users with a hacking tool. The operation led to 956 arrests of users; Europol reported 368 suspects arrested or convicted in Europe alone by May 2017. The lead administrator was sentenced to 30 years in May 2017; two co-administrators got 20 years each.
C.cite: Europol press release, 5 May 2017; Wikipedia, 'Playpen (website)'

C.n: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
C.who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
C.cover: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.
C.d: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.
C.cite: US Department of Justice press release, 16 September 2021; BBC News, 5 August 2013; RTÉ, 20 March 2019

C.n: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
C.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
C.d: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.
C.cite: US Department of Justice press release, 8 January 2013; NBC News, 3 August 2011

C.n: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
C.vn: 230 children safeguarded; 670 suspects identified worldwide
C.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
C.d: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.
C.cite: Europol press release, 16 March 2011

C.n: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
C.who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
C.d: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.
C.cite: Europol press release, 29 February 2012

C.n: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
C.who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
C.d: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.
C.cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Torpedo' (citing US court filings and DOJ)

C.n: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
C.who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
C.cover: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.
C.d: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.
C.cite: VG (Norway), 'Breaking the dark net', 7 October 2017; US Department of Justice press release on Giftbox Exchange sentencing, August 2019

C.n: Elysium darknet platform
C.place: Bad Camberg, Hesse (servers); trial at Limburg
C.vn: at least 29 victims identified by July 2017, 13 from Austria
C.who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
C.d: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.
C.cite: Europol press release, 7 July 2017; German Wikipedia, 'Elysium (Website)' (citing Spiegel, hessenschau)

C.n: Boystown darknet platform
C.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
C.d: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.
C.cite: Europol press release, 3 May 2021; Wikipedia, 'Boystown (website)'

C.n: Kidflix / Operation Stream
C.place: Bavaria (Bavarian State Criminal Police and ZCB)
C.vn: 39 children protected; 1,393 suspects identified
