C.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
C.d: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.
C.cite: Europol press release, 2 April 2025

C.n: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
C.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
C.d: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.
C.cite: Europol press release, February 2025

C.n: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
C.who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
C.d: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.
C.cite: The Guardian, 28 October 2024

C.n: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
C.vn: at least 103 confirmed victims, including 26 minors
C.who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
C.cover: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.
C.d: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram chatrooms; at least 10,000 people used the 'Doctor's Room' chats, some paying up to $1,200. At least 74 victims, including 16 minors, were exploited there. After petitions signed by millions, police named the operator, Cho Ju-bin, in March 2020 — the first official identity disclosure for a sex offender in South Korea — and on 26 November 2020 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to 40 years (reported raised to 42 years on appeal in 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, who created the original 'Nth Room' chatrooms, was sentenced to 34 years by the Andong court on 8 April 2021. The law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.
C.cite: CNN, 25 November 2020; BBC News, 25 March 2020; Korea Times (Yonhap), 8 April 2021

C.n: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
C.who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
C.d: In August 2024 a journalist's reporting revealed Telegram chatrooms, some dedicated to specific high schools and middle schools, where users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female students, teachers and others; one room for pupils at a single school had more than 2,000 members. Within a week activists had identified more than 500 schools and universities as targets. Police said they had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024 by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, and that most victims and perpetrators were teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possessing or watching sexual deepfakes; earlier that month police opened an investigation into whether Telegram was complicit.
C.cite: BBC News, 3 September 2024; Reuters via CNN, 26 September 2024

C.n: Scale of Harm — prevalence of livestreamed abuse in the Philippines (IJM / Rights Lab)
C.vn: IJM: 1 in every 100 children in the Philippines was a victim of OSEC in 2022 (study title: nearly half a million Filipino children trafficked to produce new material in 2022)
C.who: Family members and neighbours paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse
C.d: IJM and the University of Nottingham Rights Lab estimated the prevalence of trafficking to produce child sexual exploitation material in the Philippines. IJM states that 1 in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022, that the median victim age in its earlier 2020 study was 11, average abuse lasted two years, and 9% of victims were 3 or younger. IJM UK says the UK is among the top three consumer countries.
C.cite: IJM UK, 'Online Sexual Exploitation of Children' page citing IJM 2020 and IJM 2023 (Scale of Harm)

C.n: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
C.place: The Hague (sprint); victims in the Philippines
C.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
C.d: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.
C.cite: Europol press release, 2 July 2024

C.n: AUSTRAC v Westpac — payments linked to child exploitation in the Philippines
C.who: Westpac Banking Corporation (failure to monitor transfers)
C.d: In November 2019 AUSTRAC alleged Westpac had breached anti-money-laundering law more than 23 million times, including failing to report international funds transfer instructions worth more than A$11 billion; the breaches included failures over suspicious transactions associated with possible child exploitation. The scandal forced the resignation of chief executive Brian Hartzer. On 24 September 2020 Westpac and AUSTRAC agreed a record A$1.3 billion penalty, the largest in Australian corporate history.
C.cite: RNZ / ABC News, 24 September 2020 (reporting AUSTRAC statement)

C.n: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
C.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
C.d: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.
C.cite: ABC News (Australia), 14 June 2018; The Guardian, 7 March 2015 and 9 November 2022 (AFP)

C.n: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
C.who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
C.d: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.
C.cite: The Guardian, 4 November 2013

C.n: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
C.who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
C.d: Men in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts, posing as a girl, to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. A federal grand jury indicted the brothers in November 2022; they were extradited from Nigeria in August 2023. The indictment said they tried to extort more than 100 people. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to sexually exploit teenage boys (announced 10 April 2024) and were each sentenced to 17.5 years in September 2024. A third defendant, Ezekiel Robert, appealed a Nigerian extradition order; charges against him remain pending.
C.cite: US Attorney's Office, W.D. Michigan, press release, 10 April 2024; NBC News, September 2024

C.n: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
C.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
C.d: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.
C.cite: US DOJ press release, 29 April 2025; CBC News, 10 December 2025; Beneath the Surface News (Erath County, Texas), 16 May 2023

C.n: CVLT — neo-Nazi child exploitation group leaders arrested
C.vn: at least 16 minors worldwide
C.who: CVLT (part of 'The Com')
C.d: On 30 January 2025 US HSI arrested two men for participating in CVLT, which groomed and coerced at least 16 minors worldwide into producing abuse material and self-harm imagery. Europol said earlier-arrested members included one in French custody since 2022 and one serving a 50-year US sentence. Europol describes these communities as part of 'The Com'.
C.cite: Europol press release (2025), 'Law enforcement targets online cult communities dedicated to extremely violent child abuse'

C.n: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
C.vn: 62 identified or partially identified victims; 4 safeguarded
C.who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
C.d: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.
C.cite: Europol press release, 26 February 2026; Wikipedia 'The Com'

C.n: A.M. v. Omegle — site shut after child exploitation lawsuit
C.who: Omegle (random video chat)
C.d: A plaintiff known in court documents as A.M., paired at age 11 on Omegle with an adult man who then sexually exploited her for three years (he was jailed for eight years in Canada), filed a lawsuit in November 2021 alleging the site paired minors with predators; she had sought $22 million at a jury trial. BBC reported Omegle had been mentioned in more than 50 cases against paedophiles in the previous couple of years. On 8 November 2023 founder Leif K-Brooks announced the site's closure; under an out-of-court settlement for an undisclosed sum, which A.M. said included closure, he added the line 'I thank A.M. for opening my eyes to the human cost of Omegle' with a link to the lawsuit.
C.cite: BBC News, 9 November 2023 and 22 November 2023

C.n: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
C.who: Telegram (messaging platform)
C.d: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.
C.cite: Reuters via RNZ, 29 August 2024; The Guardian, 24 August 2024; BBC News, August 2024; AFP via The Star, 4 December 2024

C.n: US state lawsuits against Roblox and Discord over child exploitation (alleged)
C.place: Louisiana, Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, Tennessee, Indiana, Arkansas and others
C.who: Roblox Corporation; Discord Inc.
C.d: From 2025 US state attorneys general sued Roblox alleging it failed to protect children from predators, starting with Louisiana on 14 August 2025, whose attorney general called the platform 'the perfect place for pedophiles'; Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, Tennessee, Florida and Nebraska pursued similar claims, and in 2026 some states also sued Discord. In April 2026 Roblox began settling: Nevada (about $10–12 million), then Alabama ($12.2 million) and West Virginia ($11 million) on 21 April, with Roblox agreeing to age checks for all users by facial age estimation or government ID and other chat restrictions. These are allegations, not findings.
C.cite: NBC News, 14 August 2025; Reuters, 15 April 2026 (headline: 'Roblox agrees to pay $10 million, make platform changes in Nevada settlement'); Malwarebytes Labs, April 2026 (summarising state AG announcements)

C.n: NCMEC: 6.9 million fewer Facebook reports after Messenger encryption
C.who: Meta (Facebook Messenger default end-to-end encryption)
C.d: NCMEC reported that CyberTipline reports fell from 36.2 million in 2023 to 20.5 million in 2024 (29.2 million incidents after adjusting for 'bundling'). It attributed part of the fall to Meta's default end-to-end encryption in Facebook Messenger (December 2023 to summer 2024), with 6.9 million fewer reports from Facebook, and to Google, X, Discord, Microsoft and Synchronoss reporting 20% fewer. NCMEC says the drop came even though the 2024 REPORT Act added mandatory reporting of enticement and child sex trafficking.
C.cite: NCMEC, 2024 CyberTipline Report

C.n: Apple cancels iCloud Photos CSAM scanning plan
C.who: Apple Inc.
C.d: In August 2021 Apple announced a plan to scan photos stored in iCloud for known child sexual abuse material on users' devices. After criticism from privacy and security researchers it paused the plan, and on 7 December 2022 told Wired it had decided not to move forward with the CSAM detection tool for iCloud Photos, focusing instead on its opt-in 'Communication Safety' features for children's accounts. Wikipedia reports that Apple had scanned iCloud Mail attachments for abuse imagery since 2019.
C.cite: Wired, 7 December 2022

C.n: EU Child Sexual Abuse Regulation ('chat control') and interim derogation
C.who: European Commission, Council and Parliament
C.d: The Commission proposed the CSA Regulation (COM(2022) 209) to require platforms to assess risks and allow detection orders; it has been deadlocked over mandatory scanning. The interim derogation from the ePrivacy Directive (Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, in force 2 August 2021, extended in 2024) let providers voluntarily detect abuse material; with no agreement it lapsed on 3 April 2026. A new temporary derogation, Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, was adopted on 24 July 2026 and published 28 July 2026. As of October 2026 the permanent regulation has not been adopted.
C.cite: Wikipedia, 'Regulation to Prevent and Combat Child Sexual Abuse' (citing EUR-Lex, Council documents)

C.n: UK Online Safety Act 2023
C.who: UK Parliament / Ofcom
C.d: The Online Safety Act 2023 received royal assent on 26 October 2023. It provides for the regulation by Ofcom of certain internet services, including their handling of illegal content such as child sexual abuse material and content harmful to children. Its child-protection duties, including age checks for sites with certain adult content, came into force in late July 2025.
C.cite: Online Safety Act 2023 (c. 50), legislation.gov.uk; The Guardian, 28 July 2025

C.n: US Kids Online Safety Act, EARN IT Act and REPORT Act
C.who: US Congress
C.d: The EARN IT Act, which would condition platforms' liability shield on child-safety practices, was introduced in 2020, 2022 and 2023 and died in committee. The Kids Online Safety Act passed the Senate 91–3 on 30 July 2024 but did not pass the House that Congress; it was reintroduced in May 2025, and in June 2026 the House Energy and Commerce Committee reportedly agreed a revised version. The REPORT Act, passed in 2024, expanded platforms' mandatory reporting to NCMEC to include online enticement and child sex trafficking and raised fines for failing to report; NCMEC attributed a jump in child sex trafficking reports, from 5,976 in the first half of 2024 to 62,891 in the first half of 2025, to the law. The TAKE IT DOWN Act was signed in May 2025.
C.cite: NBC News, 30 July 2024; NCMEC, 'Spike in online crimes against children', 2025

C.n: Australia: eSafety Commissioner, Online Safety Act 2021 and under-16 social media ban
C.who: Office of the eSafety Commissioner
C.d: Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 (Act No. 76 of 2021) gives the eSafety Commissioner removal and transparency powers over online services. On 28 November 2024 parliament approved a ban on children under 16 using social media, to be enforced by the eSafety regulator with fines of up to A$50 million for non-compliant companies, taking effect at least 12 months later. Wikipedia reports that Roblox, initially excluded, was to be covered by protocols from March 2026, and that in June 2020 Australia passed the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Sexual Crimes Against Children and Community Protection Measures) Act, which IJM said recognised Australians' role in demand for livestreamed abuse.
C.cite: BBC News, 28 November 2024; Federal Register of Legislation, Online Safety Act 2021 (No. 76, 2021)

C.n: Stanford finds abuse material links in LAION-5B AI training dataset
C.who: LAION-5B dataset (German non-profit LAION)
C.d: In December 2023 a Stanford Internet Observatory study found 3,226 suspected instances of child sexual abuse material in LAION-5B, a dataset used to train Stable Diffusion and other image generators, 1,008 of them externally validated. LAION, the German non-profit that created it, temporarily took down LAION-5B and LAION-400M to check them before republishing. NCMEC has reported that its 2025 CyberTipline data included more than 12,000 reports involving CSAM found in AI training data.
C.cite: 404 Media, 20 December 2023 (reporting Stanford Internet Observatory study)

C.n: Grok image tool used to sexualise photos of minors (alleged)
C.who: X Corp / xAI (Grok)
C.d: After X rolled out an 'edit image' button for its Grok chatbot in late December 2025, users complained that it was being used to partially or completely remove clothing from pictures of women and children. On 2 January 2026 Grok posted that it had 'identified lapses in safeguards' and was 'urgently fixing them', adding that CSAM is illegal and prohibited; xAI replied to AFP with an automated message saying 'the mainstream media lies'. In August 2026 a plaintiff ('Jane Doe') sued, alleging Grok was trained on abuse material of her and that the Canadian Centre for Child Protection had found Grok-generated AI CSAM depicting her. NCMEC listed X.AI LLC among companies most of whose CyberTipline reports lacked enough information to locate offences, while noting improvements in early 2026. These are allegations.
C.cite: AFP via RNZ, 3 January 2026; NCMEC CyberTipline data page (2025 data)

C.n: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
C.vn: 1,263 children appeared in images; only 17 identified
C.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
C.d: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.
C.cite: The Guardian, 11 February 2001; CNN, 13 February 2001

C.n: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
C.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
C.cover: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.
C.d: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
C.cite: BBC News Magazine, 'Paedophile net: Did Operation Ore change British society?', 17 December 2012; The Guardian, 19 April 2007 and 17 May 2007

C.n: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
C.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
C.d: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.
C.cite: US ICE/DHS press release, Newark, 9 August 2006; CBS News/AP, 15 January 2004

C.n: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
C.who: Blue Orchid website
C.d: A Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. The investigation began in May 2000 when Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help; Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By 26 March 2001 US Customs announced that four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, with customers arrested in California, New York and Indiana and leads passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.
C.cite: CNN, 26 March 2001; CBS News/AP, March 2001

C.n: LS Models / 'Alex Model' raids, Ukraine
C.who: 'Alex Model' agency (LS-Models brands)
C.cover: Despite surveillance and arrests the legal outcome was described as lenient.
C.d: A Kyiv modelling agency with branches in Kharkiv and Simferopol recruited children through TV, newspaper and radio adverts and produced sexualised images sold worldwide under 'LS' brands from 2001. Police raided it in July 2004; at the same time over 150 people were arrested in Australia for possession and distribution.
C.cite: Wikipedia, '2004 Ukrainian child pornography raids'

C.n: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
C.who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
C.cover: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.
C.d: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.
C.cite: AP via CBS News, 7 February 2007; Sydney Morning Herald, 9 February 2007

C.n: 'Kids the Light of our Lives' forum
C.vn: 31 children rescued; 700 arrests
C.who: Online chat forum with live streaming of abuse
C.d: An internet chat room, hosted from Buxhall in Suffolk, featuring images and live streams of the sexual abuse of children. Forensic teams found 75,960 indecent images on the host's computer and evidence he had supplied 11,491 images to other users. The trail began in Canada with the arrest of 24 offenders; in a 10-month operation by the Virtual Global Taskforce, led by the UK's CEOP and involving agencies from 35 countries, officers posed as the host and ran the chat room for 10 days. British authorities said on 18 June 2007 that more than 700 suspects had been identified worldwide and 31 children rescued, some only a few months old. The host, Timothy David Martyn Cox, admitted nine counts of possessing and distributing indecent images and was given an indeterminate sentence at Ipswich Crown Court that day.
C.cite: CBS News/AP, 18 June 2007

C.n: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
C.vn: 386 children said rescued (US figure of 330+ questioned)
C.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
C.cover: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.
C.d: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
C.cite: NBC News, 14 November 2013; CBC News (Canadian Press), August 2016

C.n: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
C.vn: 11 boys under 13 rescued in Thailand; about 50 children overall
C.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
C.d: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.
C.cite: INTERPOL news release, 23 May 2019

C.n: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
C.who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
C.d: A year-long global investigation into the Tor child-abuse site 'Babyheart' and its administrator involved the UK NCA and West Midlands Police, Australian Federal Police and Queensland's Task Force Argos, Toronto Police, the Brazilian Federal Police, INTERPOL, Europol and US ICE, with nine countries listed (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Portugal, the US and the UK). Intelligence narrowed the administrator's location to Portugal, where the Portuguese Judicial Police arrested and charged him in 2017; examination of his devices identified seven victims directly related to him. INTERPOL and Portuguese police presented the case publicly on 23 January 2020. Brazil's Federal Police ran related 'Operação Lobos' phases.
C.cite: INTERPOL news release, 23 January 2020

C.n: DarkScandals site administrator arrested
C.who: DarkScandals (dark and clear web site)
C.d: A site on both the dark and clear web that advertised rape and blackmail videos of girls and included child abuse material (over 2,000 videos and images). After US IRS-CI, HSI and DOJ, Dutch police and FIOD, the BKA and Europol cooperated, Dutch police arrested the administrator at his home in Barendrecht on 9 March 2020 and the site was taken down.
C.cite: Europol press release, 12 March 2020

C.n: Operation Gargamel — Belgian-led investigation of 9 million files
C.who: Offenders producing their own abuse material
C.d: Belgian federal judicial police found more than 9 million images and videos, mostly never seen before, in a house search. With Europol victim-identification taskforces, 90 suspects (24 in Belgium) and 110 victims were identified by March 2020; an Australian suspect was sentenced to 15 years. Police in over 40 countries received intelligence packages.
C.cite: Europol press release, 31 March 2020

C.n: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
C.vn: 146 children safeguarded worldwide
C.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
C.d: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.
C.cite: Europol press release, 2 March 2022

C.n: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
C.vn: three children safeguarded
C.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
C.d: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.
C.cite: Europol press release, 8 July 2026

C.n: Operation Tantalio — WhatsApp groups sharing abuse material
C.who: 25 invitation-only WhatsApp groups linked from Tor
C.d: Spanish National Police found Tor users being directed to invitation-only WhatsApp groups (25 under investigation). Action days on 28–29 March 2017 with Europol and Interpol led to 39 arrests in Europe and South America; more than 100 targets in 13 Central and South American countries were pursued through Interpol.
C.cite: Europol press release, 18 April 2017

C.n: Operation Chemosh — minors sharing abuse 'stickers' in WhatsApp groups
C.who: Encrypted chat groups, many members minors
C.d: Begun in 2017 after a public report about children forming WhatsApp groups to create and exchange abuse material, including emoji 'stickers'. Thirty-three investigations were opened (26 in Spain) with arrests in Spain, Italy and France; the average age of those arrested in Spain was 22 because many were minors.
C.cite: Europol press release, 11 December 2019

C.n: Tbilisi photo studio producing abuse material for foreign buyers
C.vn: up to 10 girls aged 8–14
C.who: Photo studio owners and foreign clients
C.d: Georgian police, with Australian and US authorities and Europol, arrested 11 members of a group including studio owners and American and Australian citizens who arranged the production of sexual images of girls aged 8 to 14 in rented apartments in Tbilisi. Some girls were abused with parental consent in exchange for 500–3,000 GEL (about €150–900).
C.cite: Europol press release, 20 September 2019

C.n: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
C.vn: close to 70 children
C.who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
C.d: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.
C.cite: Europol press release, 8 September 2014

C.n: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
C.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
C.d: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.
C.cite: Europol press release, 13 November 2015

C.n: Operation Sky — Skype group sharing abuse material
C.who: Invitation-only Skype group with members from 14 countries
C.d: Spanish police followed Tor links to a private Skype group whose members from 14 countries exchanged abuse material; by May 2018 eight people had been arrested in France, Hungary, Italy, Spain and Canada.
C.cite: Europol press release, 8 May 2018

C.n: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
C.vn: 65 children freed by October 2021
C.who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
C.d: In October 2019 police found a large cache of child abuse images and videos at a house in Bergisch Gladbach; the man there had repeatedly abused his daughter, born in 2017, and shared recordings in chat groups. On 6 October 2020 Cologne Regional Court sentenced him to 12 years plus preventive detention. Investigators found more than 30,000 pseudonyms used in the network, many untraceable; by January 2022 Cologne police had identified 439 suspects, secured numerous convictions and rescued 65 children aged from three months to 17. Two other men, from Krefeld and Viersen, were sentenced to 14.5 and 13.5 years.
C.cite: Associated Press, 12 January 2022; Der Spiegel, 6 October 2020; Süddeutsche Zeitung / Spiegel on later verdicts

C.n: Operación Roblox — extortion network in Panama
C.who: A man in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera (Panamá Oeste), arrested in 'Operación Roblox'
C.d: On 23 October 2024 Panama's National Police and Public Ministry carried out 'Operación Roblox' in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera district, arresting a man accused of illicit contact with minors through the Roblox gaming platform and of threatening them to demand child sexual abuse material. The alert came from Spanish police investigating a child sexual abuse material network; phones and laptops were seized and investigations were continuing.
C.cite: La Prensa (Panamá), 23 October 2024

C.n: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
C.who: Roblox Corporation
C.d: In August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox (13 August) and Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked it (21 August) after parents and community groups raised child-safety concerns; Turkey had blocked it on 7 August. Roblox had been banned in Oman and Jordan since 2020, and was banned in the UAE from 2018 to 2021. Wikipedia additionally reports that Bahraini MPs drafted a ban, Palestine announced a ban in November 2025, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.
C.cite: The National (UAE), 27 August 2025

C.n: Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreaming (2026)
C.who: Discord Inc.
C.d: On 12 August 2026 Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) ordered Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature nationwide, saying it had found 'robust evidence' that Discord failed to take reasonable steps to stop minors being exposed to content promoting violence, self-harm and suicide. The order followed the death in July 2026 of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil who, authorities said, was encouraged during a Discord livestream to take her own life. Five teenagers were arrested in connection with her death, and police said the investigation also led them to another girl at risk, whom they reached in time. A Justice Ministry cyber-intelligence official called the case 'a terrible failure in moderation'.
C.cite: Al Jazeera (AFP/Reuters), 12 August 2026

C.n: Operation Hamlet — parents sharing abuse of their own children
C.vn: 45 children rescued, 37 in the US
C.who: International online network of offenders, many abusing their own children
C.d: Danish National Police, acting on information from Save the Children about images found online, arrested a man and his wife who had posted images of the abuse of their nine-year-old daughter; from November 2001 the US Customs CyberSmuggling Center coordinated US inquiries with Danish police, INTERPOL and NCMEC. On 9 August 2002 US Customs announced 10 arrests of US citizens, with 10 more suspects arrested in Denmark, Belgium, Germany, England, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and 45 children rescued, 37 of them in the US; in many cases parents were abusing their own children. Fifteen suspects, five of them foreign nationals, were indicted on federal conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of California on 8 August 2002.
C.cite: US Customs Service press release #02-040, 9 August 2002

C.n: Operation Long Arm — 'Bamse' bulletin board (1992)
C.who: Bamse BBS (Danish bulletin board, ~900 users)
C.d: US Customs' first major case against internet child abuse material. In late 1992 a US Customs controlled delivery led to a suspect who said he had obtained images from a Europe-based bulletin board; agents found 'Bamse', a Danish bulletin board with child abuse rooms, and two other Danish boards using its images, where users paid a subscription or supplied images of their own. Working with Danish authorities, the operation led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. Start year approximate.
C.cite: Government Technology magazine, 'International Cooperation' (quoting US Customs Service supervising agent Don Huycke)

C.n: Operation Soteria Shield (North Texas, 2025–2026)
C.vn: 109 children rescued in 2025 and 89 in 2026
C.who: FBI Dallas, North Texas ICAC Task Force, over 70 agencies, NCMEC
C.d: FBI Dallas and the North Texas Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, with about 70 law enforcement agencies, ran the operation against online child exploitation. The first round, which began in April 2025 and lasted about a month, led to 244 people being charged and 109 children rescued, announced in June 2025. A second, two-month round, announced on 29 May 2026, led to 276 arrests and 89 children rescued across Texas, mostly on charges of possessing or distributing child sexual abuse material; authorities said cases remained active.
C.cite: CBS Texas, June 2025; FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth, 29 May 2026

C.n: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
C.vn: 137 charges from 46 complainants
C.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
C.cover: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.
C.d: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
C.cite: BBC News, 19 February 2018 and 16 October 2018

C.n: NCMEC 2025: generative AI in 1.5 million reports
C.who: NCMEC CyberTipline
C.d: NCMEC's first look at 2025 data: over 1.5 million reports had a generative-AI connection, 1.1 million of them from Amazon AI Services with no actionable information. Excluding those: 12,000+ involved CSAM in AI training data, 7,000+ users generating or possessing AI CSAM, 30,000+ attempts to generate CSAM from uploaded images, 145,000+ altering CSAM files. NCMEC says more than 275 victims of AI-generated CSAM have been identified since 2023.
C.cite: NCMEC blog 'The work never stops: first look at NCMEC's 2025 data' (2026); CyberTipline data page

C.n: Spanish town: boys made AI nude images of 20 girls
C.who: Teenage boys using a 'nudify' website
C.d: In September 2023, at the start of the school year in Almendralejo (Extremadura), AI-generated nude images of schoolgirls made with an app circulated in at least four of the town's five middle schools; more than 20 girls were affected, including girls aged 12 and 14. Police received at least seven complaints and identified several of the alleged authors, and the case was referred to the Juvenile Prosecutor's Office.
C.cite: El País (English), 18 September 2023

C.n: Kik Messenger — groups distributing abuse material
C.who: Kik Messenger
C.d: In March 2016 the arrest of a registered sex offender uncovered more than 200 Kik groups dedicated to distributing and selling child abuse material. A UK police investigator said delays in getting information from the company increased risk to children. Kik joined the Virtual Global Taskforce in 2015 and added image-detection in October 2016.
C.cite: Wikipedia, 'Kik Messenger'

C.n: Operation Protect Our Children — domain seizures (2011)
C.who: US ICE HSI
C.cover: Seizure of one shared domain redirected about 84,000 unrelated subdomains to a seizure warning.
C.d: In February 2011 ICE Homeland Security Investigations and the US Justice Department, under a court order obtained without notice to owners, seized about ten domain names alleged to be advertising or distributing child sexual abuse material. One seized domain belonged to a free shared DNS provider, so late on 11 February 2011 all 84,000 of its subdomains, mostly unrelated small websites, displayed the ICE seizure notice; the seizure was reversed within about two days.
C.cite: NBC News / SecurityNewsDaily, 17 February 2011; The Register, 18 February 2011

C.n: Rotherham — Jay inquiry (1,400 children, 1997–2013)
C.vn: conservative estimate, Jay report
C.who: Group-based exploitation networks; Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council; South Yorkshire Police
C.cover: Three earlier reports (2002, 2003, 2013) on exploitation were effectively suppressed or ignored; police did not treat the abuse as a priority.
C.d: Professor Alexis Jay's independent inquiry, published 26 August 2014, estimated that about 1,400 children were sexually exploited in Rotherham between 1997 and 2013, some as young as 11. It described the collective failures of the council and South Yorkshire Police as 'blatant'. The report said most known perpetrators were of Pakistani heritage, and that frontline staff were confused about what might be seen as racist. The council leader resigned within hours of publication.
C.cite: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation in Rotherham 1997–2013 (Alexis Jay), 26 August 2014; Al Jazeera, 26 Aug 2014

C.n: Operation Stovewood — NCA Rotherham investigation
C.vn: potential victims identified by the NCA
C.who: National Crime Agency investigation into non-recent exploitation in Rotherham
C.d: The National Crime Agency took over the Rotherham investigation in 2014. Its page reports about 1,150 potential victims identified, more than 220 people arrested or interviewed voluntarily, and 39 people convicted with about 470 years of prison sentences. On 8 August 2025 the NCA agreed to take over an investigation, directed by the Independent Office for Police Conduct, into allegations of child sexual abuse by former South Yorkshire Police officers (allegations; no finding yet).
C.cite: National Crime Agency, Operation Stovewood page and statement of 8 August 2025

C.n: Rochdale — Operation Span convictions and 2024 review
C.who: Grooming network linked to two takeaway restaurants; Greater Manchester Police; Rochdale Council
C.cover: Police identified ring-leaders in 2007 but did not pursue them; Operation Span launched over two years after the first reports.
C.d: In May 2012 nine men were convicted after Operation Span, which Greater Manchester Police began in December 2010, more than two years after it was first told of abuse linked to two takeaways. Girls as young as 12 were plied with drink and drugs and passed between men for cash. A 173-page review published 15 January 2024 found children were 'left at the mercy' of gangs between 2004 and 2013 through a 'lamentable strategic failure' of senior police and council leaders; it identified hundreds of potential victims, mainly white girls from poor backgrounds, abused by Asian men, and said 96 men were still a potential risk to children.
C.cite: Greater Manchester Combined Authority, Operation Span review (Spicer/Woodhouse), January 2024; ITV News, 15 Jan 2024

C.n: Oxford — Operation Bullfinch and 2015 Serious Case Review
C.vn: Serious Case Review estimate: more than 350, possibly 373, over 16 years
C.who: Grooming network; Thames Valley Police; Oxfordshire County Council
C.d: Seven men were jailed in May 2013 for a combined minimum of 95 years after Operation Bullfinch; the trial judge said police and social services missed tell-tale signs. The Oxfordshire Serious Case Review, published 3 March 2015, estimated that more than 350 young people were sexually exploited in the county from 1999 to 2014. It found police did not believe the girls and treated them as if they had chosen their situation, and social services knew of grooming but failed to protect them. Both the police and council apologised.
C.cite: Oxfordshire Safeguarding Children Board Serious Case Review (Bullfinch), March 2015; Public Sector Executive, 2 March 2015

C.n: Telford — Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation
C.vn: 'more than 1,000' children over at least 30 years
C.who: Group-based exploitation networks; West Mercia Police; Telford & Wrekin Council
C.cover: Concerns raised by officers, youth workers and teachers in the 1990s were not taken seriously; specialist CSE teams were cut to near zero after Operation Chalice.
C.d: The inquiry chaired by Tom Crowther QC, published 12 July 2022, found more than 1,000 children were sexually exploited in Telford over at least 30 years. Agencies dismissed the abuse as 'child prostitution', blamed children for 'lifestyle choices', and failed to investigate partly from nervousness about race. Seven men were jailed in 2013 after Operation Chalice. West Mercia Police and the council apologised; the inquiry found no evidence of corruption.
C.cite: Independent Inquiry Telford Child Sexual Exploitation (Tom Crowther QC), 12 July 2022; ITV News, 12 Jul 2022

C.n: Newcastle — Operation Sanctuary
C.vn: about 700 across the Northumbria Police area, 108 in Newcastle (Joint Serious Case Review)
C.who: Grooming networks; Northumbria Police
C.d: Operation Sanctuary began in 2014 and led to 18 people being jailed for sexually abusing girls and young women they had groomed in Newcastle. The Joint Serious Case Review, published 23 February 2018, put the number of victims at about 700 across the Northumbria area, 108 of them in Newcastle. It found no evidence that concerns about political correctness or accusations of racism made police reluctant to investigate, and called for law changes on sexual exploitation.
C.cite: Newcastle Safeguarding Children Board, Joint Serious Case Review concerning sexual exploitation (David Spicer), February 2018; Euronews, 23 Feb 2018

C.n: Huddersfield — Operation Tendersea
C.who: Grooming networks; West Yorkshire Police investigation
C.d: In October 2018, 20 men were convicted at Leeds Crown Court of abusing girls as young as 11 in Huddersfield between 2004 and 2011; the ringleader's convictions involved 11 girls. By April 2023 Operation Tendersea had convicted 42 men in several trials for abuse between 1995 and 2013, with 505 years and six months of sentences.
C.cite: ITV News, 19 Oct 2018; Pocklington Post/Yorkshire Post, April 2023

C.n: Derby — Operation Retriever
C.who: Grooming network; Derbyshire Police investigation
C.d: Derbyshire Police's Operation Retriever led to the conviction of nine men in 2010 for grooming and sexually abusing 26 girls, one aged 12. Thirteen men had been charged and eleven stood trial.
C.cite: Heart East Midlands, 2010; BBC News 'Derby sex gang convicted of grooming and abusing girls', 24 Nov 2010

C.n: Halifax/Calderdale — West Yorkshire grooming trials
C.who: Grooming networks; West Yorkshire Police
C.d: On 6 November 2024, 20 men were jailed for more than 200 years combined for raping and abusing four girls aged 12 to 16 in Calderdale between 2001 and 2010, after three West Yorkshire Police investigations. In May 2026 six more men were convicted over the abuse of one girl from 2006 to 2009, which she reported to police in 2019.
C.cite: ITV Calendar, 6 Nov 2024; Crown Prosecution Service, May 2026

C.n: Keighley — 2016 convictions
C.who: Grooming network
C.d: In February 2016 twelve men were jailed, with sentences of up to 20 years, for sexually exploiting a vulnerable teenage girl in Keighley. A further six men were jailed in 2022 for the systematic rape of another teenage girl in the town.
C.cite: BBC News 'Keighley abuse: Twelve men jailed for sexually exploiting girl', 8 Feb 2016; Yorkshire Evening Post 2022

C.n: Oldham — 2022 assurance review
C.who: Oldham Council; Greater Manchester Police; shisha bars, residential homes and taxis
C.d: The review published 20 June 2022 found 'serious failings' by Oldham Council and Greater Manchester Police: police and council knew of risks from shisha bars by late 2010 yet children of 13 and 14 still visited them in 2013, and multi-agency child-protection procedures were often not started. It criticised how a former council welfare rights officer, later convicted of rape and trafficking, was investigated. The review found no evidence of a cover-up by senior managers or councillors. Oldham is the first confirmed area for local investigation under the 2025 national inquiry.
C.cite: Greater Manchester Combined Authority, Review into historic safeguarding practices in Oldham, June 2022

C.n: Casey national audit on group-based child sexual exploitation
C.who: Home Office; police forces in England and Wales
C.d: Baroness Casey's audit, published 16 June 2025, found that data flaws meant the scale of group-based exploitation could not be assessed, and that perpetrator ethnicity was not recorded for about two-thirds of cases. Local data from three police force areas showed 'disproportionate numbers of men from Asian ethnic backgrounds amongst suspects', which she said warranted further examination; she said flawed data had been used to dismiss concerns. The government accepted all 12 recommendations, including mandatory ethnicity and nationality data for suspects, charging adult sex with under-16s as rape, an NCA-led national operation, and a national inquiry with statutory powers.
C.cite: National Audit on Group-based Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (Baroness Casey), 16 June 2025

C.n: Home Office paper on group-based CSE characteristics (2020)
C.who: Home Office
C.d: The Home Office paper published 15 December 2020 reviewed the evidence on group-based child sexual exploitation. It said research found group-based offenders were 'most commonly White' and that available data did not support conclusions that any one ethnic group was over-represented, while stressing that data were poor and inconsistently recorded. The Home Secretary's foreword said community and cultural factors were 'clearly relevant'. The 2025 Casey audit later said such flawed data had been used to dismiss concerns.
C.cite: Home Office, Group-based child sexual exploitation: characteristics of offending, 15 Dec 2020; UCL analysis, Dec 2020

C.n: Independent Inquiry into Grooming Gangs (2025–)
C.who: National panel overseeing local investigations
C.d: On 9 December 2025 the Home Secretary named Baroness Anne Longfield, former Children's Commissioner, as chair of a national inquiry with full statutory powers overseeing local investigations into grooming gangs, following Casey's recommendation. It is time-limited to three years with a £65m budget, will hold individuals and institutions to account, and Oldham is the first confirmed local investigation. Final terms of reference were due by March 2026.
C.cite: Local Government Lawyer, 9 Dec 2025; GOV.UK Independent inquiry into grooming gangs collection

C.n: Backpage.com — seizure, CEO plea and owners' convictions
C.who: Backpage.com classified advertising website
C.d: US authorities seized Backpage.com in April 2018. On 12 April 2018 CEO Carl Ferrer pleaded guilty to conspiracy to facilitate prostitution and money laundering; the Justice Department said the site earned hundreds of millions of dollars from 'escort' ads and that traffickers used it to advertise children and adults alike. In November 2023 a Phoenix jury convicted co-owners Scott Spear and John Brunst on Travel Act and money-laundering counts and Michael Lacey on one count of international concealment money laundering; co-founder James Larkin died on 31 July 2023 before trial. On 28 August 2024 Spear and Brunst were sentenced to 10 years and Lacey to five; DOJ said the scheme earned more than $500 million.
C.cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 12 April 2018 and 28 August 2024

C.n: Craigslist adult services closure (2010)
C.who: Craigslist
C.d: In September 2010 Craigslist removed its 'adult services' section from its US site, replacing it with a 'censored' label, after a letter from 18 state attorneys general led by Connecticut's Richard Blumenthal. The letter said the section carried rampant prostitution ads and facilitated human trafficking, including ads involving children. Blumenthal estimated the section could generate over $36 million in revenue. Much of the advertising later moved to Backpage, which AGs urged to close its own section that month.
C.cite: JURIST, Sept 2010; Illinois Attorney General, 21 Sept 2010
C.url2: https://illinoisattorneygeneral.gov/News-Room/2006-2018-Press-Archive/201009-21 URGES BACKPAGEdotCOM TO REMOVE ADULT SERVICES SECTION.pdf

C.n: Pornhub/MindGeek (Aylo) — card cut-off, DOJ agreement and FTC/Utah settlement
C.place: Brooklyn, New York (EDNY); Salt Lake City (FTC/Utah)
C.who: Aylo Holdings (formerly MindGeek), owner of Pornhub
C.d: After a New York Times column by Nicholas Kristof on 4 December 2020 reported child sexual abuse material and non-consensual videos on Pornhub, the site banned uploads from unverified users and Mastercard (10 Dec 2020) and Visa stopped card acceptance. On 21 December 2023 Aylo entered a deferred prosecution agreement in Brooklyn over unlawful monetary transactions involving sex-trafficking proceeds (linked to GirlsDoPorn, whose victims were adult women), paying over $1.8 million plus victim compensation and accepting a three-year monitor; Aylo did not plead guilty. On 3 September 2025 Aylo agreed to pay $5 million to the FTC and Utah, which alleged it knowingly profited from child sexual abuse material and that its fingerprinting system was ineffective from at least 2017 to August 2021.
C.cite: TechSpot 11 Dec 2020; AP via WOWT 22 Dec 2023; TechCrunch 3 Sept 2025 (FTC and Utah Division of Consumer Protection settlement)

C.n: FBI Operation Cross Country XIII (2023)
C.vn: 59 minor victims of child sex trafficking/exploitation identified or located; 200 victims in total
C.who: FBI and partner agencies
C.d: During a two-week operation in July 2023, announced 1 August 2023, the FBI and partners identified and located 200 sex-trafficking victims, including 59 minor victims of child sex trafficking and sexual exploitation, and located 59 actively missing children. 68 trafficking suspects and 126 suspects of child sexual exploitation and trafficking offences were identified or arrested.
C.cite: US Department of Justice, 'Operation Cross Country XIII', 1 Aug 2023

C.n: Carreto family — Tenancingo to New York trafficking
C.who: Carreto family pimping network based in Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
C.d: From 1991 to 2004 the Carreto family, based in San Miguel de Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, recruited young, poor women and girls in Mexico by deception and forced them into prostitution in brothels in Queens and Brooklyn, using rape, threats and forced abortion. Josue and Gerardo Flores Carreto were sentenced to 50 years each in April 2006 and Daniel Perez Alonso to 25 years. Their mother Consuelo Carreto Valencia was extradited in January 2007 and pleaded guilty to sex trafficking on 22 July 2008.
C.cite: US Department of Justice press release, 22 July 2008; UNODC SHERLOC, United States v. Carreto et al.

C.n: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
C.vn: at least 8 victims named in five sentencings, including one minor
C.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
C.d: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.
C.cite: US Attorney's Office EDNY press release, 7 January 2019

C.n: Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network
C.who: Brothel and trafficking ring in Tucumán province
C.cover: Campaigners and the victim's family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect prostitution rings; trial court acquitted all 13 in 2012.
C.d: Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, provoking national protests and calls to impeach the judges. In December 2013 Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of the 13 guilty. Her mother's foundation, created in 2008, says it has helped free hundreds of women and girls from brothels. (Verón was an adult; the case is included because it exposed the national network that also trafficked minors.)
C.cite: Al Jazeera, 13 Dec 2012; AP via Fox News, 17 Dec 2013

C.n: Netherlands — National Rapporteur estimate of exploited Dutch girls
C.vn: at least 1,320 Dutch girls aged 12–17 per year (estimate, 2012–2016 data)
C.who: Domestic pimps and 'loverboy' recruiters
C.d: A report by National Rapporteur Corinne Dettmeijer, prepared with UNODC and published 18 October 2017, estimated that at least 1,320 underage Dutch girls aged 12 to 17 fall victim to sexual exploitation in the Netherlands each year, using 2012–2016 data. Underage girls made up nearly half of female victims in the Dutch sex industry. In October 2025 the current rapporteur reported reported exploitation cases rising from 868 (2023) to 944 (2024), with more teenage victims.
C.cite: National Rapporteur on Trafficking in Human Beings and Sexual Violence against Children, report of 18 Oct 2017 (Reuters via Arab News); DutchNews 17 Oct 2025

C.n: Canada — police-reported trafficking 2013–2023 (Ontario hub)
C.vn: about 23% of 3,558 police-reported victims were under 18
C.who: Mostly domestic traffickers known to victims
C.d: Statistics Canada reported on 1 November 2024 that police recorded 4,543 trafficking incidents from 2013 to 2023; about 23% of 3,558 victims were under 18 and 93% were women and girls. Ontario accounted for roughly two-thirds of incidents and Toronto alone for 20%. 91% of victims knew their trafficker and 34% were trafficked by an intimate partner; only 10% of completed adult court cases with a trafficking charge ended in a guilty decision.
C.cite: Statistics Canada, The Daily, 'Trafficking in persons in Canada, 2023', 1 Nov 2024

C.n: Australia — passport ban for registered child sex offenders (2017)
C.who: Australian Government
C.d: Laws taking effect on 13 December 2017 allow Australia to cancel the passports of up to 20,000 registered child sex offenders to stop them travelling to abuse children. The Foreign Minister said about 800 registered offenders travelled overseas in 2016, often to developing countries in Asia, and about 40% did so without notifying police. Reporting at the time said about half of the trips were to Southeast Asia.
C.cite: Jakarta Post, 13 Dec 2017; WGBH/NPR, 30 May 2017

C.n: Philippines blacklists Australian sex offender after AFP warning (2013)
C.who: Philippine Bureau of Immigration; Australian Federal Police
C.d: In April 2013 Philippine immigration officers at Manila airport intercepted and blacklisted an Australian convicted in Perth in 2010 of indecent assault on children, travelling on a New Zealand passport and planning to stay in Iloilo, after an Australian police warning that he posed a risk to Filipino children. It is an example of offender travel notifications between countries.
C.cite: Philippine Daily Inquirer (Global Nation), 26 April 2013

C.n: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
C.who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
C.d: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.
C.cite: BlogSicilia, 21 May 2018; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 9 Nov 2019

C.n: IOM: up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy may be sex-trafficking victims
C.vn: more than 11,000 Nigerian women and girls arrived by boat in 2016 (from 1,500 in 2014), at least four in five forced into prostitution, per IOM data cited by Thomson Reuters Foundation
C.who: Nigerian trafficking networks via Libya
C.d: In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration said perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian migrant women and girls arriving by sea in Italy could be sex-trafficking victims, and that its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. IOM indicators included age (most victims 13–24) and being 'controlled' by other migrants. Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM data that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.
C.cite: UN News (IOM report), 21 Jul 2017; Thomson Reuters Foundation via The Peninsula, 19 Sep 2018

C.n: Oba of Benin revokes trafficking 'juju' oaths (March 2018)
C.who: Oba of Benin, Ewuare II; Edo traditional priests
C.d: In March 2018 the Oba of Benin, Ewuare II, publicly revoked the curses that juju priests had used to bind trafficking victims to their traffickers and laid a curse on anyone involved in trafficking within his domain. Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in September 2018 that anecdotal evidence suggested trafficking had slowed, and cited UNODC that at least nine in ten Nigerian women trafficked to Europe come from Edo State.
C.cite: New York Times, 24 Mar 2018 (via Wikipedia 'Ewuare II'); Thomson Reuters Foundation via The Peninsula, 19 Sep 2018

C.n: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
C.d: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.
C.cite: US Department of State, 2025 Trafficking in Persons Report — Nigeria

C.n: Libya — sex trafficking of sub-Saharan girls in southern brothels; abuse of transiting children (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Commercial sex rings; armed groups; officials
C.cover: Observers report systemic official complicity, including Libyan Coast Guard, immigration and security officials; the government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking.
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says commercial sex rings subject sub-Saharan women and girls to sex trafficking in brothels, particularly in Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq, and that Nigerian women and girls are at increased risk. It cites an international organization finding that 77 per cent of children and youth transiting Libya experienced indicators of exploitation amounting to trafficking.
C.cite: US Department of State, 2025 TIP Report — Libya

C.n: Operation Twisted Traveler — ICE crackdown on US offenders in Cambodia (2009)
C.who: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement; Cambodian police
C.d: In August 2009 three previously convicted US sex offenders arrested by Cambodian police in February — Ronald Boyajian, Erik Peeters and Jack Sporich — were returned to Los Angeles as the first defendants charged under 'Operation Twisted Traveler'. ICE head John Morton called Cambodia 'ground zero for child sex tourism'; ICE had stationed an agent in Cambodia full-time. Peeters was accused of abusing at least three Cambodian boys and Sporich of abusing a boy in Siem Reap (accusations at the time).
C.cite: Associated Press via NBC News, 31 Aug 2009

C.n: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
C.who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
C.cover: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.
C.d: Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became notorious as a place where foreign men bought sex with children; CNN in 2017 reported girls there being sold by their families. After crackdowns by the government, police and international agencies, open street sales ended and the trade moved to more hidden venues such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. ABC News reported in 2017 that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35% to 1–2%.
C.cite: ABC News (US), 'Reporter's notebook: Covering brothel raids and Christian missionaries rescuing girls in Cambodia', 2017; CNN, 'The girls sold for sex by their mothers', 24 Jul 2017

C.n: Cambodia — child sex tourism and brothels; scam compounds (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Brothel and entertainment operators; foreign and Cambodian offenders
C.cover: The report says official complicity, including at senior levels, inhibited effective law enforcement.
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says Cambodian men and men from Australia, South Africa, the United States and other countries in Asia and Europe sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly via social media; children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts; and women and girls are exploited in online scam compounds.
C.cite: US Department of State, 2025 TIP Report — Cambodia

C.n: Lake Volta, Ghana — child trafficking in fishing (IJM prevalence study 2023)
C.who: Fishing-boat owners and intermediaries on Lake Volta
C.d: A 2023 International Justice Mission household survey of 1,286 children in three fishing districts around Lake Volta estimated that about 37.7 per cent were likely trafficked and a further 45.1 per cent were in likely exploitative child labour. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit children as young as four in Lake Volta's fishing industry, controlling them with violence and limited food, and that girls in the fishing sector are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; it notes observers reported forced child labour on the lake has decreased.
C.cite: International Justice Mission, 2023 Fishing Prevalence Study Report; US TIP Report 2025 — Ghana

C.n: Senegal — forced begging and abuse of talibé children in Quranic schools (HRW 2019)
C.vn: HRW estimates over 100,000 talibé children are forced to beg; 2017–2018 documentation: 16 deaths, 61 beatings, 15 cases of actual or attempted rape or sexual abuse
C.who: Some marabouts (Quranic teachers) running residential daaras
C.d: Human Rights Watch and the Senegalese PPDH platform reported on 11 June 2019 that over 100,000 talibé children in Senegal are forced by some Quranic teachers to beg daily, often under quotas enforced by beatings. For 2017–2018 they documented 16 deaths of talibés from beatings, neglect or endangerment, 61 cases of beatings, 15 cases of actual or attempted rape or sexual abuse and 14 cases of children chained or imprisoned, in 8 of Senegal's 14 regions. The 2025 US TIP report says the government identified 573 child forced-begging victims in the year.
C.cite: Human Rights Watch & PPDH, 'There Is Enormous Suffering', 11 Jun 2019; US TIP Report 2025 — Senegal

C.n: Kédougou, Senegal — sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites
C.who: Trafficking networks supplying mining camps
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 in sex trafficking throughout Senegal's southeastern gold-mining region of Kédougou; most victims are from Nigeria, with others from Senegal, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. It also reports some tourists exploit children in Dakar and Saint-Louis, and to a lesser extent Cap Skirring and La Petite Côte.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Senegal

C.n: Kenya coast — UNICEF/Government study on child sex tourism (2006)
C.vn: 2,000–3,000 girls and boys in full-time commercial sex in the coastal resorts; up to 30% of 12–18-year-old girls in the areas involved in casual sex work
C.who: Tourists and local clients in Kenya's beach resorts
C.d: On 19 December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs launched a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 per cent of 12–18-year-old girls living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex; 38 per cent of clients were Kenyan and 44 per cent Italian, German or Swiss tourists. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and acknowledged police and community failure to enforce the law.
C.cite: UNICEF & Government of Kenya, 'The Extent and Effect of Sex Tourism and Sexual Exploitation of Children on the Kenyan Coast' (2006), as summarised in US Embassy Nairobi cable 06NAIROBI5304, 20 Dec 2006

C.n: Kenya — child sex trafficking in Kilifi/Kwale villas; Karamoja girls to Nairobi (US TIP 2025)
C.vn: NGO 2023 estimate of more than 2,000 children exploited in Kilifi and Kwale
C.who: Family members, taxi drivers, recruiters; foreign and local offenders
C.cover: The report notes ongoing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials.
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 NGO study estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in child sex trafficking in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and vacation homes rather than hotels. It also reports cross-border rings moving women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and truck drivers, miners and Lake Victoria fishermen exploiting children.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Kenya

C.n: The Gambia — child sex tourism on the Senegambia Strip (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Organized networks using European and Gambian travel agencies
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children, and that organized sex-trafficking networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination, especially the Senegambia Strip. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for tourism jobs and then sexually exploited. The Tourism Offences Act provides life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — The Gambia; Wikipedia 'Prostitution in the Gambia'

C.n: Madagascar — child sex tourism and karaoke-bar exploitation (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Malagasy and foreign offenders
C.cover: The report calls corruption and official complicity significant concerns; one official was investigated.
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says most child sex-trafficking victims are exploited by Malagasy men, but foreign tourists, often from France, also exploit children; parents sometimes encourage daughters into commercial sex with tourists, and children are exploited in Antananarivo karaoke bars. Courts convicted 15 traffickers, the first convictions in four years. A Nosy Be anti-trafficking committee exists. In July 2025 police in Nosy Be arrested two women suspected of filming abuse of their own children and selling the videos to foreign buyers via mobile money (charged; L'Express de Madagascar).
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Madagascar; L'Express de Madagascar, Jul 2025

C.n: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
C.vn: at least eleven Moroccan children
C.who: Daniel Galván Viña
C.cover: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.
C.d: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.
C.cite: CNN, 'Morocco's king revokes pardon for Spanish pedophile after protests', 4 Aug 2013

C.n: Morocco — foreign offenders in Tangier vacation rentals (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Foreign nationals, primarily from Europe and the Middle East
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says some foreign nationals, primarily from Europe and the Middle East, sexually exploit children in major Moroccan cities, and NGOs report tourists exploit children in Tangier in vacation rentals owned and managed by European nationals. It also reports alleged exploitation of children after the September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake. Courts convicted 60 traffickers in 2024.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Morocco

C.n: Tanzania — child sex trafficking in Zanzibar and cities (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Traffickers, brokers, foster families
C.cover: The report says the government did not adequately address corruption and official complicity.
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit children in sex trafficking, including by foreign offenders ('extraterritorial sexual exploitation'), and in forced labour and domestic servitude in Zanzibar, and that women and girls from the mainland are brought to Zanzibar with false promises. Child sex trafficking also occurs in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Tanzania

C.n: Uganda — Karamojong children sold at border markets (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Traffickers including community 'elders'
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says NGOs estimate the majority of child sex-trafficking victims in Uganda are ethnically Karamojong, especially from Napak district. Traffickers, sometimes community 'elders', force children to meet them at international borders, where markets are organized to sell children into domestic servitude or sex trafficking. Women, girls and boys are exploited in Kampala brothels, bars and homes.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Uganda; Kenya

C.n: Malawi — Dzaleka refugee camp girls recruited for sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Transnational crime syndicates operating from bars and compounds in the camp
C.cover: The report says official complicity continued to impede enforcement.
C.d: The 2025 US TIP report says organized transnational syndicates operating from informal bars and housing in Dzaleka camp (about 53,000 refugees in a space for 10,000) recruit girls for sex trafficking inside the camp and in roadside bars along the highway to Lilongwe; the camp is a waypoint on the 'Southern Route' to South Africa. Girls are also exploited in bars and illegal brothels in Lilongwe and Blantyre.
C.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Malawi

C.n: Mozambique — girls exploited along the Maputo–South Africa highway and at mines (US TIP 2025)
C.who: Traffickers at rest stops, bars, mining areas; non-state armed groups
