C.who: Catholic Church in England and Wales; Cardinal Vincent Nichols
C.cover: Accused priests reassigned to other parishes; Holy See and Apostolic Nuncio refused to provide a witness statement
C.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 10 November 2020 that the Church in England and Wales received more than 900 complaints involving over 3,000 instances of child sexual abuse between 1970 and 2015, with more than 100 allegations a year since 2016. It found the church put its reputation before children and criticised Cardinal Nichols. The Holy See declined to provide a witness statement.
C.cite: IICSA, The Roman Catholic Church: Safeguarding in the Roman Catholic Church in England and Wales, 10 November 2020

C.n: IICSA — Ampleforth and Downside Benedictine schools
C.who: English Benedictine Congregation — Ampleforth Abbey and Downside Abbey schools
C.cover: Both institutions for decades avoided giving police and social services information; 'tell them nothing' approach after 2001
C.d: The IICSA report of 9 August 2018 found a culture of acceptance of abuse at Ampleforth and Downside, where children as young as seven and eleven were abused over about four decades. Ten people linked to the schools, mostly monks, were convicted or cautioned for sexual or indecent-image offences. Both abbeys tried for decades to avoid passing information to police and social services.
C.cite: IICSA, Ampleforth and Downside (English Benedictine Congregation case study), 9 August 2018; RTÉ

C.n: IICSA — Archdiocese of Birmingham
C.vn: More than 130 allegations
C.who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Birmingham
C.cover: Fr James Robinson moved parish after 1980s complaints, police not told; he fled to the US in 1985 and received archdiocesan payments for seven years; the Vicar General helped Fr Samuel Penney avoid arrest and leave the UK
C.d: The IICSA case study report of 20 June 2019 found more than 130 allegations against 78 people associated with the archdiocese since the 1930s. It examined priests James Robinson, Samuel Penney and John Tolkien. Robinson was moved to another parish after complaints in the 1980s without police being told, then fled to the US in 1985 while still receiving archdiocesan support; he was later extradited and jailed for 21 years.
C.cite: IICSA, Archdiocese of Birmingham Investigation Report, 20 June 2019

C.n: Deetman Commission — Catholic Church in the Netherlands
C.vn: 'Several tens of thousands' of children had unwanted sexual contact with church officials (survey estimate; other coverage cites 10,000–20,000)
C.who: Catholic dioceses and religious orders in the Netherlands
C.cover: Policy of 'not hanging out the dirty washing'; bishops and officials knew and did not act
C.d: The commission led by former minister Wim Deetman, set up by the church in March 2010, reported on 16 December 2011. It identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated tens of thousands of victims. It found bishops and officials knew of the abuse and followed a policy of avoiding scandal.
C.cite: Commissie-Deetman, 'Seksueel misbruik van minderjarigen in de Rooms-Katholieke Kerk', 16 December 2011, as reported by DutchNews.nl

C.n: Adriaenssens commission and Vangheluwe resignation, Belgium
C.vn: 475 complaints in the first half of 2010; 13 suicides reported
C.who: Catholic Church in Belgium, about 29 religious orders; Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges
C.cover: Judicial raid in June 2010 seized the commission's files (later ruled disproportionate); commission members resigned
C.d: Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned in April 2010 after admitting he abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. The church-backed commission led by psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens received 475 complaints in six months; its report of 10 September 2010 recorded 13 suicides linked to clerical abuse and 102 verified alleged abusers in about 29 orders. In June 2010 police raided church premises and seized the commission's files (Operation Chalice/Kelk); an appeals court later ruled the raids disproportionate.
C.cite: Commission for the Treatment of Complaints of Sexual Abuse in a Pastoral Relationship (Adriaenssens report), 10 September 2010, as reported by RTÉ

C.n: MHG study — German Bishops' Conference
C.who: German Catholic dioceses
C.cover: Researchers found personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated
C.d: The study by researchers from Mannheim, Heidelberg and Giessen, commissioned by the German Bishops' Conference and presented on 25 September 2018, found 1,670 clerics (4.4% of clergy) accused of abusing 3,677 minors between 1946 and 2014. The authors called the figures conservative and found that personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated.
C.cite: MHG study, 'Sexueller Missbrauch an Minderjährigen durch katholische Priester, Diakone und männliche Ordensangehörige', 25 September 2018, as reported by JURIST

C.n: Munich and Freising abuse report (Westpfahl Spilker Wastl)
C.vn: At least 497 (247 male, 182 female, 68 unassigned)
C.who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; former archbishops incl. Joseph Ratzinger, Friedrich Wetter, Reinhard Marx
C.cover: Report found misconduct by archdiocesan leaders, including Joseph Ratzinger in four cases; only 4 of 173 accused priests were dismissed from the clerical state
C.d: The report commissioned by the archdiocese from law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, published 20 January 2022, covered 1945–2019 and found at least 497 victims and 261 possible perpetrators and accomplices, 173 of them priests. It found misconduct by Joseph Ratzinger (Archbishop 1977–1982, later Pope Benedict XVI) in four cases, Cardinal Friedrich Wetter in 21 and Cardinal Reinhard Marx in two (the full report lists three). Ratzinger corrected his statement that he had not attended a January 1980 meeting about priest Peter Hullermann, who was admitted to Munich in 1980 and later reoffended.
C.cite: Vatican News (German), 'Münchner Gutachten über Missbrauch durch Kleriker und Angestellte', 20 January 2022; Deutschlandfunk, 27 January 2022

C.n: Peter Hullermann — transferred from Essen to Munich 1980
C.who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; Diocese of Essen
C.cover: Accused priest accepted into Munich for therapy in January 1980 with Cardinal Ratzinger's approval, then reassigned to pastoral work where he abused again; remained a priest until 2010
C.d: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger agreed to receive Fr Peter Hullermann from the Diocese of Essen for therapy after he had been suspended there over abuse of a boy. He was then given pastoral work, abused minors again, and in June 1986 was convicted, fined 4,000 marks and given an 18-month suspended sentence with five years' probation. He kept serving in Bavarian parishes until the archdiocese suspended him in March 2010. Then vicar general Gerhard Gruber took 'full responsibility' for letting him back into pastoral work.
C.cite: New York Times (Nicholas Kulish), 'German Priest in Church Abuse Case Is Suspended', 15 March 2010 (copy at BishopAccountability.org); Catholic News Agency, 6 January 2022

C.n: Regensburger Domspatzen choir — Weber report
C.vn: 547 victims of physical and/or sexual violence, of whom 67 suffered sexual violence
C.who: Regensburger Domspatzen cathedral choir and boarding schools, Diocese of Regensburg
C.cover: Report faulted choir director Georg Ratzinger for 'looking away' and said former bishop Gerhard Ludwig Müller bore 'clear responsibility' for weaknesses in investigating
C.d: Lawyer Ulrich Weber's final report of 18 July 2017 found that 547 boys at the cathedral choir's schools were, 'with a high degree of plausibility', victims of physical or sexual abuse or both between 1945 and 1992: about 500 cases of physical violence and 67 of sexual violence, by 49 people in all. Violence was worst at the choir's preparatory school. The report faulted Georg Ratzinger, choir director 1964–1994, for 'looking away' and failing to intervene; he said he knew of physical abuse but not sexual abuse.
C.cite: AP via CBC News, 'Decades of sexual abuse reported in choir once led by retired pope Benedict's brother', 18 July 2017

C.n: Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and Jesuit schools
C.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and St. Blasien
C.cover: Superiors helped one admitted abuser, Fr Wolfgang S., emigrate to South America; offences time-barred
C.d: In January 2010 Fr Klaus Mertes, rector of the Jesuit Canisius-Kolleg in Berlin, wrote to about 600 former pupils who attended between 1975 and 1989, apologising for 'systematic assaults' by two priests who had taught there and asking other victims to come forward; he said there had been 'a culture of looking away'. The revelations opened the German church abuse scandal. Legal action was unlikely because of time limits. One of the former teachers, Wolfgang S., then living in South America, admitted he had abused children and young people for years and said he had told his Jesuit superiors in 1991.
C.cite: Irish Times, 'Apology over sex abuse by Jesuit priests', January 2010; The Local (Germany), 'Former Jesuit teacher admits abuse', 30 January 2010

C.n: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
C.vn: By 31 August 2021, payments approved in 2,550 cases (cases not necessarily individual people); about €33 million awarded
C.who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
C.d: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others, accused him of sexual abuse; in 1998 Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded, and the Holy See opened an inquiry. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021, according to the church's victims' foundation, payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey, the former head of the boarding school was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for crimes against 24 former pupils, 15 of them victims of sexual abuse.
C.cite: Unabhängige Opferschutzkommission / Stiftung Opferschutz figures, as summarised in German Wikipedia

C.n: CIASE (Sauvé Commission) — Catholic Church in France
C.vn: Estimate from a population survey: about 216,000 abused by clergy and religious; more than 330,000 including lay church workers
C.who: Catholic Church in France (commissioned by bishops and religious orders)
C.cover: Commission called the abuse 'massive' and 'systemic' and said the church must accept institutional responsibility
C.d: The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, reported on 5 October 2021. Using a population survey, it estimated about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020, and about 330,000 including lay people working in church institutions. Archive research put the number of abusive clergy and religious at 2,900 to 3,200, a floor of 2.5% to 2.8% of the roughly 115,000 who served, and it described the abuse as massive and its causes as systemic.
C.cite: CIASE, 'Les violences sexuelles dans l'Église catholique, France 1950–2020' — summary of the final report (Sauvé report), 5 October 2021 (PDF published by La Croix)

C.n: Bernard Preynat and Cardinal Barbarin, Lyon
C.vn: Accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts; 10 victims were civil parties in the 2020 trial
C.who: Archdiocese of Lyon; Fr Bernard Preynat; Cardinal Philippe Barbarin
C.cover: Cardinal Barbarin convicted in March 2019 of failing to report abuse (suspended six months), cleared on appeal and by France's highest court in April 2021
C.d: Fr Bernard Preynat was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts between 1971 and 1991; many cases were time-barred and he was tried for assaults on 10 minors from 1986 to 1991. A church tribunal found him guilty and removed him from the priesthood (announced 4 July 2019), and on 16 March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison. Cardinal Philippe Barbarin was convicted in March 2019 of not reporting him and given a six-month suspended sentence; an appeal court acquitted him in January 2020 and the Cour de cassation upheld that in April 2021. Pope Francis accepted his resignation on 6 March 2020.
C.cite: Catholic News Agency, 'Former French priest convicted of sexual abuse of minors', March 2020; DW, 'France's top court clears Cardinal Barbarin in abuse case', 14 April 2021; Crux/AP, 6 March 2020; Vatican News, 4 July 2019

C.n: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
C.vn: Survey estimate: 200,000 to 440,000 victims since 1940 (upper figure includes lay church workers)
C.who: Catholic Church in Spain
C.d: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, a nearly 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo presented to parliament on 27 October 2023 after an 18-month investigation of 487 cases, criticised the church's response as often minimising or denying the problem. A GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults in the report found 1.13% said they had been abused as children by clergy or lay church members and 0.6% by clergy. Gabilondo did not extrapolate a victim count; media applying the percentages to Spain's adult population put the figure at about 440,000 (or about 200,000 for clergy alone). The Spanish bishops apologised but disputed the media figures.
C.cite: AP via Boston Globe, 'Spain's report on Catholic Church sex abuse estimates victims could number in hundreds of thousands', 27 October 2023; Vatican News, 31 October 2023

C.n: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
C.who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
C.d: Historians at the University of Zurich, led by Monika Dommann and Marietta Meier and commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, published a pilot study in September 2023 on sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century. They documented 1,002 cases involving 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned abuse of minors. More than half the cases occurred in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers called the cases 'the tip of the iceberg' and found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied, with many cases kept secret, covered up or trivialised.
C.cite: University of Zurich press release, 'Wide-Ranging Cases of Sexual Abuse in Swiss Catholic Church', 12 September 2023

C.n: Independent Commission — Catholic Church in Portugal
C.vn: 'At least 4,815' children abused since 1950 (commission's minimum estimate)
C.who: Catholic Church in Portugal (commission set up by the bishops)
C.d: An independent commission set up by the Portuguese church and led by child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported on 13 February 2023, after hearing from more than 500 survivors, that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950. Most offences were time-barred; 25 cases were passed to prosecutors.
C.cite: The Guardian (AFP), 'Portugal: Catholic clergy abused nearly 5,000 children since 1950, inquiry finds', 13 February 2023

C.n: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
C.vn: Church count: 625 children reported 1990–mid 2018; critics say an underestimate
C.who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
C.cover: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula
C.d: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Polish archbishop refers child sex abuse case to Vatican', 16 May 2020; National Catholic Register/CNA, 17 October 2020; Catholic News Agency, 6 November 2020; New York Times, 14 March 2019 (bishops' study, via Wikipedia)

C.n: Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf, Verona
C.vn: 65 former students signed statements in 2010 that they or others were abused
C.who: Compagnia di Maria per l'educazione dei sordomuti (Provolo Institute); Diocese of Verona
C.cover: Fr Nicola Corradi, accused in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, was working at the institute's branch in Argentina, where he went on to abuse children
C.d: In 2009 former students of the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona went public: 67 people said they had been abused by 24 priests, lay people and religious brothers, and named Fr Nicola Corradi as being in Argentina. In 2012 the Diocese of Verona asked victims for forgiveness and sanctioned accused members, but Corradi was not among them and was never charged in Italy. He kept working at the Provolo school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and convicted in 2019.
C.cite: AP via Crux, 'Priests guilty of abusing deaf children at Argentine school', 25 November 2019; BBC News, 25 November 2019

C.n: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
C.who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
C.cover: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up
C.d: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Argentina: Catholic priests jailed for abusing deaf children', 25 November 2019; AP via Al Jazeera, 25 November 2019; The Independent, 6 May 2017

C.n: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
C.who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
C.cover: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015
C.d: The Vatican found Fr Fernando Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011 and sentenced him to a life of prayer and penance; Pope Francis dismissed him from the priesthood on 27 September 2018, announced the next day. Four of his protégés became bishops, including Juan Barros of Osorno, whom Francis had defended. After receiving a 2,300-page report from Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken in his assessment of the situation in Chile. Every bishop in Chile offered to resign in May 2018; by the end of June five resignations, including Barros's (11 June), had been accepted. In October 2018 an appeals court found the Archdiocese of Santiago liable for covering up for Karadima in a suit by three survivors naming Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati.
C.cite: Catholic News Service (via Archdiocese of Baltimore), 'Pope expels Karadima, notorious Chilean abuser, from priesthood', 28 September 2018; CNN, 28 September 2018; AP via VOA, 28 June 2018; Crux, 22 October 2018

C.n: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
C.vn: 'At least 14' minors per the order
C.who: Marist Brothers in Chile
C.cover: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru
C.d: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.
C.cite: Marist Brothers Chile statement 2017, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana — suppressed by the Vatican 2025
C.who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae; founder Luis Fernando Figari
C.cover: Abuse reported by journalists in 2015 after years of internal silence; journalists faced legal action; Vatican commission in 2023 led to mass expulsions
C.d: Journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz exposed abuse by founder Luis Fernando Figari and associates in the 2015 book 'Mitad monjes, mitad soldados'. An apostolic visitor was appointed in 2015. In February 2017 the group gave Peruvian prosecutors information from an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred Figari from contact with members. After an investigation by Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, the Vatican expelled Figari in August 2024 over physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors. The society was formally suppressed by a decree signed on 14 April 2025.
C.cite: Vatican News, 'Vatican suppresses Sodality of Christian Life', 15 April 2025; Catholic News Agency, 'Sodalits provide information on abuse of minors to Peruvian prosecutors', 20 February 2017

C.n: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
C.vn: Legion acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 of them by Maciel
C.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
C.cover: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried
C.d: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
C.cite: Irish Times (Reuters), 'Legionaries founder sexually abused 60 boys, order's report finds', 23 December 2019; Catholic News Service via The Southern Cross, December 2019; Catholic News Agency, 1 May 2010

C.n: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
C.who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
C.cover: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019
C.d: On 14 January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it was investigating 426 priests over the previous ten years: 271 cases of abuse of minors in church settings and 155 other proceedings. It said 217 priests had been removed from their duties. El Universal reported in February 2020 that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, but four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences.
C.cite: Anadolu Agency, 'Investigan en México a 426 sacerdotes por casos de abuso sexual de menores', 15 January 2020; El Universal, 'El cura abusador acecha poco a poco a los niños', 17 February 2020

C.n: Venezuela — priests accused or convicted 2001–2022
C.who: Catholic Church in Venezuela
C.cover: Three of the priests served little or no sentence and returned to ministry
C.d: A 2022 Washington Post investigation found at least 10 Catholic priests accused or convicted of sexual abuse in Venezuela between 2001 and 2022, with complaints in at least eleven states. Three served little or no sentence and returned to the priesthood. The church confirmed the report's accuracy and announced an investigation.
C.cite: Washington Post, 2022, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Crimen sollicitationis — secrecy instruction (1962)
C.who: Holy See — Holy Office (now Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith)
C.cover: Church proceedings to be kept absolutely confidential under automatic excommunication, binding tribunal members, accusers and witnesses
C.d: The Holy Office instruction Crimen sollicitationis, approved by Pope John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and restating a 1922 instruction, governed canonical cases of solicitation in confession and also obscene acts with pre-adolescent children. It required absolute secrecy under pain of automatic excommunication. Many bishops did not know it was in their archives until press reports in 2003. Canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called the secrecy rules 'an explicit written policy to cover up cases', while others argue it did not bar reporting to police. It stayed in force until 2001.
C.cite: Holy Office, Instructio de modo procedendi in causis sollicitationis, 1962, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela / De delictis gravioribus (2001)
C.who: Holy See — Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect)
C.cover: All abuse-of-minor cases reserved to the CDF under pontifical secret
C.d: Pope John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001), with the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001 signed by its prefect Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, reserved to the CDF the delict of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor under 18, required bishops to notify the CDF after a preliminary investigation, and stated that such cases were subject to the pontifical secret, which remained until December 2019. In May 2014 the Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture that from 2004 to 2013 the CDF had studied 3,420 credible cases of abuse of minors and that 884 priests had been dismissed from the clerical state.
C.cite: Holy See: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (motu proprio, 30 April 2001) and CDF letter De delictis gravioribus (18 May 2001, signed by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger), vatican.va; La Nación (Argentina), 'El Vaticano destituyó a 884 sacerdotes por abusos a menores en última década', 6 May 2014

C.n: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — Holy See review (2014)
C.who: Holy See
C.cover: Committee found abusive clergy were reassigned without police notification, bishops not required to report to civil authorities, and a code of silence
C.d: On 5 February 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said it was gravely concerned that the Holy See had not acknowledged the extent of the crimes, had not taken the necessary measures against child sexual abuse, and had adopted policies that allowed abuse to continue. It said the Holy See had consistently placed the church's reputation and the protection of perpetrators above children's best interests, accused it of transferring abusive priests to new parishes, urged it to require clergy to report abuse to police, and criticised a 'code of silence' under which whistleblowers were ostracised, demoted and fired.
C.cite: Los Angeles Times, 'Catholic Church systematically protected abusive priests, U.N. says', 5 February 2014

C.n: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
C.who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
C.d: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.
C.cite: Holy See, 'Letter sent by the Holy Father to the Bishops of Chile following the report of Archbishop Charles J. Scicluna', 8 April 2018, vatican.va; CNN, 28 September 2018

C.n: Vos estis lux mundi (2019) and February 2019 summit
C.who: Pope Francis
C.d: Three months after a February 2019 Vatican summit of bishops' conference presidents on abuse, Pope Francis issued Vos estis lux mundi, published on 9 May 2019. It requires clerics and religious to report suspected abuse and cover-ups promptly to church authorities, requires every diocese to set up a public reporting system, and lets bishops be investigated for abuse or cover-up. It applies 'without prejudice' to state reporting laws but does not itself require reporting to civil authorities. A revised permanent version was decreed on 25 March 2023 and took effect on 30 April 2023.
C.cite: Vatican News, 'New norms for the whole Church against those who abuse or cover up', 9 May 2019; Catholic News Agency, 'Pope Francis decrees permanent Vos estis lux mundi legislation', 25 March 2023

C.n: Pontifical secret lifted for abuse cases (December 2019)
C.who: Pope Francis
C.d: On 17 December 2019 Pope Francis issued the instruction 'On the confidentiality of legal proceedings', removing the pontifical secret from cases of sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, child abuse material and concealment of such crimes. Information must still be treated with 'security, integrity and confidentiality' but can be made available to state authorities, and church officials were told to comply with civil laws. In a separate change the same day, the age limit in the Vatican's definition of child abuse material was raised from 14 to 18.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Pope lifts pontifical secret rule in sex abuse cases', 17 December 2019

C.n: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
C.who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
C.cover: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000
C.d: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II appointed Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a letter from Cardinal John O'Connor dated 28 October 1999 warning that the appointment would risk serious scandal, and after McCarrick denied the allegations. Benedict XVI did not order an investigation but had McCarrick told to retire in 2006 and keep a lower profile, which he did not do. The report said Francis did not learn that McCarrick was accused of abusing a minor until 2017. On 11 January 2019 the CDF found him guilty of solicitation in confession and sexual offences with minors and adults, and he was dismissed from the priesthood (announced 16 February 2019). A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old at a 1974 wedding reception was dismissed on 30 August 2023 after he was found incompetent to stand trial because of dementia. He died in April 2025.
C.cite: NPR via Georgia Public Broadcasting, 'Vatican Report Says Pope John Paul II Knew About Allegations Against Former Cardinal', 10 November 2020; America Magazine, 10 November 2020; Holy See Press Office CDF communiqué, 16 February 2019; AP via CBS Austin, 30 August 2023; Boston Globe, 4 April 2025

C.n: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
C.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
C.cover: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic
C.d: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Vatican ex-envoy Wesolowski dies ahead of abuse trial', 28 August 2015; CNN, 4 September 2013; National Catholic Register, 27 June 2014; NPR, 15 June 2015; AP via KSL, 25 March 2015

C.n: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
C.who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
C.d: On 23 June 2018 the Vatican tribunal convicted Mgr Carlo Capella, recalled in 2017 from the Holy See's embassy in Washington, of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. In October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began: Fr Gabriele Martinelli was accused of abusing an altar boy at the St Pius X pre-seminary inside the Vatican, and former rector Enrico Radice was charged with aiding and abetting.
C.cite: The Daily Beast (AP), 'Former Vatican Diplomat Convicted on Child Porn Charges', 23 June 2018; NPR, 'Vatican Court Hears Unprecedented Sexual Abuse Criminal Trial', 26 October 2020

C.n: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
C.vn: At least 143 children
C.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
C.cover: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994
C.d: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
C.cite: Baltimore Sun, 'Few voice sympathy at death of molester', 24 August 1997; Irish Times, 'Sean Brady says abuse kept secret to save church's good name', 25 June 2015; RTÉ, 20 January 2017 (HIA Inquiry report)

C.n: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
C.who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
C.d: Fr Eugene Greene, the most notorious offender in the Diocese of Raphoe, was sentenced in 1999 to 12 years in prison for abusing 26 boys over 20 years. A church safeguarding review published on 30 November 2011 found allegations against 14 Raphoe priests between 1975 and 2010, four of whom had been convicted, and pointed to 'significant errors of judgement' by successive bishops. Former bishop Séamus Hegarty said his past practice was 'sometimes poor' and apologised.
C.cite: BBC News, '85 priests were accused of abuse - Catholic Church reviews', 30 November 2011

C.n: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland — review 2020
C.vn: 275 known or suspected abusers shielded by CBSI and the Scout Association of Ireland combined
C.who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (with Scout Association of Ireland), now Scouting Ireland
C.cover: Organisations shielded known or suspected abusers after abuse was reported
C.d: A review published in May 2020 found that over several decades before their 2004 merger into Scouting Ireland, the Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and the Scout Association of Ireland shielded 275 known or suspected abusers. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised.
C.cite: Scouting Ireland historical abuse review, May 2020, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Sisters of Nazareth
C.vn: Police received more than 300 complaints from former residents
C.who: Poor Sisters of Nazareth
C.d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry found in May 2019 that children in Nazareth House orphanages from 1933 to 1984 suffered sexual abuse 'of the utmost depravity'. Police received more than 300 complaints. In 2025 the Sisters agreed to pay up to £5.75 million to survivors and three former staff were convicted.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 2 findings (Nazareth Houses), 2019

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Smyllum Park and Bellevue (Daughters of Charity)
C.who: Daughters of Charity of St Vincent de Paul
C.d: About 11,600 children passed through Smyllum Park orphanage, run by the Daughters of Charity from 1864 to 1981. The inquiry's October 2018 findings said children were sexually abused by priests, a trainee priest, sisters, staff and a volunteer, and beaten with implements. Seventeen people were later charged; in 2025 the order agreed to pay up to £10 million.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Case Study no. 1 findings (Daughters of Charity), October 2018

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Fort Augustus Abbey and Carlekemp (Benedictines)
C.who: English Benedictine Congregation — Fort Augustus Abbey School and Carlekemp Priory School
C.cover: Complaints to senior monks were inadequately handled; after one complaint the school did not tell police and sent the monk, Denis Chrysostom Alexander, back to Australia
C.d: On 11 August 2021 Lady Smith published the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on residential care run by the Benedictine monks of Fort Augustus Abbey between 1948 and 1991, concluding that children at Carlekemp Priory School, North Berwick, and Fort Augustus Abbey School suffered sexual, physical and emotional abuse; 43 witnesses gave evidence in 2019. A 2013 BBC investigation had presented evidence against seven Fort Augustus monks. Denis Chrysostom Alexander, sent back to Australia after parents complained, was arrested in Sydney in 2017, returned to Scotland in January 2020, pleaded guilty in June 2021 to abusing two boys and was jailed for four years and five months. Robert MacKenzie was extradited from Canada in 2020 but the case was dropped in 2021.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Newsletter issue 10 (autumn 2021) on the Benedictines case study findings published 11 August 2021; BBC News, 29 July 2013; STV News, 30 July 2021

C.n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Marist and Christian Brothers schools
C.vn: St Ninian's convictions in 2016 concerned 35 boys
C.who: Marist Brothers (St Joseph's College Dumfries, St Columba's College Largs); Christian Brothers (St Ninian's, Falkland)
C.d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on the Christian Brothers, published on 17 February 2021, concluded that the regime at St Ninian's Residential Care Home, Falkland, exposed children to risks of sexual, physical and psychological danger, and that between 1953 and 1983 those risks materialised for many children; 42 witnesses gave evidence. The inquiry also examined the Marist Brothers' St Joseph's College, Dumfries and St Columba's College, Largs, with findings published later in 2021. Two Brothers were jailed in 2016 for abuse at St Ninian's.
C.cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, Newsletter issue 9 (spring 2021) on the Christian Brothers case study findings published 17 February 2021

C.n: Fr Paul Moore — moved by his bishop to Toronto
C.vn: Three children (1977–1981) and a student priest (1995)
C.who: Diocese of Galloway; Bishop Maurice Taylor
C.cover: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore to Toronto and Fort Augustus
C.d: Fr Francis 'Paul' Moore was found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow in 2018 of abusing three boys in Ayrshire in the 1970s and indecently assaulting a student priest in 1995, and was jailed for nine years. He had confessed his attraction to boys to Bishop Maurice Taylor of Galloway in 1996; Taylor sent him to a treatment centre in Toronto and to Fort Augustus Abbey, removed him from ministry but let him live in a church-bought house, and did not report him.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Disgraced priest appeals sex abuse conviction and jail term', 3 May 2018 (copy at BishopAccountability.org)

C.n: Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology
C.place: Maskwacis, Alberta (site of the 2022 papal apology)
C.vn: About 150,000 children attended residential schools; 31,970 sexual or serious assault claims resolved through the Independent Assessment Process (all denominations)
C.who: Catholic dioceses and orders (incl. Oblates of Mary Immaculate) that ran about 44 of 80 schools at the 1931 peak (TRC says about 70% overall)
C.cover: Federal government funded and mandated attendance; Catholic entities cited lack of funds to compensate
C.d: More than 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were forced to attend Canada's government-funded residential schools between the 1870s and 1997; the Catholic Church ran over half of them. In 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's chair said the commissioners had concluded that 'cultural genocide' was the best description of the system. In July 2022 at Maskwacis, Alberta, Pope Francis asked forgiveness 'for the wrong done by so many Christians to the Indigenous peoples', and on his return flight described the system as genocide.
C.cite: CBC News, 'Pope says genocide took place at Canada's residential schools', 30 July 2022; CBC News, 'Residential schools findings point to cultural genocide, commission chair says', 29 May 2015

C.n: Basilian Fathers — Canadian convictions
C.who: Congregation of St. Basil (Basilian Fathers)
C.d: Basilian priest William Hodgson Marshall pleaded guilty in 2011 to 16 counts of indecent assault and one of sexual assault from 1952–1986 in Windsor, Toronto and Sudbury schools. Robert Whyte pleaded guilty in 1990 to abusing 18 children (1962–1982); Kenneth O'Keefe received house arrest in 2012–2013. In April 2020 the Supreme Court of Canada let stand an award of over $2.5 million, including $500,000 punitive damages, against the Basilians.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Canada, citing court rulings

C.n: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
C.who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
C.d: Belgian-born Oblate missionary Eric Dejaeger had served a five-year sentence in the early 1990s for 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children in Baker Lake, Nunavut. When charged over Igloolik he fled to Belgium, where he lived in Oblate homes for 16 years despite an international warrant; Oblate officials acknowledged they knew he was about to leave. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 further counts, and with eight guilty pleas was sentenced in 2015 for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children in Igloolik between 1978 and 1982. He received 19 years (eight after time served); appeals were dismissed in 2018.
C.cite: CBC News, 'Eric Dejaeger found guilty of 24 out of 68 sex-related charges', 12 September 2014; CBC News, 26 November 2018

C.n: Archdiocese of Los Angeles — settlements 2007 and 2024
C.who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Cardinal Roger Mahony
C.cover: In 2013 Archbishop Gómez removed Cardinal Mahony from public duties over his handling of abusive clergy
C.d: In July 2007 the Archdiocese of Los Angeles agreed a $660 million settlement with more than 500 people who said they were abused by more than 220 priests, teachers and other church employees, and Cardinal Roger Mahony apologised. In October 2024 it agreed to pay $880 million to 1,353 people, which experts called the largest single child sex abuse settlement with a Catholic archdiocese; total payouts reached more than $1.5 billion. In February 2013 Archbishop José Gómez barred Mahony from public ministry over his handling of abusers.
C.cite: Associated Press, 'What to know about the Los Angeles Catholic Church's $880M settlement with sexual abuse victims', 17 October 2024; The Guardian, 'LA archdiocese agrees $660m payout for sex abuse victims', 16 July 2007

C.n: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
C.vn: Admitted in 2005 to abusing at least 25 children
C.who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
C.cover: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.
C.d: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Oliver O'Grady, citing court records

C.n: Diocese of Lafayette — Gilbert Gauthe (first national case)
C.who: Diocese of Lafayette; Fr Gilbert Gauthe
C.cover: Bishop assigned him as Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy in 1976 and returned
C.d: Fr Gilbert Gauthe admitted abusing 37 children while serving in the Diocese of Lafayette from 1972 to 1983. In 1974 the bishop made him a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations about altar boys. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years; the diocese paid more than $20 million. His 1984–85 case was the first widely publicised clergy abuse prosecution in the US.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Gilbert Gauthe

C.n: US diocesan bankruptcies and settlements
C.vn: About 17,000 victims paid about $4 billion since the 1980s (Wikipedia summary); BishopAccountability reported more than $3 billion by 2012
C.who: US Catholic dioceses (Portland, Tucson, Spokane, San Diego, Davenport, Milwaukee, Albany and others)
C.cover: Milwaukee: Cardinal Timothy Dolan, with Vatican approval, moved $57 million into a cemetery trust, which kept it from victims; released files showed priests moved without telling police
C.d: Starting with Portland in 2004, at least 13 US dioceses filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy by 2023 under abuse claims. US dioceses have paid about $4 billion to roughly 17,000 victims since the 1980s. In Milwaukee, which filed in 2011 after paying $29 million on about 200 cases, released documents showed abusive priests were moved between assignments without notifying law enforcement.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic sexual abuse scandal in the United States

C.n: Christian Brothers in Australia — Ballarat and WA orphanages
C.place: Ballarat (St Alipius, St Patrick's); Bindoon, Clontarf, Castledare, Tardun (WA)
C.vn: 853 children (Ballarat region claims); 22% of Brothers in Australia alleged perpetrators since 1950
C.who: Congregation of Christian Brothers
C.cover: Convicted Brothers Dowlan and Best were moved from junior to senior campus and continued offending; leaders knew of abuse at WA orphanages for decades
C.d: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. The order made the most compensation payments of any Catholic authority: 763, totalling A$48.5 million. In Ballarat, former Brothers Edward Dowlan and Robert Best, the principal of St Alipius school, were jailed for sexual crimes against pupils.
C.cite: Irish Times, '4,444 allegations of clerical sex abuse in Australia's Catholic institutions', 6 February 2017; The Guardian, 'Australian Catholic church has paid $276m to abuse victims so far', 16 February 2017; ABC News, 21 December 2017

C.n: Maitland-Newcastle diocese — Fletcher, Cunneen inquiry and Archbishop Wilson (acquitted)
C.who: Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle; Archbishop Philip Wilson
C.cover: Monsignor Cotter's letter about Fr Denis McAlinden said 'we do not think it can be real serious'
C.d: A NSW Special Commission of Inquiry led by Margaret Cunneen SC, triggered by Detective Chief Inspector Peter Fox's public allegations in November 2012, reported on 30 May 2014. It found no evidence that senior police obstructed investigations, but found senior diocesan officials knew of complaints against Fr Denis McAlinden from 1954 and took over 40 years to tell police. On 22 May 2018 Newcastle Local Court found Archbishop of Adelaide Philip Wilson guilty of concealing abuse by Fr James Fletcher that a victim had told him about in 1976; on 6 December 2018 Judge Roy Ellis upheld his appeal, finding reasonable doubt, and quashed the conviction.
C.cite: ABC News, 'Archbishop of Adelaide Philip Wilson found guilty of covering up child sexual abuse', 22 May 2018; RNZ, 'Former Adelaide archbishop's conviction for concealing child sexual abuse quashed', 6 December 2018; ABC News, Special Commission of Inquiry report, 30 May 2014

C.n: Marist Brothers in Australia
C.who: Marist Brothers
C.cover: Royal Commission found the order failed to act on complaints against a Brother at Marist College Ashgrove; a Brother pleaded guilty in 2020 to concealing abuse
C.d: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 20% of Marist Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. Brother William Wade, a former headmaster at Marist schools in Canberra, Hamilton (Newcastle) and Kogarah, was jailed for 18 months in 2017 for abusing two boys (in 1976 and about 1980). In February 2020 he became the first senior Catholic in Australia to plead guilty to concealing child sexual abuse by colleagues, and in September 2020 was sentenced to four months, served in the community. The Marist Brothers listed 154 members accused of abusing children in June 2019.
C.cite: Marist Brothers statement, June 2019; Royal Commission findings, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
C.vn: 118 sex abuse allegations / over 120 complaints; 21 of 37 Brothers in Christchurch accused
C.who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
C.cover: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements
C.d: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.
C.cite: RNZ, 'Royal Commission: Marylands School abuse extreme, children's cries for help ignored', 2 August 2023; Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, 'Stolen Lives, Marked Souls', 2023

C.n: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
C.who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
C.d: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.
C.cite: Otago Daily Times 2018 and court reports, as summarised by Wikipedia

C.n: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
C.vn: A 2020 report cited about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases in Fiji involving clergy, some from Australia and New Zealand (figure as reported, not an official finding)
C.who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
C.cover: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged
C.d: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Australia and New Zealand, citing 1News (July 2020)

C.n: Richard Daschbach — Topu Honis shelter, Oecusse
C.vn: Convicted for four girls; charges covered 14 cases; lawyers represented 17 victims
C.who: Society of the Divine Word (SVD); US-born Fr Richard Daschbach
C.d: US-born Divine Word missionary Richard Daschbach founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1992. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted the abuse to them in March 2018, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood on 6 November 2018; the church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14, plus child abuse material and domestic violence counts. On 21 December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years, basing the verdict on the testimony of four victims. A report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission had defended him.
C.cite: Al Jazeera, 'US ex-priest jailed for child sex abuse in East Timor', 21 December 2021; The Guardian, 'A ticking time bomb', 23 May 2021

C.n: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
C.who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
C.cover: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022
C.d: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
C.cite: Al Jazeera, 'Vatican affirms sanctioning Nobel-winning bishop over sex scandal', 29 September 2022

C.n: St Michael's School, Soni — Rosminian priests
C.who: Institute of Charity (Rosminians); English priest Kit Cunningham and three others
C.cover: The order knew of Cunningham's abuse before his death in 2010; it became public only through a BBC documentary in June 2011
C.d: In the 1960s four Rosminian priests, including English priest Kit Cunningham, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's boarding school in Soni, Tanganyika (now Tanzania). The order openly acknowledged the crimes of the four priests but in 2010 refused to pay compensation; Cunningham died in December 2010. The abuse became public in the BBC documentary 'Abused: Breaking the Silence', broadcast on 21 June 2011. A group of 22 former Soni pupils pursued a compensation claim, and former pupils of Soni and the order's Grace Dieu school in Leicestershire announced they would sue.
C.cite: The Guardian (Peter Stanford), 'He was my priest and my friend. Then I found out he was a paedophile', 19 June 2011; BBC News, 'Former 1950s students to sue Catholic order over abuse', 22 June 2011

C.n: Slovenia — Fr Franc Frantar
C.vn: 'Up to 16' minors
C.who: Archdiocese of Ljubljana; Fr Franc Frantar
C.cover: Avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary until an Interpol notice was issued
C.d: Slovenian priest Franc Frantar was detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors and later sentenced (sources give three and a half and five years). He first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary and returned to Slovenia after Interpol issued a notice.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

C.n: Croatia — first priest convictions
C.vn: Čuček: 37 girls; Ljubičić: five teenage boys
C.who: Catholic dioceses in Croatia
C.cover: Nediljko Ivanov, whose abuse 1983–1991 was reported in 2012, was time-barred; a church court ordered only prayer, fasting and an apology and he continued to say Mass
C.d: In 2000 Fr Ivan Čuček was convicted of abusing 37 girls; his three-year sentence was cut to 18 months by the Supreme Court. In 2007 Fr Drago Ljubičić of Rab became the first Croatian priest to serve prison time, three years for molesting five teenage boys. Fr Nediljko Ivanov of Bibinje became the first priest convicted by a Croatian church court, but civil prosecution was time-barred.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe and by country

C.n: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta
C.vn: More than 20 boys
C.who: Archdiocese of Olomouc; Archbishop Jan Graubner (alleged failure to report)
C.cover: Archbishop Graubner allegedly did not report him and moved him between parishes
C.d: In 2000–2001 Fr František Merta was found guilty of abusing more than 20 boys and received a two-year suspended sentence. Archbishop Jan Graubner allegedly failed to report him and moved him between parishes when problems arose.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

C.n: Malta — St Joseph Home convictions
C.vn: 84 allegations recorded by April 2010
C.who: Missionary Society of St Paul (St Joseph Home); Maltese clergy
C.d: By April 2010 the church in Malta had recorded 84 allegations. Fr Charles Pulis was sentenced to six years and Fr Godwin Scerri to five years for abusing boys at a church children's home; Donald Bellizzi received three years in 2020.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country (Malta)

C.n: Belgium — Halsberghe commission (2000) and convictions
C.vn: Over 300 complaints to the 2000 commission
C.who: Catholic Church in Belgium
C.cover: In about half the 32 upheld cases the accused refused to appear; 31 cases were time-barred and only one reached court; in June 2010 police seized 450 internal dossiers from the Mechelen archbishop's palace
C.d: A church commission chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe from 2000 received over 300 complaints and upheld 32 of 33 formal ones; 31 were time-barred. Convictions included Fr Bruno Vos (nine years in 2009 for raping four minors), Robert Borremans (five years, 2008) and two Brothers jailed for ten years each in 2005 for abusing disabled people. On 24 June 2010 police raided the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, seizing 450 dossiers, and searched Cardinal Danneels' residence.
C.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Belgium

C.n: Italy — no national inquiry; Rete l'Abuso count
C.vn: Rete l'Abuso: about 300 cases in the courts since 2000, 150–170 convictions (victims' group estimate)
C.who: Catholic Church in Italy; Italian Bishops' Conference
C.cover: In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said priests had no obligation to report suspected abuse to police
C.d: Italy has no official statistics or national inquiry. The victims' network Rete l'Abuso counted about 300 cases of priests and nuns before Italian courts since 2000, with 150 to 170 convictions (October 2018). In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said its priests had no duty to report suspected abuse to police. Cases include Fr Mauro Galli (6 years 4 months, 2014) and a former Roman Rota judge who pleaded guilty to child abuse image offences in 2018.
C.cite: Rete l'Abuso, 2018; Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Italy

C.n: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
C.place: San Ramón de la Nueva Orán, Salta
C.vn: Two adult seminarians (not minors)
C.who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
C.cover: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019
C.d: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
C.cite: El País, 'Condenado a cuatro años y medio de cárcel por abuso sexual un exobispo argentino cercano al Papa', 4 March 2022; Catholic News Agency, 28 May 2019

C.n: Denis Chrysostom Alexander — extradition from Australia
C.who: Benedictine monk, Fort Augustus Abbey School
C.cover: Sent back to Australia by the school after parents complained; police not informed
C.d: Benedictine monk Denis 'Chrysostom' Alexander abused pupils at Fort Augustus Abbey School in Scotland in the 1970s. A 2013 BBC investigation reported that after a pupil told his parents, who complained to the school, Alexander was sent back to Australia with no warning about his offending; he became a parish priest in Sydney. Scotland requested his extradition in August 2016 and he was arrested in Sydney in January 2017. After contesting extradition he was returned to Scotland in January 2020. In June 2021 at the High Court in Edinburgh he pleaded guilty to indecent behaviour against two boys aged 12 to 14 between 1973 and 1976, and on 30 July 2021 he was jailed for four years and five months.
C.cite: STV News, 'Priest who sexually abused two schoolboys jailed', 30 July 2021; BBC News, 'Abuse claims at former Catholic boarding school', 29 July 2013; ABC News (Australia), 24 January 2017

C.n: IICSA — Anglican Church investigation report
C.place: England and Wales (Church of England, Church in Wales)
C.who: Church of England; Church in Wales
C.cover: Inquiry found the Church gave 'excessive attention' to alleged perpetrators over victims, ignored safeguarding advice, and used forgiveness to justify failing to respond to allegations.
C.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its Anglican Church investigation report on 6 October 2020. It counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and warned the true scale cannot be known. In 2018 alone, dioceses received 2,504 safeguarding concerns, 449 of them about recent child sexual abuse. It found deference to authority, clericalism and taboos about sexuality kept victims from disclosing, and that bishops kept safeguarding decision-making power.
C.cite: IICSA, The Anglican Church: Safeguarding in the Church of England and the Church in Wales, 6 October 2020; Church Times, 9 October 2020

C.n: Diocese of Chichester — clergy abuse (IICSA case study)
C.who: Church of England, Diocese of Chichester
C.cover: Clergy with known concerns (Rideout, Cotton, Graves, House) were given or kept permission to officiate; Cotton's prior conviction for indecent exposure involving a child sat in his diocesan file but was not shared with police; an archdeacon declined to report a serious indecent assault; Sussex Police dropped a 1997–98 investigation and later destroyed its records.
C.d: IICSA found the Diocese of Chichester had more child sexual abuse convictions than any other Church of England diocese. Roy Cotton had been ordained in the 1960s despite a prior conviction involving a child. Sussex Police investigated Cotton and Colin Pritchard in 1997–98 without charges; when Northamptonshire Police revived the case in 2006, Sussex Police had destroyed its records. The diocese's 2008–09 Past Cases Review missed the scale of abuse, and real action against abusers began only with Operation Perry in 2011.
C.cite: IICSA, Anglican Church Case Studies: Chichester/Peter Ball, conclusions

C.n: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
C.vn: 18 young men at sentencing (2015); IICSA describes 17 teenagers and young men, 1977–1992
C.who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
C.cover: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.
C.d: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.
C.cite: IICSA Chichester/Peter Ball conclusions; Gibb, An Abuse of Faith (GS Misc 1172), June 2017; sentencing coverage 7 October 2015

C.n: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
C.place: Iwerne camps (Dorset) and Winchester College; later Zambesi Ministries camps, Zimbabwe; Cape Town
C.vn: Makin Review: between 115 and 130 boys and young men; at least 85 of them in Zimbabwe and South Africa (Church Times, citing the review)
C.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
C.cover: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.
C.d: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
C.cite: Makin, Independent Learning Lessons Review: John Smyth QC (Church of England), published 7 November 2024; Church Times, 15 November 2024

C.n: Royal Commission data — Anglican Church of Australia
C.vn: 1,082 complainants about 1,115 alleged incidents reported 1980–2015; some incidents dated back to 1950
C.who: Anglican Church of Australia
C.d: Data released at the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in March 2017 showed 1,082 people lodged complaints of child sexual abuse about 1,115 incidents in the Anglican Church of Australia between 1980 and 2015. The complaints identified 569 alleged perpetrators who were clergy, teachers or volunteers, plus 133 whose church roles were unknown (702 in total).
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 52 data, March 2017; Gulf News/AP

C.n: Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
C.vn: About 37,000 of roughly 80,000 Common Experience Payment applicants also claimed sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts (all churches combined); about 180,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended over 150 years
C.who: Anglican Church of Canada (ran over 30 schools), United Church, Presbyterian Church, with the Catholic Church and federal government
C.cover: The schools were a federal government system run by churches.
C.d: Canada's Indian residential schools were run for the federal government by the Anglican, Catholic, Presbyterian and United churches; the Anglican Church of Canada operated more than 30. In April 2013 Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair Justice Murray Sinclair said about 37,000 former students had filed claims for sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts, and asked the public to imagine 'a school where half of the students suffered sexual and physical abuse'. The TRC's final report followed in 2015. Under the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, to which the Anglican, Presbyterian and United churches were parties (Anglicans ran about 30% of schools, the United Church about 10%), the Independent Assessment Process for sexual and serious physical abuse had paid C$3.18 billion to 31,103 former students by 31 March 2019 (all churches combined).
C.cite: Anglican Journal, 25 April 2013 (TRC Quebec National Event)

C.n: Southern Baptist Convention — 'Abuse of Faith' investigation
C.place: Southern Baptist churches nationwide (most convicted offenders in Texas)
C.vn: 'more than 700' victims over about 20 years
C.who: Southern Baptist Convention churches
C.d: The Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News published 'Abuse of Faith' on 10–11 February 2019. They found about 380 Southern Baptist ministers and volunteers had faced allegations of sexual misconduct over the previous 20 years, with more than 700 victims. Many pleaded guilty or were convicted, more from Texas than any other state.
C.cite: Houston Chronicle / San Antonio Express-News, 'Abuse of Faith', February 2019; Baptist Standard, 11 February 2019

C.n: Southern Baptist Convention — Guidepost report and secret list of accused ministers
C.vn: The list released on 26 May 2022 had 703 entries of accused ministers, mostly 2000–2019
C.who: Southern Baptist Convention Executive Committee
C.cover: Former Executive Committee officials D. August Boto and Roger Oldham kept a private list of abusive ministers, but no one acted to keep them out of SBC pulpits; survivors met 'resistance, stonewalling, and even outright hostility' and were told church autonomy prevented action; a few senior leaders and outside counsel focused on avoiding liability.
C.d: Guidepost Solutions, hired after SBC delegates demanded an outside probe in 2021, released its report on 22 May 2022. It found a few senior Executive Committee leaders had for about two decades controlled the response to abuse reports to limit legal liability, ignoring or disbelieving survivors. The Executive Committee then published the previously secret list, 205 pages and 703 entries, on 26 May 2022.
C.cite: Guidepost Solutions report, 22 May 2022; AP (Spokesman-Review), 23 May 2022; WSOC-TV/AP, 27 May 2022

C.n: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
C.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
C.cover: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.
C.d: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 18 findings, November 2015

C.n: ForuM study — German Protestant Church (EKD)
C.place: EKD, Hanover (all regional churches and Diakonie)
C.vn: 2,225 documented victims in files reviewed; researchers estimated up to 9,355 minors
C.who: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland (EKD) and Diakonie
C.cover: Researchers said regional churches delivered documents slowly despite a contract, so the study could not be completed; co-author Martin Wazlawik called the figures 'the tip of the tip of the iceberg'.
C.d: The ForuM study, commissioned by the EKD in 2020 and led by Hanover University of Applied Sciences and Arts, was released on 25 January 2024. Files reviewed showed 2,225 victims and 1,259 potential perpetrators among ministers, employees and volunteers since 1946, with a projected estimate of up to 9,355 abused minors. EKD head Kirsten Fehrs called it a 'massive failure' toward victims.
C.cite: ForuM research network, 25 January 2024; AFP (Citizen Digital), 25 January 2024

C.n: Jehovah's Witnesses — Royal Commission Case Study 29
C.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Australia (Jehovah's Witnesses)
C.cover: None of the 1,006 alleged perpetrators recorded since 1950 was reported to police by the church. The 'two-witness rule' required two witnesses before elders' judicial committees could act, blocking 125 allegations; 401 members were expelled after internal hearings and 230 later readmitted.
C.d: At hearings in July–August 2015, the Royal Commission was told the Watch Tower Society's files held 1,006 alleged perpetrators of child sexual abuse since 1950, including 579 confessions, and that none had been reported to secular authorities. The Commission referred 514 alleged perpetrators to police. Its November 2016 report found the organisation did not respond adequately to child sexual abuse and that its two-witness rule showed a serious lack of understanding of abuse.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 29 report, November 2016; AFP (News24), 27 July 2015

C.n: Conti v. Watchtower — Fremont congregation, California
C.who: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
C.d: In June 2012 an Alameda County jury found the Watchtower Society liable for abuse of a girl by a congregation member and awarded punitive damages, later reduced. In April 2015 the California appeals court reversed punitive damages but upheld $2.8 million in compensatory damages; the case settled during further appeal. Other US civil cases followed, including a $13.5 million San Diego judgment in 2014 (vacated 2016, settled 2018) and a $35 million Montana verdict in 2018 reversed in 2020.
C.cite: Doe (Conti) v. Watchtower, California Court of Appeal, April 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

C.n: Warren Jeffs — FLDS child 'marriages' conviction
C.place: Yearning For Zion ranch, Eldorado, Texas; Short Creek (Colorado City AZ / Hildale UT)
C.vn: Texas conviction concerned girls aged 12 and 15
C.who: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
C.d: FLDS president Warren Jeffs was added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list on 6 May 2006 and arrested in Nevada on 28 August 2006. A 2007 Utah conviction for accomplice to rape was reversed in 2010, and Arizona charges were dismissed in 2010. In August 2011 a Texas jury convicted him of two counts of sexual assault of a child, girls aged 12 and 15 he had taken as 'spiritual wives', and he was sentenced to life plus 20 years. Texas authorities had raided the YFZ ranch on 7 April 2008 and taken custody of about 416 children, who were later returned after courts found the removal unjustified.
C.cite: AP, 4–9 August 2011; Wikipedia 'Warren Jeffs' (index)

C.n: Bountiful, B.C. — parents convicted of taking 13-year-old to marry Warren Jeffs
C.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
C.d: In February 2017 a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Cranbrook convicted Brandon James Blackmore and Emily Gail Blackmore of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes: in 2004 they took their 13-year-old daughter to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were jailed in August 2017. In the same trial James Oler was acquitted of a related charge.
C.cite: Salt Lake Tribune, 7 February 2017; AP, 11 August 2017

C.n: James Oler — removing a 15-year-old from Canada to marry
C.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
C.d: Former FLDS Bountiful bishop James Oler was first acquitted in 2017; the B.C. Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. In May 2019 he was found guilty of removing a child from Canada, having taken a 15-year-old girl to the United States in 2004 to be married to an older FLDS member. On 29 August 2019 he was sentenced to 12 months in jail and 18 months' probation. Separately, Oler (5 wives) and Winston Blackmore (24 wives, 1990–2014) were convicted of polygamy in July 2017.
C.cite: CBC News, 29 August 2019; RNZ/AFP, 25 July 2017

C.n: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
C.vn: Warrant listed at least eight pupils; convicted over abuse of two sisters
C.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
C.cover: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.
C.d: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
C.cite: County Court of Victoria verdict 3 April 2023 (Al Jazeera); Wikipedia 'Malka Leifer affair' (index)

C.n: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
C.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
C.cover: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.
C.d: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.
