C.cite: AP, 8 August 2022

C.n: Charity Commission inquiry — Manchester New Moston Jehovah's Witnesses congregation
C.who: Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (charity); Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
C.cover: Trustees dismissed one allegation as a matter between two teenagers, did not enforce restrictions on the accused, and the victims were effectively required to repeat their allegations at an internal hearing in front of the abuser, who was allowed to question them. The charity did not give the Commission accurate and complete answers. The Watch Tower Society fought the inquiry through five courts and tribunals until 2016.
C.d: Allegations of child abuse against a trustee of the New Moston congregation were made in 2012 and 2013; he was later convicted of two counts of indecent assault. The Charity Commission opened a statutory inquiry on 27 May 2014 and published its report on 26 July 2017, finding the trustees had not adequately dealt with the allegations. The Commission also ran a wider inquiry into the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain.
C.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses inquiry report, 26 July 2017

C.n: A v Watchtower — High Court damages over Peter Stewart abuse
C.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
C.d: On 19 June 2015 the High Court (A v Watchtower Bible and Tract Society [2015] EWHC 1722 (QB)) awarded £275,000 damages to a woman abused as a child by Jehovah's Witness ministerial servant Peter Stewart, holding the organisation liable. Separately, in July 2014 Barry congregation elder Mark Sewell was found guilty of eight sex offences including rape and sentenced to 14 years; a church judicial committee had earlier cleared him after the women reported him, and victims said other elders told them not to 'gossip' about the attacks.
C.cite: BBC News, 'Jehovah's Witness Mark Sewell jailed for abusing girls', 2 July 2014; A v Watchtower Bible and Tract Society [2015] EWHC 1722 (QB), 19 June 2015 (BAILII, not opened — bot check)

C.n: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
C.vn: 751 people shared experiences through the study's contact point; 27% of cases led to a police report
C.who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
C.d: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.
C.cite: Utrecht University / WODC, 'Sexual abuse and willingness to report sexual abuse within the Jehovah's Witnesses community', 23 January 2020

C.n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Jehovah's Witnesses child sexual abuse charges
C.place: Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (defendants from Philadelphia, Delaware, Butler and Berks counties)
C.who: Jehovah's Witnesses congregations in Pennsylvania
C.d: A statewide investigating grand jury in Harrisburg, opened after a county prosecutor's referral, heard dozens of witnesses about abuse in Jehovah's Witness congregations. On 7 July 2023 Attorney General Michelle Henry announced charges against five more men, bringing the total to 14 charged; one earlier suspect killed himself before arrest. One former elder was later convicted in Lancaster County.
C.cite: AP (WITF), 7 July 2023

C.n: Latter-day Saints abuse help line — Bisbee, Arizona case (AP investigation)
C.who: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
C.cover: After the father confessed to his bishop, the bishop called the church's abuse help line; church lawyers told him the clergy-penitent privilege meant he had to keep it secret. AP reported the abuse continued for about seven years afterwards. The help line, set up in 1995, routes calls that pose legal risk to church attorneys.
C.d: Paul Douglas Adams, a Border Patrol employee and church member in Bisbee, abused his daughter from age 5 and later a second daughter, and filmed the abuse; he stopped only when arrested in 2017 and died by suicide in jail before trial. An AP investigation published 4 August 2022 found church officials had known for years through confessions. Arizona law, like more than 20 states, lets clergy withhold abuse learned in confession. The church disputed the AP's account.
C.cite: Associated Press investigation, 4 August 2022

C.n: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
C.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
C.cover: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.
C.d: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
C.cite: NBC News/Reuters, April 2016; German Foreign Office, 26 April 2016; Deutsche Welle 2018 and BBC 18 May 2019 (via Wikipedia)

C.n: Re ST (A Minor) — High Court judgment on The Family (Children of God)
C.who: The Family / Children of God (now The Family International)
C.d: In a custody case in the High Court Family Division, Lord Justice Alan Ward gave judgment in chambers on 26 May 1995 and handed it down publicly on 19 October 1995. He found that a high proportion of children in The Family were exposed to adult sexual activity and that a significant number had sexual activity forced on them by adults, and he described harsh discipline including silence restriction and exorcisms of children. He found the group had made changes he judged likely to be irreversible, let the mother keep custody on conditions, required the group to ban corporal punishment of children in the UK by anyone other than parents, and said it must denounce founder David Berg and acknowledge that through his writings he was personally responsible for children being subjected to sexually inappropriate behaviour.
C.cite: High Court of Justice, Family Division, In the matter of ST (a minor), judgment of Lord Justice Ward, given in chambers 26 May 1995 and handed down 19 October 1995 (full text as hosted at exfamily.org)

C.n: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
C.vn: 137 children taken into custody; the judge said 9 showed signs of maltreatment
C.who: The Family / Children of God
C.d: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.
C.cite: Christianity Today, 25 October 1993; Washington Post/Reuters, 2 September 1993 (via Wikipedia)

C.n: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
C.who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
C.d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.
C.cite: US Attorney's Office EDNY press release, 27 October 2020

C.n: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries — leader convicted of transporting girls across state lines
C.vn: girls as young as 9
C.who: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries
C.d: On 24 July 2009 a federal jury convicted Tony Alamo on all 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; women testified he had taken them as 'wives' when they were children, some as young as 9. On 13 November 2009 he was sentenced to 175 years and fined $250,000. In 2013 federal authorities moved against 27 properties held by members to collect $2.5 million restitution. He died in custody in 2017.
C.cite: FBI Little Rock press release, 13 November 2009

C.n: Agape Boarding School — Christian boys' school, Missouri
C.vn: 132 students enrolled in late 2021
C.who: Agape Boarding School (independent Baptist ministry)
C.cover: The state Attorney General's office said 22 workers should have been charged with serious crimes, but the county prosecutor charged five with low-level counts; in Missouri only the local prosecutor can file charges.
C.d: Former students came forward in 2020. In 2021 the school's longtime doctor, David Smock, was charged with child sex crimes and five staff with low-level abuse counts; two later pleaded guilty to misdemeanours. Missouri passed a 2021 law tightening oversight of religious boarding schools. Agape closed on 20 January 2023.
C.cite: AP (CBS News), 11 January 2023

C.n: Royal Commission Case Study 22 — Yeshivah Melbourne and Yeshiva Bondi
C.place: Yeshivah Centre, East St Kilda (Melbourne) and Yeshiva Centre, Bondi (Sydney)
C.vn: Four survivors gave evidence
C.who: Yeshivah Centre / Chabad Institutions of Victoria; Yeshiva Centre – Chabad NSW
C.cover: The Commission found that the principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) as applied in the community discouraged reporting, and survivors who went to police were treated as outcasts. Bondi's Rabbi Yossi Feldman testified he 'was not aware it was illegal to touch a child's genitals'; the Commission found him ignorant of the duty to report.
C.d: The Royal Commission held hearings in February 2015 on responses to abuse by David Cyprys, David Kramer and Aron Kestecher at Yeshivah Melbourne and Daniel Hayman at Yeshiva Bondi. Its report (released October–November 2016) found 'a marked absence of supportive leadership' for survivors at Yeshivah Melbourne. Its 2017 final report recommended Jewish institutions state that mesirah does not apply to reporting child sexual abuse.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 22, 2016

C.n: Nechemya Weberman — Satmar counsellor, Williamsburg
C.who: Satmar Hasidic community, Brooklyn
C.cover: During the case men were arrested for trying to bribe the victim and her husband to drop it; four were later convicted of coercion or witness tampering. Others photographed her on the witness stand and posted the images online.
C.d: Nechemya Weberman, an unlicensed counsellor in the Satmar community, abused a girl from age 12 to 15. He was convicted on all 59 counts on 10 December 2012 and sentenced on 22 January 2013 to 103 years, later cut on appeal. Brooklyn DA figures showed about 100 of 5,389 sex abuse cases since 2009 came from the Haredi community; critics said DA Charles Hynes's policy of not naming Haredi defendants protected the community.
C.cite: AP (Times of Israel), 22 January 2013; Wikipedia 'Sexual abuse cases in Brooklyn's Haredi community' (index)

C.n: AP investigation — sexual abuse in Pakistan's madrassas
C.place: Pakistan (cases in Kehrore Pakka, Mansehra, Punjab)
C.vn: 359 cases reported in newspapers over 10 years (Sahil tally); a Pakistani official disclosed more than 500 complaints against madrassa teachers in 2004
C.who: Islamic seminaries (madrassas), over 22,000 registered with at least 2 million pupils
C.cover: Police are often paid off and refuse to register cases; families of poor victims are pressured to 'forgive' clerics and accept money, which Pakistani law allows; the religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted.
C.d: An AP investigation published 21 November 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics was pervasive in Pakistan's madrassas and seldom prosecuted. In one case a 9-year-old's teacher confessed but was freed after the mother 'forgave' him for $300. A follow-up AP investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the same pattern.
C.cite: Associated Press, 21 November 2017; AP/RFE-RL, 14 April 2020

C.n: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
C.vn: 151 women and girls aged 3 to 65
C.who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
C.cover: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.
C.d: Men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate households, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. The attacks came to light in June 2009. In August 2011 a Bolivian court convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls; seven were sentenced to 25 years and an eighth man got 12 years for supplying the drug.
C.cite: BBC News, 'The rapes haunting a community that shuns the 21st Century', 16 May 2019; The Guardian, 'The work of the devil', 10 September 2009

C.n: Royal Commission data — Uniting Church in Australia
C.vn: about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse across the church's 40-year history
C.who: Uniting Church in Australia
C.d: At a Royal Commission hearing on 10 March 2017, the Uniting Church was reported to have faced about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse over its 40-year history (it was formed in 1977). The Commission's Case Study 23 also examined Knox Grammar School, a Uniting Church school in Sydney.
C.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, hearing 10 March 2017 (Guardian Australia via BishopAccountability)

C.n: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
C.who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
C.cover: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.
C.d: Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001 and became Governor-General in June 2001. In December 2001 he faced allegations that he had handled sexual abuse cases poorly as archbishop. His successor, Phillip Aspinall, set up a church inquiry in February 2002 into the handling of nine abuse cases; its report was tabled in the Queensland Parliament on 1 May 2003, and Aspinall said Hollingworth had made a 'grave and serious' error of judgement. Hollingworth announced his resignation as Governor-General on 25 May 2003.
C.cite: ABC News, 'Timeline: Peter Hollingworth's career', 26 May 2003; The Age, 'He who heard the call now faces the fall', 11 May 2003

C.n: Salvation Army boys' homes — Australia
C.place: Bexley and Goulburn (NSW); Indooroopilly and Riverview (Queensland); Victoria
C.vn: 474 abuse cases settled in Victoria (A$15.5 million, reported 2013); about 30,000 children passed through its homes 1940s–1980s
C.who: The Salvation Army (Australia)
C.cover: The Royal Commission heard that officers accused of abuse were moved interstate.
C.d: The Salvation Army sheltered about 30,000 Australian children from the 1940s to the 1980s and apologised in 2006 for abuse that may have occurred. Private settlements totalling A$15.5 million for 474 cases in Victoria were reported in 2013. In January–February 2014 the Royal Commission's Case Study 5 examined abuse at Bexley Boys' Home, Gill Memorial Home (Goulburn), Alkira (Indooroopilly) and Riverview Training Farm, and how accused officers were investigated and transferred.
C.cite: Royal Commission Case Studies 5, 10 and 33 (2014–2015); Wikipedia 'The Salvation Army' (index)

C.n: Rev. Gordon Nakayama — Anglican dioceses of New Westminster and Calgary
C.place: Vancouver (Diocese of New Westminster) and Alberta (Diocese of Calgary)
C.vn: 'over 300' children, mostly boys aged 3–20, over 62 years of ministry
C.who: Anglican Church of Canada; Japanese Canadian congregations
C.cover: Nakayama made a written confession in 1994; the dioceses did not report it to police. He was allowed to resign and died in 1995.
C.d: Gordon Goichi Nakayama served for more than 50 years as an Anglican priest to Japanese Canadian communities in the dioceses of Calgary and New Westminster. In 1994 he admitted a history of sexually abusing minors and shortly before his death in 1995 signed a written confession to Archbishop Barry Curtis; he was charged with immorality under church law and resigned from ministry, but police were not told. On 15 June 2015 the two dioceses formally apologised to survivors in Vancouver. The church said it is not known how many minors were abused.
C.cite: Anglican Journal, 'Bishops apologize for Japanese-Canadian priest's abuse', 17 June 2015

C.n: Terry Knight — Diocese of Portsmouth
C.who: Church of England, Diocese of Portsmouth
C.cover: Bishop Timothy Bavin did not report Knight to police when parents raised concerns in 1985.
C.d: Terry Knight, active in the Diocese of Portsmouth, was convicted of child sexual offences in 1996 and again in 2016. Parents had raised concerns with the bishop in 1985, who did not inform police.
C.cite: The News (Portsmouth), 2015–2016 (via Wikipedia 'Anglican Communion sexual abuse cases')

C.n: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
C.vn: police estimated 233 student victims; inquiry recorded 175 reports of sexual abuse
C.who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
C.cover: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.
C.d: Police arrested and charged six men on 14 September 2020 over offences at Dilworth alleged to date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. An independent inquiry led by Dame Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild KC, released on 18 September 2023 and covering 1950 to the present, found that sexual abuse was committed consistently from the mid-1950s to the end of 2005: 126 of 171 former students who gave information reported being sexually abused, and the inquiry knew of 49 more. Police estimated 233 student victims. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.
C.cite: RNZ, 'Dilworth independent inquiry releases report into historical abuse at school', 18 September 2023; RNZ, 'Six men arrested and charged in relation to historical offences', 14 September 2020

C.n: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
C.vn: Police said in 2021 at least 60 people in the community had been involved in 'harmful sexual behaviour'
C.who: Gloriavale Christian Community
C.cover: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.
C.d: Founder Neville Cooper ('Hopeful Christian') was sentenced in December 1995 to five years in prison on three charges of indecent assault against a young woman, after an earlier conviction on 10 counts involving five young complainants was overturned on appeal. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled that three former members had been employees from age six, doing 'strenuous, difficult and sometimes dangerous' work. Leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to indecently assaulting six girls and young women between 2002 and 2022, resigned as leader, and on 12 December 2025 was jailed for 26 months.
C.cite: RNZ, 'Disgraced former Gloriavale leader Howard Temple sentenced to 26 months' jail', 12 December 2025; NZ Herald, on founder's 1995 conviction; RNZ, Employment Court ruling, 10 May 2022

C.n: Jesus Fellowship (Jesus Army) — Operation Lifeboat and redress scheme
C.vn: 601 redress applicants; the trust found about one in six children in the community were sexually abused
C.who: Jesus Fellowship Church / Jesus Fellowship Community Trust
C.d: After founder Noel Stanton died in 2009, Northamptonshire Police ran Operation Lifeboat into historic abuse; about ten to twelve former members were convicted of sex offences. The church's redress scheme, whose final report was published on 11 September 2024, received 601 applications, paid £7.7 million, identified 539 alleged perpetrators and accepted responsibility for 264 of them, 61% of whom were former leaders.
C.cite: Jesus Fellowship Redress Scheme Final Report, 11 September 2024; BBC News 2019–2024 (via Wikipedia 'Jesus Army')

C.n: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches — Star-Telegram investigation
C.place: IFB churches in the US and Canada
C.vn: 412 abuse allegations in 187 churches and institutions
C.who: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions
C.d: A Fort Worth Star-Telegram investigation published in December 2018 identified 412 allegations of sexual misconduct in 187 Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions across 40 US states and Canada, some dating back to the 1970s. Reporters spoke to more than 200 current or former members, and described accused men being able to move to other churches through informal networks of church-college alumni.
C.cite: HuffPost, 'Investigation Unearths Hundreds Of Abuse Allegations In Independent Baptist Churches', 12 December 2018, reporting the Fort Worth Star-Telegram investigation of 9 December 2018

C.n: Samuel Bateman — FLDS splinter group, Short Creek
C.vn: at least 10 minor 'wives', youngest 9
C.who: Splinter group of the FLDS led by Samuel Bateman
C.d: Samuel Bateman began claiming to be a new prophet in 2019 and led a group that broke off from the FLDS church. In a plea agreement he admitted 'spiritually marrying' 20 women and girls, 10 of them under age, with the intent of sexual activity with the girls. He was arrested in 2022, when nine child 'brides' were removed from homes. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transport a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to commit kidnapping, and on 9 December 2024 a federal judge in Phoenix sentenced him to 50 years. Two male followers who went to trial were convicted.
C.cite: Salt Lake Tribune, 'Samuel Bateman gets 50 years in prison', 9 December 2024

C.n: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
C.who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
C.d: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on 3 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor, production of child pornography and human trafficking. On 3 June 2022, days before trial, he pleaded guilty to three counts involving minors (two of forcible oral copulation and one lewd act on a 15-year-old), and on 8 June 2022 was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty to four counts in 2020. In October 2023 a federal grand jury indicted him for producing and possessing child pornography involving a 16-year-old follower.
C.cite: Los Angeles Times, 'La Luz del Mundo church leader pleads guilty to sex abuse charges', 3 June 2022; Los Angeles Times, 4 June 2019; NBC News/AP, 26 October 2023

C.n: Apollo Quiboloy — Kingdom of Jesus Christ
C.who: Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC)
C.d: A federal grand jury in the Central District of California returned a 42-count superseding indictment on 10 November 2021 (unsealed 18 November) charging Quiboloy and eight church administrators, including with sex trafficking of children. It alleges females aged about 12 to 25 were recruited as personal assistants and required to have sex with him, and that church members were brought to the US on fraudulently obtained visas and forced to solicit donations for a sham charity. In 2024 the Philippine Department of Justice charged him with sexual abuse and a court ordered his arrest; after a two-week police operation at the church's Davao City compound he surrendered and was taken into custody on 8 September 2024. He denies the charges.
C.cite: US Attorney's Office, Central District of California, superseding indictment press release, 18 November 2021; Al Jazeera, 'Philippine authorities arrest church leader charged with sex trafficking', 8 September 2024

C.n: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
C.place: Selangor and Negeri Sembilan (later raids in 8 more states)
C.vn: 402 children rescued on 11 September 2024; 625 victims aged 2–28 by end of operation; 13 suspected sodomy cases among 384 screened; 415 arrests by 23 October 2024
C.who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
C.d: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 charity homes linked to GISB Holdings in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, after six months of intelligence work; police said they had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. By 10 October police put the total rescued at 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022–2023, another teaching assistant with sexually assaulting four boys, and others with physical abuse of children; police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.
C.cite: Bernama, 'Global Op: Chronology of GISBH Case', 20 September 2024 (also in New Straits Times); The Star, '625 victims total rescued from GISB by police', 10 October 2024

C.n: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
C.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
C.d: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.
C.cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, 'Two Senior Leaders of Lev Tahor Sect Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison for Kidnapping and Sex Crimes', 31 March 2022

C.n: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
C.who: Lev Tahor
C.d: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 minors from a Lev Tahor farm compound in Oratorio after abuse and trafficking complaints; in January 2025 Interpol arrested a member in Guatemala on trafficking charges. The group had earlier fled child-protection proceedings in Quebec (2013, where authorities sought care for 127 children) and Ontario.
C.cite: Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor' (citing Reuters, Times of Israel, 2024–2025)

C.n: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
C.place: ISKCON rural community boarding schools, US and India
C.who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
C.d: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.
C.cite: Wikipedia 'International Society for Krishna Consciousness' (citing Rochford 2007 and others)

C.n: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
C.vn: 80 testimonies heard by the commission
C.who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
C.cover: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.
C.d: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.
C.cite: Independent Commission of Inquiry report, April 1998; Christianity Today, 2010 (via Wikipedia 'Christian and Missionary Alliance')

C.n: New Tribes Mission — Fanda boarding school, Senegal
C.who: New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360)
C.d: A 2010 report by GRACE (Godly Response to Abuse in the Christian Environment), commissioned by New Tribes Mission after pressure from survivors, accused the mission of a culture of systemic abuse at the Fanda boarding school it ran in Senegal for missionaries' children, including sexual abuse of more than 20 children; a former dorm parent was identified as the most prolific perpetrator. 1992 field committee notes said allegations should not be reported to police. The mission then set up its own investigation process, IHART, to examine historical allegations at other schools.
C.cite: NBC News, 'Ungodly abuse: The lasting torment of the New Tribes missionary kids', 2019

C.n: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
C.vn: Liberation ceremonies freed 400 (2000), 126 (2001), 465 (2003), 94 (2004), 120 (2005) and 52 (2010) people from specific shrines; no national count
C.who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
C.d: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.
C.cite: Ghana Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 1998 (Act 554); BBC 2001; Africa Recovery 2001 (via Wikipedia 'Trokosi')

C.n: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
C.vn: Karnataka government study: 40,600 devadasis (2008); Karnataka State Women's University: over 80,000 (2018); Andhra Pradesh identified 16,624
C.who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
C.d: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite laws against the practice, including Karnataka's 1982 ban. The Karnataka government's last survey, in 2008, counted 40,600 devadasis; NGOs and a 2018 Karnataka State Women's University study found more than 80,000. Girls as young as seven have been pushed into the tradition.
C.cite: The New Indian Express, 'Over 80K Devadasis in Karnataka, say NGOs', 28 February 2020; The New Indian Express, 'The women who lived as sex slaves to an Indian goddess', 23 January 2023

AFG.story:
During the war in Afghanistan, commanders in the Afghan security forces and the Afghan Local Police sexually abused boys, a practice known as bacha bazi. In 2011 two US soldiers, Capt. Dan Quinn and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland, beat a local police commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy. Quinn was relieved of his command and Martland was at first discharged. In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told not to intervene when their Afghan allies abused boys, in some cases even on US bases.

Nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR), the US official who audits spending in Afghanistan, to investigate. Its report, made public in January 2018, found that by August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them sexual assaults on children. A US law, the Leahy Law, requires aid to be cut to military units that commit such violations, but the Pentagon used an exception in the law to keep supporting them. In December 2015 it approved continued funding for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.

After the Taliban took power, the UN verified sexual violence against 13 children in 2022, 12 in 2023 and 6 in 2024, and attributed most of these cases to the Taliban. In March 2024 boys aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs, religious schools, told the broadcaster Radio Azadi that teachers had pressured them into sexual acts. One 16-year-old reported a teacher to the school's qari, a senior religious teacher, who only told the teacher to stop, and the abuse continued. The Taliban run 6,836 madrasahs for boys and have sought 100,000 new teachers for them.

Under the former government and under the Taliban, boys have been abused by men with official power, and the United States kept funding units accused of it. The UN's small yearly counts are the only figures, and no representative survey has measured online sexual exploitation of children in South Asia.

BEN.story:
Among the Fon people of Benin, and the Ewe in neighbouring Ghana and Togo, some traditional shrines practise trokosi. A family gives a girl, usually a young virgin, to a shrine to atone for a wrong that a relative is said to have committed. The girl serves the shrine's priest without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as part of her duty, which defenders of the practice deny. Ghana made ritual servitude a crime in 1998, with a minimum sentence of three years, but the practice continued there and no prosecutions are recorded. The records for this map do not describe any law or prosecution in Benin.

There is also no survey that measures the sexual exploitation of children in Benin. Childlight, a research centre that combines national surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa had no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children.

How many girls are held in shrines in Benin, and how many children are exploited in other ways, is not known.

BHR.story:
The records for this map hold no case, inquiry or count of child sexual abuse or trafficking in Bahrain. Childlight, a research centre that combines national surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that there was no representative survey data on the online sexual exploitation of children for the Middle East and North Africa, the region that includes Bahrain. Without such surveys, counts depend on the cases that reach the authorities or that technology companies report.

The extent of child sexual exploitation in Bahrain is therefore not known.
---

CAF.story:
In December 2013 France sent soldiers to the Central African Republic in Operation Sangaris, under French and not UN command. Six boys aged 9 to 13 later told UN staff that French soldiers had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the camp for displaced people at M'Poko airport in Bangui, in exchange for food rations. The UN did not pass its internal report to the French authorities, and Anders Kompass, the UN official who did, was suspended and resigned in 2016. The Paris prosecutor's investigation grew to cover accusations by 15 children, but in January 2018 French judges closed the case for lack of sufficient evidence, and no soldier was charged.

The UN's own mission, MINUSCA, faced similar accusations. Under UN rules, only the country that sends a peacekeeper can prosecute them, and the UN can only send soldiers home. Two allegations about Gabonese and Burundian troops in Dékoa led to interviews with about 136 alleged victims, 48% of all victims the UN recorded worldwide in 2016. Press reports said 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges. In 2015 girls in Bambari told Human Rights Watch they had been raped by peacekeepers guarding the airport, and in January 2016 the UN withdrew a battalion from the Democratic Republic of the Congo whose soldiers had been accused of rape. In September 2021 it sent home all of Gabon's units, about 450 soldiers, after more allegations.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in the country: 58 by the CPC coalition of armed groups and 35 by government and pro-government forces. It also verified the abduction of 141 children, most of them for recruitment or sexual violence.

None of the foreign soldiers accused of abusing children in the Central African Republic is recorded here as convicted. The country's own forces are now among those the UN finds abusing girls, and no survey has measured the abuse of children across West and Central Africa.

CHN.story:
China opened intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by parents in other countries, in 1992. About 160,000 children were sent abroad, most of them to the United States, which issued visas to 87,704 children adopted from China between 1994 and 2014. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought babies from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with families in China and abroad. In 2005, 23 officials were fired and three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years in prison. The New Yorker reported that the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking, and on 5 September 2024 China ended it.

Girls and women are also brought into China from neighbouring countries and sold as brides. Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States in Myanmar, many displaced by war, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to $13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the AP news agency that the investigation largely stopped because of pressure from officials worried about relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals.

In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports of online abuse from technology companies, received 9,406 reports for China, compared with 1,933,900 for India, because most American platforms are blocked there. The extent of online abuse of children in China is therefore not known, and the trade in brides from neighbouring countries continues.

CIV.story:
Girls are moved within and into Côte d'Ivoire for work and sex. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and other West African countries to Abidjan, promising school or training, and then keep them as domestic servants, where they are vulnerable to sexual exploitation. Ivorian women and girls are sold for sex, especially in Abidjan. Nigerian traffickers recruit women and girls with offers of jobs in shops and then exploit them in the gold-mining and cocoa regions, as part of networks that also move Nigerian girls to mines in Senegal, Mali and Burkina Faso.

How many children in Côte d'Ivoire are sexually exploited is not known, because no representative survey has been done in West and Central Africa.

GBR.story:
Complaints about Jimmy Savile, a BBC presenter who also raised money for NHS hospitals, first reached the police in 1958. Police investigations during his lifetime, the last by Surrey Police in 2007–09, produced no charges, and in December 2011 after his death the BBC programme Newsnight shelved its own report on him. After an ITV documentary in October 2012, the Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree. Its 2013 report recorded 214 crimes from 1955 to 2009, and 73% of the 450 people who made allegations were under 18 at the time.

Cyril Smith, the Liberal MP for Rochdale from 1972 to 1992, was first reported to the police in 1968, by a pupil who was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man". The Director of Public Prosecutions, the official who decides on prosecutions, advised against charging him in 1970, and reviews in 1998 and 1999 brought no charge. He died in 2010, and in 2012 prosecutors said he should have been charged. In 2020 the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), a national inquiry for England and Wales with legal powers, found no organised network of abusers at Westminster but found "overt and direct deference by police towards powerful people".

In Rotherham, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited by groups of men between 1997 and 2013. It called the failures of the council and South Yorkshire Police "blatant", and three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Telford, a 2022 inquiry found more than 1,000 children exploited over at least 30 years, which agencies had treated as "child prostitution". In 2025 Baroness Casey's national audit found that police records were too poor to measure the scale of this abuse, and the government agreed to a new national inquiry with statutory powers.

IICSA's final report in 2022 made 107 recommendations. The first to be fully carried out, removing the three-year deadline for civil claims over child sexual abuse in England and Wales, took effect in June 2026, and the new inquiry into group-based exploitation is starting with Oldham.

GMB.story:
In 2003 The Gambia passed the Tourism Offences Act. It defined a child as anyone under 18, made hotel operators liable if they knowingly allowed child prostitution on their premises, and set life imprisonment as the penalty for tourists who traffic children. By 2017 the US State Department reported that traffickers were increasingly hosting foreign men who came to abuse children in private homes outside the main tourist areas, where they were harder to detect.

The State Department's 2025 trafficking report says European tourists, mainly from the United Kingdom, reportedly still travel to The Gambia to sexually exploit children. Organised networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country, and especially the Senegambia Strip, a beach resort area, to these visitors. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for jobs in tourism and then sexually exploited.

After the 2003 law, traffickers moved some of the abuse into private homes, and visitors from Europe still come for it. The number of children affected is not known, because no representative survey of child sexual exploitation has been done in West and Central Africa.
