IRQ.story:
On 3 August 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State (ISIS) attacked Sinjar, the home district of the Yazidi religious minority in northern Iraq. Its fighters moved captured Yazidis by bus and truck to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj, including Badoush prison and a wedding hall in Mosul, and then took women and girls to Raqqa in Syria. Women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at markets and held as sexual slaves, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. In June 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis and that more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, most of them in Syria. Thousands remain missing.

After ISIS lost its territory, the risk to children moved into the camps for displaced people. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says women and girls in these camps whose relatives are accused of links to ISIS may be sexually exploited by security and military officials. An international organisation reported in 2024 that officials made family members of detained children perform sex acts in exchange for security clearances or civil documents, such as identity papers. The government reported no action against these officials. The same report says Yazidi survivors remain at risk of being trafficked again. Armed groups also still take children: the UN verified 18 abductions in 2022, 10 of them by ISIS and 4 by the Kurdish armed group HPG/PKK, and 8 in 2024.

Thousands of Yazidi women and children taken in 2014 are still missing. Children in the displacement camps whose families are linked to ISIS depend on officials for their papers, and some of those officials are accused of exploiting them. No representative survey has measured the sexual exploitation of children in the Middle East and North Africa.

ISL.story:
Iceland appears in the records for this map mainly as a place where abuse material is stored online. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds abuse images and has them removed, took action against 7,455 web addresses hosted on servers in Iceland, 2 percent of all the addresses it acted on that year.

The records also link Iceland to two international police operations in 2025. In Operation Stream, police from 38 countries working with Europol, the European Union's police agency, took down Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users, and identified 1,393 suspects. In Operation Cumberland, police from Denmark and 18 other countries acted against a paid platform that distributed abuse images made with artificial intelligence, identifying 273 suspects and arresting 25. Europol said many countries had no national laws covering such images.

Abuse material is still hosted on servers in Iceland. The records for this map hold no inquiry or count of abuse of children within the country.

ITA.story:
Italy has never held a national inquiry into the abuse of children in the Catholic Church or other institutions, and there are no official statistics on it. In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference, the body of the country's Catholic bishops, said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty that governs relations between Italy and the Holy See, its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The victims' group Rete l'Abuso has asked for years for an independent inquiry.

Fr Nicola Corradi was accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, and the diocese flagged him in 2011. He continued working at the order's school in Luján de Cuyo in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016, and in 2019 a court in Mendoza convicted him of abusing deaf children there and sentenced him to 42 years. Joseph Henn, a priest indicted in Arizona in 2003, went to Italy and avoided extradition, the legal handing over of a suspect to another country, until he was arrested in Rome in May 2019.

Italy is also the destination of a trafficking route for women and girls, most of them from Edo State in Nigeria, who are moved overland through Niger and Libya and then by boat, bound by debts and oaths. The UN migration agency IOM recorded an almost 600 percent rise in potential victims arriving by sea between 2014 and 2017. In Palermo, police arrested 19 alleged members of a cell of Black Axe, a Nigerian confraternity, in 2016 over the exploitation of prostitution and other crimes; a judge convicted 14 in 2018, and in 2019 another court rejected the charge of mafia association against five others. In 2016 Europol, the European Union's police agency, said that at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy.

No national inquiry has counted abuse in Italy's churches and institutions, so its extent is not known. It is also not known how many of the 5,000 migrant children who went missing in Italy were exploited.

KEN.story:
In December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs published a study of four beach resort areas on the coast. It found that up to 30 percent of girls aged 12 to 18 living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex. Kenyans made up 38 percent of the clients, and tourists from Italy, Germany and Switzerland 44 percent. The vice president, Moody Awori, accepted the findings and said the police and communities had failed to enforce the law. A 2023 study by a charity, cited in the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report, estimated that more than 2,000 children were sold for sex in Kilifi and Kwale counties on the coast, now more often in private villas and holiday homes than in hotels. The same report described concerns about officials taking part, with no action reported against them.

Children are also sold in Nairobi. In 2020 a year-long investigation by BBC Africa Eye found people who snatched babies from homeless mothers and sold them for about £350 to £550, and illegal street clinics that sold newborns. A clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings, using the hospital's real transfer papers. The BBC said he appeared to keep his job. Rings also bring women and underage girls across the border from the Karamoja region of Uganda to Nairobi for domestic work or sex.

At the Nyumbani Children's Home in Nairobi, a Catholic charity's home for children with HIV that drew large donations from the United States, a 2021 investigation by the US aid agency USAID found claims that volunteers, caregivers and other children had raped children to be credible. A 2022 USAID memo said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006.

Twenty years after the government accepted the 2006 findings, children are still sold for sex on the coast, now mostly in private villas. No action has been reported against the officials accused of taking part.

KWT.story:
On 21 August 2025 Kuwait's telecommunications regulator temporarily blocked Roblox, an online game platform popular with children, after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety. Qatar had blocked it on 13 August and Turkey on 7 August, and Oman and Jordan had banned it since 2020.

Little else about the abuse or exploitation of children in Kuwait is counted. Childlight, a research centre that combines national surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that there was no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children for the Middle East and North Africa. Without such surveys, counts depend on the cases that reach the authorities or that technology companies report.

The extent of child sexual exploitation in Kuwait is not known.

LUX.story:
Between 1984 and 2008, 561 children from South Korea were sent to Luxembourg for adoption, part of about 163,898 Korean children sent abroad from 1953 to 2008. Four Korean agencies held guardianship of the children and sent them abroad under government policy. In March 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body investigating past abuses, found that these agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet the demand of foreign partner agencies, had falsely registered children as orphans and had sometimes swapped children's identities, and that the Korean state had failed to supervise them.

Luxembourg is also linked in the records to Operation Stream, the 2025 police action by 38 countries and Europol, the European Union's police agency, against Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users. The operation identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79.

The Korean commission found fraud in the system that sent children to Luxembourg, and the records for this map hold no inquiry by Luxembourg into these adoptions.

MAR.story:
In December 2010 Moroccan police arrested Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, and in September 2011 a court sentenced him to 30 years in prison for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. On 30 July 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned him along with 47 other Spanish prisoners, as a gesture towards Spain. Galván left Morocco on an expired passport, with the authorities' knowledge. Protesters gathered outside parliament in Rabat and were violently dispersed. On 4 August the king revoked the pardon and said he had not been told the details of the case. Spanish police arrested Galván on 7 August, and he was imprisoned in Spain to finish his sentence. It was not the first such pardon. A 2010 US diplomatic cable reported that in 2006 the king had pardoned Hervé Le Gloannec, a Frenchman convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh, and he was released.

Foreign offenders still come to Morocco. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says foreign nationals, mainly from Europe and the Middle East, sexually exploit children in the major cities, and that charities report tourists abusing children in Tangier in holiday rentals owned and run by Europeans. It also reports alleged exploitation of children after the earthquake in Al Haouz in September 2023. Moroccan courts convicted 60 traffickers in 2024.

Morocco has also sent soldiers abroad as UN peacekeepers, and Moroccan military personnel are named in UN records of sexual exploitation and abuse allegations in the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Foreign men continue to abuse children in Moroccan cities, and in two known cases foreigners convicted of it were freed by royal pardon. How many children are affected is not known, because no representative survey of online or other exploitation has been done in the Middle East and North Africa.

MYS.story:
On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 children's homes in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan run as charities by Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), a company linked to Al-Arqam, a religious movement that is banned in Malaysia. Police had received 41 reports about the group since 2011 and had gathered intelligence for six months before the raids. They rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, and by 10 October the number of children rescued had risen to 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022 and 2023, another teaching assistant was charged with sexually assaulting four boys, and others were charged with physically abusing children. Police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

In 2016 an undercover investigation by Al Jazeera's 101 East programme found babies being advertised online with photographs and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by sex, race and skin colour. Some went to couples who wanted a child, and the programme reported that others were sold to traffickers. Among those giving up babies were immigrant sex workers, who are not legally allowed to bear children in Malaysia.

Malaysian servers also hold abuse material. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, took action against 17,046 web addresses hosted in Malaysia, 5 percent of its total, the same share as in 2024.

The GISB cases were at the charge stage in the records for this map, so the courts have not yet decided them. Malaysia's share of the world's hosted abuse material did not fall between 2024 and 2025.

NLD.story:
In March 2010 the Catholic Church in the Netherlands set up a commission led by the former minister Wim Deetman to examine abuse by its clergy. Its report in December 2011 identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who had abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 minors had been abused. It found that bishops and church officials had known and followed a policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing". In 2012 a state commission received 800 claims of sexual abuse in children's homes and foster families and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor.

The Netherlands also received thousands of children through intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. About 4,000 came from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, where babies were bought or taken from hospitals and handed to paid "acting mothers" who posed as birth mothers in court. A government committee chaired by Tjibbe Joustra reported in February 2021 that adoptions from Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia and other countries from 1967 to 1997/98 involved serious violations and that the Dutch government had failed for decades to prevent them. On 8 February 2021 the government suspended all intercountry adoption with immediate effect, and in 2024 announced that its citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

In 2018 the Netherlands held 47% of the material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images. Its share fell to 11% in 2025, or 33,788 web addresses, but INHOPE, the international network of reporting hotlines, still ranked it first for confirmed material that year.

The Netherlands has examined abuse in the church, in state care and in adoption, and has closed adoption from abroad. Its share of the abuse material found online has fallen, but Dutch servers still hold more confirmed material than those of any other country in INHOPE's count.

PRY.story:
In 2002 Fr Carlos Urrutigoity, an Argentine priest, was accused in the Diocese of Scranton in the United States of sleeping in the same beds as boarding-school students at St Gregory's Academy, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved with his group of followers to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este in Paraguay. In 2014 its bishop, Rogelio Livieres, made him vicar general, the bishop's second-in-command. Pope Francis removed Livieres later in 2014, reportedly in part because of this case, and in June 2015 Urrutigoity was moved again, to Mendoza in Argentina. He has not been convicted. The Paraguayan newspaper La Nación reported that at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or of crimes against humanity had taken shelter in Paraguay.

Paraguay has also been a place to live for offenders from abroad. In April 2021 police arrested a German man in Paraguay who was one of the administrators of Boystown, a website on the hidden part of the internet used to share the abuse of boys, which had 400,000 registered users. He and three other German administrators were sentenced in December 2022 to between 7 and 12 years.

Inside the country, the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report describes criadazgo, a common practice in which families take in children from poorer households and make them work as unpaid domestic servants. An estimated 47,000 children live in criadazgo, most of them girls, and many are highly vulnerable to sex and labour trafficking.

About 47,000 children remain in criadazgo, which the US government treats as a form of trafficking. Accused priests from neighbouring Argentina have found posts in Paraguay, and the records show none of them convicted there.

PSE.story:
In June 2024 the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, a body appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, reported on sexual violence in the war that began on 7 October 2023. It found that Israeli security forces had subjected Palestinians in detention and during arrests to sexual and gender-based violence, including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that "men and boys were targeted in particular ways". It found that the persecution of Palestinian men and boys on the basis of gender was a crime against humanity. The same commission found that sexual violence was committed in Israel on 7 October, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage.

In November 2025 the Palestinian authorities announced a ban on the online game platform Roblox, after several countries in the region blocked it over concerns about children's safety.

The UN commission's finding is the only official record on this map of sexual violence against Palestinian boys. Other abuse of children in Palestine is not measured, because no representative survey has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa.

RWA.story:
Rwanda appears in the records for this map as a country that sent children abroad through intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. On 10 October 2007 Ireland's Adoption Board, the state body that then approved adoptions, suspended adoptions from Rwanda and Ethiopia.

The records give no further detail about adoptions from Rwanda, about the reasons for the suspension, or about the abuse or trafficking of children inside the country.
---

SSD.story:
In 2022 the UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls in South Sudan, some as young as seven. Soldiers of the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, the national army, were responsible for 74 of them, and armed opposition groups and the national police for most of the rest. In 2024 the UN verified seven cases, five of them by the army.

People displaced by the fighting shelter in UN-run camps called Protection of Civilians sites. In 2022 The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022, aid workers at the UN-run camp in Malakal had sexually exploited displaced women and girls, including by demanding sex in exchange for aid. Women and girls said they had been raped and become pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named. UN peacekeepers in South Sudan can be prosecuted only by the countries that sent them, and the UN can only send them home. In the UN's 2025 data on allegations against peacekeepers, few cases were finished: one Togolese officer was sent home and jailed for 60 days, and others were waiting for information from the country concerned.

Earlier, from 1994 to 2006, the Lord's Resistance Army, a Ugandan armed group, held children it had abducted in northern Uganda at its bases in southern Sudan. In 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, of 61 crimes including sexual slavery and forced marriage.

The UN records South Sudan's own army as the main abuser of girls there, and the records show no punishment of the aid workers named at Malakal. Online abuse is barely counted: in 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports of online abuse from technology companies, received 863 reports for South Sudan.

SWE.story:
In February 2011 a Swedish government inquiry reported on abuse and neglect in municipal children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980. It recommended a public apology, which was made at Stockholm City Hall that year, and a payment of SEK 250,000 to each person who had suffered serious abuse. A compensation board opened in 2013, and by July 2015 it had decided just over 4,000 applications and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

Sweden was also one of the main receiving countries for intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. It took in 9,051 children from South Korea between 1957 and 2005. When South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia in January 1975, the Swedish ambassador urged it to keep sending children. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body investigating past abuses, found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Children also came to Sweden from Chile, where many were taken from poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, when babies were bought from "baby farms", and from Greece between 1950 and 1975.

After campaigning by Chilean adoptees, Sweden set up an independent inquiry. Its report of 2 June 2025, nearly 1,600 pages long, covered 65 years of adoptions and documented many irregular and illegal adoptions that state authorities had some knowledge of. By then Sweden had stopped adoptions from South Korea.

In 2016 Europol, the European Union's police agency, said that about 1,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Sweden, and that it had evidence some of the children who went missing in Europe had been sexually exploited.

Sweden has examined both its own care system and the adoptions it arranged from abroad, and found that state authorities knew of some of the illegal adoptions. The records for this map give no later account of the 1,000 migrant children who went missing in Sweden.

TUR.story:
Türkiye has hosted about 2.9 million people displaced from Syria. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says Syrian girls in Türkiye, especially in poor rural regions, are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, which are not registered with the state, and are then held as domestic servants and sold for sex. The report says corruption and official complicity remain significant concerns, but no investigations of complicit officials were reported.

Türkiye was earlier a destination for trafficking from Moldova. In March 2007 the State Department reported that women and children from Moldova were trafficked for sexual exploitation, more and more often to Russia and to the Middle East, including Türkiye, Israel and the United Arab Emirates. UNICEF found that children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more likely than other children to be trafficked.

In December 2025 prosecutors in Ankara reportedly opened an inquiry after an opposition MP, Turhan Çömez, cited US Justice Department files on Jeffrey Epstein. The document in question is a 2009 civil complaint by an anonymous woman that alleged, "upon information and belief", that Epstein had brought minor girls from Turkey and other countries. No findings or charges have been reported.

The forced marriage of Syrian girls in Türkiye continues, and no official has been investigated for taking part. The records for this map give no count of the girls affected.

UKR.story:
Between 2012 and 2015 the US-based group Disability Rights International investigated 33 Ukrainian orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities, and concluded that the orphanage system served traffickers as a way to recruit children. La Strada Ukraine, an anti-trafficking charity, told it that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that sexual exploitation in institutions usually began around age 13, often started by staff. A coordinator for IOM, the UN migration agency, said most documented trafficking cases began in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. Ukraine also sent 18,612 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and the United States issued visas to 10,544 children adopted from Ukraine from 1994 to 2014.

After Russia's full invasion in February 2022, a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped children. The war also put children left in Ukrainian institutions at risk. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report said children evacuated from at least 195 facilities were at high risk, that officials at several state institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running.

Children who remain in Ukraine's institutions are at risk from traffickers, and no official has been convicted of taking part.

VAT.story:
The Holy See is both the central government of the Catholic Church and a state with its own diplomats and courts. In 1922, and again in 1962 in an instruction called Crimen sollicitationis, it ordered that church trials of priests accused of sexual acts with children be kept absolutely secret, on pain of automatic excommunication. In 2001 it required bishops to send every case of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, its office for church discipline, and kept those cases under the pontifical secret, its highest level of confidentiality. Between 2004 and 2013 that office studied 3,420 credible cases and dismissed 884 priests from the priesthood.

In August 2013 it recalled Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, its nuncio, or ambassador, to the Dominican Republic, amid allegations that he had abused minors, before Dominican prosecutors opened their investigation. He was charged by a Vatican prosecutor in 2015 and died before trial. In 2017 it recalled Mgr Carlo Capella from its embassy in Washington, and in 2018 its own court convicted him of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years; he was not tried in the United States or Canada. Archbishop Luigi Ventura, its nuncio to France, was tried in Paris in his absence and in December 2020 received an eight-month suspended sentence. Ireland's Murphy Commission, a state inquiry, received no files from the Vatican.

In 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said the Holy See had placed the church's reputation and the protection of offenders above children's interests and had moved abusive priests to new parishes. In 2019 Pope Francis required clergy to report suspected abuse to church authorities, though not to the police, and in December 2019 he lifted the pontifical secret so that case files could be given to state authorities.

Since December 2019 church files on abuse can be given to state authorities, but the Holy See still decides whether to hand them over, and its own rules do not require clergy to report abuse to the police.

WSM.story:
Between 2002 and 2005 Focus on Children, an adoption agency in Utah run by Scott and Karen Banks, arranged for about 80 Samoan children to be taken to the United States. The agency told the parents that their children would go to America for a time to attend school. Instead, the children were adopted permanently by American families. In February 2007 a US federal court charged the Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. In January 2009 they all pleaded guilty to misdemeanour charges, the less serious class of crime, of helping foreigners enter the country improperly, and the agency pleaded guilty to a more serious conspiracy charge. A judge sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.

A Salesian priest, a member of a Catholic religious order, who had been convicted of abuse in Melbourne, Australia, was allegedly moved to Samoa so that he would not face further police investigation.

Families in Samoa lost children to adoption abroad through an agency that misled them, and the people responsible were given probation. The case of the priest sent from Australia is an allegation, and the records do not show whether it was investigated in Samoa.

ZAF.story:
In 1979 Fettes College, a private school in Edinburgh, dismissed the teacher Iain Wares but gave him a glowing reference. He went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children. South Africa approved his extradition, the legal handing over of a suspect to another country, to Scotland, and in 2025 he was still contesting it. A German priest, Fr Georg Kerkhoff, also worked in South Africa for years while abuse cases were pending against him at home. He was tried in South Africa for abusing boys at a camp in 2008, then extradited to Germany and jailed in Krefeld in 2015.

The British barrister John Smyth came to South Africa from Zimbabwe. An internal report by the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity whose holiday camps he chaired, described in 1982 how he had beaten boys, and he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 without the police being told. When Zimbabwe refused to let him back into the country, he moved to South Africa in 2001. He was never charged anywhere. A review for the Church of England published in 2024 called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa" and found it highly likely that he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town in 2018.

Inside South Africa, the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas and sell them for sex in the cities, especially in Gauteng and the Western Cape. Brothel owners use drugs to control them, some parents sell their own children for money or drugs, and low-level officials are complicit. In a separate case against Timothy Omotoso, which began in 2017, the trial was delayed for eight years by motions and recusals, and the witness Pamela Mabini, who had reported him, was shot dead on 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict.

Abusers who left Britain and Germany found new work with children in South Africa, and two were later extradited or approved for extradition. The trafficking of rural children into the cities continues, with officials still complicit.

ZWE.story:
Between 1946 and 1956, 276 children from British care were sent to the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College in Southern Rhodesia, as Zimbabwe was then called, under British child migration programmes. These were schemes, backed by the UK government and run by charities such as the Fairbridge Society, that sent children from Britain to the colonies and dominions. At the college, children who told the headmaster that a padre, a chaplain, had sexually abused them were beaten and warned against "spreading malicious lies". In 2018 the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse for England and Wales called child migration "a deeply flawed government policy".

In 1984 the English barrister John Smyth moved to Zimbabwe. Two years earlier, an internal report for the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity whose holiday camps he had chaired, had described how he beat boys, but its readers did not tell the police. In Zimbabwe he founded Zambesi Ministries in 1986, which ran camps for boys. A 16-year-old died at one of the camps in December 1992. Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged. A review for the Church of England published in 2024 found no evidence that anyone in England had tried to warn the Zimbabwean authorities about him, and described him as "a problem solved and exported to Africa". Zimbabwe later refused to let him back into the country, and in 2001 he moved to South Africa.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says women and children are sold for sex around Zimbabwe's gold and diamond mines, sometimes for money or food, and that children work there as panners and ore carriers. Some families trade daughters for food or money, and under the custom of ngozi a girl may be given to another family to make amends for a killing. Low-level officials are complicit.

In both cases, British institutions that knew of abuse did not act to protect children in Zimbabwe. The risks the records describe today come from inside the country, where girls are traded by families and sold for sex around the mines.

SOM.story:
In 2013 and 2014 the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), a force of soldiers sent by African countries to support the Somali government, had its headquarters and bases in Mogadishu. Human Rights Watch interviewed 50 people there, including 21 survivors. In a report published on 8 September 2014 it documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by AMISOM soldiers, mainly Ugandan soldiers at and around the headquarters and Burundian soldiers at their base.

Many of the women and girls had gone to the bases to ask for medicine or aid. Interpreters helped soldiers reach them, and some were pressed into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine. Four of the rapes and one sexual assault involved girls under 18. The youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013.

Children are also taken by the armed group Al-Shabaab, which is fighting the government. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia, 850 of them by Al-Shabaab, mainly to recruit them. In the same year it verified sexual violence against 267 children, 265 of them girls. Al-Shabaab was responsible for 120 of these cases and unidentified perpetrators for 110. Somali government security forces were responsible for 14, 11 of them by the Somali National Army, and Ethiopia's Liyu Police for 7. The UN Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

The UN's figures for 2024 show children in Somalia abused both by Al-Shabaab and by forces on the government's side, including its own army. The sources for this map record no prosecution of the AMISOM soldiers named in the 2014 report.

PAN.story:
In early February 2021 a subcommission of Panama's National Assembly, the country's parliament, reported that it had found abuse in shelters for children at social risk. The shelters were run privately or by charities and were supervised by the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf), the government agency for children and families. By March 2021 the Public Ministry, the national prosecution service, had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved elsewhere. Five people had been charged with offences including mistreatment of children, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman, an official who investigates complaints against public bodies, found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected and found that 70% of 44 shelters lacked suitable staff. The Ombudsman also said Senniaf did little to follow up on the shelters.

Panama also appears in cases that began in other countries. In Cartagena, Colombia, Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello, known as "La Madame", ran a network that supplied young women and girls under 18 to parties and sent women abroad to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas, coached to avoid checks at airports. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month in prison. On 23 October 2024 Panama's National Police and Public Ministry arrested a man in Puerto Caimito, in La Chorrera district, who was accused of contacting children through the gaming platform Roblox and threatening them to make them send sexual images. The alert came from Spanish police investigating a network that shared abuse material.

In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 5,275 web addresses hosted in Panama, 2% of its total.

The 2021 inspections found that the agency responsible for children's shelters did little to check on them, and the sources for this map do not record what changed afterwards. The online cases in Panama came to light through reports from foreign bodies, the British charity and the Spanish police.

LBR.story:
In early 2002, during Liberia's civil war, a joint mission of UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, and the charity Save the Children UK reported that employees of charities, of UNHCR and of other UN bodies, as well as peacekeepers, were sexually exploiting refugee children in the three countries, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), the UN's internal investigators, then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10. In October 2002 OIOS said it had not substantiated any allegation against a UN staff member and had found no evidence of "widespread" abuse. Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think its report was wrong.

The war ended in 2003. In the years that followed, the number of private orphanages in Liberia rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia, the capital, was closed, and 89 of its 102 "orphans" were returned to their families. A 2007 report by UNICEF and Holt International, an adoption agency, found that many children had entered the adoption system through fraud, including false promises made to their birth parents, and the UN mission in Liberia found orphanages run for profit without accreditation. Between the US fiscal years 1994 and 2014 the United States issued 1,553 immigrant visas to children adopted from Monrovia, with the highest number, 353, in 2006. Canada placed a moratorium, a temporary ban, on adoptions from Liberia.

The sources for this map do not say how many of the children adopted abroad still had parents who had not agreed to give them up. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update, so the present scale of abuse in Liberia is not measured.

LBY.story:
Many migrants from Nigeria travel to Italy by way of Libya. In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN migration agency, said that perhaps 80 per cent of the Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy by sea could be victims of sex trafficking. Most of those it identified were between 13 and 24 years old, and its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. The Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM figures showing that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says commercial sex rings hold sub-Saharan women and girls in brothels in Libya, particularly in the southern towns of Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq, and that Nigerian women and girls are at greater risk. It cites an international organization's finding that 77 per cent of children and young people crossing Libya showed signs of exploitation amounting to trafficking. Observers quoted in the report describe officials taking part across the system, including the Libyan Coast Guard and immigration and security officials. The government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking.

Children crossing Libya pass through a country whose officials are reported to take part in trafficking and where no one has been prosecuted for it. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

ALB.story:
The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers exploit Albanian women and children for sex and forced labour, especially during the tourist season. Children from the Roma and Balkan-Egyptian minorities are forced to beg. Albanians who migrate to Western Europe, particularly to Britain, are at risk of being forced to commit crimes for others. In Britain in 2024, Albanians were the second most common nationality among people referred to the authorities as possible victims of trafficking, with 2,492 referrals, and 95 per cent of them were adults.

In the period the report covers, Albania's courts convicted two sex traffickers and two labour traffickers. These were the first trafficking convictions in the country since 2021.

The four convictions followed several years with none. Much of what is known about Albanian victims, such as the 2,492 referrals in Britain, comes from the records of the countries they reach.

FJI.story:
In 1999 the Salesians of Don Bosco, a Catholic religious order present in more than 130 countries, moved the priest Julian Fox from Australia to Fiji after Australian police began investigating allegations that he had abused children. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. He was jailed in Australia in 2015.

In July 2020 the New Zealand broadcaster 1News reported about 1,300 alleged cases of child abuse by clergy in Fiji, and said some of them involved clergy from Australia and New Zealand. A survivor advocate told 1News that Fiji was a common destination for clergy transferred from those countries. Under the Vatican's rules, abuse cases against priests were reserved from 2001 to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the Vatican office for church discipline, under "pontifical secret", a rule of strict confidentiality that was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Australia and other countries found that bishops moved accused clergy and avoided going to the police.

No inquiry named in the sources for this map has examined the 1,300 alleged cases in Fiji, so it is not known how many involved priests sent from abroad.

TZA.story:
In the 1960s four priests of the Institute of Charity, a Catholic order known as the Rosminians, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's, a boarding school in Soni in Tanganyika, as Tanzania was then called. One of them was the English priest Kit Cunningham. The order acknowledged the crimes of the four priests, but in 2010 it refused to pay compensation. Cunningham died in December 2010. The abuse became public on 21 June 2011, when the BBC broadcast the documentary "Abused: Breaking the Silence". After the broadcast, 22 former Soni pupils pursued a compensation claim, and former pupils of Soni and of the order's Grace Dieu school in Leicestershire, England, announced they would sue. The case is recorded as settled.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking describes the present situation. It says children in Tanzania are exploited for sex, including by foreign visitors, and in forced labour and domestic servitude in Zanzibar, the islands off the coast, and that women and girls from the mainland are brought to Zanzibar with false promises. It also records child sex trafficking in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza, and says the government did not adequately deal with corruption and the involvement of officials.

The Soni abuse became public only after Cunningham had died, and the sources for this map record no criminal case against any of the four priests. For children in Tanzania now, the 2025 report is the main record, and it found that the government had not dealt adequately with officials' part in trafficking.

CMR.story:
In 2023 the UN verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon. It attributed 10 of the cases to the Cameroon Armed Forces, the national army, 6 to unidentified perpetrators and 1 to JAS, a faction of the armed group Boko Haram, which is active around Lake Chad. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 6 girls, one of them by the armed forces, and the abduction of 50 children. The UN publishes only the cases its staff have been able to confirm.

In 2023 most of the confirmed sexual violence against girls in Cameroon was committed by the country's own army. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update, so the full number of children affected is not known.

YEM.story:
In 2023 the UN verified sexual violence against 24 children in Yemen, 8 boys and 16 girls. It attributed 20 of the cases to the Yemen Armed Forces, the government's army, and to forces affiliated with them, including the police and the units called the Security Belt and the Amaliqah. The army itself was responsible for 9 cases and the police for 4. In 2024 the UN verified 11 cases, involving 6 boys and 5 girls. It attributed 2 to the Houthis, the armed movement fighting the government, 2 to the army and 7 to affiliated forces, 4 of them to the police. The UN publishes only the cases its staff have been able to confirm.

In both years most of the confirmed sexual violence against children in Yemen was committed by forces on the government's side, including the police. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

JOR.story:
Jordan hosts refugees from the war in Syria. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Syrian refugee women and girls in Jordan have been sold into forced marriages. In 2022 Jordanian authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.

The sources for this map record one investigation and do not say how many refugee girls in Jordan have been married by force. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

TWN.story:
Between 2003 and 2022 Taiwan sent 4,289 children abroad for intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child by parents in another country, according to figures compiled by the researcher Selman. Taiwan has not closed or suspended these adoptions.

In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, from two houses in Bangkok. They had been held there by Baby 101, a company that took orders for newborn babies from childless couples, and their passports had been taken from them. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking. Four of the women said they had been tricked, and Thailand's health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

Intercountry adoption from Taiwan continues, and the sources for this map record no investigation of how the children sent abroad came to be placed.

STP.story:
The research for this map found no documented case of child sexual abuse networks or child trafficking in São Tomé and Príncipe. The main source on online abuse of children is Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys, in which a sample of people are asked about their own experiences, into global estimates. In its 2026 update it had such surveys from only 60 countries, too few to represent West and Central Africa.

Without surveys or published cases, there is no count of how many children in São Tomé and Príncipe are affected.

The research for this map found no documented case of child sexual abuse networks or child trafficking in Guinea-Bissau. The main source on online abuse of children is Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys, in which a sample of people are asked about their own experiences, into global estimates. In its 2026 update it had such surveys from only 60 countries, too few to represent West and Central Africa.

Without surveys or published cases, there is no count of how many children in Guinea-Bissau are affected.

The main source on online abuse of children is Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys, in which a sample of people are asked about their own experiences, into global estimates. In its 2026 update it had such surveys from only 60 countries, too few to represent West and Central Africa.

The main source on online abuse of children is Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys, in which a sample of people are asked about their own experiences, into global estimates. In its 2026 update it had such surveys from only 60 countries, too few to represent South Asia.

HUN.story:
In 2022 a Hungarian court sentenced Endre Kónya, the former deputy director of the children's home in Bicske, to three years and four months in prison for helping the home's director cover up his sexual abuse of children. In April 2023, before a visit by the Pope, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, and Kónya was among them. A presidential pardon in Hungary must be countersigned by a minister, and the justice minister at the time, Judit Varga, signed it. The news site Telex made the pardon public on 2 February 2024. After protests, on 10 February Novák resigned, saying she had made a mistake. On the same day Varga announced that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Orbán then proposed a change to the constitution that would bar pardons for crimes against children.

Hungary also appears in several international police operations against online abuse. In 2018 Spanish police traced a private Skype group whose members in 14 countries exchanged abuse material, and by May 2018 eight people had been arrested in France, Hungary, Italy, Spain and Canada. An operation led by New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, begun in 2019 after an online service reported users exchanging images of the sadistic abuse of infants and children, had safeguarded 146 children by March 2022, and in Austria and Hungary some of the suspects were abusing their own children. In 2016 Europol, the EU's police agency, said at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, that some had been sexually exploited, and that criminals had built an organisation over 18 months to exploit migrants arriving in Europe, and that there had been many arrests in Germany and Hungary.

Between 2003 and 2022 Hungary sent 2,868 children abroad for intercountry adoption, according to figures compiled by the researcher Selman, and it has not closed these adoptions.

The president and the former justice minister left public life because of the pardon. The sources for this map do not say whether the proposed ban on pardons for crimes against children was passed.

BOL.story:
In 1964 the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas first abused a child in Lima, Peru, and afterwards he settled in Bolivia. The Jesuits, the Catholic religious order called the Society of Jesus, made him deputy director of the Juan XXIII boarding school in Cochabamba in October 1971, and about three years later he became its director. In 1978, in Spain, he told his Jesuit instructor about the abuse. No church process was opened and he was not removed. He died in Cochabamba in September 2009 and was never prosecuted. On 30 April 2023 the Spanish newspaper El País published his diary, in which he admits abusing dozens of children at schools in Latin America, mainly in Cochabamba, and estimates the number at about 85. El País reported that at least seven provincial superiors, the heads of the order's regional branches, and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics had covered up his crimes.

Bolivia also has closed farming colonies of conservative Mennonites, a German-speaking Protestant community. In the Manitoba Colony, men sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate whole households, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. At first the attacks were blamed on ghosts or demons. They came to light in June 2009, and in August 2011 a Bolivian court convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls. Seven were sentenced to 25 years and an eighth man to 12 years for supplying the drug. A 2013 investigation reported similar attacks continuing.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says foreign offenders exploit children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, around Rurrenabaque, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It says the production of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz.

Pedrajas was never tried, because his superiors kept what they knew from 1978 within the order and his diary appeared only after his death. The sources for this map do not record any consequence for the Jesuits who covered for him.

SDN.story:
In April 2023 war broke out between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force. The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan, a body of investigators appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, found that rape and gang rape were widespread, committed mostly by men in RSF uniform and by militias allied with them, and that the victims included girls as young as 8. It found that the RSF's abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes amounted to sexual slavery. Some cases were committed by the Sudanese Armed Forces. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023, 57 of them by the RSF, and against 74 children in 2024, 54 by the RSF and 9 by militias affiliated with it. He listed the RSF among the forces responsible for the rape and abduction of children.

Girls from neighbouring countries are also brought into Sudan. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes controlled with drugs. In 2022 the UN attributed 4 of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to the Chadian National Army.

In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France, saying they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region. The authorities found that most of the children were from Chad and were not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children, and a Sudanese defendant was sentenced to four years.

The sources for this map record no prosecution of RSF fighters for these crimes. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

MLI.story:
In 2012 and 2013 the armed groups Ansar Eddine and AQIM, an affiliate of al-Qaeda, ran an Islamic police force in Timbuktu. The International Criminal Court (ICC), the permanent international court for war crimes, later tried Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz for his role in that period. On 26 June 2024 it convicted him of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including torture and persecution, but acquitted him of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery, charges that included the forced marriage of women and girls.

The fighting continued in the following years. In 2023 the UN verified the rape of 15 girls in Mali, 4 of them by the Malian armed forces. In 2024 it verified the rape of 32 girls: 22 by unidentified perpetrators, 4 by ISGS, the Islamic State group in the Sahel, 3 by JNIM, an al-Qaeda-linked coalition, 2 by the Malian armed forces and 1 by the militia Ganda Lassal Izo. It also verified the abduction of 119 children that year, 4 of them by foreign security personnel.

Children from Mali are also moved across West Africa. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Nigerian networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire, and that in Senegal's Kédougou gold-mining region girls as young as 12 are exploited for sex, some of them from Mali. In September 2019 police in Kaduna, Nigeria, raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them chained; some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana, and seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested.

The UN's yearly counts show the Malian army among those responsible for raping girls, and the ICC case ended without a conviction for sexual violence. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update, so the wider scale of abuse is not known.

IDN.story:
Between 1967 and 1997 or 1998 Dutch couples adopted children from Indonesia and other countries through licensed Dutch agencies. In 2019 the Netherlands set up the Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, chaired by Tjibbe Joustra. In February 2021 it reported "serious violations" in adoptions from countries including Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia, and concluded that the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent the abuses. The government said its officials had known of wrongdoing for years and had not intervened, and on 8 February 2021 it suspended all intercountry adoptions.

Babies are still being sold abroad from Indonesia. In July 2025 police in West Java said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some of them "reserved while still in the womb", for 11 to 16 million rupiah each. The syndicate prepared false family cards and passports in Pontianak. Police arrested 13 people, rescued six babies who were about to be sold, and asked Interpol, the international police organisation, to help trace the adoptive parents.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says the sexual exploitation of children by foreign visitors is common in the Riau Islands, which border Singapore, and that women and girls are forced into commercial sex, notably in Batam. It also says tourists from the Middle East pay more than $700 for week-long "contract marriages" in Puncak, in Bogor, involving girls as young as nine, and that the government tacitly accepted the practice. The report says corruption and the complicity of officials seriously held back efforts against trafficking.

In the recent cases the buyers came mainly from Singapore and the Middle East, and the government is reported to have tolerated the contract marriages. The Dutch inquiry covered only adoptions into the Netherlands, and the sources for this map record no inquiry into adoptions from Indonesia to other countries.

THA.story:
In 1996 Thailand passed a law that made sex with anyone under 18 in a prostitution establishment a crime, whether or not the child agreed. The same year a Swiss man who had already been convicted of abusing children in Fribourg in 1980 and in Valais in 1991 returned to Thailand. Mainly between 2002 and 2013 he abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room used by European men, and in Nong Hoi in the north, and he forced boys to perform sexual acts with European clients. He was tried in Switzerland, and on 1 March 2018 a Swiss court sentenced him to 16 years. Between 2011 and 2013 the British former teacher and scout leader Mark Frost abused boys from poor families in Thailand. In February 2017 he was sentenced in Britain to 13 life terms after pleading guilty to 45 offences there and in Thailand.

Thailand passed its Anti-Human Trafficking Act in 2008, and in 2017 it refused entry to 74 known foreign sex offenders. Abuse of Thai children was also sold online. In 2017 Interpol, the international police organisation, found material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website on the dark web with nearly 63,000 users. Its main administrator, in Thailand, was arrested in January 2018, and in June 2018 a Thai court sentenced him to 146 years. Interpol said 50 children had been removed from harm.

In 2023 police raided an illegal bar on Bangla Road in Patong, Phuket, and rescued six children under 18 who were being sexually exploited there. Five senior Patong police officers were transferred to other posts after the raid. On 19 July 2024 the Phuket Provincial Court sentenced seven Thai and foreign defendants, and the owner received a total of 1,073 years.

Thai courts now give very long sentences to the offenders they convict. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly sold for sex in brothels, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels in Thailand.

PRT.story:
Casa Pia is a state institution in Lisbon that cared for about 4,500 children. A teacher reportedly began telling the institution's leaders and the police about abuse there in 1975. In 1981 police accused a caretaker, and no legal action followed. One of the men later convicted, the diplomat Jorge Ritto, had been removed as consul in Stuttgart, Germany, around 1969 to 1971 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but he stayed in the diplomatic service. The abuse became public in 2002, 27 years after the first report.

A trial began in 2004, and on 3 September 2010 six of the seven defendants were convicted. Carlos Silvino, a former Casa Pia driver, confessed to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others and was sentenced to 18 years. The television presenter Carlos Cruz and the doctor João Ferreira Diniz received seven years each, Ritto, by then a retired ambassador, six years and eight months, the lawyer Hugo Marçal six years and two months, and the former Casa Pia governor Manuel Abrantes five years and nine months. All of them except Silvino denied the charges. A former minister, Paulo Pedroso, was detained during the investigation but was not tried.

In January 2022 Portugal's Catholic bishops set up an independent commission, led by the child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht, to study abuse in the church. Its report of 13 February 2023, based on 512 validated testimonies, concluded that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950, and it described the church's archives as "the tip of the iceberg". Most of the offences were past the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a prosecution, so only 25 cases were passed to prosecutors.

Because the legal deadlines have passed, most of the church abuse counted by the commission can no longer be prosecuted, and the commission considered the true number to be higher than 4,815.

VNM.story:
The United States issued 7,498 immigrant visas to children adopted from Hanoi between 1994 and 2014, with a peak of 828 in 2007. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi reported that the number of babies recorded as abandoned had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the United States when it expired that September. In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two provincial social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, for "abuse of power and authority". They were accused of asking poor families for their babies and falsifying papers to say the babies had been abandoned, and 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers in border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriage, and that Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024. In Britain, 416 Vietnamese children were referred to the authorities as possible trafficking victims in 2024, many of them exploited on cannabis farms and in nail salons.

Vietnam limited adoption to the United States after the embassy's report of fraud, and officials were put on trial for selling babies for adoption. The 2025 figures show children from poor and minority families still being trafficked abroad, to China and Britain among other places.

KHM.story:
In 1992 and 1993 the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), a UN mission of about 22,000 personnel, was based in the country. Over two years the estimated number of sex workers in Cambodia rose from 6,000 to more than 25,000. The UN did not keep thorough records of abuse allegations at the time.

Cambodia passed a law against trafficking and sexual exploitation in 1996. By 2002 observers described child prostitution in Svay Pak, a poor village on the edge of Phnom Penh, as thriving, driven by Western men after Thailand had cracked down. On 22 January 2003 police raided the Svay Pak brothels, but the raid had been widely announced beforehand. Almost all the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville, and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had been extorting money from the brothel owners. The government shut the Svay Pak brothels in 2005, and the trade moved to less visible places such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. ABC News reported in 2017 that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35% to 1–2%.

Children were also bought for adoption. From 1997 to 2001 the American facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions of Cambodian children by US families, more than half of all adoptions from Cambodia, and the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. The United States suspended adoptions from Cambodia in late 2001, and in 2004 Galindo pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering, admitting she had falsified documents that erased children's identities.

The State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Cambodian and foreign men still exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly through social media, and that children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts. It says the complicity of officials, including senior ones, hinders law enforcement.

The open trade in children in Svay Pak ended after 2005, and the 2025 report describes the abuse continuing in brothels, in tourism and through social media.

POL.story:
During the German occupation from 1940 to 1945, the SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), a Nazi agency for racial screening, took Polish children it judged "racially valuable". They were held in homes run by Lebensborn, an SS organisation, and placed with German families under new identities. Estimates reported by the German broadcaster DW put the number of Polish children kidnapped in this way at up to 200,000. In 1948 a US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted 13 of 14 leading officials of RuSHA, Lebensborn and related bodies, and sentenced Ulrich Greifelt to life imprisonment.

Józef Wesołowski, a Polish archbishop, was the nuncio, the Vatican's ambassador, in the Dominican Republic from 2008. In August 2013, amid allegations that he had abused children, the Vatican recalled him, and Dominican prosecutors opened an investigation that September. The Vatican later told Polish prosecutors that its law did not allow him to be extradited. He died in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before his trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest accused alongside him, returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him in 2014, and in 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six children in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference, the body of Poland's bishops, reported that 382 priests had been accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. Documentaries by the Sekielski brothers in 2019 and 2020 led the Vatican to investigate bishops for protecting abusers, and in 2020 Bishop Edward Janiak resigned, Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was removed and Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz was disciplined. A State Commission on child sexual abuse was created by a law of 30 August 2019. In August 2022 it was criticised because church documents sent to the Vatican were out of its reach, and because under church law files are destroyed ten years after a conviction.

Because the state commission cannot see church records held in the Vatican, the full number of children abused by Polish clergy is not known.

COL.story:
The FARC-EP, a guerrilla army that fought the Colombian state, recruited children into its ranks. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), a court set up to try crimes of the armed conflict, opened Case 07 on this recruitment, and in August 2021 it identified a provisional total of 18,677 victims. It has indicted former FARC-EP commanders for war crimes including the recruitment of children and sexual violence against children, and former members of the FARC-EP leadership have publicly acknowledged responsibility. Armed groups that are still active continue to abuse girls. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in Colombia, 12 by the ELN guerrilla group, 12 by FARC-EP dissident groups and 7 by the Clan del Golfo.

Colombian children were also sent abroad for adoption. In 1981 the New York Times reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a ring that took or bought hundreds of poor Andean children from their mothers and sold them abroad with forged papers. Colombia went on to send 20,864 children abroad between 2003 and 2022, according to figures compiled by the researcher Selman. In February 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found "serious violations" in adoptions from countries including Colombia between 1967 and 1998, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption.

The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in Colombian institutions. In May 2019 the journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos asked the Archdiocese of Medellín and the Salesian order for the records of 43 priests, and both refused, calling them private. On 3 March 2020 the Constitutional Court, the court that rules on constitutional rights, ordered the archdiocese to hand them over. A later order required it to disclose files on 915 cases of accused clergy within 48 hours, and it did not fully comply.

Colombia still sends children abroad for adoption after a foreign inquiry found abuses in those adoptions. Without a national inquiry, the extent of abuse in Colombian institutions is not known.

NGA.story:
On the night of 14 April 2014 gunmen from Boko Haram, an armed Islamist group in north-eastern Nigeria, raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and drove 276 girls away in trucks. In April 2024 Amnesty said 82 of the Chibok girls were still held and that 20 of those released had been forced to marry former fighters. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 991 children in Nigeria, 690 of them by JAS, the main Boko Haram faction, and 294 by ISWAP, the Islamic State's West Africa branch. It also verified sexual violence through forced marriage against 419 children, 412 of them girls.

In the south, the trafficking of women and girls for sex abroad is centred on Edo State. They are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound to the traffickers by debt and by oaths sworn before juju priests, traditional religious priests. In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration, the UN migration agency, said perhaps 80 per cent of the Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy by sea could be sex-trafficking victims, most of them aged 13 to 24. In March 2018 the Oba of Benin, Ewuare II, the traditional ruler, publicly revoked the curses used to bind victims and laid a curse on anyone involved in trafficking, and reporters later found anecdotal evidence that trafficking had slowed.

Offenders in Nigeria also target children abroad. Two brothers in Lagos, Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, posed as a girl on Instagram to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. They were extradited to the United States and each sentenced to 17.5 years in 2024.

Children in Nigeria are still abducted by armed groups in the north-east and trafficked abroad from the south. Childlight found too few representative surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse in the region.

KOR.story:
From 1953 to 2008 South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad for adoption, 109,242 of them to the United States. In 1974 it tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia, and Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats sent nine requests asking it to continue, after which it resumed. In 1989 the government adopted a policy of phasing out intercountry adoption, but 18,578 children were still sent abroad between 2003 and 2022.

In December 2022, after petitions from adoptees, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body that investigates past human rights abuses, opened an inquiry. On 26 March 2025, having examined petitions from 367 adoptees, it found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. The four private agencies authorised to arrange adoptions had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand, registered children with known parents as orphans and failed to obtain proper consent, and the government had not supervised them. The commission said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to welfare at home. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.

From 2000, six staff at the Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students, including the headmaster, sexually harassed or raped at least nine students. The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired, and two of the six escaped punishment because the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for prosecution, had expired. After the 2011 film "Silenced" (Dogani) about the school, the National Assembly removed that deadline for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people.

Son Jong-woo ran Welcome to Video, a dark web site that sold access to more than 250,000 abuse videos for Bitcoin. US investigators traced the payments to a server in South Korea, and he was arrested on 5 March 2018. Son served 18 months in South Korea, and on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused to extradite him to the United States.

The state has accepted responsibility for the adoption abuses. The law on child sex crimes was changed after a film brought the Gwangju case to public attention, years after the abuse.

IND.story:
In Bihar, many children's homes are run by charities paid by the state's Social Welfare Department. At the department's request, Koshish, a unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, visited 110 homes in 38 districts and on 27 April 2018 submitted a social audit, an independent review of how the homes were run. It graded the girls' home in Muzaffarpur, run by Brajesh Thakur's charity, as criminally negligent, and raised abuse at 14 other homes. Police opened a criminal case on 31 May 2018. Medical examinations indicated that 34 girls, most of them children, had been sexually abused. The district child protection officer was among the accused, and the state's social welfare minister, Manju Verma, resigned. Because the accused were influential in Bihar, the Supreme Court moved the trial to Delhi at the request of the CBI, the federal investigation agency. On 20 January 2020 the Delhi court convicted Thakur and 18 others, and Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment; he has appealed.

In Unnao district, Uttar Pradesh, a girl said she had been raped in 2017 by Kuldeep Singh Sengar, a member of the state legislature for the BJP. Her father died in police custody, and Sengar was arrested only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018. In December 2019 a special CBI court in Delhi convicted him and sentenced him to life imprisonment.

India also sent 12,511 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, according to figures compiled by the researcher Selman. In 2001 police in Hyderabad found that a children's home had earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, and in 2005 ten people from it were sentenced for cheating and forgery. Andhra Pradesh then became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.

The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in Indian institutions, and Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few representative surveys in South Asia. What is known about abuse in children's homes comes from audits, such as Bihar's, that a state government chose to commission.

USA.story:
In 2002 the US Conference of Catholic Bishops commissioned a national study from John Jay College, published in February 2004. It counted 10,667 allegations of abuse against 4,392 clergy, about 4% of the 109,694 clergy covered.

Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years, and in many states the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, used to run out in a person's early twenties. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern states from 2011 to 2018, a total that covers all the issues it lobbied on. Where the deadlines were lifted, at least 41 Catholic dioceses and religious orders filed for bankruptcy, as did USA Gymnastics and the Boy Scouts of America, which faced more than 82,000 abuse claims.

Complaints against people with status often waited years for action. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997. USA Gymnastics told the FBI in July 2015, the FBI did not act, and in 2021 the Justice Department's Inspector General, its internal watchdog, found that at least 70 more athletes had been abused before his arrest in 2016. In March 2005 a woman told Palm Beach police that her 14-year-old stepdaughter had been paid to give the financier Jeffrey Epstein a massage. Police identified about 35 girls, but in 2006 a state grand jury returned a single count of soliciting prostitution. A federal non-prosecution agreement in 2007 ended the federal case, and Epstein served 13 months in a county stockade under a state plea in 2008. Federal sex-trafficking charges came in July 2019, after a series in the Miami Herald. In July 2025 the Justice Department and FBI said Epstein had harmed more than a thousand victims.

No national inquiry has examined abuse in American institutions, so what is known comes from a church-commissioned study, state investigations and lawsuits. In Pennsylvania, which has not reopened time-barred claims, many people abused as children still cannot sue.

AUS.story:
In the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat, in Victoria, Bishop Ronald Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children. He kept appointing him to new parishes. Ridsdale was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children. In 2017 the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, a national public inquiry with the power to require documents, called the bishop's decisions a "catastrophic" failure. It also found that in 1972 a senior police officer had offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating another Ballarat priest, Monsignor John Day.

In March 2008 the Adass Israel School in Melbourne paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. She was arrested in Israel in 2014. Her extradition, the legal handover of a suspect to another country, took until January 2021, partly because Israel's deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, interfered with her psychiatric assessments. She was convicted in Australia on 3 April 2023.

The Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017. It held 8,013 private sessions with survivors and heard evidence about 3,489 institutions.
