Of the survivors in those sessions, 58.1 percent had been abused in a religious institution and 32.5 percent in one run by government. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began in July 2018. Between 2015 and 2018 every state and territory removed or changed the legal deadline for suing over child abuse.

A 1994 law let Australians be prosecuted at home for abusing children abroad. In 2016 about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled overseas, 40 percent without telling police. In 2020 the bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty that included failing to check payments to the Philippines that could be linked to child exploitation.

Survivors abused in Australian institutions can now sue whenever the abuse happened. A 2020 study by International Justice Mission ranked Australians third among the buyers of abuse streamed live from the Philippines.

NZL.story:
In 2018 New Zealand set up the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, a public inquiry into what happened to children and adults placed in state and church care. Its final report, in July 2024, estimated that 200,000 of the roughly 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 had been abused, and that sexual abuse was commonplace. Māori were more likely to be abused. The commissioners found that the state had not responded to signs of systemic abuse.

Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice, a state psychiatric hospital, about half of them Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks given without anaesthetic as punishment, and evidence was given of children raped by staff and adult patients. The psychiatrist in charge, Selwyn Leeks, denied abuse and was never charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission found that many of the children had been tortured, and in December 2024 the government offered each survivor NZ$150,000 and a new apology.

In church care, the commission found that abusers were moved to other posts where they offended again. At Marylands, a Christchurch school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended between 1955 and 1984 reported abuse, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served there faced allegations. After allegations against Brother Bernard McGrath in 1977, the order moved him to Australia; he was later put in charge of its Hebron Trust in Christchurch and has since been convicted of more than 100 offences in the two countries. The commission recommended an inquiry into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after allegations.

New Zealand now has an estimate of how many people were abused in its care, and Lake Alice survivors have been offered payments. For other survivors, the redress system the commissioners recommended in 2021 had made little progress by 2024.

ESP.story:
After the Civil War of 1936 to 1939, the Franco government placed about 30,000 children in state care. A 2008 ruling by Judge Baltasar Garzón described most of them as children whose parents were dead, imprisoned, exiled, in hiding or disappeared. Their names were changed so they could be given to families who supported the regime. Unmarried mothers held in homes run by the Women's Protection Board, a state body, were also pressured to give up their babies, and this continued into the early 1980s. The 1977 Amnesty Law, which barred prosecution for crimes of the dictatorship, made these removals hard to investigate, and many of the Board's files went missing in 1996.

In 2011 families of 261 babies who had disappeared from Spanish hospitals asked the attorney general to investigate an alleged network of doctors and nurses, and lawyers claimed up to 300,000 babies had been taken. The first trial, of Dr Eduardo Vela in 2018, ended in acquittal because the legal deadline for prosecution had passed. In 2026 forensic geneticists at Spain's National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences found no evidence of systematic theft from hospitals and called the 300,000 figure a hoax, while not disputing the coercion in Francoist institutions.

The Catholic Church was examined later. On 27 October 2023 the Ombudsman, Ángel Gabilondo, presented Spain's first official inquiry into abuse in the church to parliament, based on 487 cases. It said the church had often minimised or denied the problem. In a survey of about 8,000 adults for the report, 11.7 percent said they had been abused before 18, 1.13 percent by clergy or lay church members and 0.6 percent by clergy. Gabilondo did not turn these percentages into a total; newspapers that did put it at about 440,000, and the bishops apologised but disputed that figure.

How many children Franco's institutions took and where they went is still unsettled, and the amnesty law still stands in the way of prosecutions. The church inquiry gave Spain its first survey-based estimate of abuse by clergy.

MEX.story:
In 1941 the priest Marcial Maciel founded the Legion of Christ, a Catholic religious order, in Mexico. Former seminarians wrote to the Vatican about his abuse in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and filed formal charges in 1998, without result. In 2010 the Vatican said his acts were "true crimes" and that the Legion had shielded him. He was never tried. In 2019 the Legion's own report found that 33 of its priests had abused 175 minors since 1941, at least 60 of them abused by Maciel.

In 2003 several girls in Cancún complained about the hotel owner Jean Succar Kuri, who was detained in the United States in 2004 and sent back. In 2005 the journalist Lydia Cacho published a book linking him to the Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and the Puebla governor, Mario Marín. Puebla state police then arrested Cacho in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla, and she says she was tortured. Leaked phone calls recorded the two men discussing jailing her as a favour. In 2007 Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6 to 4 that Marín had no case to answer. Succar Kuri was convicted in 2011 and died in 2024 while serving his sentence. Marín was arrested in 2021 on torture charges and his trial continues; neither he nor Nacif has been convicted.

When federal police raided the La Gran Familia shelter in Zamora in 2014 they freed 432 children, some of whom had been sexually abused; more than 40 complaints from parents had reached state and federal authorities before the raid. In 2009, 14 children disappeared from Casitas del Sur, a church-run shelter in Mexico City where city prosecutors had placed them.

In 2020 Mexico's bishops said they had investigated 426 priests over ten years and removed 217. The newspaper El Universal found that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such offences by religious figures between 2009 and 2019, and four prosecutors' offices recorded six convictions.

Most abuse reported in Mexican churches and shelters has not reached a court, and the torture trial over Cacho's arrest is still not finished.

RUS.story:
From the 1990s Russia sent large numbers of children from its orphanages to families abroad. The United States issued visas to 60,266 children adopted from Russia between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 5,865, in 2004.

In May 2000 Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help with Blue Orchid, a Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By March 2001 four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, and leads were passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 5,797 web addresses in Russia, 2 percent of its total.

After a criminal case was opened against him in St Petersburg in November 2013, the priest Gleb Grozovsky fled to Israel. He was detained and extradited to Russia, the legal process of sending a suspect back for trial, and in 2018 he was jailed for 14 years. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped Ukrainian children.

In the cases recorded here, offenders were caught when Russian and foreign police worked together or when a suspect who had fled abroad was sent back. No trial over the UN commission's finding that Russian forces raped children is recorded in the sources for this map.

NOR.story:
Between 1955 and 2008 Norway received 6,295 children for adoption from South Korea. In 1974 and 1975, when South Korea tried to stop sending children abroad, Scandinavian diplomats pressed it to continue. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body that investigates past abuses, found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, registered children who had known parents as orphans and did not properly obtain consent. It said the Korean state had failed to supervise them.

Norway opened its own investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions, the adoption of children from abroad, and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them. The foreign ministry said it was aware of serious findings. In September 2025 a woman adopted from Korea gave notice that she would sue the Norwegian state, alleging that her adoption was illegal.

Children in Norway's own institutions had been examined earlier. An official report in 2004, NOU 2004:23, found neglect and abuse, including sexual abuse, in municipal children's homes and state special schools between 1945 and 1980. In 2005 a committee of the Storting, the parliament, recommended a state compensation scheme with payments of up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof, and Bergen and other municipalities set up their own schemes.

In 2026, after US authorities released documents about Jeffrey Epstein, Norway's economic crime agency charged the former prime minister Thorbjørn Jagland with aggravated corruption, examining whether he received gifts, travel and loans in connection with his position. He denies the charges, and the case concerns corruption, not abuse.

Norway has paid compensation to people abused in its children's homes. What its own officials knew about the adoptions from Korea is still under investigation.

LKA.story:
In the 1980s thousands of Sri Lankan babies were adopted by families abroad, about 4,000 of them in the Netherlands and others in Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Germany. Babies were bought, or taken from hospitals, and handed to paid "acting mothers", who posed as the birth mothers in court; brokers and some hospital doctors and nurses acted as intermediaries for Western agencies. In 1987 police raided one of these "baby farms" and found 20 newborns and 22 women held in prison-like conditions, and Sri Lanka temporarily stopped foreign adoptions. In 2017, after a Dutch television documentary, the health minister, Rajitha Senaratne, admitted that there had been "a lot of baby farms" and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank for families searching for each other. In 2021 a Dutch government committee found that officials had known of the abuses for years without acting, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption. Switzerland's government acknowledged its authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023.

Sri Lankan soldiers served in Haiti with MINUSTAH, the UN peacekeeping mission there. The UN's internal investigators found that between 2004 and 2007 members of the Sri Lankan contingent sexually exploited and abused children frequently and at almost every place they were posted. In 2007, 114 were accused and 108 were sent home. Under UN rules only the soldiers' own country can prosecute them, and Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts "consensual". No one was jailed, and one victim received a one-off payment in 2016.

Inside Sri Lanka, complaints about a children's home in Vavuniya, run by a Buddhist monk and housing children affected by the war, reached the National Child Protection Authority from 2010. The monk was arrested in 2013 for abusing a 9-year-old, and was released on bail after the Authority said it did not object.

No Sri Lankan soldier has been jailed for the abuse in Haiti. South Asia has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so how common it is in Sri Lanka is not known.

AUT.story:
In 1995 Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër, the Catholic Archbishop of Vienna, stepped down after a former pupil, and then others, accused him of sexual abuse. In 1998 the Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded. After a wave of new disclosures in 2010, the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission, chaired by Waltraud Klasnic, to decide on payments to people abused in the church. It paid in tiers of €5,000, €15,000 and €25,000, with more in extreme cases, and by August 2021 payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. In 2013 a court jailed the former head of the boarding school at Kremsmünster Abbey for 12 years for crimes against 24 former pupils.

The City of Vienna examined its own children's home at Wilhelminenberg, which it ran from 1948 to 1977. A commission it appointed interviewed 217 people, including 140 former residents, and reported in 2013 that children there had been raped and sexually exploited by caregivers and by men from outside, some girls as young as about six. It found that staff in the city department responsible knew of the abuse and did nothing, and that city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it. Its findings were sent to prosecutors, and some former residents received up to €35,000.

Austria has also been a starting point for international investigations of online abuse. In 2006 an employee of a Vienna file-hosting company reported suspicious material, and within a day investigators recorded visits from 2,361 internet addresses in 77 countries. In 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being abused.

In Austria most payments to people abused as children were set by commissions, one created by the church and one by the city of Vienna. The Wilhelminenberg findings reached prosecutors more than 35 years after the home closed.

GTM.story:
After Guatemala's civil war ended in 1996, adoptions of Guatemalan children by foreigners rose every year. About 98 percent were handled by private notaries, lawyers who arranged both sides of the adoption without review by a court and charged $35,000 or more per child. Almost all the children, 97 percent, went to the United States, which issued visas to 32,863 children adopted from Guatemala between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 4,728, in 2007. In August 2007 police found 46 children at Casa Quivira, a private adoption home in Antigua, after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children every day. The attorney general said most lacked proper documents and that his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or taken from mothers under pressure.

In December 2007 Guatemala passed a law following the Hague Convention, the international treaty that sets safeguards for adoptions between countries, and stopped new adoptions to the United States from January 2008. In 2010 CICIG, a UN-backed commission investigating crime in Guatemala, studied 153 adoption cases and found that 78 percent broke the law in some way.

Children in state care were also at risk. About 700 children lived in the Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, a state home built for 500, and most had committed no crime. Prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, girls had alleged sexual abuse by staff, and in 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman reported a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On 8 March 2017, after an escape, police locked a group of girls in a room; one set a mattress on fire, and 41 girls died. In August 2025 a judge convicted six former officials, including the former social welfare secretary, who received 25 years, and said the fire followed abuses that had been reported and not acted on.

International adoption from Guatemala has been closed since 2008. Officials responsible for the state home have been convicted, and the judge ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.

PER.story:
In 1971 Luis Fernando Figari founded the Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana, a Catholic lay society, in Lima. In 2015 the journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz published a book describing abuse by Figari and those around him, and they then faced legal action. The Vatican appointed an official to examine the group the same year. In 2017 the society gave Peruvian prosecutors an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred him from contact with members. After a further Vatican investigation, Figari was expelled in August 2024 for physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors, and the society was formally dissolved in 2025.

Religious orders also moved abusers into and out of Peru. In 2010 Brother Abel Pérez of the Marist Brothers, a teaching order, confessed to his superiors in Chile that he had abused minors, and the order transferred him to Peru; in 2017 it acknowledged at least 14 victims. In the other direction, the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas first abused a child in Lima in 1964, then moved to Bolivia, where he abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools.

Children are also exploited in places where the state has little control. In 2019 more than 1,500 soldiers and police moved against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in Madre de Dios, and the women's minister said child sexual exploitation had been among the worst crimes there. In 2021 a 16-year-old girl who had earlier been rescued from a trafficking group in La Pampa was found murdered. The US State Department reported in 2025 that tourists from the United States and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon, and that in Loreto criminal groups take tourists by boat to remote places on the river where women and children are exploited.

The Sodalicio no longer exists, and its founder has been expelled by the church but not convicted by a Peruvian court. Exploitation of children in mining camps and by tourists continues.

MDA.story:
In the mid-2000s Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children. Children left them at 15 or 16 with about US$70 and no further support or follow-up. UNICEF reported that research showed these children were several times more likely than others to be trafficked. In its 2007 human rights report, the US State Department said women and children were being trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia, Turkey, Israel and the United Arab Emirates, and that 12 percent of the trafficking victims helped by the International Organization for Migration were minors.

Women and girls from Moldova were also taken to the Balkans after the wars there. Human Rights Watch reported in 2002 that women and girls trafficked mainly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine were held in debt bondage in bars and brothels in Bosnia, where local police, UN police monitors and US military contractors were among those involved. Amnesty International reported in 2004 that women and girls from Moldova and neighbouring countries were brought through Serbia to Kosovo, where the international peacekeeping presence produced 80 percent of traffickers' income.

The State Department's 2025 report says traffickers now recruit Moldovan children through social media, video calls and fake job advertisements, and still target children who are in or leaving state institutions. Moldovan courts convicted 33 traffickers in 2024, and a former police officer was given 20 years for labour trafficking. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, took action against 9,941 internet addresses hosted in Moldova, 3 percent of its total.

Children leaving Moldova's institutions are still the group traffickers look for, and recruitment has moved online. Moldova is also among the countries whose servers hold a measurable share of the abuse images found on the internet.

DOM.story:
In 2008 the Vatican sent the Polish archbishop Józef Wesołowski to the Dominican Republic as its nuncio, the Vatican's ambassador. In August 2013, amid allegations that he was abusing minors, the Vatican recalled him to Rome, and in September Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation. Once he was in the Vatican he was out of reach of Dominican courts, and the Vatican later told Polish prosecutors that its law did not allow him to be extradited. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was dismissed from the priesthood in 2014. In 2015 a Vatican prosecutor charged him with abusing children in the Dominican Republic between 2008 and 2013 and with possessing abuse images, but he was found dead in August 2015, before the trial.

A Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, Fr Wojciech Gil, was suspended in May 2013 and returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence, and in 2015 a Polish court sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

Children are also sold for sex to visitors in the Dominican Republic's tourist towns. In April 2015 Dominican authorities, working with US Homeland Security Investigations, freed 29 victims, 20 of them aged 14 to 17, in the north-coast town of Sosúa and arrested seven Dominican nationals. US men have been prosecuted at home for abusing children on the north coast. The US State Department's 2025 report says teenage girls are often exploited on streets, in parks and on beaches, and charities link the growing number of child victims to weak regulation of tourism.

The cases against the two clergymen were decided in Poland and the Vatican, not in the country where the children lived. Exploitation of children in tourist areas continues.

BIH.story:
During the war in 1992 and 1993, Bosnian Serb forces in Foča held Bosniak women and girls at sites such as the Partizan Sports Hall, next to the town's police building, and took them from there to apartments and houses to be raped. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), a UN court for war crimes in the region, found that rape was used as a means of terror and that local police guarded the women and joined in their mistreatment. In 2001 it sentenced Dragoljub Kunarac to 28 years, Radomir Kovač to 20 years and Zoran Vuković to 12 years for crimes including rape and enslavement. Kovač had held two girls in his apartment for about four months and sold victims to other soldiers, and Vuković raped a girl he knew to be 15.

After the war, from 1995, women and girls were trafficked into Bosnia, mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine, and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Human Rights Watch reported in 2002 that local police acted as owners, guards and customers. Foreign staff of the international mission were also involved. Eighteen monitors of the UN International Police Task Force who bought women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges were sent home, and Human Rights Watch found none prosecuted. A US Army report documented employees of DynCorp, a US company contracted to the NATO-led force, buying women from brothels; they too were sent home, so they could not be used as witnesses. DynCorp fired the police monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking, and in 2002 a British employment tribunal found the dismissal unfair.

The commanders at Foča were convicted by an international court. The foreigners who bought trafficked women and girls in Bosnia after the war were sent home without trial, because only their own countries could prosecute them.

PAK.story:
In August 2015 it became known that in Hussain Khanwala, a village in Kasur district in Punjab, a gang had filmed the sexual abuse of at least 280 children between 2006 and 2014 and used the videos to blackmail their parents. Parents had asked the police for help and the police had not acted. Arrests followed only after relatives clashed with police and the media reported the case. The Punjab police and the local provincial assembly member were alleged to have tried to cover it up, and the Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court sentenced two men to life in prison, and by 2018, 12 other accused men had been acquitted.

In 2017 an Associated Press investigation found that sexual abuse by clerics was common in Pakistan's madrassas, Islamic religious schools, of which more than 22,000 are registered with at least 2 million pupils. Police were often paid not to register cases. Pakistani law allows a victim's family to "forgive" an offender, and poor families were pressured to accept money; in one case a teacher who confessed to abusing a 9-year-old was freed after the mother forgave him for $300. Police told the AP that clerics are almost never convicted, and a 2020 follow-up found the same pattern.

Girls are also sold abroad. In 2019 the AP obtained a list compiled by Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency of 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019, many from poor Christian families. Officials said the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 under pressure from government officials worried about relations with China, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or paid.

In each of these cases few accused people were convicted. South Asia has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so its extent in Pakistan is not known.

SVN.story:
The Slovenian Catholic priest Franc Frantar was accused of abusing up to 16 minors. He first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary, and returned to Slovenia only after Interpol, the international police organisation, issued a notice for him. He was detained in 2006 and later sentenced to prison; sources give the term as three and a half or five years.

During the Second World War, Nazi Germany took children judged "racially valuable" from occupied Poland and other occupied areas, held them in homes run by the SS organisation Lebensborn and placed them with German families under new identities. In 1948 a US military court at Nuremberg convicted 13 officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies for crimes that included kidnapping these children. Slovenia is recorded among the countries involved in this programme.

How many other accused priests in Slovenia were sent abroad in this way is not known.

GAB.story:
Gabon sent soldiers to MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission in the Central African Republic. Under UN rules, only a soldier's own country can prosecute him; the UN can only send him home. In 2016 two sets of allegations against Gabonese and Burundian soldiers, about events in the town of Dékoa in 2014 and 2015, led UN investigators to interview some 136 alleged victims, 48 percent of all the victims the UN recorded that year. Press reports said at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges. In 2017 the UN said the investigations by the soldiers' own countries were still pending.

The allegations continued. In September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA, about 450 soldiers, would be sent home after new allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse, and Gabon opened an investigation.

No Gabonese soldier is recorded as charged over the abuse in the Central African Republic. West and Central Africa has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so its extent in Gabon itself is not known.

SEN.story:
In Senegal many boys, called talibés, live at residential Quranic schools, known as daaras, run by teachers called marabouts. In 2019 Human Rights Watch and a Senegalese group, the PPDH, reported that some of these teachers force more than 100,000 talibés to beg every day, often enforcing quotas by beating them. In 2017 and 2018 the groups documented 16 deaths of talibés from beatings or neglect, 61 cases of beatings, 15 cases of rape, attempted rape or sexual abuse and 14 cases of children chained or locked up. The US State Department's 2025 report says the government identified 573 children forced to beg that year.

Foreign institutions have also abused children in Senegal. New Tribes Mission, a US evangelical mission, ran the Fanda boarding school there for missionaries' children. A 2010 report it commissioned after pressure from former pupils found sexual abuse of more than 20 children and a culture of systemic abuse, and showed that notes from a 1992 mission meeting said allegations should not be reported to police.

Girls are also brought to Senegal to be sold for sex. The 2025 State Department report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 throughout Kédougou, the gold-mining region in the south-east. Most come from Nigeria, where organised networks move women and girls to mining regions in several West African countries. The report also says some tourists exploit children in Dakar and Saint-Louis.

Forced begging and abuse of talibés continue, and girls are still sold at the mining sites. West and Central Africa has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so its extent in Senegal is not known.

NER.story:
In Niger, armed groups take children in the course of the conflicts in the Sahel and around Lake Chad. The UN, which checks and publishes these attacks each year, verified the abduction of 202 children in Niger in 2024, 102 of them girls. It attributed 35 of the abductions to JAS, the faction of Boko Haram that abducted schoolgirls in neighbouring Nigeria, two each to the Islamic State groups ISWAP and ISGS, and 163 to people it could not identify. It also verified sexual violence against five girls that year. In 2023 it had verified sexual violence against eight girls, one of them by Niger's own security forces.

Most of the children abducted in Niger in 2024 were taken by people the UN could not name, so no one can be held to account for them. West and Central Africa has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so its extent in Niger is not known.

LBN.story:
After the war in Syria began, criminal groups recruited Syrian refugee women and girls with false job offers and forced them into prostitution in Lebanese brothels. In late 2011 police raided Chez Maurice, a brothel in the Maameltein district of Jounieh, and found a 17-year-old Syrian girl trapped there. It closed for about three months and then reopened. In March 2016 security forces raided it again, together with another brothel, Silver-B, freed as many as 75 Syrian women and charged more than a dozen people with sex trafficking. A survivor said a trafficker had told her he had "bought the state". Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims that year, most of them from these two brothels. The US State Department reported in 2025 that the recruitment of Syrian women and girls continues, and that Syrian children are held in bonded labour, work to pay off a debt, in the Beqaa valley.

Syrian refugee women and girls are still recruited into Lebanese brothels. The Middle East and North Africa have no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so its extent in Lebanon is not known.

CRI.story:
Fr Mauricio Víquez had been a spokesman for the Catholic Church in Costa Rica on family issues. When accusations against him became public in 2018, he left the country through Panama for San Nicolás de los Garza in Mexico, where he was caught. He was extradited, sent back to Costa Rica, in 2021. The church had expelled him from the clergy in 2019. In March 2022 a court sentenced him to 20 years for abusing an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002 and 2003. Three other complaints could not be tried because the legal deadline for bringing them had passed. In August 2022 a civil court ordered the archbishop of San José, the bishops' conference and the church's property company to pay 65 million colones, about US$100,000, in damages; the victims' lawyer said the church had known since 2002 and done nothing.

Children are also exploited for sex in other settings. The US State Department reported in 2025 that traffickers exploit Costa Rican children, especially in the tourist areas of the Pacific coast and near the northern and southern borders, and that girls from Nicaragua, Panama, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela are also among the victims.

A Costa Rican court has held the church liable for damages in an abuse case, while three older complaints against Víquez expired before they reached court. Sexual exploitation of children in coastal and border areas continues.

COG.story:
The Republic of Congo sent soldiers to MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission in the neighbouring Central African Republic. In January 2016 Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by peacekeepers in the town of Bambari, including a 14-year-old girl who said she was gang-raped near the airport. Most of the incidents took place between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport, and survivors believed the soldiers were from either the Republic of Congo or DR Congo. Under UN rules, only a soldier's own country can prosecute him, and the UN can only send him home.

No prosecutions in the Republic of Congo are recorded for these cases. West and Central Africa has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so its extent in the country is not known.

XKX.story:
In 1999 NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in Kosovo after the war there. Amnesty International reported in 2004 that Kosovo had since become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution, and that the international staff, soldiers and police were the customers who produced 80 percent of traffickers' income. The women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia, and girls from Kosovo were also abducted. In 2004 the UN's peacekeeping department acknowledged that peacekeepers had "come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution". Soldiers serving abroad can only be prosecuted by their own countries, and Amnesty found no criminal case brought against any of them there.

No case against a foreign soldier over this trade is recorded, and the reports give no count of the girls trafficked into Kosovo in those years.

GRL.story:
The sources gathered for this map hold no case of sexual abuse, exploitation, sale or trafficking of children in Greenland. The one Greenland record they contain concerns a removal of children by the Danish state in 1951, and it documents none of these, so it is not shown.

No figures on sexual abuse or trafficking of children in Greenland are included in the sources for this map, so how many children there are affected is not known.

KAZ.story:
Kazakhstan has sent many children abroad for adoption. The United States issued visas to 6,612 children adopted from Kazakhstan between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 826, in 2004, and 6,541 children were sent abroad between 2003 and 2022. Kazakhstan has not closed intercountry adoption. The US State Department reported in 2025 that traffickers offer girls and women from rural areas jobs as waitresses, models or nannies in large cities and then exploit them, and that Kazakh women and girls are exploited in Russia, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Europe, East Asia and the United States.

Adoption from Kazakhstan remains open, and girls from its rural areas are still recruited with false job offers.

JEY.story:
From 2007 to 2010 Jersey's police investigated abuse at Haut de la Garenne, a children's home, in an inquiry called Operation Rectangle. The Independent Jersey Care Inquiry then heard from about 450 people connected with the island's care system since 1945 and reported in July 2017. It found that the States of Jersey, the island's government, had been "an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent", that its child-welfare law was decades out of date and that some children in care might still be at risk. It found the authorities had not been open, which led people to believe there had been collusion and cover-up, and described a "small island culture" that no one had challenged. It recommended demolishing the Haut de la Garenne buildings, and the chief minister, Ian Gorst, apologised.

The inquiry warned in 2017 that some children in Jersey's care might still be at risk.

MNG.story:
The US State Department reported in 2025 that women and girls in Mongolia are trafficked for sex in hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, in provincial centres and in border areas. It said this is sometimes made easier by a lack of police enforcement and that some families take part. Traffickers also use online platforms to groom children and blackmail them, and some children taken abroad for competitions have been put to work instead, for example as horse jockeys.

The only account of child trafficking in Mongolia recorded here is this one report, so little is known about how many children are affected.

PNG.story:
In 2024 New Zealand's Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found that the Catholic Church in New Zealand had moved abusers to other ministries, and it recommended an investigation into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after allegations against them. The commission did not say how many priests were sent or what they did there.

Whether priests moved from New Zealand abused children in Papua New Guinea has not been investigated.

CPV.story:
Cape Verde has no documented cases on this map. Most estimates of how many children are abused online come from surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries, too few to cover West and Central Africa, the region that includes Cape Verde.

How many children in Cape Verde are abused or exploited online is not known.

MDV.story:
The Maldives has no documented cases on this map. Most estimates of how many children are abused online come from surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries, too few to cover South Asia, the region that includes the Maldives.

How many children in the Maldives are abused or exploited online is not known.

CAN.story:
From the 1870s until 1997, the Canadian government paid churches to run Indian residential schools, boarding schools that First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were made to attend. About 150,000 children went to them, and the Catholic Church ran more than half. Under a 2006 settlement, former students could claim compensation for sexual and serious physical abuse through the Independent Assessment Process; it received 38,276 claims, and adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants.
In St John's, Newfoundland, the Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order, ran the Mount Cashel orphanage. In December 1975, after two Brothers admitted molesting boys, the police chief and assistant chief ordered the detective to end his investigation. References to sexual assault were removed from his report, the Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province. Police reopened the case in 1989 and nine Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission, a provincial public inquiry, reported in 1991 that neither the police nor the Justice Department had handled the files normally.

Two priests of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a Catholic order with missions in the Arctic, left Canada before trial. Fr Eric Dejaeger fled to Belgium in 1995 when he was about to be charged, and lived in Oblate houses there for 16 years despite an international warrant; after he was returned in 2011 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik. Fr Johannes Rivoire left for France in 1993. Canada issued warrants in 1998 and 2022, France refused to extradite him, and he died there in 2024 without trial.

Under the settlement, the records of residential school abuse claims are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep them. Much of what is known about abuse in Canadian institutions comes from inquiries and compensation claims, and some of the accused were never tried in Canada.

IRL.story:
From the 1930s to the 1990s, Catholic religious orders ran more than 250 industrial schools and other institutions for the Irish state, holding over 30,000 children. The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse, known as the Ryan Commission, reported in 2009 after nine years of work. It found sexual abuse "endemic" in the boys' institutions, most of them run by the Christian Brothers, a teaching order, and found that Department of Education inspections had failed to stop it. The Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep their members' names out, and the report names no abusers. A state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.

Inquiries into individual dioceses followed. The Ferns report of 2005 found that Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts for a time and then reinstated them. The Murphy report of 2009 found that four archbishops of Dublin had not told the Gardaí, the Irish police, what they knew, and that the archdiocese had taken out insurance against abuse claims from 1987. The Gardaí themselves had treated priests as outside their remit. In Cloyne, the 2011 report found that nine complaints made after the church adopted reporting rules in 1996 were not passed to the Gardaí, and said the Vatican's response to those rules had allowed bishops to ignore them.

The Norbertine order moved Fr Brendan Smyth between parishes, dioceses and countries, including the United States, without reporting him. At church meetings in 1975 two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy, and their evidence never reached the police. The Irish government's delay in acting on a request from Northern Ireland's police to extradite him led to the fall of the government in 1994. In 1997 he was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children.

In 2024 a state scoping inquiry recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, and the government announced a full commission of investigation. More than half of those alleged abusers are dead.

CHL.story:
In 1959 authorities in Siegburg, Germany, issued a warrant for Paul Schäfer for abusing two boys. He fled, and in 1961 he founded Colonia Dignidad, a closed German commune in southern Chile. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic. In 1966 a teenager who escaped took refuge at the West German embassy, which sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. Chilean politicians rejected other escapees' accounts in the 1960s because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup. After the coup, DINA, the Pinochet dictatorship's secret police, used the colony to hold and torture opponents, as Chile's Rettig Commission reported in 1991. An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer hid in Argentina until 2005, and in 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children.

From the 1960s to 2000, children were taken from mainly poor Chilean mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent for adoption in the United States and Europe, including Sweden. The practice peaked under Pinochet. A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad, and a congressional committee concluded the state was responsible. As of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice.

In the Catholic Church, parishioners reported Fr Fernando Karadima to the archbishop of Santiago in 1984, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a church investigation in 2004–05. In 2015 one of his protégés, Juan Barros, was made a bishop. After a Vatican investigator delivered a 2,300-page report, Pope Francis wrote in 2018 that he had made serious errors in judging the situation, and every bishop in Chile offered to resign.

In 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the state responsible for grave violations, including sexual abuse, over 40 years in residences of SENAME, the national child protection service.

In 2019 Chile removed the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for prosecution, for child sexual abuse, so old cases can still be brought. No one had been tried for the adoptions abroad by 2023.

PHL.story:
When Clark Air Base, a US military base in Angeles City north of Manila, closed in 1992, the bars around it lost the American soldiers who had been their customers. The same year Manila's mayor, Alfredo Lim, began closing Ermita, the city's main sex-industry district, and many of its businesses moved to Angeles City and took up foreign tourists as customers. In 2025 the US State Department's trafficking report still named Angeles City among the places where sex trafficking frequently occurs. It said most foreign offenders come from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Britain and the United States, and many are already convicted or charged sex offenders at home.

From 2006 the charity International Justice Mission (IJM) worked with police in several Philippine cities, and by 2016 the number of children trafficked for sex in bars and other establishments there had fallen by 79 to 86 percent. Over 2014 to 2017 the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for child sexual exploitation grew more than twelvefold. Parents, relatives or neighbours were paid by buyers abroad to abuse children in front of a webcam. Because the buyers were abroad, 64 percent of the cases taken up by the police anti-trafficking unit in 2017 began with a referral from a foreign police force. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaking money-laundering law, including failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation in the Philippines. In 2024 Europol, the EU police agency, examined chats between about 12,000 buyer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines, gathered over 12 years, and sent leads on 197 buyers to 24 countries.

In 2002 the Catholic bishops apologised and said about 200 of the country's 7,000 priests had committed sexual misconduct over two decades. No national inquiry into abuse in church or state institutions has been found.

IJM estimated that 1 in every 100 children in the Philippines was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022. The people paying for it live mostly in a few wealthy countries, so finding them depends on police and banks there.

HTI.story:
From 2004 the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, included a contingent of about 950 soldiers from the Sri Lanka Army. In 2007 the UN's internal investigators reported that its members had sexually exploited and abused children frequently, usually at night, at almost every place they were posted. A 2017 Associated Press investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children between 2004 and 2007. Under UN rules only the country that sends peacekeepers can prosecute them, so the UN could only send the accused home. Sri Lanka took back 114 of them, its authorities judged the acts "consensual", and none was jailed.

Haiti has also sent many children abroad for adoption, 13,986 of them between 2003 and 2022. Most of its orphanages are private and funded from abroad. The charity Lumos found in 2017 that at least US$70 million a year reached about a third of them, that 92 percent of funders were in the United States and 90 percent were faith-based, and that the donations led people to open orphanages and recruit children away from their families. In 2007 one centre was forced to return 47 children it had been holding for adoption after misleading their parents with payments. After the 2010 earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained while taking 33 children to the Dominican Republic without proper papers; their leader, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel. In 2019 the government's social welfare agency, after assessing more than 750 orphanages, identified 3,019 children in them as potential trafficking victims.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence by armed groups against 566 children in Haiti, up from 41 girls in 2023, and attributed 411 of the cases to the Viv Ansanm gang coalition. The US State Department reported in 2025 that close to half of gang members are children.

Children in Haiti now face sexual violence from gangs, and many still work as restaveks, unpaid domestic servants in other families' homes, where displacement has raised their risk of sexual exploitation.

COD.story:
In 2002 and 2003, during the war in Ituri province in the east, the Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC), an armed group, enlisted children under 15 as soldiers. The International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries people for war crimes when their own country does not, convicted the UPC's leader, Thomas Lubanga, in 2012 of conscripting and using these children; sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at his trial but not charged. In 2019 the ICC convicted his commander Bosco Ntaganda of crimes including the rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers.

The UN peacekeeping mission sent to the same area was investigated as well. In 2004 the UN's internal investigators found that peacekeepers in Bunia, Ituri's main town, regularly had sex with girls under 18, some as young as 13, in exchange for food or small sums of money. Of 72 allegations, six were fully substantiated, largely because most reports were too vague to investigate. Peacekeepers can only be prosecuted by the country that sent them, and in a 2025 UN report few cases had been finalised. During the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in North Kivu and Ituri, aid workers arrived in the same region. An independent commission appointed by the World Health Organization found in 2021 that WHO staff and other responders, mostly local temporary hires, had used offers of jobs to obtain sex, and that the youngest of those it heard was a 13-year-old girl.

The fighting has continued. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC, by the M23 rebel group, the CODECO militia, the national army and others, and the abduction of 815 children. In the eastern mines, the US State Department reported in 2025, mining bosses, family members, officials and armed groups force children into labour, and girls are trafficked for sex and forced marriage.

In eastern DRC, armed groups and the army continue to abuse and abduct children, and few of the commanders, soldiers or responders accused have been tried. No representative survey has measured online sexual exploitation of children in West and Central Africa, which includes the DRC.

GRC.story:
In its 2025 trafficking report, the US State Department said unaccompanied migrant children in Greece are vulnerable to sex trafficking, and that Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg there. In April 2025 the US Department of Justice announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of '764 Inferno', a subgroup of the online network 764, which extorted minors into producing abuse material and harming themselves. One was arrested in North Carolina and the other in Greece.

Unaccompanied children arriving in Greece remain at risk of sex trafficking. No inquiry into the sexual abuse of children in Greek institutions was found in the sources for this map.

DNK.story:
In 2011 the Godhavn Report examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other Danish state children's homes from 1945 to 1976. It found neglect and physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22 percent of Godhavn's boys had been given psychiatric drugs by a psychiatrist. No prosecutions followed, and Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in 2019.

Denmark has also received many children from abroad, including 9,297 from South Korea between 1965 and 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that agencies there had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Denmark suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2016 after abuses there, and in 2024 the Danish International Adoption agency, the country's only intercountry adoption agency, said it was closing.

Danish police have led or joined several international investigations of online abuse, from the Bamse bulletin board in the early 1990s to Operation Cumberland in 2025, one of the first cases of AI-generated abuse material, in which 273 suspects were identified.

The children abused in the state homes have received an apology from the prime minister, and no one was prosecuted. With its only agency closing, Denmark's part in intercountry adoption is ending.

UGA.story:
From 1987 the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), a rebel group in northern Uganda led by Joseph Kony, abducted children to use as fighters, porters and "wives" for its commanders. UNICEF estimated that at least 25,000 children had been taken by 2006, and the LRA held many of them at bases in southern Sudan. One of those abducted as a child, Dominic Ongwen, became a brigade commander. In 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted him of 61 crimes, including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage and the use of children under 15 as soldiers, and sentenced him to 25 years. The court's warrant for Kony has not been carried out.

Uganda also sent children abroad for adoption, 1,933 of them between 2003 and 2022. Between 2013 and 2016 European Adoption Consultants, an agency in Ohio, arranged adoptions of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families. Parents were told their children would go to school in Kampala, and the children were taken to an unlicensed home. An employee pleaded guilty in 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials to obtain adoption orders, and in 2020 two other employees and a Ugandan lawyer were charged and the US government sanctioned two Ugandan judges and two lawyers. Uganda's social development ministry now says only 185 children's homes are licensed and more than 500 operate without oversight, many funded from abroad, and that many children in them are not orphans.

Ugandan soldiers have also been accused abroad. In 2014 Human Rights Watch documented rape and sexual exploitation by African Union soldiers in Somalia, mainly Ugandans, including of girls as young as 12.

Inside Uganda, the US State Department reported in 2025 that most child sex-trafficking victims are Karamojong children from the north-east, whom traffickers, sometimes community elders, sell at markets on the borders. Unlicensed children's homes and cross-border trafficking from Karamoja continue to put children at risk.

CZE.story:
In 2000 and 2001 a Czech court found Fr František Merta, a Catholic priest in the Archdiocese of Olomouc, guilty of abusing more than 20 boys, and gave him a two-year suspended sentence, meaning he did not go to prison unless he offended again. Archbishop Jan Graubner was alleged to have failed to report him to the police and to have moved him between parishes when problems arose. No national inquiry into abuse in the Czech church appears in the records gathered for this map.

Most of the other Czech cases concern abuse images sold abroad. In 2014 Czech police, supported by Europol, the EU police agency, and Eurojust, its agency for cooperation between prosecutors, led Operation Atelier against a Czech photographer. He had photographed close to 70 children from poor and disadvantaged families and, with a Swedish partner, sold the images to customers in the EU and Canada. Ten people were arrested, five of them in the Czech Republic, and 30 terabytes of data were seized. In 2026 Czech police joined police in Norway and five other countries in arresting 28 men suspected of paying cryptocurrency to watch abuse videos on forums reached through anonymising software, after Norwegian police developed a way to trace the payments.

The records for Czechia show one convicted priest and a few international police operations. How many children were abused in Czech churches, schools or children's homes has not been studied.

BLR.story:
Until 2003 a company in Minsk called Regpay Co. Ltd took paid memberships for about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it ran itself, and sold access to thousands of subscribers around the world. Subscribers paid by credit card, the payments passed through Latvian banks, and a Florida payment firm, Connections, helped hide where the money came from. Because the company was in Belarus, beyond the reach of US police, US agents used a ruse to draw its president, Yahor Zalatarou, and its marketing director to a hotel in Paris, where they were arrested in July 2003; the technical administrator was arrested in Spain and extradited. All three pleaded guilty in New Jersey, and in 2006 Zalatarou and the administrator were each sentenced to 25 years. The customer records led to the arrest of hundreds of subscribers in the US and other countries, in what the US government called Operation Falcon.

Regpay's managers were tried only after US agents drew them out of Belarus. The sources for this map record no other case of child abuse networks run from Belarus.

BGR.story:
In its 2025 trafficking report the US State Department cited a UN special rapporteur, an independent expert appointed by the UN, who found that sexual exploitation, including possible sex trafficking, was common among children in government-run institutions. The same report said traffickers exploit Bulgarian girls and women in Sofia, in resort and border towns and across Western Europe. It found corruption widespread in the police and the courts, and of 31 traffickers convicted, only eight were sent to prison.

Bulgaria sent 5,067 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and its adoptions remain open.

Bulgaria now hosts more of the online abuse material found by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes such material, than any other country. In 2025 the foundation acted on 87,959 web addresses in Bulgaria, 28 percent of its total, up from 9 percent in 2024, and said most of them belonged to a few particular sites. Bulgarian cybercrime police have also taken servers down, as in 2017–18, when they removed the servers of a subscription site showing the abuse of boys in Thailand.

Children in Bulgarian state institutions remain at risk of sexual exploitation, and most convicted traffickers do not go to prison. In 2025 a few sites hosted in Bulgaria accounted for more than a quarter of the abuse material the foundation found.

SYR.story:
On 3 August 2014 the Islamic State (ISIS) attacked Sinjar, where many Yazidis, a religious minority, lived. Its fighters moved the people they captured by bus and truck to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj, and then took the women and girls on to Raqqa in Syria. There they were sold at markets and held in sexual slavery, some of the girls as young as nine, and boys were sent to ISIS training camps. In June 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis. At that date more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

Syrians who fled the war were also exploited in neighbouring countries; Türkiye alone hosted about 2.9 million of them. In Lebanon in March 2016, security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels in Jounieh. Police had raided one of them in 2011, finding a 17-year-old Syrian girl there, and it had reopened about three months later. The US State Department reported in 2025 that Syrian girls in Türkiye are married in unofficial religious ceremonies and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking, and that Syrian refugee girls in Jordan have been sold into forced marriages.

Inside Syria, the UN verified the abduction of 14 children in 2024 by armed groups and government forces, often to recruit them as fighters.

Thousands of Yazidi women and children taken to Syria are still missing. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, so its scale in Syria and among Syrian refugees is unknown.

BDI.story:
In 2013 and 2014 Burundian soldiers were serving in Somalia with AMISOM, the African Union's peace mission there. Human Rights Watch documented in 2014 cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by soldiers at the Burundian base in Mogadishu, alongside cases involving Ugandan troops. Many of the women and girls had come to the bases to ask for medicine or aid, and some were pressured into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine.

Soldiers on such missions can be tried only by their own country. In the Central African Republic, Burundian and Gabonese soldiers served with MINUSCA, the UN mission there. In 2016 the UN recorded two allegations from the town of Dékoa involving these contingents, which led to interviews with about 136 alleged victims, almost half of all victims the UN recorded that year. UN data list allegations against Burundian personnel involving 46 children. The UN's 2017 report said the investigations by Burundi and Gabon were still pending, and press reports said 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without being charged.

Within Burundi itself, little is recorded. In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online abuse material from technology companies, received 1,028 reports linked to Burundi, one of the countries from which almost no reports reach the international systems.

No trial in Burundi of the soldiers sent home from the Central African Republic is recorded. Because so few reports come out of Burundi, the extent of abuse of children inside the country is not known.

BGD.story:
In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said that traffickers take Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India, Pakistan and the Gulf states, and observers estimate that children are 40 percent of the Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. In India, police in Kolkata rescued nine girls under 18 from a house in the north of the city in September 2025 and charged the couple running it; the State Department says significant numbers of Bangladeshi and Nepali women and girls are recruited for sex trafficking in India.

Near Cox's Bazar, more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Many fled Myanmar, where a UN fact-finding mission found that the army raped hundreds of Rohingya women and girls during its 2017 operations. In Bangladesh, tourists have increased the demand for sexual exploitation near Cox's Bazar, including of Rohingya girls, and the State Department described corrupt policing in the camps. Bangladeshi courts convicted 103 traffickers in the year covered by the 2025 report, down from 407.

Bangladesh was also one of the countries from which children were adopted into the Netherlands. In 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from Bangladesh and other countries between 1967 and 1998, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption.

Girls continue to be taken from Bangladesh and exploited near the camps, and fewer traffickers are being convicted. No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in South Asia.

GIN.story:
In 2001 a joint mission by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, and the charity Save the Children UK visited refugee camps in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Its report in early 2002 said refugee children were being sexually exploited by employees of aid groups and UN agencies and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services, the UN's internal investigators, then examined 43 cases in full and substantiated 10. They included the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou. The investigators said in October 2002 that they had found no evidence of "widespread" abuse, and Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN had found made it think its report was wrong.

Guinea was also the site of Mamou Alliance Academy, a boarding school for the children of missionaries of the Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA) working in West Africa. Former pupils wrote to the church's headquarters about abuse from the 1980s, and an inquiry was set up only after 30 of them asked for one in 1995. In 1998 an independent commission found that the church had been negligent and identified nine offenders, whose abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The church's US board then wrote an open letter asking the victims' forgiveness.

Both cases were found by inquiries set up by the organisations involved. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its extent in Guinea is not known.

BFA.story:
In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 309 children in Burkina Faso. Armed Islamist groups took most of them, 157 by JNIM and 80 by ISGS, the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, and 47 were taken by groups that could not be identified. The other 25 were abducted by the state's own security forces and the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP), civilian auxiliaries who fight with them. It also verified the rape of four girls that year, two of them by the VDP, and in 2022 the rape of 16 girls, two by state forces.

Children from Burkina Faso have also been trafficked across borders. In 2019 police in Kaduna, in northern Nigeria, raided a building presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them in chains; some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana, and local media reported that captives had been sexually abused. The US State Department reported in 2025 that Nigerian networks move women and girls to mining areas in several West African countries, including Burkina Faso, for sex trafficking.

Children in Burkina Faso are abducted by both the armed groups and the forces fighting them. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its wider extent is not known.

ARE.story:
Telegram, the messaging service, has its operational centre in Dubai. In August 2024 French investigators charged its founder, Pavel Durov, with offences including suspected complicity in running a platform used to share images of child sexual abuse, and with refusing to give information to the authorities. A BBC investigation that month found that Telegram had not joined the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children or the Internet Watch Foundation, two organisations that collect and share records of known abuse images, and had ignored repeated requests to do so. In December 2024 Telegram agreed to use the Internet Watch Foundation's list of known images to detect them in public parts of the platform. The foundation said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse images on Telegram since 2022.

UAE police have taken part in international operations against people sharing abuse images. In 2015 they were one of ten members of the Virtual Global Taskforce, a group of police forces, that together arrested 303 people and identified 106 victims in Operation Atlas.

No other cases from the UAE appear in the records for this map. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, so how many children in the UAE are affected is not known.

VIR.story:
The financier Jeffrey Epstein owned Little St. James, a private island in the US Virgin Islands, and used it as one of the homes where he and Ghislaine Maxwell sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005. Maxwell was convicted in 2021, and Epstein died in 2019. After his death the territory's government brought civil cases. It reached a $105 million settlement with Epstein's estate and a $62.5 million settlement with the billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, Epstein's bank, claiming the bank had ignored warning signs and made his activities possible by keeping him as a client. In 2023 JPMorgan agreed to pay $290 million to nearly 200 of Epstein's victims and $75 million to the Virgin Islands. In 2020 New York's financial regulator had fined Deutsche Bank $150 million for ignoring warning signs about Epstein.

Where the girls brought to the island came from is still being examined. In December 2025 prosecutors in Ankara opened an inquiry after a Turkish MP cited a 2009 civil complaint that alleged Epstein brought girls from Turkey, the Czech Republic and other countries; no findings or charges have been reported.

The Virgin Islands recovered money through civil settlements, which carried no criminal findings, and no bank was criminally charged over Epstein. How many girls were brought to the island, and from where, is still not established.

TLS.story:
In 1992 Richard Daschbach, a US-born missionary priest of the Society of the Divine Word, a Catholic order, founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse, a district of Timor-Leste. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted to them that he had abused children there, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood in November 2018. The church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14. A report by the Justice and Peace Commission of the Dili archdiocese defended him, and in December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years.

In 2019 the Vatican received allegations that Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo, a member of the Salesian order and a winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, had abused boys in Fatumaca and Dili before and during his time as bishop. In 2020 it barred him from contact with minors and with Timor-Leste and limited his movement and ministry. It did not announce this, and confirmed the sanctions only in September 2022, the day after the Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer published the accounts of two men. Belo had left Timor-Leste in 2002 and worked in Mozambique from 2004.

In both cases the church learned of the abuse and acted internally without telling the public, and the cases became known through a criminal court and a magazine. Belo has not been tried.

URY.story:
In the 1970s the military governments of Argentina, Uruguay and other South American countries cooperated in hunting down their opponents, under an arrangement known as Operation Condor. In August 1976 a pregnant 19-year-old Argentine woman was detained in Buenos Aires and secretly moved to Montevideo by a joint Argentine–Uruguayan unit. She gave birth in a military hospital, and in December 1976 her baby was taken from her and left with the family of a police officer, who raised the girl under another identity for 23 years. The mother disappeared.

In 1986 Uruguay passed the Expiry Law, an amnesty that protected military and police officers from prosecution for crimes under the dictatorship, and in 2003 it was used to close the investigation into this case. In 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the court that rules on whether American states have kept their human rights treaties, found Uruguay responsible for the mother's enforced disappearance and for hiding the child's identity, and ruled that the amnesty could not be used to block the investigation.

After the 2011 ruling the amnesty could no longer be used to close this case. It is the only Uruguayan case in the records for this map, so how many other children were taken in Uruguay under the dictatorship is not shown here.

MHL.story:
From 2015 to 2019 Paul Petersen, an adoption lawyer who was also the elected assessor of Maricopa County, Arizona, paid recruiters to bring about 40 pregnant Marshallese women to Arizona, Utah and Arkansas. He paid the women about $10,000 each to give up their babies and charged the adoptive couples about $35,000. This broke the Compact of Free Association, the treaty between the Marshall Islands and the United States, which bars Marshallese citizens from travelling to the US to give up a child for adoption. He also obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds, the public health insurance for people on low incomes, for the women by fraud. He was charged in all three states in October 2019, pleaded guilty in June 2020 to human smuggling and fraud, and was sentenced in December 2020 to more than six years in prison.

The case was prosecuted in the United States. Records from the Marshall Islands of how many children were taken through such schemes are not in the sources for this map.

QAT.story:
On 13 August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox, an online game platform popular with children, after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety on it. Kuwait's telecoms regulator blocked the platform temporarily later that month, and Oman and Jordan had banned it since 2020.

No other cases from Qatar appear in the records for this map. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children, online or offline, has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, so how many children in Qatar are affected is not known.

GUM.story:
In 2016 Guam lifted the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a civil lawsuit, for child sexual abuse, so people abused decades earlier could sue. More than 200 lawsuits followed against the Catholic Archdiocese of Agaña, naming 35 priests, teachers and scoutmasters for abuse going back to the 1950s. In March 2018 a Vatican tribunal found the former archbishop, Anthony Apuron, guilty of charges including the sexual abuse of minors, and rejected his appeal in February 2019. He was removed from office and barred from living in Guam, but remained a priest, and he denies the allegations.

In January 2019, facing the lawsuits, the archdiocese filed for bankruptcy, which placed all the claims in a single court process and limited what it would pay to what a judge approved. The number of claims rose to nearly 280. In January 2020 the archdiocese offered a plan worth $21 million, and it sold a property in Yona for $6.1 million.

Survivors' claims are being settled through the bankruptcy court. The only judgment against Apuron in these records came from a church tribunal.

DJI.story:
In its 2025 trafficking report, the US State Department said that traffickers bring Ethiopian girls into neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, and exploit them in domestic servitude and sex trafficking, sometimes using drugs to control them. The report said officials continued to be reported as complicit.

No other cases from Djibouti appear in the records for this map. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, the region in which the survey researchers grouped Djibouti, so the number of children affected there is not known.

ERI.story:
Eritrea's army, the Eritrean Defence Forces, was among the forces that fought in the war in Ethiopia's Tigray region from 2020. In 2022 the International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, a UN-appointed inquiry, documented widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray, and by Tigrayan forces against women and girls as young as 11 in neighbouring Amhara. In February 2021 the BBC reported that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health facilities in Mekelle, in Tigray, as survivors of rape.

Almost nothing is reported from inside Eritrea. In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online abuse material from technology companies, received 11 reports linked to the country.

No Eritrean soldier is recorded in these sources as having been tried for the sexual violence in Tigray, and abuse of children inside Eritrea goes almost entirely unrecorded.

KGZ.story: In 2009 Kyrgyzstan suspended intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by families abroad, and in April 2010 the US State Department issued an alert to American families about the suspension. The records for this map give no reason for the suspension and contain no other cases from Kyrgyzstan, so the scale of abuse and trafficking of children there has not been documented here.

DZA.story: No cases of networked abuse or trafficking of children in Algeria appear in the records gathered for this map. Childlight, a research institute that collects survey data on sexual exploitation of children, found in 2026 that no representative survey of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation of children had been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, which includes Algeria. How many children there are affected is therefore not known.

EGY.story: No cases of networked abuse or trafficking of children in Egypt appear in the records gathered for this map. Childlight, a research institute that collects survey data on sexual exploitation of children, found in 2026 that no representative survey of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation of children had been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, which includes Egypt. How many children there are affected is therefore not known.

TKM.story: No cases of networked abuse or trafficking of children in Turkmenistan appear in the records gathered for this map. In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online child sexual abuse material, mostly from American technology companies, received 591 reports linked to Turkmenistan, which places it among the countries from which almost no reports reach the international systems. With so few reports, the extent of abuse of children in Turkmenistan is not known.

ARG.story:
Between 1976 and 1983 Argentina was ruled by a military junta, a government of the heads of the armed forces. Security forces secretly detained people they saw as opponents, and many were never seen again; they became known as the disappeared. Children kidnapped with their parents or born to mothers in detention were taken and registered as the biological children of military families or supporters of the regime. Many did not know they were adopted. The practice crossed borders under Operation Condor, an agreement among South American military governments to hunt each other's opponents.
