In one case, a pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, and her baby was given to a Uruguayan police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years.

In 1977 the children's grandmothers formed the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo to search for them. Their work led to the creation of a National Bank of Genetic Data, which allowed DNA tests to match children with their families. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken. The Grandmothers had found 97 by 2008 and announced the 140th in July 2025. In 2012 a federal court in Buenos Aires found that the junta had run a systematic plan to take these children. It sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years.

The Italian priest Nicola Corradi was accused at a school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, and he went on working at the same order's school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, in Mendoza province. He was arrested there in 2016, and in 2019 a Mendoza court sentenced him to 42 years and another priest to 45 for abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016.

Most of the children taken under the junta have still not been identified, and those who are found learn their true identity as adults.

BEL.story:
In 1992 Belgium released Marc Dutroux early from a 13.5-year sentence for rape, against the objections of a prosecutor and a psychiatrist. In 1995 and 1996 he kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19. His mother wrote to the authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls, but police took 14 months to arrest him. Police missed voices heard in his cellar and did not review his videotapes, and rivalry between two police forces slowed the search. In October 1996 hundreds of thousands of people marched in Brussels in protest. A parliamentary inquiry criticised the police investigation, and Belgium later reorganised its police forces. In 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life. Witnesses also told investigators of an abuse network involving prominent people, but prosecutors dismissed the statements and the claims remain unproven.

The Catholic Church set up its own commission in 2000. It upheld 32 of 33 formal complaints, but 31 were past the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, and only one reached court. In April 2010 the Bishop of Bruges, Roger Vangheluwe, resigned after admitting he had abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. A second church-backed commission then received 475 complaints in six months, and its report recorded 13 suicides linked to abuse by clergy. In June 2010 police raided church buildings, including the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, and seized the commission's files and 450 internal dossiers.

Eric Dejaeger, a Belgian missionary in the Canadian Arctic, fled to Belgium in 1995 and lived in homes of his order for 16 years despite an international warrant. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was sentenced in 2015 for 32 offences against Inuit children.

After the church cases, abuse in Flemish youth institutions and boarding schools from 1930 to 1990 came to light, and in 2014 the Flemish Parliament formally apologised to the victims.

Much of the abuse in Belgian church institutions was reported after the legal deadlines had passed. Victims of abuse in Flemish institutions are still coming forward, and the commission set up in 2014 to hear them received 121 reports in 2024.

BRA.story:
In 2000 Brazil made it a crime, punishable by 4 to 10 years in prison, to subject a child or adolescent to prostitution. Foreign men continued to travel to the coast of the northeast for sex with children, and in 2006 the Federal Police said this happened most often in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal. In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said that taxi drivers and staff of hotels, bars and nightclubs in coastal tourist towns help arrange the sale of children for sex. It cited a study suggesting that up to 16 percent of girls aged 14 to 17 in one northeastern city area were likely victims. It also said a 2016 case against an elected official in Paraná was unresolved.

Children are also sold along the country's main roads. For about 19 years the Federal Highway Police and the charity Childhood Brasil have mapped roadside places such as truck stops, bars and motels where children are at risk. Their survey for 2021 and 2022 assessed more than 9,700 places and rated 640 critical. An earlier survey found that 38 percent of victims came from elsewhere and may have been trafficked.

Brazil also sent children abroad for adoption, 5,456 of them between 2003 and 2022. In 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from several countries, Brazil among them, between 1967 and 1998, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption.

Brazil has the largest Catholic population in the world, but no national inquiry into abuse in the Church or other institutions has been found. In 2010 former altar boys in Arapiraca complained about three priests, and a secretly filmed video was shown on television. In 2011 a court convicted the three of abusing altar boys and sentenced them to between 16 and 21 years, but they were not jailed while they appealed.

Without a national inquiry, the extent of abuse in Brazil's churches, schools and care homes is not known. Children are still sold for sex along the main roads and in tourist towns, and Brazil reported no investigations of officials involved.

CHE.story:
Swiss federal and cantonal authorities, the national and regional governments, detained people without any court order. An independent expert commission reported in 2019 that more than 60,000 people had been held in about 650 institutions, mainly between 1930 and 1981, and that many were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. Among them were the Verdingkinder, children placed with farmers as unpaid labourers. The government had apologised in 2010, and a 2016 law gave each victim of these measures a payment of CHF 25,000.

Switzerland also received children for adoption from abroad, including 1,111 from South Korea between 1968 and 1997 and others from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet. Swiss authorities realised early that the children were often wrongly described as orphans and that some adoptions were linked to organised child trafficking, yet they decided cases on incomplete or false documents. After parliament commissioned a study in 2018, the Federal Council, Switzerland's government, acknowledged these failures in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 it recommended banning intercountry adoption altogether.

In 2023 historians at the University of Zurich, working for the Catholic bishops and religious orders, documented 921 victims of abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the 1950s; 74 percent of the documents concerned abuse of minors. They described their count as the tip of the iceberg.

Switzerland has examined and apologised for detentions and forced placements carried out by its own authorities, and has paid victims of these measures. The researchers' count of victims in the Catholic Church is a minimum, and the full number is not known.

DEU.story:
From 1967 the youth authorities of West Berlin, the city's child welfare service, followed the advice of the sexologist Helmut Kentler and placed homeless boys and other children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers. University of Hildesheim reports in 2020 and 2024 found the Berlin authorities responsible and showed that a network of academics, welfare officials and educators across West Germany tolerated or supported this until after 2000. Kentler died in 2008 without being prosecuted.

One member of that network was Gerold Becker, headmaster of the Odenwaldschule, a private boarding school. Former pupils reported abuse in 1998 and a newspaper wrote about it in 1999, but a promised review did not take place, and prosecutors dropped the case because the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, had passed. In 2010 a report commissioned by the school named Becker and a music teacher as the main abusers, and later counts put the victims at 132 pupils or more. Becker died that year without facing a court.

After abuse at another school, the Canisius-Kolleg, became public in January 2010, the federal government set up a Round Table on child sexual abuse and an Independent Commissioner. In 2013 the Bundestag, the federal parliament, extended the deadline for civil claims from 3 to 30 years. A 2022 report for the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising counted at least 497 victims since 1945 and found misconduct by Joseph Ratzinger, archbishop from 1977 to 1982 and later Pope Benedict XVI, in four cases.

At a campsite in Lügde two men abused 32 children from 1998 to 2018, and a youth office had placed a foster daughter with one of them. Police received two tips in 2016, and 155 pieces of evidence went missing from a police office. A state parliamentary inquiry said the men could have been stopped two years earlier. Both were convicted in 2019.

The main figures in the Kentler and Odenwaldschule cases died without trial. The Lügde abuse continued until 2018, after the 2010 reforms, while police and a youth office had information about the offenders.

ETH.story:
In the 2000s the number of Ethiopian children adopted abroad grew quickly. The number sent each year rose from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008, and between 2003 and 2022 a total of 33,303 children left the country this way. The United States alone issued 15,166 visas to adopted Ethiopian children between 1994 and 2014. Families in Canada found that children had been given papers as orphans when their parents were alive. In 2011 the US State Department found that one agency, Better Futures Adoption Services, was involved in child trafficking, and the agency lost its licence to work in Ethiopia.

Ireland suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2007, Australia in 2009 and Denmark in 2016. Ethiopia suspended foreign adoptions in November 2017, and in January 2018 its parliament banned adoption by foreigners. It cited abuse and neglect of children abroad after a US couple were convicted in 2013 over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

During the war in Tigray, which began in 2020, forces on both sides raped women and girls. A UN-appointed commission of human rights experts reported in 2022 that Ethiopian and Eritrean forces had committed widespread sexual violence in Tigray, and that Tigrayan forces had raped women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages in 2021. In February 2021 the BBC reported that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health centres in Mekelle as survivors of rape. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia, and attributed 38 of these cases to the national army.

Ethiopian girls are also taken abroad. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers exploit them as domestic servants and for sex in Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs to control them, and that begging rings exploit women and children in Saudi Arabia. It said reports of officials taking part continued.

Foreign adoption from Ethiopia has been closed since 2018. The national army was responsible for more than half of the sexual violence against children that the UN verified in Ethiopia in 2024.

FRA.story:
Between 1968 and 2008 France took in 11,165 children from South Korea for adoption, among others from abroad. In March 2024 a government assessment acknowledged that the authorities had long known of "illicit practices of a systemic nature" in intercountry adoption and had been late to act.

In 2018 the Catholic bishops set up an independent commission chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé. Its 2021 report used a population survey to estimate that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, or about 330,000 if lay people working for the Church were included.

In 2004 the US FBI traced downloads of abuse images to the surgeon Joël Le Scouarnec, and in 2005 a French court gave him a four-month suspended sentence. Prosecutors did not tell the medical authorities, a warning to the health ministry in 2007 led to no action, and in 2008 a hospital hired him knowing of the conviction. He went on abusing patients until 2014. In 2025 he admitted abusing 299 victims, many of them under anaesthesia, and was sentenced to 20 years.

In April 2025 a parliamentary inquiry estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services are victims of prostitution. Teenagers in care are often housed in hotels with little supervision.

France has estimated the scale of abuse in the Church through a national survey and has given victims more time to bring a case. By the inquiry's estimate, about 15,000 children in the state's own care are being sold for sex now.

GHA.story:
Among the Ewe people of Ghana, some traditional shrines practise trokosi. A shrine takes a girl, usually a young virgin, to atone for a wrong a relative is said to have committed. She serves the priest without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as part of her duty, which defenders of the practice deny. In 1998 Ghana amended its Criminal Code to make ritual or customary servitude a crime, with a minimum sentence of three years. The practice continued, and no prosecutions are recorded.

Children are also sold into work. On Lake Volta, traffickers put children as young as four to work in fishing and control them with violence and little food. In 2023 International Justice Mission, a charity, surveyed 1,286 children in three fishing districts and estimated that 37.7 percent were likely to have been trafficked. The US State Department said in 2025 that girls in the fishing trade are at risk of sexual exploitation, and that observers reported forced child labour on the lake had decreased.

Some Ghanaian boys were taken further away. In 2019 police in Kaduna, in northern Nigeria, raided a building presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them in chains. Some had been brought from Ghana, Burkina Faso and Mali, and local media reported that captives had been sexually abused.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its extent in Ghana is not known. Children are still put to work on Lake Volta, and trokosi continued after it was made a crime.

GNQ.story:
No case, inquiry or flow of children involving Equatorial Guinea is recorded on this map. In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research organisation that gathers data on the sexual exploitation of children, found no representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children in West and Central Africa, the region that includes Equatorial Guinea. A representative survey asks a sample of people chosen to reflect the whole population, so it can estimate how common something is.

Without such surveys, reports or inquiries, the extent of abuse and trafficking of children in Equatorial Guinea is not known.

HKG.story:
In December 2003 Hong Kong passed the Prevention of Child Pornography Ordinance. Among other things, it gave 24 sexual offences extraterritorial effect, which means that a Hong Kong resident who commits one of these offences against a child in another country can be prosecuted in Hong Kong. Laws of this kind were passed by several places from which men travelled abroad to abuse children, so that offenders could not escape prosecution by going to a country with weaker laws or weaker courts.

Hong Kong also became one of the places where abuse material is stored online. The Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes images and videos of child sexual abuse, counted 24,063 web addresses with such material hosted in Hong Kong in 2023 and 2024. In those years Hong Kong was the third or fourth largest host in the world. In 2025 the number fell sharply.

No inquiry into abuse in Hong Kong's own institutions is recorded, so how many children there have been abused is not known. The reasons for the fall in hosting in 2025 are also not known.

ISR.story:
In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox school in Melbourne, paid for its headmistress, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of allegations that she had abused pupils. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences. Her lawyers in Israel sought more than 70 hearings and appeals, and in 2019 she was found to have faked mental illness. The deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, had pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric evaluations so that she would appear unfit for extradition, the legal process of sending a suspect to another country for trial. Leifer was extradited in 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in 2023 of 18 charges including rape. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a plea deal, resigned from the Knesset, Israel's parliament, and received eight months' probation.

In June 2024 a UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israeli security forces had subjected Palestinians to sexual violence during arrests and in detention, that men and boys were targeted in particular ways, and that this amounted to gender persecution as a crime against humanity. It also found that sexual violence was committed in the attacks of 7 October 2023, when 36 children were among 252 people taken hostage.

Leifer was convicted in Australia in 2023 after years of hearings in Israel, and the minister who obstructed her extradition received probation.

JAM.story:
In 2023 a study of the prevalence of trafficking in Jamaica estimated that 6.3 percent of children aged 12 to 17 had lived in conditions that indicate trafficking. The US State Department cited the study in its 2025 report on trafficking. The report says children are sold for sex in resort areas visited by tourists, sometimes with the involvement of their parents. In some communities men pay girls or their families for sex. The people named as taking part include family members, local and foreign buyers, and "dons", the men who control some neighbourhoods.

The report also says that corruption is widespread in Jamaica and that the complicity of officials, including police officers, remained a significant problem.

Children in Jamaica's resort areas and in some communities continue to be sold for sex. Some of the police officers responsible for stopping this trade are reported to be complicit in it.

JPN.story:
Johnny Kitagawa founded Johnny & Associates, which became Japan's dominant agency for boy bands, which trained boys to become pop singers. A weekly magazine first reported on his abuse of boys in 1965. In 1999 the magazine Shūkan Bunshun published a series of reports, and Kitagawa sued it for defamation, a claim of false and damaging reporting. The courts upheld the reporting on sexual abuse in 2003 and 2004. Japanese newspapers and television barely covered the rulings; journalists said this was because the agency controlled which of its stars appeared on their programmes. Kitagawa died in 2019 without being charged.

A BBC documentary in March 2023 and a former trainee's public statement in April led the company to set up an outside investigation. Its report in August 2023 found that Kitagawa had abused boys and young men from the early 1970s to the mid-2010s. The company admitted the abuse, split off its talent business, and set up a committee of three former judges to handle compensation. By August 2026 it had decided to compensate 585 people.

In June 2023 Japan reformed its Penal Code, the main criminal law. It raised the age of consent from 13 to 16 and extended the time limit for prosecuting rape from 10 to 15 years.

Other institutions have been counted only in part. In 2020 the Catholic bishops published a survey of all 16 dioceses that found 16 cases of abuse of minors from the 1950s to the 2010s. Most victims had taken 10 to 30 years to report, and eight of the accused had been transferred. In 2021 the newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun found that at least 47 staff in children's homes had committed indecent acts against 69 children in their care over five years.

In Japan most abuse became known only when victims spoke decades later or foreign media reported it. Children are still sold for sex through "JK businesses", which sell dates with high-school girls; the police counted 91 such businesses at the end of 2024, and the US State Department says many have links to organised crime.

LVA.story:
The records for this map contain little about the abuse or trafficking of children in Latvia itself. No national inquiry into abuse in Latvian institutions, and no case brought in Latvia, is recorded here.

The one recorded change concerns adoption abroad. Latvia had been among the countries sending children to families in the United States for adoption. A Latvian law that prevents adoptions to the United States took effect on 1 July 2022, according to the US State Department's adoption report for 2024. The records do not say what led to the law or how many Latvian children had been adopted in the United States before it.

Because no inquiry or survey has been recorded, how many children in Latvia have been abused in institutions, trafficked or exploited online is not known.

MDG.story:
When Mozambique tightened its laws against the sexual exploitation of children, child sex tourism in Madagascar increased. Most of the foreign offenders were French and Italian.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says most children sold for sex in Madagascar are exploited by Malagasy men, and that foreign tourists, often from France, also exploit children. Some parents encourage their daughters to sell sex to tourists, and children are exploited in karaoke bars in Antananarivo, the capital. The report described corruption and officials taking part as significant problems, and only one official was investigated. Courts convicted 15 traffickers in the year, the first convictions in four years.

Abuse of children is also sold online. In July 2025 police on the island of Nosy Be, a tourist area with its own anti-trafficking committee, arrested two women suspected of filming the abuse of their own children and selling the videos to buyers abroad, who paid by mobile money, a system for sending money by phone. The two women were charged.

Children in Madagascar are sold both to tourists who visit and to buyers abroad who pay by phone for videos. Few of the people involved, officials among them, have been brought to court.

MMR.story:
In 2017 Myanmar's armed forces, the Tatmadaw, carried out what they called "clearance operations" against the Rohingya, a minority people in Rakhine State. A UN inquiry, the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar, found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during these operations, and that 80 percent of the corroborated cases were gang rapes. In 2019 it reported that sexual violence was a hallmark of the army's operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan States. It also found that in 2012 Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, had been subjected to sexual violence while held at Buthidaung prison.

In 2019 Human Rights Watch documented women and girls from these areas, many of them displaced, who had been sold for US$3,000 to $13,000 to families in China as brides. They were locked up and raped so that they would become pregnant. One girl was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. Human Rights Watch said police in both countries gave traffickers little reason to fear arrest. In 2025 the US State Department said displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain at risk of forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.

The war has continued. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 85 children, most of them to be used as fighters, 41 by the armed forces and their militias and 33 by the Kachin Independence Army, an ethnic armed group.

Children in Buddhist monasteries are another group with little protection. Up to 300,000 children may live in monasteries, and few records are kept. In 2018 four girls aged 10 to 14, who stayed at a monastery in Pathein so they could go to school, said its administrator monk had raped them repeatedly. He disappeared when their parents went to the police. Reporters found that police usually defer to the religious authorities in cases against monks.

The armed forces that the UN inquiry found responsible for widespread rape are still fighting, and children in the conflict areas are still being abducted and trafficked to China.

MOZ.story:
After a peace treaty ended Mozambique's war in 1992, the United Nations sent a peacekeeping mission, ONUMOZ, to oversee the settlement. A UN study of children in armed conflict, led by Graça Machel and published in 1996, found that ONUMOZ soldiers had recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. The same study found that in six of twelve countries it examined, the arrival of peacekeeping troops was followed by a rapid rise in child prostitution. Peacekeepers can be tried only by their own countries, and the UN can do no more than send them home.

Since 2017 armed groups linked to the Islamic State have fought in Cabo Delgado, in the north. In 2024 the UN verified that they had abducted 468 children, 371 boys and 97 girls, most of them to use as fighters, and that five girls were subjected to sexual violence. Government forces were also named. Of the 12 girls the UN verified as victims of sexual violence in 2023, five were attributed to the national army and three to a police unit, the Rapid Intervention Unit.

In the south, according to the US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking, traffickers exploit girls at rest stops, bars and restaurants along the highway from Maputo to South Africa and around mines. Girls as young as 11 who work as nannies are at risk when their jobs end.

Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, left Timor-Leste in 2002 and worked in Maputo from 2004. In 2019 the Vatican received allegations that he had abused boys in Timor-Leste, and in 2020 it limited his ministry and barred him from contact with minors, but it did not make this public until a magazine reported the case in 2022.

Children in Cabo Delgado are still being abducted by armed groups and abused by some of the forces sent to fight them. In the south, girls are exploited along the main trade route to South Africa.

MWI.story:
Dzaleka refugee camp, near Lilongwe, holds about 53,000 refugees in a space built for 10,000. According to the US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking, criminal groups working across borders run informal bars and housing in the camp and use them to recruit girls for sex trafficking, both inside the camp and in roadside bars on the highway to Lilongwe. The camp is also a stop on the Southern Route, the path criminal networks use to move migrants to South Africa, where some end up in sex trafficking or forced labour. Girls are also exploited in bars and illegal brothels in Lilongwe and Blantyre. The report said officials taking part in the trade continued to hold back enforcement.

Franc Frantar, a Catholic priest from Slovenia accused of abusing up to 16 minors, went to Malawi as a missionary and so escaped prosecution at home for a time. He returned to Slovenia after Interpol, the international police organisation, issued a notice for him, and in 2006 he was detained and later sentenced to prison.

Girls in Dzaleka remain within reach of trafficking groups that work inside the camp and along the route south to South Africa.

NPL.story:
In March 2007 the British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported that babies in Nepal were being bought for intercountry adoption, with bribes paid and birth families deceived. The next month Nepal's new minister halted all adoptions abroad. About 440 pending cases were processed from November 2007. The United States later stopped adopting Nepali children declared abandoned, because their documents could not be relied on. Between 2003 and 2022, 1,991 children were sent abroad for adoption.

Children are also placed in children's homes for money. In 2021 and 2022 Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered homes holding 10,905 children, and UNICEF estimates that about 85 percent of children in them have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from poor rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by the homes. In one case documented by charities, a child was admitted with a forged certificate of a parent's death. Researchers say the homes use the children to attract donations from abroad. A 2018 law requires local governments to appoint child welfare officers, but only about 200 of 753 had done so.

Girls and women are also taken to India, across a 1,850 km open border. Estimates collected by researchers put the number at 5,000 to 10,000 a year. Traffickers recruit them with false offers of jobs or marriage, and now also through online romance scams, and sell them to brothels in Kolkata, Mumbai and other cities. Traffickers give underage girls false documents stating they are adults. Inside Nepal, a 2024 study cited by the US State Department found that most workers in the adult entertainment sector were trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers in the year covered by the 2025 report, which also raised serious concerns about officials taking part.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in South Asia, so its extent in Nepal is unknown. Most children in Nepal's homes have a parent, and the officials meant to check on them have mostly not been appointed.

OMN.story:
Very little has been counted about the sexual abuse or exploitation of children in Oman. In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research organisation that gathers data on the sexual exploitation of children, found no representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children anywhere in the Middle East and North Africa. A representative survey asks a sample of people chosen to reflect the whole population, so it can estimate how common something is.

The one recorded action concerns a gaming platform. Oman has banned Roblox, an online game used by many children, since 2020. In August 2025 Qatar and Kuwait also blocked it after parents and community groups raised concerns about the safety of children on the platform.

Without surveys or an inquiry, how many children in Oman are abused or exploited, online or offline, is not known.

PRK.story:
Internet companies that find images or videos of child sexual abuse on their services report them to the CyberTipline, run by the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). Each report is linked to the country where the material was uploaded or the user was located. In 2025 NCMEC received 12 reports for North Korea.

Very few people in North Korea can use the internet, so the low number reflects how little access there is and gives no measure of how often children there are abused. No other case, inquiry or survey involving North Korea is recorded on this map.

Almost nothing is known from outside about the abuse or trafficking of children in North Korea.

ROU.story:
In 1966, under Nicolae Ceaușescu, Romania banned abortion by Decree 770, and many of the children born in the following years were abandoned in state institutions. There they were neglected, sedated, and physically and sexually abused; abuse was reported to be common at the children's psychiatric hospital in Siret. After Ceaușescu fell in 1989, television showed about 100,000 children in Romanian orphanages, and foreign families began adopting them in large numbers. Private agencies charged €7,500 to €25,000 per child, and the system soon became corrupt. The United States alone issued 5,285 visas to children adopted from Romania between 1994 and 2008.

Romania tried several times to stop the trade. It halted adoptions in 1991 and outlawed selling babies, imposed a temporary ban in 2001 after a government commission found that middlemen and officials had taken the money, and in June 2004, under pressure from the European Union, banned foreign adoption except by grandparents. In 2006 there were no intercountry adoptions.

Girls from Romania continued to be sent abroad by other means. From 2009 one criminal group used the "loverboy" method, in which a man pretends to be in love with a vulnerable girl. The group exploited girls in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18 and then moved them to Britain, Ireland and Germany. Romanian and British investigators working together arrested 21 members in 2020. In its 2025 report the US State Department said most identified victims of trafficking from Romania are women and girls exploited at home or in Western Europe. It also said children in state institutions, particularly girls in homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking. Romanian courts convicted 161 traffickers in 2024.

Romania also hosted 21,188 web addresses with abuse material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity, in 2025, 7 percent of the total.

Foreign adoption from Romania has been closed since 2004. Children still live in state institutions, where girls are at risk from traffickers and some staff are alleged to have been complicit or negligent.

SAU.story:
Little has been counted about the abuse and trafficking of children in Saudi Arabia. The records for this map come mostly from reports about the countries the children come from. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking in Ethiopia says that traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia in forced begging, sometimes through organised begging rings. It also says that reports of Ethiopian officials taking part in trafficking continued.

That report also covers Ethiopian girls who are sold as domestic servants and for sex, but it names Djibouti and Sudan, not Saudi Arabia, as the main destinations for them. The State Department's report on Indonesia says tourists from the Middle East pay for short "contract marriages" with Indonesian girls as young as nine in Puncak, West Java, but it does not say which countries the tourists come from.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa. Without such surveys or a national inquiry, the number of children abused or trafficked in Saudi Arabia, including children brought from abroad, is not known.

SLE.story:
In 1998 about 29 children staying at a centre in Makeni run by the charity Help A Needy Child International (HANCI) were taken to Freetown, the capital, for medical checks. They never came back. Their parents later learned that the children had been adopted by families in the United States. Between 1994 and 2014 the United States issued 385 visas to children adopted from Sierra Leone. The government suspended adoptions in May 2009, and in April 2012 a commission set up by the president closed HANCI down. It concluded that the children's families "cannot be said to have genuinely consented".

In early 2002 a joint mission of the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, and the charity Save the Children UK reported that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by staff of aid groups and UN agencies, by peacekeepers and by community leaders, often in exchange for food and other aid. The UN's internal investigation office then examined 43 cases fully and found 10 of them proven, one involving a peacekeeper, who was sent home. It said it found no evidence of widespread abuse. Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think its report was wrong.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, and the main account of the exploitation of refugee children in Sierra Leone dates from 2002. How many children are abused there now is not known.

SLV.story:
During El Salvador's civil war, from 1980 to 1992, the armed forces took children from their families. Pro-Búsqueda, an organisation founded in 1994 to search for these children, has documented close to a thousand cases, most of them carried out by the armed forces. Many of the children were adopted abroad through flawed procedures, to the United States, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands.

In 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the court of the Organization of American States, ruled on the case of two sisters, the Serrano Cruz sisters, who disappeared in 1982 during a military operation known as the Guinda de Mayo. In 2010 El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children. The armed forces have still not opened their archives on the disappeared children, although families and campaigners have asked for this for years.

Children in El Salvador now face other risks. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says foreign tourists sexually exploit children there, and that the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks. It estimates that 140,000 to 200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent who is abroad or in detention.

Because the armed forces have kept their archives closed, many families of children taken during the war still do not know what happened to them.

SRB.story:
Serbia kept children and adults with mental disabilities in large state institutions. In 2007 Mental Disability Rights International, a US-based advocacy group, published the results of a four-year investigation covering more than 17,000 people in these institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, dirty conditions, contagious disease and no outside oversight, and it described the treatment as "tantamount to torture". It also warned of a risk of sexual exploitation. At the institution in Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards, and staff said they made no effort to find out whether sex was consensual. In 2006 the director of one institution had refused to let the investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave, and Serbian officials dismissed the findings as propaganda.

Serbia was also a transit route for trafficking. After NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in neighbouring Kosovo in 1999, women and girls were brought there for forced prostitution, mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia by way of Serbia. Amnesty International reported in 2004 that the international presence produced 80 percent of the traffickers' income at the time.

No official inquiry into these institutions is recorded, so it is not known whether conditions for the children in them changed after 2007.

TCD.story:
In October 2007 members of a French charity, Zoé's Ark, were detained in Abéché as they tried to fly 103 children to host families in France. The charity said the children were orphans from Darfur, a region of neighbouring Sudan, but the authorities found that most were from Chad and were not orphans. In December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years of forced labour. They were transferred to France, and in March 2008 Chad's president, Idriss Déby, pardoned them.

Chad's own army has also been named by the UN. In 2022 the UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province, near Lake Chad, where armed groups are active. It also attributed to the Chadian army four of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan. In the Lake Chad region, the UN verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and in Diffa.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, and no national inquiry is recorded, so the extent of abuse of children in Chad is not known.

TGO.story:
Among the Ewe people, who live in Togo and Ghana, some traditional shrines practise trokosi. A shrine takes a girl, usually a young virgin, to atone for a wrong that a relative is said to have committed. She serves the priest without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as part of her duty, which defenders of the practice deny. Ghana made ritual servitude of this kind a crime in 1998, but the practice continued there, and the records for this map include no law or prosecution in Togo.

In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research organisation that gathers data on the sexual exploitation of children, found no representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children in West and Central Africa.

How many girls are held in shrines in Togo, and how many children there are exploited online, is not known.

TUN.story:
No case, inquiry or flow of children involving Tunisia is recorded on this map. In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research organisation that gathers data on the sexual exploitation of children, found no representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children in the Middle East and North Africa, the region that includes Tunisia. A representative survey asks a sample of people chosen to reflect the whole population, so it can estimate how common something is.

Without such surveys, reports or inquiries, the extent of abuse and trafficking of children in Tunisia is not known.

N.n: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)
N.d: Federal Oral Tribunal No. 6 found in July 2012 that the junta ran a systematic plan to take children born to detained or disappeared mothers and give them to military families and regime allies; Videla received 50 years and Bignone 15. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken; 140 had been identified by July 2025.
N.cite: Tribunal Oral Federal No. 6, 5 July 2012; Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo
N.reach_note: Uruguay: Gelman case (IACHR 2011), in which the child of an Argentine detainee was taken in Montevideo under Operation Condor. reach_est lists Condor partner states. They are listed because Condor ran there, not because a child-appropriation finding there was opened in this research. Paraguay: a military doctor accused in the Silvia Quintela case fled there in 1986.

N.n: Franco regime child removals and Spain's 'stolen babies'
N.d: The Franco regime, Auxilio Social and the Women's Protection Board removed about 30,000 children of Republican prisoners and took babies of confined women into the early 1980s; later hospital 'stolen baby' cases reached the courts from 2011, with the first trial (Dr Eduardo Vela, 2018) ending in acquittal on limitation grounds.
N.cite: Wikipedia 'Lost children of Francoism'; RTÉ, 8 October 2018

N.n: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
N.d: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.
N.cite: Nuremberg Military Tribunal, US v. Greifelt et al. (RuSHA case)
N.reach_note: Norway: Lebensborn homes are documented in the Lebensborn article but adoption-of-kidnapped-children findings here cover Poland, Bohemia-Moravia, Slovenia, Yugoslavia, Belarus, USSR.

N.n: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
N.d: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).
N.cite: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Korea, 26 March 2025; AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024; The Guardian, 28 September 2023
N.reach_note: Receiving countries from the Korean Ministry of Health and Welfare table of adoptees by country 1953–2008; the TRC petitions came from 11 receiving countries.

N.d: Agency run by Scott and Karen Banks that arranged about 80 adoptions of Samoan children whose parents were told it was temporary schooling; the defendants pleaded guilty in January 2009 and were banned from adoption work.

Defunct Ohio agency that, per a 2020 federal indictment, procured more than 30 Ugandan children for US clients in 2013–2016 through bribery of Ugandan officials, and arranged a fraudulent Polish adoption. One employee pleaded guilty in 2019; others were charged in 2020.
N.cite: US DOJ, 17 August 2020; The Guardian, 18 August 2020

N.d: Baptist group whose ten members were arrested on 29 January 2010 taking 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic; leader Laura Silsby was convicted of arranging irregular travel.
French charity whose six members were convicted in Chad in December 2007 for trying to fly 103 children, falsely presented as Darfur orphans, to French host families.

N.n: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)
N.d: Facilities posing as maternity homes, clinics or orphanages where pregnant girls and women are held (some raped) and their babies sold, including for illegal adoption. Raids: Enugu 2008, Aba 2011 (32 girls), Ihiala 2011, Imo 2013, Lagos 2018 (162 children).
N.cite: Makinde et al., Trauma, Violence & Abuse (2015); BBC 26 April 2018; The Guardian 2 June 2011
N.reach_note: Makinde et al. list high incidence in Ondo, Ogun, Imo, Akwa Ibom, Abia and Anambra.

N.n: Pro Juventute 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse'
N.d: Programme of the Swiss foundation Pro Juventute, backed by federal authorities, that removed about 590 Yenish children from their families; recognised by the Swiss government as a crime against humanity in February 2025.

N.n: Kentler network (West German youth welfare and pedagogy)
N.d: A network of academics, youth welfare officials and educators around sexologist Helmut Kentler who supported, legitimised or tolerated paedophile positions. Berlin youth authorities placed children with paedophile foster fathers from the late 1960s into the 2000s.
N.cite: University of Hildesheim final report, February 2024
N.reach_note: University of Hildesheim research names Berlin, Göttingen, Hannover, Lüneburg, Tübingen and Heppenheim (Odenwaldschule) as central nodes.

N.d: Federally funded schools run by churches to assimilate First Nations, Métis and Inuit children; about 150,000 attended. Tens of thousands of claims of sexual and serious physical abuse were compensated under the 2007 settlement.
417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or territories, 1819–1969, documented by the Department of the Interior with at least 973 child deaths and physical, sexual and emotional abuse.
N.cite: DOI Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Vol. II, 2024

N.d: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.
National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.
N.reach_note: Only the US case is verified in this file so far. Scouting abuse findings in Canada, the UK, Ireland, Australia and other countries have not yet been checked; add them to reach when verified.

N.n: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
N.hq: No single headquarters — a pattern across private, donor-funded orphanages
N.d: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.
N.cite: US State Department TIP Report 2019; Lumos 2017; Australian Parliament 'Hidden in Plain Sight' 2017
N.reach_note: Documented here: Haiti (IBESR assessment, 3,019 potential victims; Lumos 2017), Cambodia (US TIP 2019: orphanages purchasing children), Nepal (NCRC/UNICEF: ~85% of children have a parent; agents paid commissions), Uganda (500+ unlicensed homes), Australia (2017 parliamentary recognition as modern slavery; source of volunteers and donors), USA (largest donor source to Haitian orphanages). reach_est: the US 2019 TIP report also names Nigeria and Sri Lanka; Kenya, Liberia and India have related cases in this and other files but no finding that names orphanage trafficking as such was opened.

N.n: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
N.d: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.
N.cite: Reports of the Secretary-General, Special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (A/59/782 to A/79/789)
N.reach_note: Reach = host countries of missions with documented child-victim SEA allegations or findings in the UN/OIOS documents cited (MONUC/MONUSCO, MINUSCA, MINUSTAH, UNMIL, UNAMSIL-era West Africa, UNMISS, MINUSMA, UNOCI, ONUMOZ, UNTAC-era Cambodia); Sudan (UNAMID) and Lebanon (UNIFIL) appear in UN allegation tables but child victims not confirmed there.

N.d: French military operation in the Central African Republic, December 2013 – October 2016. Allegations of child sexual abuse by its soldiers in Bangui (2013–2014) ended in a judicial dismissal (non-lieu) in January 2018.
AU peace operation in Somalia. HRW in 2014 documented rape and sexual exploitation of women and girls as young as 12 on Mogadishu bases by Ugandan and Burundian soldiers.

N.status: dismantled as territorial state; active as insurgency
N.d: ISIS abducted thousands of Yazidi women and children from Sinjar in August 2014 and ran markets for their sale; the UN COI found genocide. Affiliates in West Africa, the Sahel and Mozambique are verified by the UN as abducting children.
N.reach_note: Iraq/Syria: Yazidi enslavement (UN COI). West Africa (ISWAP), Sahel (ISGS) and Mozambique affiliates: child abduction verified by the UN; affiliates counted as documented reach.

N.d: Abducted 276 schoolgirls at Chibok (2014) and 110 at Dapchi (2018); UN verified 991 child abductions and 419 cases of sexual violence through forced marriage in Nigeria in 2024. Active across the Lake Chad basin.

N.hq: Northern Uganda (originally); later DRC/CAR border areas
N.status: largely defeated; leader Kony at large
N.d: Abducted tens of thousands of children for use as fighters and 'wives'. ICC convicted commander Dominic Ongwen in 2021 of 61 crimes including forced marriage and sexual slavery; ICC warrant for Joseph Kony outstanding.

Paramilitary force at war with the Sudanese army since April 2023. The UN fact-finding mission found large-scale rape and sexual slavery, including girls as young as 8; the UN verified RSF responsibility for most sexual violence against children in Sudan in 2023–2024 and two cases in CAR in 2024.

N.n: Russian state system for transfer, adoption and 're-education' of Ukrainian children
N.hq: Moscow (Office of the Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights)
N.d: ICC arrest warrants (17 March 2023) for Vladimir Putin and Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL identified at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea where at least 6,000 Ukrainian children were held in 2022. Ukraine counts 20,651 deported and/or forcibly displaced children and 2,752 returned (Oct 2026).
N.cite: ICC press release 17 March 2023; COI Ukraine A/78/540; childrenofwar.gov.ua
N.reach_note: Belarus: Belarusian opposition group reported at least 2,100 Ukrainian children taken to Belarus (Aug 2023); Belarus Red Cross head said transfers for 'health improvement' would continue.

N.status: leader convicted; settlement continues as Villa Baviera
N.d: German sect enclave in Chile led by Paul Schäfer, convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors. Used by Pinochet's secret police DINA as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991). Germany's president acknowledged diplomatic failures in 2016.

Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.
N.cite: Court records via AP/PBS; DOJ OIG 2023; Wikipedia 'Jeffrey Epstein'
N.reach_note: Documented by courts: New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, London (Maxwell trial), US Virgin Islands (USVI suits), Paris (French criminal probe). Turkey and Czech Republic appear only in a 2009 civil complaint stated 'upon information and belief'. Norway and Israel are listed for documented political/financial ties (Jagland charge; Barak business ties), not abuse findings.

N.n: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
N.d: Savile used his BBC celebrity and NHS fundraising roles to gain access to children and patients for decades. Inquiries found 72 victims linked to the BBC (Smith, 2016) and victims aged 5–75 across NHS sites (Lampard, 2015); the Met recorded 214 crimes (2013).
N.cite: Smith Review 2016; Lampard 2015; Giving Victims a Voice 2013

N.d: Metropolitan Police investigation opened 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations; 19 arrests and 7 convictions of entertainment figures.

Japan's dominant boy-band talent agency. Its founder Johnny Kitagawa abused boys and young men from the early 1970s to the mid-2010s (independent investigation, 2023); the company admitted it and by Aug 2026 had decided to compensate 585 people.
National governing body of US gymnastics whose team doctor Larry Nassar abused at least 265 girls and young women; USAG filed for bankruptcy in 2018 and paid $380m with the USOPC (2021).
Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.
N.reach_note: US officials: arrests in 38 countries; only those listed are named in the source (Hungary via the case of its ambassador to Peru).

N.d: Tor forum with over 215,000 users; FBI ran it 19 Feb–4 Mar 2015 (Operation Pacifier) and unmasked users with malware; 956 arrests.
N.reach_note: Europol: 368 suspects arrested or convicted in Europe by May 2017 (countries not listed).

N.d: Largest Tor web host in 2013, hosting Lolita City and other abuse sites; operator sentenced in the US to 27 years (2021).
Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).
'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).
N.reach_note: Europol sent intelligence to 25 EU states and 8 others; France and Spain from Operation Atlantic follow-up.

N.d: Tor forum; operated by Queensland Police Task Force Argos for about 11 months after the owner's arrest.
Darknet forum with over 87,000 members used to share material and arrange abuse; four operators convicted 2019.
N.reach_note: Chat groups in German, French, Spanish and Italian; Europol partners included New Zealand, Italy and Australia.

N.d: Tor platform with 400,000 registered users; four German administrators sentenced 7–12 years (2022).
N.reach_note: Taskforce members: Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada, US; server registered in Moldova (Wikipedia).

N.hq: Germany (server seized by German and Dutch authorities)
N.d: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.
N.reach_note: The 38 countries whose authorities took part in Operation Stream.

N.d: Telegram blackmail rings selling coerced sexual material of women and girls; leaders sentenced to 42 and 34 years.
Messaging platform; founder charged in France in August 2024 incl. complicity in distribution of CSAM; joined IWF in December 2024. Legal domicile Tortola (BVI), operational centre Dubai (Wikipedia).
N.reach_note: Cases documented here: Nth Room and 2024 school deepfakes (South Korea), French charges against its founder. IWF says it confirmed thousands of abuse-imagery reports on Telegram since 2022.

N.d: Online network extorting minors into producing abuse material and self-harm; fragmented into subgroups (CVLT, 676, etc.) within 'The Com'.
N.reach_note: Der Spiegel: 764-related arrests in at least eight countries. Listed as terrorist entity by Canada and New Zealand.

N.d: Transnational network of online groups (incl. 764, CVLT) involved in sextortion, child sexual exploitation, swatting and other crimes; FBI public warning 23 July 2025; Europol Project COMPASS since 2025. Start year approximate.
N.reach_note: Project COMPASS covers 28 countries.

N.n: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
N.d: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.
N.reach_note: Buyers documented from Australia, UK, US and (Sweetie sting) 13 countries; Europol 2024 sprint: buyers in 24 countries.

N.d: Offenders posing as young women on social media extort teenage boys for money; NCMEC counts at least three dozen US teenage boys who died by suicide after financial sextortion since 2021 (all offender nationalities).
Placeholder grouping for individual sextortion prosecutions; IWF: 92% of sextortion reports it assessed 2023–2025 involved boys.

N.n: North Rhine-Westphalia abuse complexes (Lügde, Bergisch Gladbach)
N.d: Linked series of investigations into men abusing children and sharing recordings in chat groups; Bergisch Gladbach alone produced 439 suspects. Münster complex (2020) not documented here — page not retrieved.
Online classified site whose 'adult' and 'escort' ads were used by traffickers to sell children and adults. Seized April 2018; CEO pleaded guilty; owners convicted 2023 and sentenced 2024.
N.reach_note: Backpage ran city sites in many countries, but only US prosecutions were verified here.

N.d: Owner of Pornhub. Lost card payments in December 2020 after reports of child abuse material; entered a 2023 US deferred prosecution agreement over sex-trafficking proceeds (GirlsDoPorn) and a 2025 FTC/Utah settlement over child abuse material.

Family-based pimping networks from Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, that recruited Mexican and Central American women and girls by deception and forced them into prostitution in New York and other US cities. Several were prosecuted in Brooklyn (Carreto family, 2005–2008; Rendon-Reyes organization, 2019).
N.reach_note: Rendon-Reyes case documents Central American victims smuggled via Mexico; Central American recruitment sites not separately documented here.

N.n: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)
N.d: Nigerian confraternity whose members in Italy were arrested in 2016 for 'mafia conspiracy, drug trafficking, exploitation of prostitution and violent crimes'. A Palermo court convicted 14 in 2018; in 2019 another Palermo court rejected the mafia-association charge for five others.
N.cite: Wikipedia 'Black Axe (confraternity)'; BlogSicilia 2018; Il Fatto Quotidiano 2019
N.reach_note: US TIP 2025 says cult-linked Nigerian groups traffic women and girls in Italy, Spain, the UK and Germany but does not name Black Axe; only Italian prosecutions were verified here.

N.d: Transnational criminal organization originating in Venezuela. US TIP 2025 says it operates sex-trafficking networks in Colombia, using daily-debt lodging (pagadiarios) to control victims, and has affiliated groups in Peru.
N.cite: US TIP Report 2025 — Colombia, Peru, Bolivia
N.reach_note: US TIP 2025 reports Tren de Aragua trafficking in Colombia, Peru and Bolivia, and transfers from Cúcuta to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru; operations in Ecuador/Argentina are stated only as destinations.

N.n: Amish and Old Order Anabaptist church districts
N.hq: Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (largest settlement; no central HQ)
N.d: Amish communities are organised in autonomous church districts under bishops. Pennsylvania prosecutions in 2017 and 2020 charged bishops for handling abuse confessions internally through excommunication and confession rather than reporting them, as state law requires of clergy.
N.reach_note: Decentralised church districts led by bishops; cases here involve bishops failing to report abuse confessions. Old Colony Mennonites in Bolivia are a separate net ('old-colony-mennonites').

N.d: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.
N.cite: UN CRC Concluding observations on the Holy See, 2014; national inquiry reports listed in cases
N.reach_note: reach = countries with a case record in this dataset. Abuse findings exist far beyond these; many countries with large Catholic populations have had no national inquiry (see notes).

N.d: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.
N.cite: Legion of Christ report, 21 December 2019; Holy See communiqué 1 May 2010
N.reach_note: Documented: Maciel abused seminarians in Spain and Rome; Legion confirmed abuse by Fr William Izquierdo in Ireland and the US; Cancún school case in Mexico. Estimated: countries where the Legion runs institutions; the 2019 report's 175 cases were not broken down by country in sources opened.

N.n: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana)
N.d: Lay society founded in Lima in 1971 by Luis Fernando Figari. Exposed by journalists in 2015; investigators found sexual abuse of minors and adults by Figari and others. Figari and over a dozen members were expelled in 2024 and Pope Francis signed its suppression on 14 January 2025.
N.cite: Holy See decrees 2024–25; Salinas & Ugaz, Mitad monjes, mitad soldados (2015)
N.reach_note: Abuse findings documented in Peru; the group operated in the other listed countries.

N.d: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.
N.cite: Ryan Report 2009; Royal Commission (Australia) 2017; Wikipedia, Congregation of Christian Brothers
N.reach_note: Documented findings or convictions in Ireland (Ryan, 2024 scoping), Canada (Mount Cashel), Australia (Royal Commission, WA orphanages), UK (St Ninian's Scotland; Northern Ireland convictions), US (2011 bankruptcy and settlement). India: allegations only. Malta: child migrants were sent to Christian Brothers' WA institutions (per inquiries; not detailed in sources opened).

N.d: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.
N.reach_note: Peru: Chilean Brother Abel Pérez was transferred there after confessing. Fiji: compensation disparities with NZ reported, not detailed.

N.d: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.
N.cite: Wikipedia, Abuse by members of Roman Catholic orders; Salesians of Don Bosco
N.reach_note: Samoa: a priest convicted in Melbourne was allegedly moved there to avoid police. Timor-Leste: Bishop Belo is a Salesian.

N.d: The 2010 Canisius-Kolleg disclosures in Berlin started Germany's abuse reckoning. In 2023 El País published the diary of Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas recording abuse of more than 80 minors in Bolivia, with superiors aware from 1978.
N.cite: El País, 30 April 2023; Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Germany
N.reach_note: Germany: Canisius-Kolleg 2010; Bolivia: Pedrajas and cover-up by provincial superiors; Spain: Pedrajas was Spanish, and a German Jesuit offended in Spanish and Chilean Jesuit schools; US: cases in several schools (not detailed here).

N.n: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
N.d: Australia's Royal Commission found 40.4% of St John of God Brothers were accused, the highest of any order. In New Zealand, 21 of 37 Brothers in Christchurch faced allegations over Marylands School and the Hebron Trust.
N.cite: Royal Commission (Australia) data 2017; NZ Royal Commission 2023
N.reach_note: Sri Lanka: Bernard McGrath returned from there before arrest; no finding there.

N.d: IICSA counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and found a culture of deference and secrecy. The Peter Ball case and the Makin Review of John Smyth showed senior clergy withholding evidence; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
N.cite: IICSA Anglican Church report, 6 October 2020; Makin Review, 7 November 2024
N.reach_note: Smyth's abuse in Zimbabwe and South Africa was by a Church of England-linked evangelical, not through CofE structures; recorded under Anglican Communion.

N.d: National Anglican churches with documented findings: Australia (1,082 complainants 1980–2015), Canada (residential schools; Nakayama), New Zealand (Dilworth School), and southern Africa (Smyth).
N.cite: Royal Commission (Australia) 2017; TRC Canada; Dilworth inquiry 2023; Makin Review 2024

N.d: Largest US Protestant denomination. Journalists found about 380 accused leaders and over 700 victims in 20 years (2019); the Guidepost report (2022) found the Executive Committee stonewalled survivors and kept a private list of 703 accused ministers.

N.hq: No central body (Hammond, Indiana was a major centre)
N.d: Network of independent churches and colleges. A 2018 Star-Telegram investigation found 412 abuse allegations in 187 IFB churches and institutions.

N.n: Hillsong Church / Australian Christian Churches (Assemblies of God)
N.d: Founded 1983 by Brian and Bobbie Houston. The Royal Commission found Brian Houston did not report his father Frank Houston's abuse of a boy to police in 1999; Brian Houston was acquitted of concealment in 2023.
N.reach_note: Hillsong has churches in about 27–30 countries, but abuse findings concern Frank Houston in Australia and New Zealand.

N.d: Formed 1977; about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse reported to the Royal Commission in 2017. Knox Grammar School case.
Ran children's homes in Australia that sheltered about 30,000 children from the 1940s to 1980s; Royal Commission case studies 5, 10, 33 and 49.
N.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse
N.reach_note: Only Australian findings were verified in this pass.

N.n: Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD) and Diakonie
N.d: Federation of 20 regional Protestant churches. The 2024 ForuM study found 2,225 victims and 1,259 accused in files since 1946, with an estimate of up to 9,355 minors.

N.n: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
N.d: The 'two-witness rule' and internal judicial committees kept abuse reports inside congregations. Australia's Royal Commission found 1,006 alleged perpetrators since 1950, none reported to police. Findings and judgments followed in the UK, US, Netherlands and New Zealand.
N.cite: Royal Commission Case Study 29 report, November 2016
N.reach_note: Norway removed state registration in December 2022 over shunning of children and others (not sexual abuse); in Japan a 2023 survey of 255 former members and children reported widespread whipping of children; Ireland: two elders were removed in 2016 after reporting a child molester to police against branch advice.

N.n: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
N.d: Runs an abuse help line (since 1995) staffed by social workers that routes legally risky calls to church lawyers; an AP investigation in 2022 found it helped keep abuse secret in the Bisbee, Arizona case. The church disputes this.
N.reach_note: Individual cases outside the US (e.g. an Australian leader jailed in 2017) were not verified in this pass.

N.n: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
N.hq: Colorado City, Arizona / Hildale, Utah (Short Creek)
N.d: Polygamous sect led by Warren Jeffs (convicted 2011 of sexually assaulting girls aged 12 and 15). Girls were moved from Bountiful, British Columbia, to the US for 'marriages'. In 2015 the US Department of Labor fined members $1.96 million over child labour in the 2012 pecan harvest.
N.cite: AP 2011; BC Supreme Court 2017, 2019; US DOL 2015
N.reach_note: The FLDS page says members live in the western US, Mexico and Canada; no Mexican case verified.

N.d: The principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) has been documented as discouraging reports of abuse in Melbourne, Brooklyn and Israel. Cases include Malka Leifer (Australia/Israel) and Nechemya Weberman (Brooklyn).
N.cite: Royal Commission final report 2017, rec. 16.30; Wikipedia 'Mesirah'
N.reach_note: Times of Israel and Channel 4 reported a UK Haredi leader used mesirah to shield suspects; not verified further.

N.n: Yeshivah Centre Melbourne and Yeshiva Centre Bondi (Chabad)
N.d: Chabad institutions examined in Royal Commission Case Study 22 (2015–2016) over responses to abuse by staff and volunteers.

Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.
N.cite: Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor' (citing BBC, Reuters, court records)
N.reach_note: Also detained in Iraq (2021) and passed through Turkey and Romania; deported from Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2022 over child abuse concerns; 17 minors rescued in Yarumal, Colombia, November 2025.

N.d: Founded by David Berg. A UK High Court judge found in 1995 that the group, including top leaders, had sexually abused minors in the past, and ordered it to denounce Berg's writings.
N.reach_note: Police investigated the group in these countries in the 1990s, without convictions; colonies in an estimated 70 countries by the mid-1970s.

N.d: Communal Christian group that canes children. German authorities removed 40 children in 2013 (upheld by the ECHR in 2018); New York found child labour violations at a Twelve Tribes farm in 2018.
N.cite: ECHR, Wetjen v. Germany, 2018; Times Union, 4 June 2018
N.reach_note: Australia: police searched a NSW farm in 2020, no charges announced; France listed the group in a 1995 parliamentary report on cults.

N.d: Self-help group run by Keith Raniere, convicted in 2019 of racketeering and sex trafficking; the racketeering acts included sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old.
N.reach_note: Victims included people from Mexico; not verified as a separate finding here.

N.d: Leader convicted in 2009 on 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; 175 years.
Church whose leader Naasón Joaquín García pleaded guilty in 2022 to sexually abusing children in California.
N.reach_note: Present in about 58 countries; findings only in the US (and a time-barred 1997 complaint in Mexico).

N.d: Church of Apollo Quiboloy, indicted in the US in 2021 for sex trafficking including of minors, and charged in the Philippines in 2024. FBI raided its offices in California, Texas and Hawaii in January 2020.

N.n: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB)
N.d: Company linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement that ran children's homes; 2024 police raids rescued 402 children and led to 415 arrests.

Network of ashrams and gurukuls; founder Asaram convicted in 2018 of raping a 16-year-old and in 2023 in a Surat sisters' case. Two boys died at the Motera gurukul in 2008; an inquiry blamed ashram negligence.
Acknowledged abuse in its boarding schools in the 1970s–80s; $15 million settlement in 2008.
Evangelical mission to indigenous peoples. Abuse documented at its Fanda school in Senegal (GRACE 2010) and by a missionary convicted for abusing Katukina girls in Brazil (2014).
N.reach_note: Fields examined by the 2023 IHART historical abuse review; findings per country not verified.

N.d: Closed Christian community; founder convicted 1995 of sexual abuse of young members; multiple later convictions and Employment Court rulings on child labour and servitude.
Charismatic communal church; its redress scheme identified 539 alleged perpetrators and paid £7.7 million.
N.cite: Jesus Fellowship Redress Scheme Final Report, 2024

N.hq: No central body (Manitoba Colony, Santa Cruz)
N.d: Closed German-speaking farming colonies. Bolivia had about 150,000 Mennonites by 2023 (estimate). The Manitoba Colony mass-rape case led to convictions in 2011.
N.reach_note: Colonies migrated Canada→Mexico (about 6,000, 1922–25), Canada→Paraguay (about 1,800, 1927), Mexico→Belize (about 1,700 after 1958), Paraguay→Bolivia (1954–57), Mexico/Belize→Bolivia (from 1967), Canada→Bolivia (1968). No abuse finding outside Bolivia verified here.
