F.size_note: Romania HCCH annual return for 2002 (458 intercountry adoptions in total)
F.d: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Italy in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.
F.cite: Romania, Annual adoption statistics for States of origin, 2002, submitted to HCCH

F.size_note: Romania HCCH annual return for 2002 (458 intercountry adoptions in total)
F.d: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Spain in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.
F.cite: Romania, Annual adoption statistics for States of origin, 2002, submitted to HCCH

F.size_note: Romania HCCH annual return for 2002 (458 intercountry adoptions in total)
F.d: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Israel in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.
F.cite: Romania, Annual adoption statistics for States of origin, 2002, submitted to HCCH

F.size_note: about 160,000 children sent abroad 1992–2024, more than half to the US (New Yorker); US visas FY1994–2014 recorded separately
F.d: China sent about 160,000 children abroad for adoption from 1992 until it ended the programme on 5 September 2024; others went to Spain, Canada, the UK, the Netherlands, France and Australia.

F.size_note: adoptions arranged by facilitator Lauryn Galindo
F.d: About 800 Cambodian children adopted to US families through Lauryn Galindo, convicted on visa-fraud and money-laundering charges in 2004.

F.size_note: adoptions by Focus on Children
F.d: Samoan children adopted to the US by Focus on Children; parents were told it was temporary schooling.

F.size_note: Utah investigators believed more than 40 pregnant women were brought through Utah
F.d: Pregnant Marshallese women brought to Arizona, Utah and Arkansas by Paul Petersen so their babies could be adopted.

F.size_note: more than 30 children
F.d: Ugandan children adopted by US families through European Adoption Consultants via bribery (indictment, 2020).

F.size_note: at least 25 babies sold, mostly to Singapore
F.d: Babies from West Java sold to buyers in Singapore via Pontianak with forged documents.

F.size_note: attempted; stopped at Abéché airport
F.d: Zoé's Ark attempted to fly 103 children to French host families; six members convicted in Chad.

F.size_note: attempted; stopped at the border
F.d: New Life Children's Refuge members tried to take 33 children across the border after the 2010 earthquake.
F.cite: Wikipedia, New Life Children's Refuge case

F.size_note: 20,000 Polish children identified as passing Germanization criteria (Heinemann); Polish official estimate of all abducted about 200,000
F.d: Polish children kidnapped for Germanization and placed with German families via Lebensborn/RuSHA.
F.cite: Wikipedia, Kidnapping of children by Nazi Germany

F.size_note: more than 15,000 since 1999 (BBC, 2018)
F.d: Ethiopian children adopted in the US before Ethiopia banned foreign adoption in 2018; many also went to Spain, France and Italy.

F.size_note: about 29 children
F.d: Children from the HANCI centre in Makeni adopted by Americans without genuine parental consent (presidential commission, 2012).

F.n: Berlin → paedophile foster homes in West Germany (Kentler placements)
F.to: Foster homes incl. in Lower Saxony
F.d: Berlin youth authorities placed children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, including outside Berlin; the Hildesheim report names Hannover and other Lower Saxony locations as network nodes.

F.to: Australia (Fairbridge farm schools, Barnardo's Picton, Catholic institutions)
F.size_note: About 4,000 children migrated after WWII, mostly to Australia (IICSA).
F.d: Children in British care were sent to institutions in Australia where IICSA found a catalogue of evidence of ill-treatment and sexual abuse; the last child was migrated in 1970.
F.cite: IICSA Child Migration Programmes report, 1 March 2018

F.to: Canada (incl. Fairbridge farm school, British Columbia)
F.d: British child migration to Canada began in the 19th century; IICSA found the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its schools in Canada.
F.cite: IICSA Child Migration Programmes report, 1 March 2018

F.n: Moldova → Russia, Turkey, Israel, UAE (trafficking of women and children, incl. institution leavers)
F.to: Russia, Turkey, Israel, United Arab Emirates
F.d: The US State Department (March 2007) reported women and children trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East including Turkey, Israel and the UAE; UNICEF found children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.
F.cite: US State Department Human Rights Report 2006 and UNICEF 2005–2006, compiled by ACCORD query a-5839

F.from: Orphanages and institutions across Ukraine (e.g. Vinnytsia oblast)
F.to: Vocational schools and sex trafficking, domestic and abroad (destinations not specified)
F.size_note: IOM: more than 120,000 Ukrainians trafficked since 1991 (all ages and routes; not only orphanage leavers). The source names no specific foreign destination, so the line ends at Kyiv.
F.d: An IOM staff member told Disability Rights International that orphanages are a direct feeder to domestic and international human trafficking, and La Strada said recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme'.

F.n: Rural Nepal (Karnali) → Kathmandu child care homes
F.from: Karnali Province and other rural districts (e.g. Humla, Bajura, Rukum)
F.to: Child care homes in the Kathmandu Valley
F.d: Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and deliver children to Kathmandu institutions, which pay commissions; NGOs documented a forged parental death certificate used to admit a child. UNICEF estimates about 85% of children in Nepal's registered homes have a living parent or guardian.
F.cite: The Annapurna Express, citing NCRC 2021/22 and UNICEF

F.size_note: 549 British child migrants arrived 1948–1954 (NZ Ministry of Social Development, 2009).
F.d: New Zealand's Social Development Minister said in November 2009 that 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954 and that most were placed in foster care rather than institutions; IICSA lists New Zealand among the destinations of British child migration.
F.cite: New Zealand Herald, 16 November 2009; IICSA Child Migration Programmes report, 2018

F.n: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
F.to: Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College, Bulawayo, Southern Rhodesia
F.size_note: 276 children sent 1946–1956 by the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial Association (IICSA).
F.d: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.
F.cite: IICSA Child Migration Programmes report, 2018, section 22 (Fairbridge Society)

F.n: US and Canadian faith-based donors → Haitian orphanages
F.from: United States and Canada (churches, faith-based NGOs)
F.size_note: At least US$70 million a year traced to about one-third of orphanages; total estimated above US$100 million a year (Lumos 2017).
F.d: Lumos found 92% of orphanage funders were from the US and 90% faith-based, and that the flow of donations drives the establishment of orphanages, some purely for profit, which recruit children from families.
F.cite: Lumos, 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights', 2017

F.n: Sinjar → Tal Afar/Mosul → Raqqa: ISIS trafficking of Yazidi women and girls
F.size_note: over 3,200 Yazidi women and children still held in June 2016, mostly in Syria (COI)
F.d: Captives were moved in buses and trucks to holding sites in Tal Afar and Mosul, then women and girls were transferred to Raqqa and sold.

F.size_note: 276 abducted minus 57 who escaped immediately
F.d: Girls were driven or marched away, possibly to the Konduga area of the Sambisa Forest where Boko Haram had fortified camps; military sources believed they were split among camps around Lake Chad, the Gorsi mountains and Sambisa.

F.n: Northern Uganda → South Sudan: LRA abducted children
F.to: LRA bases, southern Sudan (now South Sudan)
F.size_note: UNICEF (2006): at least 25,000 children abducted overall
F.d: LRA bases in southern Sudan held abducted Ugandan children.

F.n: LRA move to DR Congo and CAR (2008–2011)
F.size_note: more than 3,000 abducted Sept 2008–July 2011 across DRC, South Sudan and CAR
F.d: The LRA shifted operations to DRC, South Sudan and CAR and abducted thousands.

F.size_note: 114 accused; 108 repatriated
F.d: Contingent members implicated in exploitation of children were sent home; none jailed.

F.size_note: 16 soldiers named in UN-commissioned report; case dismissed 2018
F.d: Allegations of child sexual abuse; French judges dismissed the case for insufficient charges.

F.size_note: 2016 UN tables: 4 allegations, 46 child victims (Burundi military personnel)
F.d: UN data list allegations against Burundian contingent personnel involving 46 children.

F.size_note: 2016 UN tables: 4 allegations, 43 child victims; all ~450 Gabonese troops withdrawn Sept 2021
F.d: Gabonese contingent faced repeated SEA allegations; UN repatriated all units in 2021.

F.n: DR Congo → CAR: MINUSCA FARDC contingent allegations (offenders)
F.size_note: 2016 UN tables: 17 allegations, 15 child victims; 2015: 7 military allegations (all missions)
F.d: DRC battalion repatriated in January 2016.

F.n: Republic of Congo → CAR: MINUSCA contingent allegations (offenders)
F.size_note: 2016 UN tables: 9 allegations, 7 child victims
F.d: HRW linked Bambari airport cases to the Republic of Congo contingent.

F.n: Morocco → CAR/DRC: MINUSCA and MONUSCO contingent allegations (offenders)
F.size_note: 2016 UN tables: 7 allegations, 6 child victims; 2015: 4 allegations
F.d: Moroccan military personnel named in UN SEA data tables.

F.n: Moldova/Romania/Ukraine → Bosnia: trafficking of women and girls
F.size_note: 601 women and girls assisted in an IOM-type return programme, 498 repatriated (HRW)
F.d: Women and girls mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine sold to Bosnian bar owners; local police, IPTF monitors and US contractors implicated.
Amnesty (2004): international presence generated 80% of income for traffickers.

F.n: Germany → Chile: children taken to Colonia Dignidad
F.size_note: Schäfer arrived with about 70 followers and a number of children taken from their families; the colony continued to bring children from Germany
F.d: Schäfer fled abuse accusations in Germany in 1961 and the colony kept 'importing' children.

F.n: Girls taken between Epstein homes: New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico
F.d: Maxwell's trial covered abuse of teenage girls at Epstein's homes in New York, Palm Beach and New Mexico; she was convicted of sex trafficking a minor. The SDNY 2019 indictment charged trafficking of minors 2002–2005 in New York and Florida.
F.cite: AP via PBS, 6 Oct 2025; Wikipedia 'Ghislaine Maxwell'

F.n: New York → Zorro Ranch, New Mexico
F.d: New Mexico's legislative truth commission (Aug 2026 interim report) estimated at least 30 people were abused by Epstein or associates in New Mexico. Ages are not stated in the report coverage.

F.n: US mainland → Little St. James, USVI
F.d: The USVI government and victims sued the Epstein estate and JPMorgan over a sex-trafficking operation run partly from the island; the estate paid $105m and JPMorgan $75m to USVI and $290m to victims. These are civil settlements, not criminal findings.

French prosecutors investigated rape of minors and trafficking linked to Epstein and model agent Jean-Luc Brunel, whose MC2 agency in New York and Miami was reportedly funded by Epstein. Brunel was charged but died before trial, so no court finding exists.
After his 1999 UK conviction, Paul Gadd moved to Cambodia (expelled 2002–03) and then Vietnam, where he was convicted in 2006 of obscene acts with girls aged 10 and 11.
Matzneff made several trips to the Philippines in the 1980s and described sex tourism with underage boys in his published diaries; there was no prosecution.

Fettes College dismissed teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial; he went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children. South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025.

F.n: Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's
F.d: After complaints were quietly investigated at Brisbane Grammar in the early 1980s, counsellor Kevin Lynch later worked at St Paul's School, where he also abused students; he was charged in 1997.

F.n: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse
F.d: AUSTRAC alleged Westpac failed to vet transactions that could be linked to child exploitation and live child sex shows in the Philippines (A$1.3bn penalty, 2020); an Australian man paid a Filipino mother while directing abuse over Skype for nearly five years. IJM's 2020 study ranked Australians third among purchasers.

F.n: United Kingdom → Philippines demand for livestreamed abuse
F.d: IJM UK states the UK is among the top three global consumers of livestreamed abuse of Filipino children.

F.size_note: about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts over 12 years; 197 buyers identified
F.d: Europol's 2024 sprint on US HSI data: chats between about 12,000 criminal customer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines; packages may lead 24 countries to 197 buyers. Origin point is The Hague (sprint host), not a buyer country.
Credit card payments for access to about 50 abuse websites run from Minsk were routed through Latvian banks; Florida firm Connections laundered money.

F.n: Bitcoin payments → Welcome to Video, South Korea
F.size_note: 4,000 paying members; about ₩400 million (~US$360,000) received
F.d: Paying members in 38 countries bought points in Bitcoin; tracing these payments located the server and users.

F.n: Sextortion: Nigeria-based offenders ← US teenage victims
F.d: Lagos-based offenders demanded money from US teenagers after obtaining images; the Ogoshi brothers targeted hundreds of US teenagers and adults (DOJ).

F.size_note: URLs actioned, 28% of world total
F.d: Bulgaria hosted 87,959 URLs actioned by IWF in 2025, up from 9% share in 2024, driven by 'just a few particular sites'.

F.n: Abuse material hosted in the United States (IWF 2025)
F.size_note: 16% of URLs
F.d: US hosting services held 49,021 URLs actioned by IWF in 2025.

F.n: Abuse material hosted in the Netherlands (IWF 2025)
F.d: The Netherlands was the largest host of IWF-actioned material for years (47% in 2018); its share fell to 11% in 2025. INHOPE 2025 still ranks it first for confirmed CSAM (36%).

F.size_note: IWF URLs; INHOPE: 14% of confirmed CSAM
F.d: Romania hosted 21,188 IWF-actioned URLs (7%) in 2025 and 14% of INHOPE-confirmed CSAM.
France's share rose from 1% (2024) to 7% in 2025.
6% of IWF-actioned URLs in 2025.
5% of IWF-actioned URLs in both 2024 and 2025.

F.n: Abuse material hosted in Hong Kong (IWF 2023–2024)
F.d: Hong Kong was the third/fourth largest host in 2023–2024 before falling sharply in 2025.

F.n: Welcome to Video: operator in South Korea → arrests in 38 countries
F.to: Arrest countries incl. US, UK, Germany
F.d: 337 users arrested in 38 countries (223 Koreans).

F.n: Kidflix: platform seized in Germany → suspects in 38 countries
F.size_note: suspects identified; 79 arrested
F.d: Operation Stream intelligence went to 38 countries; Wikipedia reports 30 arrests in the UK from 60 identified.

F.size_note: names passed by FBI to UK police
F.d: FBI passed 7,272 UK names from the Landslide database, leading to 3,744 arrests and 1,451 convictions; some names were later found to be card-fraud victims.

F.n: Australian offender relocates to the Philippines
F.d: Peter Scully fled Melbourne for the Philippines in 2011 and ran a pay-per-view abuse site there; life sentence 2018.

F.n: US and Australian buyers commission abuse material in Tbilisi
F.d: American and Australian citizens were among 11 arrested for arranging production of sexual images of girls in Tbilisi.
One of Boystown's German administrators was living in Paraguay and arrested there in April 2021.

F.n: Czech-produced abuse images → buyers in the EU and Canada
F.d: A Czech photographer and Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to customers abroad.

F.n: Films made in Ukraine/Romania → distributed by Azov Films, Toronto
F.d: Primary producers were in Crimea (Ukraine), Romania and Germany; the Toronto firm sold to customers in over 50 countries. Start year approximate.
Women and girls recruited in Mexico by deception and smuggled to brothels in Queens and Brooklyn; proceeds sent back to Tlaxcala.

The Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US for forced prostitution. Origin shown at Honduras for display; the DOJ release says 'Central America' without naming countries.
Several Australian men have been convicted in Australia for abusing children in the Philippines, including a flight attendant who abused 26 girls from 2010 to 2017.

F.n: Australia → Southeast Asia registered offenders' travel
F.size_note: about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled overseas in 2016; reporting said about half went to Southeast Asia (destination point is a regional placeholder, not Thailand specifically)
F.d: Australia's Foreign Minister said about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, often to developing countries in Asia, with 40% not notifying police.

F.n: Edo State → Libya → Italy (sex trafficking of women and girls)
F.size_note: Nigerian female sea arrivals in Italy in 2016 (IOM data); at least four in five forced into prostitution
F.d: Women and girls, most from Edo State, are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound by debt and oaths. IOM recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims arriving by sea in 2014–2017.
F.cite: IOM via UN News, Jul 2017; Thomson Reuters Foundation, Sep 2018

F.n: Nigeria → gold-mining regions of Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire
F.d: Organized networks transport Nigerian women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire for sex trafficking; in Kédougou victims include girls as young as 12.

F.n: United States → Cambodia (travelling child sex offenders)
F.size_note: three men returned under Operation Twisted Traveler in Aug 2009; Boyajian made 35 trips to Asia in nine years
F.d: US men, several already convicted at home, travelled repeatedly to Cambodia to buy children; prosecuted in Los Angeles under the PROTECT Act.

F.n: Vietnam → Svay Pak, Cambodia (girls sold to brothels)
F.d: Most children in Svay Pak brothels were ethnic Vietnamese, many sold by destitute families; US TIP 2025 still reports ethnic Vietnamese women and girls exploited in Cambodian cities and tourist areas.

F.n: Karamoja, Uganda → Nairobi (girls for domestic servitude and sex)
F.d: Cross-border rings ferry women and underage girls from Karamoja to Nairobi for domestic servitude or sex trafficking.

F.n: Ethiopia → Saudi Arabia (children in forced begging rings)
F.d: Organized begging rings exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia.

F.n: Ethiopia → Djibouti (girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking)
F.d: Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in Djibouti and Sudan.
European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children; networks use European and Gambian travel agencies.

F.n: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)
F.d: The 2006 UNICEF–Government study found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of clients of exploited children on the coast; Kenyans were 38 per cent.
Foreign tourists, often from France, exploit Malagasy children.

F.n: Europe → Tangier, Morocco (tourist offenders in vacation rentals)
F.d: NGOs report tourists exploit children in Tangier in vacation rentals owned and managed by European nationals.

F.n: Dzaleka camp, Malawi → South Africa ('Southern Route')
F.d: The camp is a waypoint for criminal networks moving migrants south, some of whom end up in sex trafficking or forced labour, particularly in South Africa.

F.n: Nepal → India (girls and women to brothels)
F.size_note: lower bound of published annual estimates (5,000–10,000 per year); not an official count
F.d: Recruitment by false job, marriage and online romance offers across the open border to brothels in Kolkata, Mumbai and elsewhere.
F.cite: US TIP 2025 — Nepal; Wikipedia 'Human trafficking in Nepal'

F.d: Large numbers of Nepalese women and girls trafficked into Kamathipura in recent decades.
Bangladeshi women and girls exploited in sex trafficking in India; children estimated at 40% of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims abroad.

F.size_note: girls and women on FIA list, 2018–June 2019
F.d: Brokers sold poor Pakistani girls and women, many Christian, to Chinese men as brides.

F.n: Kachin State, Myanmar → Yunnan and beyond, China ('bride' trafficking)
F.size_note: cases reported by Myanmar government in 2017; HRW says real number likely much higher
F.d: Women and girls sold for $3,000–13,000 to Chinese families.
Hmong and other ethnic-minority women and girls lured or abducted to China for forced marriage.
Lao women and girls kidnapped or recruited via marriage brokers to China.
Extraterritorial child sexual exploitation is prevalent in the Riau Islands bordering Singapore.

F.n: Middle East → Puncak, West Java ('contract marriages')
F.d: Middle Eastern tourists pay for short 'contract marriages' with girls as young as nine.

F.n: Australia / UK / US / Japan / NZ → Philippines (foreign offenders)
F.d: Most foreign offenders in the Philippines are from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the UK and the US, many already convicted or charged at home.
Repeat offenders from Switzerland and the UK, previously convicted at home, abused boys in Pattaya and elsewhere; the Swiss bar also served European clients.

F.n: Burma / Cambodia / Laos → Thailand (children in sex trafficking)
F.d: Children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos increasingly sex-trafficked in brothels, massage parlours, bars and hotels; many Lao women and girls exploited in Thailand.
Displaced Venezuelan women and girls exploited in sex trafficking and webcam studios; Tren de Aragua moves victims through Cúcuta.

F.n: Venezuela → Trinidad and Tobago (women and girls)
F.d: Sex-trafficking victims are mainly women and girls from Venezuela, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Guyana; NGOs allege officials facilitate transport and entry.

F.n: Cúcuta → Ecuador, Peru, Argentina (Tren de Aragua transfers)
F.d: Tren de Aragua reportedly used Cúcuta's transport hub to move trafficking victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru.

F.size_note: US convictions linked to the Medellín offensive by May 2026
F.d: US men travelled repeatedly to Medellín (one 48 times in two years) to exploit girls; prosecuted in Miami.

F.n: Cartagena → Panama, Mexico, Miami, Bahamas ('La Madame' network)
F.d: Young women sent individually abroad, coached to avoid airport scrutiny.

F.n: United States → Puerto Plata / Sosúa (travelling offenders)
F.d: US men prosecuted under the PROTECT Act for abusing boys and girls on the north coast; joint HSI–Dominican operations in tourist towns.

F.n: Guatemala / Honduras → Mexico → United States (children in sex trafficking)
F.d: Guatemalan and Honduran adults and children exploited in sex trafficking in Mexico, the US, Belize and El Salvador.
Bolivian women and girls exploited in sex trafficking in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru.
Girls groomed as minors in Romania, then moved at 18 to the UK, Ireland and Germany for sexual exploitation.

F.n: Romania → Western Europe (sex trafficking of women and girls)
F.d: Most identified Romanian victims are women and girls exploited in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK.

F.n: Vietnam → United Kingdom (children for cannabis farms, nail bars)
F.size_note: Vietnamese children referred to the UK NRM in 2024
F.d: Vietnamese children and adults exploited in cannabis cultivation, nail salons and forced criminality; many children went missing from local-authority care.
F.cite: Home Office NRM 2024; US TIP 2025 — UK

F.n: Syria → Lebanon (refugee women and girls into sex trafficking)
F.size_note: freed from Chez Maurice/Silver-B, March 2016
F.d: Criminal groups recruit Syrian women and girls with false job offers and exploit them in Lebanese brothels; Syrian children held in bonded labour in the Beqaa.
Keith Morris was jailed for 18.5 years in the UK for 10 sexual offences against vulnerable children in Kenya, one of about eight UK prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.
Former teacher and scout leader abused boys in Thailand and streamed abuse to another European man.
A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

F.n: Tehuacán → Los Angeles → Mexico: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera
F.d: A Mexican priest was presented to the Los Angeles archdiocese by his bishop in January 1987; within a year 26 children were reported abused, and he fled back to Mexico before arrest on 19 felony counts.

F.n: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014)
F.d: Removed from ministry in Minnesota in 2005, he returned to India and continued as a priest; charged in 2006, he was arrested in Erode in 2012 and extradited back in 2014.
Indicted in Arizona in 2003, the Salvatorian priest went to Italy and evaded a confirmed extradition until his arrest in Rome in May 2019.
Rivoire left the Arctic for France in January 1993; Canadian warrants (1998, 2022) went unexecuted and France refused extradition. He died in France in 2024.

F.n: Scranton (USA) → Ciudad del Este (Paraguay): Fr Carlos Urrutigoity
F.d: After 2002 accusations in Scranton, the priest and his group moved to Ciudad del Este, where he became vicar general in 2014; he was moved to Mendoza, Argentina in 2015.

F.n: Costa Rica → Mexico: Fr Mauricio Víquez (flight, extradited 2021)
F.to: San Nicolás de los Garza, Nuevo León, Mexico
F.d: The priest fled in 2018 via Panama to Mexico, where he was caught and extradited in 2021; he was sentenced to 20 years in 2022.
F.cite: AP via Voz de América, 24 Aug 2022

F.n: Pennsylvania → El Progreso, Honduras: Fr Joseph Maurizio
F.d: A Pennsylvania priest abused minors on charity trips to a Honduran orphanage between 2004 and 2009, funded partly through illegal money transfers; convicted 2015.

F.n: Burkina Faso / Mali / Ghana → Kaduna: children held in purported Islamic school
F.d: Police said some of the 300+ captives freed in the 2019 Kaduna raid had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana.

F.n: Sisaket → United States: 'jet-set monk' Wirapol (fugitive, extradited 2017)
F.d: The former abbot fled to the U.S. after 2013 exposure and was extradited to Thailand in July 2017, then convicted of abducting and raping a girl.

About to be charged in 1995, the Oblate fled to Belgium; Oblate officials acknowledged knowing he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant until returned in 2011. In 2015 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik (1978–82).

F.n: Germany → South Africa: Fr Georg Kerkhoff (extradited back)
F.d: A German priest with abuse cases pending at home worked for years in South Africa, where he was tried for abusing boys at a 2008 camp, then extradited and jailed in Krefeld in 2015.

F.n: St Petersburg → Israel: Fr Gleb Grozovsky (extradited)
F.d: After a criminal case opened in November 2013 the priest fled to Israel, was detained and extradited to Russia, where he was jailed for 14 years in 2018.

Corradi, accused at the Provolo deaf school in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, worked at the order's school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and in 2019 sentenced to 42 years for abusing deaf children.
F.cite: Wikipedia, Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf; Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

F.n: Chile → Peru: Marist Brother Abel Pérez
F.d: After confessing to superiors in 2010 that he had abused minors, Brother Abel Pérez was transferred by the Marist Brothers to Peru.
F.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Chile; Marist Brothers

F.n: Germany → South America: Jesuit Fr Wolfgang S.
F.to: South America (he had also offended in Jesuit schools in Chile and Spain)
F.d: After he admitted abusing pupils at St. Blasien (1982–84) and Canisius-Kolleg, the Jesuits said his superiors helped him emigrate to South America, where he lived as of 2010. A separate summary says he had also offended in Jesuit schools in Chile and Spain; his exact destination country is not confirmed.
F.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Germany; Abuse by members of Roman Catholic orders

F.d: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Ratzinger accepted accused priest Peter Hullermann for therapy; he was then given parish work and abused again, and was convicted in 1986.
F.cite: Süddeutsche Zeitung 2010 via Wikipedia; Munich report 2022

F.d: Detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors, Frantar avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary, returning after an Interpol notice.
F.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

F.d: Spanish Jesuit Pedrajas settled in Bolivia after his first abuse in Lima in 1964, then abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools there; he confessed to a superior in 1978, who covered it up.
F.cite: El País, 30 April 2023, via Spanish Wikipedia

F.n: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth
F.to: Rhode Island, North Dakota and Boston, USA
F.d: The Norbertine order knew of Smyth's abuse and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including assignments in the US, sometimes without warning bishops; he abused at least 143 children.

After complaints in the 1980s Robinson was moved to another parish without police being told; he then fled to the US in 1985 and the archdiocese kept paying him for seven years. A BBC team found him in California in 2003; he was extradited and jailed for 21 years.
F.cite: IICSA, Archdiocese of Birmingham report, 20 June 2019

F.d: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore, later convicted (2018) of abusing three children and a student priest, to Toronto and to Fort Augustus.
F.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country (Scotland)

F.n: Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander
F.d: After a pupil's parents complained, the abbey school sent the monk back to Australia without telling police; he was arrested in Sydney in 2017 and pleaded guilty in 2021.

PAT.title: Moved instead of stopped
PAT.summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.
roles: Sent abusers away and received them
PAT.series_label: Documented moves on the map, by the decade they began

facts.t: Pennsylvania grand jury — six dioceses: A 23-member statewide grand jury report released by Attorney General Josh Shapiro on 14 August 2018 identified 301 'predator priests' and at least 1,000 child victims over about 70 years in six dioceses. The roughly 1,400-page report found bishops 'went to great lengths to keep it secret' and moved abusers. Most crimes were too old to prosecute.

Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.

John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review): A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

University of Zurich pilot study (Dommann and Meier), commissioned by Swiss Bishops' Conference, RKZ and KOVOS; report May/Sept 2023: 1,002 cases, 510 accused, 921 victims; superiors systematically transferred accused clerics, sometimes abroad, to avoid prosecution

PAT.uncertain: The moves drawn are only those a source documents; most church and school personnel files were never opened, and Poland's state commission reported in 2022 that files sent to the Vatican were out of its reach. A move is drawn from where the abuser was sent from to where they went; whether the receiving diocese or country was told is often not recorded.

PAT.implications:
Moving an abuser kept the matter inside the institution. No police report was made where the abuse had happened, and the people at the new posting were not told. The receiving places were often poorer or more remote than the sending ones, such as missions in Africa, the Pacific and Latin America and Indigenous communities in northern Canada, where a complaint against a foreign priest was less likely to reach a court.

The records show the same practice in Catholic dioceses and religious orders, in Anglican and evangelical circles, in an ultra-Orthodox Jewish school and in a Scottish private school, over several decades. It went on for as long as these institutions dealt with complaints themselves, and it came to light mainly when grand juries, royal commissions and courts obtained their files.

PAT.title: Years of waiting: protected by status
PAT.summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

facts.t: Jeffrey Epstein (United States): Maria Farmer reported to the FBI in 1996 with no known action; after the 2005 Palm Beach police probe, the 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement ended the federal case and he served 13 months in a county stockade on a state plea (2008). Federal sex-trafficking charges came only in July 2019 after the Miami Herald series (2018)

Jimmy Savile (United Kingdom): Two police investigations in his lifetime (earliest 1958) produced no charges; Surrey Police 2007-09 dropped; BBC Newsnight report shelved Dec 2011; press inquiries from 1973 never published

Cyril Smith MP (United Kingdom): A pupil told police in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; investigations in 1970, 1998, 1999 brought no charge; CPS said in 2012 he should have been charged over 40 years earlier

Colonia Dignidad (Paul Schäfer) (Chile): Escapees' allegations in the 1960s (Wolfgang Müller; Heinz Kuhn 1967) were rejected by politicians because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup; colony served as a DINA torture centre

Mount Cashel Orphanage (Canada): Royal Newfoundland Constabulary probe opened Dec 1975 was closed by the police chief nine days later; the Justice Department ordered the report rewritten (1976); Deputy Minister of Justice said further action unwarranted (1977)

Malka Leifer (Adass Israel School) (Australia): The school flew her to Israel in March 2008 before police were told; Israeli Deputy Health Minister Yaakov Litzman interfered with psychiatric assessments, later pleading guilty to breach of trust; extradition took six years from her 2014 arrest
Johnny Kitagawa (Japan): Shūkan Bunshun's 1999 series; Kitagawa won a defamation judgment (2002) but courts upheld the abuse reporting (2003-04); Japanese mainstream media barely covered it

PAT.uncertain: The first-report year is the earliest complaint a source documents; earlier complaints that left no record are not counted, so most waits are longer than shown. Two people included were acquitted (George Pell, Bishop Franco Mulakkal); their rows record the time to charge, not a finding of guilt.

PAT.implications:
A long gap between a complaint and any action means that someone with the power to act knew and did not. The reasons recorded in these cases are of a few kinds. Prosecutors made lenient deals, as with Jeffrey Epstein's non-prosecution agreement in Florida in 2007. Police chiefs closed inquiries, as in St John's, Newfoundland, where an investigation into the Mount Cashel orphanage was shut nine days after it opened in 1975. Complaints were set aside because of who the accused was, as with Cyril Smith. Witnesses were attacked or killed, as in the cases against Asaram Bapu in India and Timothy Omotoso in South Africa. A 1999 magazine investigation into the Japanese talent agent Johnny Kitagawa was upheld in court, but no inquiry followed until 2023.

In several cases nothing happened until the accused had died. When a powerful person is charged after many years, the earlier complaints are usually on record somewhere, together with the names of the people who received them.

PAT.title: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
PAT.summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

timeline.event: Archdiocese of Portland (Oregon) filed for bankruptcy. First US Catholic diocese to file (6 July 2004), hours before two abuse trials; argued parish assets were not archdiocesan assets. Paid $71.45m to 169 victims (2007 plan).
Diocese of Tucson filed for bankruptcy. Filed Sept 2004; $22.2m settlement approved June 2005.
Diocese of Spokane filed for bankruptcy. Filed Dec 2004; agreed to pay at least $48m.
Diocese of Davenport filed for bankruptcy. Filed 10 Oct 2006; by Nov 2007 court allocated $37m to 156 victims; sold bishop's residence.
Diocese of San Diego (1st filing) filed for bankruptcy. Filed 27 Feb 2007 hours before the first of ~150 lawsuits was heard; Sept 2007 settled 144 claims for $198.1m.

Diocese of Fairbanks filed for bankruptcy. Filed March 2008; ~140 plaintiffs, many Alaska Native, abused by priests and church workers since the 1950s; co-defendant Jesuit Oregon Province settled for $50m.
Jesuits — Oregon Province filed for bankruptcy. Filed Feb 2009; agreed in 2011 to pay $166m to abuse victims (many Native American in Alaska and the Northwest).
Diocese of Wilmington filed for bankruptcy. Filed 18 Oct 2009, the day before the first trial, after Delaware's 2007 window; 2011 plan paid 150 victims $77.425m.

Archdiocese of Milwaukee filed for bankruptcy. Filed 4 Jan 2011, two days before the archbishop's deposition. Documents released in bankruptcy (July 2013) showed Archbishop Timothy Dolan in 2007 asked the Vatican to move $57m into a cemetery trust for "improved protection of these funds from any legal claim and liability"; the Vatican approved five weeks later.
Congregation of Christian Brothers (North America) filed for bankruptcy. Filed 2011; 2013 agreed ~$16.5m to more than 400 people abused as children (incl. Mount Cashel, Newfoundland, claimants).
Diocese of Gallup filed for bankruptcy. Filed 12 Nov 2013; by Feb 2017 had paid >$17.6m to 57 victims.
Diocese of Helena filed for bankruptcy. Filed Jan 2014 as part of a $15m settlement for 362 victims.
Diocese of Stockton filed for bankruptcy. Filed 2014; plan approved 2017, ~$15m to over two dozen victims.
Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis filed for bankruptcy. Filed 16-17 Jan 2015 after Minnesota's 2013 window; $210m settlement (2018) — $170m from insurers, $40m from archdiocese and parishes.
Diocese of Duluth filed for bankruptcy. Filed 7 Dec 2015 after an $8m jury verdict; May 2019 agreed $40m to 125 plaintiffs.
Diocese of New Ulm filed for bankruptcy. Filed 3 March 2017; made Minnesota the first state with three Catholic diocesan bankruptcies.

Diocese of Great Falls-Billings filed for bankruptcy. Filed March 2017 weeks before first trials; $20m to 86 victims; critics alleged the diocese moved ~$16m of assets into an entity it controlled (CASC).
Crosier Fathers and Brothers filed for bankruptcy. Order filed 2017 after agreeing to pay $25.5m.
Diocese of Winona-Rochester filed for bankruptcy. Filed Dec 2018 over 121 lawsuits; Feb 2021 $21.5m to 145 victims.

Archdiocese of Agaña (Guam) filed for bankruptcy. Filed 15-16 Jan 2019 after Guam's 2016 permanent window; claims rose to nearly 280; Jan 2020 plan offered $21m; sold Yona property for $6.1m. Former Archbishop Anthony Apuron found guilty in a canonical trial (2018-19).
Diocese of Saint Cloud filed for bankruptcy. Filed June 2020; $22.5m for 70 survivors; plan approved Dec 2020.

Archdiocese of Santa Fe filed for bankruptcy. Filed Dec 2018 (announced Nov 2018); 395 claimants. Before filing it transferred assets worth over $150m into trusts and incorporated parishes; in Oct 2020 the bankruptcy judge allowed survivors to sue alleging these were fraudulent transfers.

Boy Scouts of America filed for bankruptcy. Filed 18 Feb 2020 in Delaware; >82,000 claims by 16 Nov 2020 bar date; $2.46bn plan confirmed 8 Sept 2022 with third-party releases for local councils, insurers and chartered organisations (churches); upheld by Third Circuit May 2025; Supreme Court denied certiorari 12 Jan 2026. ~$295.5m paid to >36,000 survivors by late 2025; trust estimates full value >$7bn and billed non-settling insurers.

Boy Scouts of America: Filed 18 Feb 2020 in Delaware; >82,000 claims by 16 Nov 2020 bar date; $2.46bn plan confirmed 8 Sept 2022 with third-party releases for local councils, insurers and chartered organisations (churches); upheld by Third Circuit May 2025; Supreme Court denied certiorari 12 Jan 2026. ~$295.5m paid to >36,000 survivors by late 2025; trust estimates full value >$7bn and billed non-settling insurers.

Opposition: Pennsylvania Catholic Conference ($615,285 lobbying in 2016; >$700,000 in each of 2012, 2017, 2018; >$7.6m 2014-2024); Insurance Federation of Pennsylvania (~$20.7m 2014-2024, all issues); Boy Scouts and a local council ($486,505, 2016-2018). Philadelphia archdiocese sent letters to all 219 parishes urging parishioners to contact lawmakers

Opposition: Catholic Church ($2,912,772 lobbying 2011-2018; 80% via Catholic Conference Policy Group); Agudath Israel opposed a look-back window in 2009 and 2017; American Insurance Association ($130,000 in 2017), Liberty Mutual and Zurich (combined >$375,000 in 2017); Boy Scouts retained lobbyists

PAT.uncertain: Lobbying totals are what these organisations spent on all issues in each state, not only on limitation reform; the disclosures do not split them. A bankruptcy filing is legal and does not itself prove an intent to avoid victims; the timing and the asset transfers are what the records show. Outside the United States, lobbying against reform was not documented in the sources reached.

PAT.implications:
The deadline decides whether a case can be heard at all, so the effort to keep it or change it determined how many institutions would ever face a court. Bankruptcy then capped what survivors could recover and stopped trials that would have brought church files and bishops into open court.

Before filing, some dioceses moved assets out of creditors' reach. In 2007 the Archdiocese of Milwaukee asked the Vatican for permission to move $57 million into a cemetery trust, writing that this would protect the money from legal claims, and the Vatican approved it five weeks later. Much of what survivors could win was decided in legislatures and bankruptcy courts before any single case reached a judge.

PAT.title: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
PAT.summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

PAT.implications:
The number of documented cases in a country depends heavily on whether an inquiry has taken place there. Ireland, Australia and the United States have many cases on record because their inquiries had the power to demand documents and hold public hearings, and used it for years. Where no inquiry has been held, few cases are on record, whatever the size of the church or the number of children who passed through its schools and homes.

Who runs the inquiry also matters. Bodies that could compel evidence, such as Ireland's commissions, Australia's Royal Commission and the Pennsylvania grand jury, found that abuse had been concealed. Studies commissioned by the institutions themselves were limited to the files those institutions opened to them.

PAT.title: States that shielded their own
PAT.summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

PAT.implications:
Diplomatic immunity, extradition rules and military jurisdiction exist to protect a country's officials and soldiers from unfair prosecution abroad. In these cases the same rules protected people accused of abusing children. The children were usually in the poorer of the two countries, such as Haiti, the Central African Republic and the Dominican Republic.

The bodies involved include the United Nations, the Holy See, a South Korean court and an Israeli minister. When a case was referred to the accused person's home country, the records show it usually ended there. The one waiver in these records came in 2019, when the Holy See lifted the immunity of its ambassador in France, who was accused of sexually assaulting adults, after French requests.

PAT.title: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
PAT.summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

facts.t: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents.

Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007): After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way.

Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights.

Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank.

China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions): Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

PAT.uncertain: Totals are adoptions reported by 23–25 receiving states (Peter Selman's tables) and miss countries that do not report; South Korea's total differs by source (163,898 per its ministry for 1953–2008; up to about 200,000 in AP reporting). A closure means the sending or receiving government stopped or suspended adoptions; the reason given was not always fraud.

PAT.implications:
The parents adopting lived mainly in a small number of wealthy countries, including the United States, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the Nordic countries. The children came from countries where families were poor and records of births and guardianship were easy to alter. The fees paid for each child gave intermediaries a reason to find children and to produce the papers that made them available for adoption. The yearly figures show the totals moving from one sending country to the next as each was closed.

In some cases officials knew. South Korea's commission found the state responsible, and the Dutch government said in 2021 that its officials had been aware of wrongdoing for years without intervening. A child could be adopted through a lawful court process while the documents describing that child as an orphan were false.

PAT.title: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
PAT.summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.
roles: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers

facts.t: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict): On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress).

Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher.

British child migration programmes — IICSA: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse.

South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases.

Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987.

PAT.uncertain: Numbers of children taken are estimates in most of these cases and differ by source. Removals by governments where the records show no sexual abuse and no false identity or sale (for example Australia's Stolen Generations, Canada's Sixties Scoop, Denmark's 1951 Greenland experiment and Russia's deportation of Ukrainian children) are not on this map, because it covers abuse and trafficking. Spain's courts have convicted nobody for the stolen babies; the one doctor tried (2018) was acquitted on the statute of limitations.

PAT.implications:
In these cases the people who took the children worked for the state or under contract to it, so the officials who would normally investigate were part of the same system. Investigation came only after a change of government, as in Argentina after 1983, or when a later inquiry was set up, as in Canada, Britain, Ireland and South Korea.

For many of the people taken as children, the harm continues today. Some still do not know who their parents are, and in Spain and Chile no one has been convicted.

PAT.title: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
PAT.summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

PAT.implications:
Enforcement in one place moved much of the trade to another, because the buyers kept coming from the same countries. The records name Australia, the United States, Britain, Germany, Japan and South Korea again and again as the offenders' home countries, and most of those countries passed laws against abuse committed abroad years after the destinations were known.

Since the 2010s much of the abuse has taken place over live video. A buyer in a wealthy country pays a relative or neighbour of a child in the Philippines and watches the abuse on a call, without travelling. A fall in the number of children found in bars and on the street in the Philippines therefore did not mean that fewer children were being abused.

PAT.title: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
PAT.summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

facts.t: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid.

MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home.

Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs.

Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels.

PAT.implications:
In these settings children are often separated from their families, short of food and dependent on outsiders for safety, and the outsiders are protected by legal immunity or by their home country's jurisdiction. The UN cannot prosecute peacekeepers. It can send them home, and only their own government can try them, which the records show rarely happened. The yearly numbers of allegations rise and fall with new missions and have not fallen steadily.

Several of the cases that became public, including the trafficking of women and girls in Bosnia around 2001 and the abuse of children in the Central African Republic in 2014 and 2015, came to light through staff who passed information outside their organisation, not through the UN's own reporting.

PAT.title: War and the taking of children
PAT.summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.
roles: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
Children deported or transferred by a state

facts.t: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria.

Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram: On the night of 14 April 2014 Boko Haram gunmen raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks; more than 50 escaped within hours, mostly by jumping off the lorries, leaving 219 in captivity, some later found in the Sambisa Forest.

Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006.

Sudan — RSF rape and sexual slavery of women and girls (UN Fact-Finding Mission 2024): The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan found that rape and gang rape were widespread, mostly by men in RSF uniform and allied militias, with victims including girls as young as 8. It found the abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes by the RSF amounted to sexual slavery.

Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07): The Special Jurisdiction for Peace's Case 07 investigates the recruitment and use of children by the former FARC-EP; in August 2021 it identified a provisional universe of 18,677 unique victims and has accredited 9,854.

PAT.uncertain: UN-verified counts are minimums: verification needs access, and the worst-hit areas are often closed. Several country records here were extracted automatically from UN annexes and should be read with the report open.

PAT.implications:
For these groups captured children are used as a resource: girls are given to fighters or sold, and boys are made to fight. The abductions in Iraq, Nigeria, Uganda and Sudan were reported by the UN and the press while they were happening.

A few commanders have since been convicted at the International Criminal Court, years later. Most of the children taken were never found, and many were never counted.

PAT.title: When spies, soldiers and police are named
PAT.summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.
roles: Proven link to a state service

facts.t: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them.

Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days: After seizing the server the FBI kept Playpen running from 19 February to 4 March 2015 under a court warrant and used malware (a 'Network Investigative Technique') to unmask users; the EFF criticised the operation as continued distribution, and the 11th Circuit (2019) held the warrant invalid but did not exclude the evidence (good-faith exception).

Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity: Abuse allegations reached the RUC by 1977 without prosecution until 1980; the Hart inquiry found a 'catalogue of failures' by police and authorities. Former army officers Colin Wallace and Brian Gemmell said in 2014 that superiors stopped them passing on or pursuing information.

Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services: In July 2019 journalist Vicky Ward (Daily Beast) reported that Alexander Acosta had told Trump transition interviewers he was told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone; the source was not named.

PAT.uncertain: The proven cases show state services that used, tolerated or failed to stop abuse; none shows an intelligence service running a child-abuse network as policy. Individual accounts about Kincora and Epstein remain unresolved, and new document releases may change what is known.

PAT.implications:
In the documented cases the state did not set up the abuse. It used it, tolerated it or failed to stop it because something else mattered more to it: a dictatorship's use of a compound, a military alliance, an official theory about foster care, or the chance to identify more offenders online.

The claims that have not held up rest mainly on single witnesses or anonymous sources. When such a claim collapses, as Operation Midland did, later allegations against powerful people become harder to have taken seriously. The difference between the two kinds is whether a court, an inquiry or the agency's own records established the facts.

PAT.title: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
PAT.summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

facts.t: Westpac Banking Corporation (AUSTRAC): Penalty of A$1.3 billion agreed 24 Sept 2020 for 23 million breaches of the AML/CTF Act covering A$11bn of transactions, including failure to properly vet transactions that could be linked to child exploitation and live child sex shows in the Philippines and south-east Asia; CEO Brian Hartzer resigned

Visa (Fleites v. MindGeek): US District Judge Cormac Carney ruled (29 July 2022) it was reasonable to conclude Visa knowingly facilitated MindGeek's monetisation of child sexual abuse material, denying Visa's motion to dismiss; Visa and Mastercard then suspended payments to MindGeek's ad arm TrafficJunky

Welcome to Video (Bitcoin tracing): IRS Criminal Investigation traced Bitcoin payments and found the server IP in the site source code, locating it in South Korea; 337 users arrested in 38 countries (Oct 2019). Fifth Circuit (US v. Gratkowski, 2020) held there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in public blockchain data

FinCEN Financial Trend Analysis (Feb 2024): 2,311 Bank Secrecy Act reports (Jan 2020 - Dec 2021) linked cryptocurrency to online child sexual exploitation and trafficking, totalling over $412m in suspicious activity; reports rose from 336 (2020) to 1,975 (2021); 95% (2,191) concerned CSAM; 2,157 named bitcoin; over 1,800 unique bitcoin wallets identified; typologies: darknet markets, P2P exchanges, mixers, crypto kiosks

PAT.uncertain: Hosting shares measure where servers are, which can change with one large site; the IWF noted Bulgaria's 2025 jump came from a few sites. CyberTipline country counts reflect where people use US platforms, not where most abuse happens.

PAT.implications:
Each stage of online abuse passes through a company that could detect it: the host, the platform, the payment service and the bank. In these records the companies acted mostly after pressure from outside, such as a sheriff's letters to Visa and Mastercard about Backpage in 2015, a newspaper column about Pornhub in 2020 and a regulator's case against Westpac. Changes made for other reasons, such as encrypting messages, have reduced the reports that police rely on.

The child, the viewer and the server are often in three different countries, but the payments and data that connect them pass through regulated businesses, which governments can require to check.
