PAT.title: Officials who took part or looked away
PAT.summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

facts.t: Rotherham — Jay inquiry (1,400 children, 1997–2013): Three earlier reports (2002, 2003, 2013) on exploitation were effectively suppressed or ignored; police did not treat the abuse as a priority.

Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care': The earlier Jillings report (commissioned 1994, completed 1996) was shelved and only released in redacted form in 2012 after a BBC Freedom of Information request. North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers rather than having them independently investigated.

Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.

Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.

PAT.uncertain: This counts cases whose sources document official involvement or obstruction; it does not measure how common that is in each country, and countries with more inquiries will show more.

PAT.implications:
In these records officials rarely set out to help abusers. More often they put another interest first: a council worried about its reputation, a police force protecting its own officers, a politician protecting an ally or a donor. The decision to set a child's complaint aside was made by different people in different places, and in many cases more than once.

Where officials were involved, the abuse usually came to light through someone outside the chain of authority, such as a journalist, a researcher, a court, or an inquiry with the power to demand documents.

PAT.title: Where nobody is counting
PAT.summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.
roles: No survey data on online abuse in its region
No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
Almost no reports reach the international systems

facts.t: Global: Childlight 2026 meta-analysis covers 103 data sources, 147 studies and only 60 countries with representative survey data on technology-facilitated CSEA (studies 2006-2024)
South Asia: Lacking in representative survey data (Childlight 2026); only 2 countries / 2 sources for past-year online solicitation (6.5%, low confidence)
West & Central Africa: Lacking in representative survey data; a single study for past-year online solicitation — no pooled estimate possible
Middle East & North Africa: Lacking in representative survey data; not represented at all for online solicitation; one source for unwanted sexual content
Online sexual exploitation (all regions): Past-year sex-disaggregated estimates rest on only four studies in three regions; lifetime estimates on three data sources
Sexual extortion (all regions): Sex-disaggregated estimates based on only 5 studies

Global (2024 index): Childlight Dec 2024: one in eight (12.6%) of the world's children — about 302 million — experienced non-consensual taking, sharing or exposure to sexual images/video in the past year; 12.5% (300 million) online solicitation. The 2026 update did not produce a new single overall estimate because no new studies measured overall prevalence

Global (2026 update): Pooled estimates: online solicitation 26.6% lifetime / 6.7% past year; CSAM/IBSA 5.2% / 1.6%; unwanted sexual content 8.7% / 7.3%; online sexual exploitation 9.6% / 2.4%; sexual extortion 9.1% / 2.5%
Global (2026, Nature Human Behaviour): 1 in 5 women and 1 in 6 men experienced sexual violence as children; more than 130 million children in 2024; from 1,412 studies in 147 countries

PAT.uncertain: The regional groupings follow UNICEF's regions, which Childlight uses; individual countries within a region may have national studies that were not pooled. "No national inquiry found" for Brazil, the Philippines and India is an absence in the sources reached, not a sourced statement.

PAT.implications:
A country with few recorded cases may be a country where no one has asked. The places least covered by surveys, official statistics and online reports overlap with places where many children live in poverty, and in some of them the institutions that would be investigated also hold the records.

For this reason the map's country score uses estimates of the trafficking trade and of how much stands in its way, which cover nearly every country, and not the number of cases found.

PAT.title: False alarms that drown real cases
PAT.summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

timeline.event: Wayfair "trafficking children in furniture listings" — Flooded the US National Human Trafficking Hotline: "hundreds of reports" in several days; Polaris said the "extreme volume of these contacts has made it more difficult for the Trafficking Hotline to provide support and attention to others who are in need of help"

Summer 2020 viral trafficking rumours (furniture websites, text-message recruitment) — Polaris: the rumours "flooded the Polaris-operated National Human Trafficking Hotline with calls and concerns that were simply not true. The barrage crowded out calls and contacts from people who truly needed help"; Polaris built an online "Human Trafficking 101" training in response

#SaveTheChildren (QAnon co-option) — QAnon followers co-opted the trademarked name of the charity Save the Children, which issued a statement on 7 Aug 2020 against unauthorised use; Facebook/Instagram redirected the hashtag (Sept 2020) and limited its reach (Oct 2020)

Pizzagate (Comet Ping Pong, Washington DC) — Edgar Maddison Welch fired an AR-15-style rifle inside the restaurant on 4 Dec 2016 (4 years' prison, June 2017); owner and staff got death threats; arson attack 25 Jan 2019 by a man who had posted a QAnon video (4 years, April 2020)
QAnon "cabal" child-trafficking narrative — An FBI Phoenix field office intelligence bulletin (May 2019) identified QAnon-driven extremists as a domestic terrorism threat
Adrenochrome "harvested from children" — Central motif of QAnon and Pizzagate claims of child torture by a Satanist cabal

Beech was himself found to be a child sex offender and jailed for 18 years (July 2019)

McMartin preschool / Satanic ritual abuse panic — Seven years and about $15m of prosecution ended with no convictions (1990); FBI expert Kenneth Lanning found "little or no evidence for ... large-scale baby breeding, human sacrifice, and organized satanic conspiracies"

PAT.implications:
False claims about secret rings of powerful people do two kinds of harm. They use up police and hotline time that could have gone to children in danger, and after they collapse, real allegations against powerful people are more easily dismissed.

The real cases on this map involving politicians, celebrities and bishops were established slowly, through police investigations, courts and inquiries. The viral claims did not go through that process, and none of those listed here led to a child being found or protected.

SER.title: Reports to the US CyberTipline (NCMEC), per year
SER.note: Reports of suspected online child sexual exploitation received each year, mostly from US technology companies. The drop after 2023 follows a change in how reports are bundled and Meta's move to end-to-end encryption, not less abuse. 1998-2023 exact counts from NCMEC appendix to OJJDP 'CY 2023 Report to the Committees on Appropriations: NCMEC Transparency' (2024). 2024 is NCMEC's rounded figure (20.5 million reports; equivalent to 29.2 million incidents after 'bundling' of viral reports, introduced by Meta in 2024). 2025 exact total from NCMEC 2025 CyberTipline Report. Drop in 2024 attributed by NCMEC partly to bundling and to Meta's default end-to-end encryption on Facebook Messenger (Dec 2023-summer 2024; 6.9 million fewer reports from Facebook).

Trafficking rings, street grooming networks, brothels, pimping families, and companies that profited from selling children for sex.

Armed groups, state armies, peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones, intelligence and security services, and children taken in war.

Where offenders travel from and to
Documented travel of offenders to abuse children abroad: sex tourism, and personnel sent abroad who abused children there.
Abusers that a church, order or other institution moved to another country instead of reporting them, as documented by inquiries, courts or the institution's own files.
Intercountry adoptions from countries where official inquiries later found children were bought, stolen or falsely registered as orphans.

Documented money paid from one country for children to be abused in another, for example livestreamed abuse.
Where the material reported to hotlines was found on servers, by hosting country.

convicted: A court convicted at least one person.
inquiry: An official inquiry, royal commission, grand jury, commission or government review found it happened.
acknowledged: The institution or state admitted it, apologised or paid redress.
settled: Paid compensation in a settlement, usually without admitting liability.
charged: Charges were brought; no verdict yet, or not reported here.
reported: Documented by a major news investigation or NGO report, without an official finding.
alleged: Allegations only; not counted in any score. The record says who alleges it.
acquitted: A court acquitted, or a conviction was overturned. Not counted in any score.
disproved: Investigated and found false or unsupported. Not counted in any score; kept because false claims shape how real ones are heard.

ABOUT:
What this map shows

Where children have been sexually abused, exploited, sold or trafficked by organised groups and inside institutions, who protected the people responsible, and the patterns that repeat across countries and decades. The map is about those patterns, not individual crimes: cases of a single offender acting alone, with no network, no institution protecting him, no officials involved, no trade across borders and no wider finding, have been left out. So have removals of children by governments, neglect in care homes and child labour where the records show no sexual abuse, exploitation or sale of children. It holds 757 documented cases in 125 countries, 88 networks and institutions, 207 documented movements of children, offenders and money, and 15 patterns behind the scenes.

Nobody keeps a world register of child abuse networks, and most of what exists is found only when someone looks: a police raid, a court, a grand jury, a royal commission, a journalist. The map keeps two kinds of evidence apart.

  • Documented cases. Each dot is a case, inquiry finding, prosecution or official report connected to a wider pattern, with the forum that established it and a link to the source.
  • Measured indicators. Country figures published by others: the size of the trafficking trade, modern slavery, reports of online abuse, and how much stands in the way. These color the countries, including the many where little has been documented.

How complete this is

Two checklists measure how much of the documented picture the map holds. The first is the kinds of abuse and trafficking, merged from four published lists: the institutional settings examined by the inquiries in England and Wales and in Australia, the forms of sexual exploitation of children in the international Terminology Guidelines, and the forms of child trafficking in the UN Office on Drugs and Crime's Global Report on Trafficking in Persons. The second is every major official finding the research for this map could find: a report by an inquiry, royal commission, truth commission, grand jury, parliament, attorney general, ombudsman, court, UN body or an institution's own commissioned investigation, covering a whole country, state or region, a whole institution or sector, or 100 or more children. Findings that were considered and left out are listed with the reason. Both checklists are in the layer's "How complete this is" box.

A complete checklist is not a complete record. The checklist holds what has been found and published; many countries have no official finding at all. The cases on the map are a small share, roughly 1 to 5 percent by this map's estimate, of all the connected cases documented anywhere, and most abuse is never reported.

Coloring the countries

Likely scale and impunity (the default) is 0 to 100. Sixty percent is the likely size of the trade and forty percent is how little stands in the way. The cases on the map are not part of the score, because the number of cases found in a country depends mostly on whether anyone has investigated there. Darker means more.

  • Likely size of the trade. The average of what is available: GI-TOC's human trafficking market score (2025, out of 10), Walk Free's estimated people in modern slavery per 1,000 (2023), and NCMEC CyberTipline reports per 100,000 people (2025), the last two on a log scale.
  • How little stands in the way. The average of GI-TOC's score for officials working with criminal groups (state-embedded actors), its resilience score and its score for help to victims and witnesses (both inverted), and the US State Department's 2025 trafficking ranking (Tier 1 = 0.1, Tier 2 = 0.4, Watch List = 0.65, Tier 3 = 0.9, special case = 0.85).

Territories with no indicator of their own borrow their sovereign's figures (Greenland from Denmark, Puerto Rico from the United States, and so on), and their box says so. No record is not the same as no abuse; see the pattern "Where nobody is counting".

The other layers show each measure on its own: cases by setting, cases where officials took part or covered up, the years from the first complaint to the first action, and each indicator.

The cases

Every case names the forum that established it. The status words mean:

  • Convicted: a court convicted at least one person.
  • Official inquiry finding: a royal commission, statutory inquiry, grand jury, parliamentary or government review found it happened.
  • Admitted: the institution or state admitted it, apologised or paid redress.
  • Settled: compensation paid in a settlement, usually without admission.
  • Charged: charges brought; no verdict yet or not reported here.
  • Investigated by the press: documented by a major news investigation or NGO report without an official finding.
  • Alleged, Acquitted, Disproved: shown as grey rings. Disproved claims are kept because false stories change how real ones are heard.

Cases are grouped in eight settings: churches and religious movements; state care, homes and youth groups; the powerful (politics, wealth, fame, sport); organised crime and trafficking rings; travelling offenders; online networks and platforms; war, armies, peacekeepers and spies; and stolen children and adoption trafficking. A filled dot is placed at the town or site, and cases at the same spot are set side by side on a small ring around it; a ring at a country's center means the source named no town. Dot size grows with the number of children where a source gives one.

"First complaint on record" is the earliest year a source says a complaint reached police, an employer, a church, a school or officials. It does not mean anyone acted on it.

No victim or survivor is named. People are named as offenders only when convicted, charged, or found responsible by an official inquiry; anyone else is described as accused, with who accused them, and acquittals are stated. Nothing on this map points to where abuse material can be found: no site addresses, no access methods, no search terms.

Lines and networks

All line types are shown when the map opens; each can be turned off in the key, or all at once with the switch beside "Lines". Trafficking routes, travelling offenders, abusers moved by their institution, children sent abroad for adoption, children removed by states, payments for abuse, and where abuse material is hosted. Every line links its source in the box of the countries at either end. Lines follow the years chosen.

Networks and institutions are shown when the map opens, placed at their headquarters and sized by how many countries they are documented in. Clicking one draws dotted lines to the countries where it is documented, and grey dotted lines to countries where its presence is only likely. Presence is not proof of abuse in that country.

Patterns behind the scenes

Each pattern layer colors the countries by their role in a structure that repeats across cases, draws its documented connections, and gives a plain summary, the figures behind it, a dated timeline, the sources, what remains unproven, and a short reading of what it means. The patterns were researched for this map from inquiry reports, court records, lobbying and bankruptcy filings, UN reports, adoption statistics and the cases themselves:

  • Moved instead of stopped: institutions relocating abusers, across borders.
  • Years of waiting: the delay between the first complaint and the first action.
  • Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy: limitation periods, the spending against reform, and bankruptcy filings.
  • Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked.
  • States that shielded their own: immunity, extradition refusals, military jurisdiction, pardons.
  • The adoption pipeline that keeps moving, from one sending country to the next.
  • Children taken by governments, then sexually abused or given false identities.
  • Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there, and then online.
  • Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones.
  • War and the taking of children.
  • When spies, soldiers and police are named: proven, disproved and still only claimed.
  • Platforms, servers and the money behind them.
  • Officials who took part or looked away.
  • Where nobody is counting.
  • False alarms that drown real cases.

Sources

  • Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, Global Organized Crime Index 2021, 2023 and 2025 (human trafficking, state-embedded actors, resilience, victim and witness support).
  • Walk Free, Global Slavery Index 2023, Table 26 (estimated prevalence of modern slavery by country).
  • US Department of State, Trafficking in Persons Report, June 2025 (tier placements).
  • National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, CyberTipline data, reports by country and by year.
  • Internet Watch Foundation annual data reports; INHOPE; Childlight, Into the Light index (2024, 2026 update); UNODC Global Report on Trafficking in Persons 2024.
  • UN Secretary-General reports on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (2004–2025) and on children and armed conflict.
  • Peter Selman, global statistics for intercountry adoption (hosted by the Hague Conference); US State Department adoption statistics.
  • Population: World Bank, 2024.
  • Each case, network, line and pattern links its own source: inquiry and commission reports, court records and judgments, government and UN documents, and major news investigations. Where a record was reached through an encyclopedia summary of an official report, the record names the report.

Built 28 October 2026.

Limits

The cases on the map measure exposure as much as abuse. Countries that held inquiries (Ireland, Australia, the United States, the United Kingdom) show more because they looked. Many countries in Africa, South and Central Asia and the Middle East have few cases here because few official findings exist in sources that can be reached, not because children there are safer. The indicators are estimates by their publishers, and none measures child sexual abuse alone. Figures can differ between sources; each record gives the one its source states.

If you or a child you know is in danger, contact local emergency services. In the United States, the National Human Trafficking Hotline is 1-888-373-7888 and the NCMEC CyberTipline is report.cybertip.org.
